Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]

Admission Date: [REDACTED] | Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Admitted Diagnosis: Atrial fibrillation with features of LVH and SARS-CoV-2 positive infection

Major Procedures: None

Hospital Course:

The patient presented to the ED with malaise and palpitations, and a confirmed diagnosis of SARS-CoV-2. Upon admission, he was noted to be febrile with left lower lobe infiltrates and patchy perihilar and right middle lobe ground-glass airspace disease on chest x-ray. The patient's vital signs were monitored closely, and he was started on intravenous diltiazem for atrial fibrillation control. The patient showed an improvement in his PR after treatment and was then started on intravenous diltiazem drip at 5mg/hour. The patient received symptomatic treatment for fever given the presence of a fever on admission. The patient was maintained in droplet and contact isolation with eye protection.

Treatment:

The patient was treated intravenous diltiazem (10 mg bolus) and a 500 ml normal saline intravenous fluid bolus, which led to an improvement in his PR to approximately 100 bpm. After this, he was started on intravenous diltiazem drip at 5 mg/hour for atrial fibrillation control and admitted for further monitoring and workup.

Outcome:

The final diagnosis was atrial fibrillation with features of LVH and SARS-CoV-2 positive infection. The patient's tachycardia and fever subsided during his hospitalization course. He was discharged in a stable condition for further follow-up.

Recommendations:

The patient was advised to continue home isolation and complete the 14-day quarantine period. The patient was provided with a list of symptoms that he should report to his primary care physician if they occur. A follow-up appointment to his primary care physician was scheduled for further management after completing the quarantine period.

Overarching Risk Factors:

The patient had a past medical history of untreated essential hypertension.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [REDACTED] 
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED] 
Date of Admission: [REDACTED] 
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED] 

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 78-year-old male, was admitted to the emergency room with complaints of dry cough, fever and malaise persisting for 1 month. He was previously treated with amoxicillin with no improvement. His medical history included diabetes and arterial blood hypertension, for which he was on metformin and amlodipine for 7 years. The patient presented with mildly lethargic orientation, febrile with mild tachycardia, hypoxemia, and crackles in the mid- and lower-lung fields on physical examination. Laboratory tests revealed elevated WBC counts, NLR, ESR, and CRP. The chest radiograph showed diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates. The HRCT showed diffuse interstitial lung involvement with a ground glass pattern. Blood and sputum cultures were negative for bacteria, urine antigen tests for Legionella pneumonia and Streptococcus pneumoniae were negative. Serum immunology tests for autoimmune diseases such as antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies were all negative. A bronchoscopy was then performed, BAL and TBLB were negative for malignancy, bacteria, nocardia, fungi, and mycobacteria. BAL increased cellularity and had a mixed cellularity pattern. In view of the above findings, a diagnosis of Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia (COP) was considered. Treatment with antibiotics was ceased, and the patient was started on prednisone 20mg daily. The patient showed immediate improvement, blood inflammatory markers decreased, and he was discharged after 5 days on prednisone. He was advised to taper off corticosteroids for a total duration of treatment of 6-12 months.

Medical Condition:
Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia (COP)

Treatment:
Prednisone 20mg daily

Follow-up:
The patient has had no recurrence of symptoms at follow-up visits after complete clinical and radiological resolution of his condition.

Hospital Course:
The 78-year-old male patient was admitted with complaints of right-sided pain and numbness in the ear, submandibular and temporal regions, and right side of the tongue root, as well as right-sided facial weakness. The patient reported paroxysms of odynophagia triggered by swallowing which lasted throughout his mealtime. The patient's pain was rated a 9-10 on the numerical rating scale, and he had difficulty taking food for several days due to the intensity of his pain. Medical therapy was initiated with the application of ipsilateral lidocaine spray to the tonsillar branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve before mealtime. 

Diagnostic findings:
The patient's peripheral facial paralysis was classified as House-Brackmann grade III, and the results of the audiogram were normal. Laboratory investigations and brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) were unremarkable. The delivery of pulsed radiofrequency (PRF) to the Gasserian ganglion was recommended to alleviate the pain of the mandibular nerve division of the trigeminal nerve.

Treatment:
The patient received pulsed radiofrequency treatment with a radiofrequency generator, which produced some pain relief, and a second application of PRF was performed a week later. Sensory testing at 50 Hz and motor testing at 2 Hz were performed to ensure the needle was on the sensory target. Infrared thermography was done to follow up lesion changes and provide effective assessment of combined therapy. The peripheral facial paralysis was treated with linear-polarized near-infrared light irradiation. The patient's treatment regimen was adjusted according to response, and gabapentin was initiated at a dose of 300 mg once per day, which was increased by 300 mg every day until a therapeutic dose (600 mg three times daily) was reached.

Outcome:
After ten sessions of linear-polarized near-infrared light irradiation, the House-Brackmann grade indicated that the patient was healthy, and the patient was discharged from the hospital. The patient was followed up with thermography to monitor the progress of therapy. At three months, the patient missed a dose of gabapentin, and infrared thermography of the pain area showed a higher temperature than that of the contralateral side. However, after gabapentin administration, the thermographic findings showed a lower temperature image.

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 27-year-old pregnant female with a history of congenital heart disease, was admitted to the hospital at 34 weeks of gestation due to pain abdomen for 2 days. On examination, the patient was found to be cyanotic with clubbed fingers and raised Jugular venous pressure, and there was a pansystolic murmur and bilateral basal crepitations present. The patient was diagnosed to have a large perimembranous ventricular septal defect (VSD) with bidirectional shunt and severe pulmonary hypertension (PAH), tricuspid regurgitation, and a dilated right atrium seen on echocardiography.

Treatment:

The patient had been on irregular treatment with sildenafil 25 mg twice a day since 4 months, and given her previous obstetric history, lower segment cesarean section (LSCS) was planned. All risks were explained, and written informed consent was obtained. Prophylaxis against bacterial endocarditis was provided, and an epidural catheter was inserted for pain management during the surgery. Ampicillin and gentamicin were administered as per standard prophylaxis guidelines.

Procedure:

Over a period of 30 min, a total of 7cc of lignocaine with adrenaline solution and 8 cc of bupivacaine with 25 μg of fentanyl produced a block height of T8 tested to touch with blunt forceps. CVP was maintained between10-12 mm throughout surgery. The procedure was uneventful, and after delivery of the baby, furosemide 10 mg was given intravenously. A total of 450 cc of colloid was given.

Postoperative:

After surgery, the patient was shifted to the intensive care unit (ICU) for monitoring and was discharged on the 10th day. Epidural analgesia was maintained with 0.125% bupivacaine and 20 μg of fentanyl every 8 hourly for 72 h.

Summary:

The patient was diagnosed to have a large perimembranous ventricular septal defect (VSD) with bidirectional shunt and severe pulmonary hypertension (PAH), tricuspid regurgitation, and a dilated right atrium seen on echocardiography. She had a history of a stillborn delivery in her previous pregnancy and was advised against conceiving again, but she refused. She had been on irregular treatment with sildenafil, and given her previous obstetric history, LSCS was planned. The procedure was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on the 10th day. Epidural analgesia was maintained for pain management after surgery.

Over 30 minutes, doctors gave 7 cc of numbing medicine with adrenaline and 8 cc of numbing medicine with fentanyl.
This created numbness up to the chest level, which was checked by touch using blunt forceps.
Central venous pressure was kept between 10 and 12 mmHg during the whole surgery to keep the heart stable.
The surgery went smoothly, and after the baby was born, she received 10 mg of a water pill into her vein.
She also received 450 cc of fluid to help maintain blood pressure and support circulation during recovery.

After surgery, she was moved to the intensive care unit for close monitoring and care.
She was sent home ten days after the operation, once her condition was stable.
Epidural pain relief continued with low-dose bupivacaine and fentanyl every eight hours for three days.

Discharge Summary:
Patient Name: [redacted]
DOB: [redacted]
Admission Date: [redacted]
Discharge Date: [redacted]
Diagnosis: Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with fever and cervical pain for which she had received antibiotics in the past. Physical examination showed multiple swollen lymph nodes in the left axillary region. CT imaging revealed axillary lymphadenopathy and bone destruction in the axis. The PET scan showed multiple lesions of the bone and bone marrow. Bone marrow aspiration revealed no large lymphoid cells. Biopsy of the left axillary lymph nodes showed absence of follicular structures and diffusely proliferative large lymphoid cells. Immunohistochemical staining confirmed that the large lymphoid cells were positive for CD20, bcl-2, and MIB-1, but negative for CD3, CD30, and EBER. The patient was diagnosed with clinical stage IV DLBCL, with low-to-intermediate risk according to the international prognostic index.

The patient received radiotherapy for the cervical lesions and declined conventional chemotherapy due to the risk of recurrent NTM infection. She was started on CAM and PSL, and her fever improved within a few days. The PSL dosage was initially 20 mg/day for 2 weeks and subsequently 15 mg/day for 2 weeks. The maintenance dosage was 10 mg/day. The patient experienced slightly reduced taste sensation, considered a side effect of long-term CAM use.

The follow-up imaging studies after 6 months showed complete remission with improvements in lymphadenopathy and lesions of the bone and bone marrow. The patient remains in complete remission 7 months after initiation of treatment.

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient was admitted with fever and cervical pain. Multiple swollen lymph nodes were found in the left axillary region. Imaging studies showed axillary lymphadenopathy and bone destruction in the axis, with multiple lesions of the bone and bone marrow. Biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of clinical stage IV DLBCL. The patient received radiotherapy for cervical lesions and subsequently started on CAM and PSL. Follow-up imaging after 6 months showed complete remission, and the patient remains in complete remission 7 months after initiation of treatment.

Hospital Course

This 51-year-old male weighing 131 kg presented to the ED with altered mental status and slurred speech after undergoing cervical epidural injection. He became unresponsive during the injection with subsequent brief convulsive activity. Emergency medical services was called and found him obtunded with shallow breathing and low oxygen saturations requiring ventilation assistance. On arrival to the ED his breathing was erratic with low oxygen saturations. He remained somnolent with slurred speech, unable to answer questions appropriately or follow commands. On cardiopulmonary monitor, he was noted to have an irregularly irregular heart rhythm. Electrocardiogram showed atrial fibrillation with a rate of 82 beats per minute. Hemodynamically he was stable. Within 60 minutes of ED arrival, the patient’s mental status was back to baseline without recollection of the events that had occurred after the start of the procedure. Imaging studies obtained were all negative. 

Hospital Course: Diagnosis and Treatment

The patient was observed overnight in the hospital and remained asymptomatic and without any further dysrhythmia. He only had chest wall pain, possibly from sternal rub or from any bystander chest compressions that may have been performed when he became unresponsive. Serum/plasma levels of lidocaine and its primary active metabolite, monoethylglycinexylidide (MEGX), were obtained and returned undetectable. Aspirin 325 mg daily was prescribed and a referral to outpatient cardiology was made. 

Condition at Discharge

The patient was discharged with no symptoms and normal mental status.

Hospital Course
A 51-year-old man weighing 289 pounds came to the emergency department confused and with trouble speaking after a neck injection.
He became unresponsive during the injection and had a brief seizure, then stopped responding for a short time.
An ambulance was called and found him very drowsy with short breaths and low oxygen levels, needing help to breathe.
When he arrived at the emergency department, his breathing was uneven and his oxygen levels remained low.
He stayed sleepy, spoke unclearly, and could not answer questions or follow directions during his stay.
His heart monitor showed an uneven heartbeat, and an electrocardiogram confirmed atrial fibrillation at about 82 beats per minute.
His blood pressure and circulation were stable, and doctors said his circulation was okay throughout his emergency department stay.
Within an hour of arriving, his thinking returned to normal and he had no memory of events after the injection.
All imaging tests, including X-rays and scans, showed no abnormalities or signs of injury in his brain or chest.
Hospital Course: Diagnosis and Treatment
The patient stayed in the hospital overnight for observation and had no symptoms or further uneven heartbeats.
He had chest pain that might have come from rubbing his breastbone or from chest compressions.
The chest compressions were likely done by a bystander trying to help him after he became unresponsive.
Tests for the numbing medicine lidocaine and its breakdown product showed none present in his blood.
The doctor prescribed aspirin 325 milligrams to take each day to help prevent heart problems.
He was also referred to a heart specialist for follow-up care after leaving the hospital.
Condition at Discharge
The patient left the hospital feeling fine and with normal thinking at the time of discharge.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: [Patient's Name]

Gender: Male

Age: 76 years

Medical Record Number: [Medical Record Number]

Admission Date: [Admission Date]

Discharge Date: [Discharge Date]

Admitting Diagnosis: Elevated creatinine levels, elevated IgE level, proteinuria, and glucosuria

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the rheumatology clinic with severe fatigue, unintentional weight loss, memory loss, and ambulatory dysfunction. The patient had a 120 pack-year smoking history and also smoked marijuana. The patient had a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, COPD, and diabetes mellitus.

The labs showed an elevated creatinine level, elevated IgE level, proteinuria, and glucosuria. An ultrasound image of the Kidneys showed echogenic foci in the right kidney. The CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast showed a scar in the interpolar region of the right kidney. CT scan of the chest with contrast showed a 10 mm low-density area in the right thyroid lobe. Thyroid ultrasound showed bilateral thyroid nodules, including a 3.5 cm hypoechoic nodule in the lower pole. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the nodule showed benign follicular nodule.

The patient had a repeat CT chest with contrast, which showed a 1.4 cm right lower lobe lung nodule, bilateral interlobular septal thickening with lower lobe predominance, multiple bilateral ground-glass opacities, cystic changes, and multiple enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes. PET scanning was done, which showed right lower lobe hypermetabolic nodule, highly suspicious for malignancy with extensive smoking history and significant weight loss.

The patient underwent right lower lobe basilar segmentectomy and mediastinal lymph node dissection. Histology was negative for malignancy and showed numerous positive IgG4 plasma cells, along with obliterative phlebitis, significant fibrosis, and arteritis as lymphoplasmacytic infiltration. IgG4:IgG ratio on the lung biopsy was greater than 40%. The lung biopsy was highly suggestive of IgG4-related disease. The lymph node also showed lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, IgG4-positive cells, irregular fibrous bands, but no obliterative phlebitis or arteritis.

Treatment and Procedures:

The patient was started on 40 mg of prednisone, which resolved his fatigue and had significant weight gain, and his prednisone was tapered down and stopped in 4 months. He was not placed on any immunosuppression and was monitored for any further relapse. He is in remission for the last one year off any medications without any relapses.

Diagnosis on Discharge:

IgG4-related disease.

Condition at Discharge:

The patient is asymptomatic with no need for further follow-up.

Follow-up Recommendations:

The patient is advised follow-up with the rheumatology clinic.

He has been in remission for the last year, taking no medicine and having no relapse reported.

The final diagnosis is IgG4-related disease, a condition where the body makes too much of a certain antibody.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: _______

Gender: Female

Age: 56 years

Admission Date: _______

Discharge Date: _______

Diagnosis: Primary Osteoarthritis of the Left Knee 

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 56-year-old female with a body mass index of 23.2, was admitted to our facility as a diagnosed case of primary osteoarthritis of the left knee. The osteoarthritis of the left knee was evaluated as grade 3 based on the Kellgren-Lawrence Scale. The patient had received an intra-articular injection of high molecular weight hyaluronic acid 2 years back which transiently improved pain symptoms. Significant improvement was not noted in the pain symptoms despite the administration of 4 injections of platelet-rich plasma (PRP) a month apart each. The patient also performed prescribed exercises that included strengthening of quadriceps and hamstrings, and stretching of the hamstrings and took precautionary measures in the activities of daily living which provided little relief in symptoms. An ultrasound of the knee joint was done to look for structural changes, and suitable changes for treatment were recommended. 

Treatment:

In view of inadequate response after 8 months of the last PRP injection, intra-articular injection of adalimumab was planned, and 10 mg of Adalimumab was administered under ultrasonography-guidance. The procedure was uneventful, and the patient did not have any transient discomfort or complications following injection adalimumab. The patient was put on Tablet Paracetamol 650 mg (as per need) as a rescue medication, and post adalimumab injection pill count was on an average 2 tablets per week. 

Outcome:

The patient reported noticeable reduction in pain beginning approximately 2 weeks from the date of injection. The 11-point visual analog scale (VAS) for pain intensity was used to evaluate the patient. VAS reduced from 8 (pre-treatment) to 3 at the 1 month follow-up, remained at 3 at the 3 months follow-up and became 4 at the 6 months follow-up. Ultrasonographic examination was repeated at the end of 12 weeks and 6 months, and pre- and post-intervention ultrasonographic findings did not show any change despite significant improvement in symptoms. The patient's knee injury & osteoarthritis outcome score (KOOS) improved from 32.20 (pre-treatment) to 61.20 at the 1 month follow-up, 60.90 at the 3 months follow-up and 57.50 at the 6 months follow-up. The patient was discharged and is under routine care in our outpatient department, and has not complained of any deterioration in symptoms. A formal evaluation of VAS, KOOS, and ultrasound examination is scheduled after 6 months. 

Recommendation:

The patient has been advised to follow the preventive measures to avoid any pain, inflammation, or stiffness in the joint. The patient has also been advised to follow-up with the treating physician regularly to avoid any complications or further injury.

The patient continues to take hydrocortisone.

Gender: Female

Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
The patient was referred for an evaluation of right periorbital pain, right eye ptosis, and diplopia that had first appeared 20 days earlier. She had restricted adduction of the right eyeball. Initial MRIs showed enlargement of the right medial rectus muscle with mild contrast enhancement, and additional lesions in the right retrobulbar optic nerve sheath and preseptal area.

MEDICAL MANAGEMENT:
The initial diagnosis was orbital IIP, and the patient was started on 60 mg of prednisone daily for 10 days, which greatly improved her symptoms. The dosage was gradually reduced over the next 8 weeks, but her symptoms relapsed when prednisone was reduced to below 20 mg per day. Azathioprine and mycophenolate mofetil also could not be administered because of potential direct hepatotoxicity. The patient was started on 3 mg of tacrolimus while discontinuing prednisolone over 8 weeks. After 6 months of tacrolimus administration, the right periorbital pain had completely disappeared, and the restriction of right eye abduction had resolved. The second follow-up MRIs were obtained at 16 months after the onset, by which time the lesions had nearly resolved. Tacrolimus was gradually reduced over a period of 7 months before being discontinued, and the patient had no further relapse during the 1-year follow-up.

CLINICAL FINDINGS:
The patient had painful tenderness of the right medial orbital region. Routine serological tests, autoimmune screening tests, and CSF studies all produced normal findings. However, her hepatitis C virus RNA level was 1,724,673 IU/mL in the quantification test, indicating active hepatitis C.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
The patient is advised to follow up with their healthcare provider for further management of hepatitis C. If any orbital IIP concerns arise, they are to contact their healthcare provider immediately.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [Redacted]
Age: 50 years
Sex: Female
Race: South Indian

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to the outpatient department with a productive cough with hemoptysis for the past 2 months. She had a history of pulmonary tuberculosis, which was discontinued within 3 weeks of starting the treatment. She also suffered from diabetes mellitus with peripheral neuropathy for the past 8 years and was taking oral hypoglycemic agents for the same. The patient was diagnosed with an indwelling aspergilloma and was treated with an oral loading dose of Voriconazole followed by an oral maintenance dose. The patient responded well to the treatment, and the hemoptysis resolved after a lobectomy. After 3 weeks, the sputum became negative for acid-fast bacilli. The patient is currently in the 4th month of treatment and is doing well.

Laboratory Results:
Admission baseline investigations showed anemia, and the renal and liver function tests were within normal limits.

Diagnostic Study:
Computed tomogram of the thorax revealed a thick-walled cavity in the right lung upper lobe with an indwelling aspergilloma. 3 sputum samples were tested positive for acid-fast bacilli by Ziehl Neelsen's staining technique. Conventional method of culture on Lowenstein Jensen's medium yielded growth of M. tuberculosis. The anti-tuberculosis drug susceptibility test showed resistance to Isoniazid and Rifampicin but sensitive to Ethambutol, Pyrazinamide, and Streptomycin in their critical concentrations.

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis and an indwelling aspergilloma.

Treatment:
The patient was initially started on a daily dose of Isoniazid, Ethambutol, Pyrazinamide, and Streptomycin. However, after culture demonstrated MDR-TB, Isoniazid was stopped, and oral Levofloxacin and Ethionamide were included in the treatment regimen. Rifampicin was not included due to its interactions with Voriconazole. The patient was given an oral loading dose of Voriconazole 400 mg 12th hourly for 2 doses, which was followed by an oral maintenance dose of 200 mg 12th hourly for 6 weeks.

Follow-up:
After the treatment, the patient was counseled on the importance of adhering to medication and follow-up visits. She was advised to return to the hospital for follow-up visits and monitoring of symptoms.

Summary:
The 50-year-old South Indian woman presented with complaints of productive cough with hemoptysis for the past 2 months. She suffered from diabetes mellitus with peripheral neuropathy and had a history of pulmonary tuberculosis. The patient was diagnosed with an indwelling aspergilloma and treated with an oral loading dose of Voriconazole followed by an oral maintenance dose. Hemoptysis resolved after lobectomy, and the sputum became negative for acid-fast bacilli after 3 weeks. The patient responded well to the treatment and is currently in the 4th month of treatment. The patient was advised to adhere to medication and follow-up visits.

Admitting Diagnosis: Exudative AMD with Subfoveal PED and an Associated MH

Hospital Course: The 73-year-old Caucasian female was admitted with decreased vision and metamorphopsia for 6 months in her left eye. Initial examination showed best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) of 20/80 left eye (LE) and 20/25 right eye (RE). Fundus biomicroscopy revealed the presence of exudative AMD with a subfoveal PED and an associated MH. Spectral domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) confirmed a full-thickness MH with attached edges and a partially detached posterior hyaloid on top of the prominent PED. Intravitreal anti-VEGF-therapy with three loading doses of a monthly bevacizumab (1.25 mg)-injections was started. After 4 weeks, the first injection resulted in the resolution of the PED with an approximation of the MH edges. However, BCVA decreased to 20/160. In the follow-up, the second injection was administered after four weeks, and SD-OCT showed complete closure of the MH along with marked visual improvement to 20/50. During further follow-up, PED recurred, but no reopening of the MH was observed. Continued intravitreal drug therapy with bevacizumab according to Pro Re Nata regimen led to resolution of PED and visual stabilization.

Discharge Diagnosis: Exudative AMD with Subfoveal PED and an Associated MH

Discharge Education: The patient was counseled on the importance of continued ophthalmic checkups and adherence to medication regimen. The potential side effects of the medication and the importance of promptly reporting any new symptoms were also discussed.

Follow-Up Care: The patient will follow-up with her ophthalmologist in three months.

- Diagnosis: Congenital Hyperinsulinism (CHI)

- Patient with CHI was admitted electively to our pediatric inpatient unit to decide on an alternative medical treatment due to the troublesome hypertrichosis caused by diazoxide.
- Trial off diazoxide was performed whereby, diazoxide was gradually weaned and stopped for 72 hours. However, this led to subsequent development of recurrent symptomatic hypoglycaemia.
- Octreotide (a somatostatin analogue) was then commenced as four times daily subcutaneous injection.
- A good glycemic response was noted at this dose and she was able to tolerate a fast for a period of 24 hours with no evidence of hypoglycaemia.
- Lanreotide (long-acting somatostatin analogue) was commenced as a subcutaneous injection 30 mg once monthly and octreotide was gradually weaned and stopped.
- Continuous blood glucose monitoring system following the administration of lanreotide revealed good glycemic control with no episodes of hypoglycemia.
- Patient developed recurrent symptomatic hypoglycemic episodes after starting fluoxetine. Fluoxetine was discontinued and hypoglycemic episodes resolved within a week.
- Two weeks after the discontinuation of fluoxetine, the patient's depressive symptoms slowly improved over time with the help of counselling.

Final Diagnosis:
- Congenital Hyperinsulinism (CHI)

Follow-up Plan:
- No further specific follow-up needed at this time.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

Patient Information:
Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 67 years
Sex: Female

Chief Complaint:
Moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon. Right hemicolectomy was performed, and the pathology confirmed stage III (pT3N1) adenocarcinoma. Adjuvant chemotherapy was initiated but was discontinued after four of eight cycles due to severe neuropathy. After completion of adjuvant treatment, the patient underwent active surveillance. In November 2012, a recurrence near the right psoas muscle was identified and excised in December. Immunohistochemical workup showed an abnormal mismatch repair profile with loss of MLH1 protein. The patient underwent radiotherapy concurrent with capecitabine, but again, significant neutropenia necessitated a capecitabine dose reduction. In October 2013, the patient relapsed with disease in the L3 spinous process and received 42 Gy of stereotactic radiotherapy in 10 fractions. In June 2014, the tumor recurred at the same site, and the patient underwent palliative resection of the mass.

Enter Personalized OncoGenomics (POG) initiative:
The patient consented to genomic analysis of the tumor resected from the L3 spinous process by the POG initiative at the BC Cancer Agency. The genomic analysis revealed overexpression of FOS and JUN genes that encode the AP-1 transcriptional complex. Immunohistochemical workup confirmed robust expression of c-JUN protein. It was suggested that irbesartan could be a potential option due to the blockade of the renin–angiotensin pathway.

Treatment:
The patient had a pretreatment baseline PET/CT scan and started irbesartan at a dose of 150 mg daily in December 2014. After 5 weeks of therapy, a follow-up PET/CT was performed, and there was virtually a complete functional radiological resolution of her disease. CEA levels decreased from 18 to 3.1.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon.

Discharge Condition:
The patient has been discharged, and her condition is stable. Follow-up visits have been scheduled, and medication and dietary instructions have been provided.

Medications:
Irbesartan 150 mg daily.

Follow-up:
Follow-up appointments have been scheduled. The patient has been advised to adhere to a healthy diet and lifestyle and continue medication as prescribed.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 58-year-old male laborer, presented with a rough scaly plaque on the right lower back. He had a history of a small annular lesion that spread peripherally to a larger plaque, which remained static for seven years before suddenly spreading in the last two years. The patient often worked with bare upper body for long hours and experienced itching and burning sensation in high mercury conditions.

Investigations:
The patients were thoroughly investigated, with all results within normal limits. The patients were negative for HIV and immunocompetent. The provisional diagnosis of porokeratosis was confirmed with biopsy specimens revealing cornoid lamellae, absent granular, and chronic inflammatory cells in papillary dermis.

Treatment:
The patients were advised to wear protective clothing and were prescribed capsule isotretinoin 20mg and halobetasol 0.05% for topical application at night. The patient who experienced itching and burning under the sun underwent partial excision, cryotherapy, and subsequently applied 0.05% tretinoin cream and 5% fluorouracil cream alternate nights. The patient experienced side effects of erythema, pruritus, oozing, crustation, and edema, after every 3-4 weeks, but ultimately showed moderate improvement over five months of treatment.

Follow-up:
One of the three patients was lost to follow up and the other two did not show any further signs of the condition. The patient who experienced side effects from treatment was lost to follow up due to the severity and frequency of side effects.

Diagnosis:
Porokeratosis

Instructions:
The patient is advised to wear protective clothing to avoid direct sunlight exposure. The patient should continue taking capsule isotretinoin 20mg and applying halobetasol 0.05% as prescribed.

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the hospital following a stab wound to the left chest. He was transferred to the emergency department with hypotension, tachycardia, tachypnea, and Glasgow Coma Scale score of 14. The initial FAST revealed a pleural effusion in the left thorax. A chest drain was inserted, and more than 700 mL of blood was drained. Subsequent FAST had revealed a pericardial effusion.

A Clamshell thoracotomy was started due to the patient's unstable hemodynamic status, and surgical exploration showed a massive hemothorax in the left thorax, left lung posterior lobe injury, pericardial injury, and hemopericardium with blood clots. A 10-mm defect was found in the right ventricle near the left anterior descending coronary artery. Chemical cardiac arrest was induced using ATP, and the cardiac wall was repaired surgically using a horizontal mattress suture. The patient recovered after the surgery and received intensive care in the hospital for 13 days.

Discharge Summary:

The patient was discharged after a 13-day hospital stay without complications. The postoperative echocardiographic check-ups showed a septal injury, but the patient did not exhibit any symptoms of heart failure.

The patient should avoid strenuous activities and get plenty of rest for at least two weeks. It is essential to monitor for signs of infection, such as fever, inflammation, and excessive wound discharge. The patient should report chest pain, shortness of breath, or lightheadedness immediately.

Follow-up care should include a visit with a primary care provider or specialist, depending on the patient's condition, within one week. They should return to the hospital immediately if new symptoms appear or existing symptoms worsen.

The patient's condition is stable currently, and they have been discharged home with follow-up treatment as suggested above.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission:
A 43-year-old male with primary hypothyroidism was admitted for evaluation of progressive fatigue, weakness, muscle and joint pain in the setting of recurrent fractures.

History of Present Illness:
The patient had been experiencing musculoskeletal pain in several locations including bilateral knees, ankles, left shoulder, left arm, and lower back which affected his overall functional status. He struggled to climb a flight of stairs, often grabbing the railing to pull himself up. A nuclear medicine bone scan showed abnormal uptake in bilateral ribs, vertebrae, right knee, hips, ankles, and feet. A lower extremity MRI showed stress fractures in left fibula, fifth metatarsal, and right tibia.

Course in Hospital:
The patient was started on calcitriol and phosphate supplements which significantly improved muscle weakness. Due to concern for TIO, a positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) scan with 68Gallium (68Ga)-DOTATATE was performed which showed multiple lytic osseous lesions with increased somatostatin positive uptake seen throughout pelvis, ribs, ankles, and feet. However, after re-review with radiology, multiple areas of increased uptake were considered to be secondary to fractures, and left posterior acetabular lesion was presumed to be the tumor of interest given a remarkably higher standard uptake values (SUVmax) in this lesion compared to other lesions (SUVmax 20 vs. 4–5).

Procedure:
The left acetabular lesion was biopsied and pathology demonstrated a 1.4 cm phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor of the left acetabulum with uninvolved margins. The patient underwent radical resection of the tumor of the posterior left acetabulum with reconstruction of the posterior wall and posterior column of the acetabulum through a Kocher-Langenbach approach. His hip joint was able to be spared utilizing a 3D-printed custom bone cutting guide (CG) and intra-operative O-arm guided surgical navigation (Medtronic© Stealth) utilizing a navigated Sonopet Ultrasonic Bone Cutting Bovie (Stryker). The posterior wall and column of his acetabulum were constructed with a tantalum augment (Zimmer) and a pelvic reconstruction plate and screw construct (Synthes) after tumor removal.

Discharge Summary:
The patient was discharged with normal phosphorus and FGF23 levels, pain-free left hip, no evidence of hardware complication, back to hiking, and walking on the treadmill. Clinical and radiographic follow-up at 6 months postoperatively found him to be pain-free in his left hip, with almost complete resolution of bone pain, and no recurrence of fractures. Phosphorus level also remained normal at 3.4 mg/dL 6 months after surgery.

HOSPITAL COURSE

This patient was admitted to our facility for an intense pruritus on her right arm, which had been ongoing for six months. She also complained of right brachial paresis.

COMORBIDITIES

The patient has a known history of multiple myeloma.

DIAGNOSTIC TESTS AND PROCEDURES

Computed tomography of the cervical spine, magnetic resonance imaging, and electromyography of the brachial plexus were performed, which showed right cervical disc herniation with nerve root compression of C6-C7 and right brachial plexus inflammation (Parsonage-Turner syndrome).

DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS

The patient was treated with methylprednisolone aceponate cream 0.1% and oral hydroxyzine 25mg every 8 hours, which resulted in little improvement of the pruritus. Gabapentin was introduced at 900mg/day, which achieved optimal control after three months of follow-up.

FOLLOW-UP INSTRUCTIONS

The patient was referred to neurosurgery and oncology consultation for additional therapeutic orientation.

SUMMARY

The patient presented with brachial plexopathy, which is attributed to neoplastic infiltration of multiple myeloma. The treatment plan included the application of methylprednisolone aceponate cream 0.1% and oral hydroxyzine 25mg every 8 hours, along with the introduction of gabapentin at 900mg/day. The patient was referred to neurosurgery and oncology for further management.

Hospital Course:

The patient, an 81-year-old female with a significant history of prediabetes and end stage renal disease on hemodialysis, underwent coronary artery bypass graft surgery and replacement of mitral valve with postoperative complications. The patient presented with a dehiscence of the sternal wound, which required wound vacuum assisted closure, as well as a sacral decubitus ulcer, and multiple episodes of sepsis and respiratory failure.

Assessment and Plan:

During the first 45 days of admission, the patient's blood glucose was well-controlled with only 2 units total of sliding scale insulin required. However, soon after the start of intravenous ascorbic acid to aid in sternal wound healing, the patient experienced multiple high FSBG levels over 200 mg/dL, resulting in a total of 9 units of insulin treatment in 24 hours and subsequent FSBG levels remaining high over the next few days. Further investigation revealed a marked discrepancy of greater than 100 mg/dL between simultaneous FSBG and BGMP readings, with BGMP readings ranging from 72 to 146 mg/dL. Given the suspicion for falsely high FSBG readings caused by intravenous ascorbic acid, it was discontinued and FSBG values returned to normal. The patient did not experience hypoglycemia while receiving unnecessary insulin treatment.

Summary:

This discharge summary documents the hospital course of an elderly female with a history of renal disease and prediabetes who underwent coronary artery bypass graft surgery and replacement of mitral valve, complicated by postoperative complications. The patient had high FSBG levels after starting intravenous ascorbic acid, which were believed to be falsely elevated, resulting in unnecessary insulin treatment. The FSBG values returned to normal after discontinuation of intravenous ascorbic acid.

Discharge Summary
Patient: 39-year-old male

Medical History:
The patient had a history of allergic rhinitis. He reported many episodes of lightheadedness and patches of urticaria, with chest tightness that happened either with or shortly after exercise over the previous 3 months. Over time, the episodes had become more frequent and severe and required several treatments to relieve his symptoms. The patient was diagnosed with eosinophilic esophagitis via biopsy. 

Hospital Course:
The patient was given several medications to treat his throat and chest tightness with exercise, but they did not completely resolve his symptoms. He later tried to avoid wheat and all food for up to 12 hours before exercise but to no avail.

To manage his condition, the patient elected to start a trial of omalizumab, which was given in doses of 300 mg every 2 weeks. No food restrictions were given during this time. The patient reported marked improvement, and he was able to exercise three times a week without any symptoms. He had only one episode of mild urticaria, but it happened when he had missed one of his omalizumab injections. The patient continued to exercise normally, reporting any symptoms that he had and was followed up monthly.

The patient later experienced episodes of urticaria, markedly increased chest tightness, and periorbital edema after at least 15 minutes of exercise. He ultimately had an episode of anaphylaxis with urticaria, difficulty breathing, and facial swelling and was admitted to the emergency department, where he received several treatments to relieve his symptoms. After this episode, omalizumab was restarted at the same doses and intervals.

Follow-up and Outcome:
The patient continued on omalizumab with no further episodes of anaphylaxis and no restrictions on his activity level. He is expected to continue being followed up monthly and continue exercising normally.

Admitting Diagnosis: Second-stage uterine prolapse

Chief Complaint: Intermittent vaginal blood spotting

Hospital Course: 

The patient was admitted at 28+0 weeks of gestation with complaints of intermittent vaginal blood spotting and diagnosed with second-stage uterine prolapse. Pelvic examination revealed point C as the leading edge according to the pelvic organ prolapse quantification staging system. Sonographic examination revealed a short cervix with 17 mm length and a T-shape. A progesterone capsule was administered vaginally daily.

Two weeks later, at 30+0 weeks of gestation, the patient was admitted again because of regular uterine contractions. She was diagnosed with second-degree uterine prolapse. A more shortened cervix with 10-mm length and a T-shape was noted on sonographic examination. To control preterm uterine contractions, tocolytic therapy was initiated with a favorable outcome. Corticosteroids were also administered. The patient was advised to rest in bed with a suggestion of a slight Trendelenburg position. Vaginal culture revealed mycoplasma infection, which was treated with a single dose of azithromycin 1,000 mg.

At 34+0 weeks of gestation, uterine contractions disappeared without tocolytics, and the patient was discharged. However, she was readmitted at 37+0 weeks of gestation due to regular uterine contractions. The cervix was still prolapsed at the same level and the cervical orifice was opened to about 3 cm width. After a latency period, a healthy male neonate was delivered with an estimated blood loss of about 400 mL, which was not different from that of a normal pregnancy. Apgar scores were 10 at 1 minute and 10 at 5 minutes. 

The prolapsed uterus was manually reduced, and the postnatal period was uneventful. Two days after delivery, the patient was discharged in good health with complete resolution of the cervical prolapse. Follow-up examination 1 and 6 months postpartum revealed no evidence of uterine prolapse.

Discharge Diagnosis: Second-stage uterine prolapse

Condition at Discharge: Good

Discharge Instructions:

- Follow up with obstetrician as recommended for postpartum care.
- Avoid heavy lifting for at least 6 weeks.
- Resume normal activities gradually as tolerated.
- Review vaginal hygiene practices with a healthcare provider.
- Seek medical attention immediately if vaginal bleeding or abnormal discharge occurs.
- Take prescribed medications as directed.
- Follow a healthy diet and maintain a regular exercise routine.

This is a hospital course summary for a 15-year-old girl who presented with oliguria and gross hematuria of 20 days' duration after catching a cold. She was diagnosed with ANCA-associated CGN with immune complex deposits, and the origin of thrombocytosis was unknown.

Treatment:
During her hospitalization, the patient received intermittent hemodialysis 3 times a week, pulse therapy with Methylprednisolone and Cyclophosphamide, and plasma exchange in conjunction with other supportive treatments such as blood pressure control and gastric mucosa protection.

Outcome:
When the patient was discharged, her serum creatinine fell to 313.8 μmol/L with a platelet count of 439 × 10^9 L. The patient continued pulse therapy with Cyclophosphamide at regular intervals for 3 times and until now, her platelet count has not gone beyond 500 × 10^9 L.

Diagnosis:
The final diagnosis was RT. 

Follow-up:
The patient underwent a follow-up of 6 months, and her platelet count remained within the normal range.

Hospital Course:
[Name], a 48-year-old female with polycystic liver and kidney diseases, was admitted to our hospital for surgical treatment. She had been followed up for 5 years at another institution and complained of progressive distension of the abdomen and abdominal fullness leading to gradual decrease in body weight without shortness of breath.

Upon admission, the patient was observed regularly without considering palliative surgery or liver transplantation. During the outpatient clinic follow-up for 1 year, the patient's condition worsened with increasing fatigue and dyspnea on exertion. Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status worsened from 2 to 3.

Medical Treatment:
Medical treatment with somatostatin analogue was not considered primarily due to the high medical cost as well as the undetermined therapeutic efficacy. After obtaining consent from the patient on the uncertain effect of fenestration treatment as well as high risk of disease recurrence, the patient underwent surgical fenestration treatment. Multiple cysts in the enlarged liver were opened, and the cyst walls were excised with electrocautery.

At the end of the fenestration procedure, the liver appeared to be markedly shrunken, and three Jackson-Pratt type drains were inserted to evacuate the ascitic fluid. After performing follow-up CT at 1 week, the drains were removed. The total liver volume by using CT volumetry was 3,870 ml before surgery and 3,125 ml at 1 week after surgery, showing a volume reduction of 19.3%.

Clinical Outcome:
After the surgery, ECOG performance status improved to 1 at 1 month and to 0 at 1 year. Gastrointestinal Quality of Life Index (GIQLI) score was significantly increased to 122 after 1 month. During regular follow-up at an interval of 6 months, follow-up CT showed no progression in cyst size and flat abdomen was observed. At 18 months after surgery, the patient is doing well and performing her normal activities with no evidence of disease recurrence.

Conclusion:
In summary, the patient underwent surgical fenestration treatment for polycystic liver and kidney diseases, resulting in significant improvement in clinical outcomes with no evidence of disease recurrence.

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 28-year-old female who presented to the Emergency Department with sudden onset chest pain and recent fall. She complained of intermittent chest pain, substernal, 8/10 in intensity, and it resolved spontaneously. The patient also reported loss of consciousness followed by a fall that resulted in minor trauma to the head and leg. She denied any history of heart failure or any symptoms suggestive of heart failure. Additionally, the patient reported marijuana use two days prior. On examination, mild epigastric tenderness was detected on abdominal examination. Laboratories revealed a mild leukocytosis and mild hypokalemia. The troponin level was elevated indicating the possibility of non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI). During hospitalization, the patient was diagnosed with Non-Ischemic Cardiomyopathy with severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction. Urgent cardiac catheterization was consistent with echocardiogram results, and severe left ventricular dysfunction was present. Upon repeat echocardiogram, there was a significant improvement in the ejection fraction (EF) with a sound resolution of mitral regurgitation upon discharge. 



Discharge Diagnoses:
-Non-Ischemic Cardiomyopathy



Discharge Medications:
-The patient was discharged on the same doses of Enalapril, and Carvedilol, in addition to, low dose oral furosemide (20mg PO daily). Counseling for abstinence of toxic substances was conducted. The patient was recommended to undergo Cardiac MRI for further evaluation to rule out etiologies but opted for secondary consultation.



Discharge Condition:
The patient's condition improved while in the hospital. She was discharged with a diagnosis of Non-Ischemic Cardiomyopathy and recommended to continue medication and abstinence from toxic substances. Cardiac MRI follow up was recommended but was scheduled to undergo consultation with a specialist.

Hospital Course Summary:

This is a hospital course summary for a 40-year-old female patient who was admitted due to ventricular arrhythmias during neoadjuvant chemotherapy for left breast ductal cancer. The patient had a history of LQTS type 2, a mutation of NM_000238.3(KCNH2):c.2593-2A>G, and had an internal defibrillator implanted in 2005. The patient was treated with slow-release Metoprolol for over 15 years with a prolonged QTc of approximately 480 ms. The patient reported no prior symptomatic arrhythmia episodes.

During the neoadjuvant therapy, the patient was shifted from Metoprolol 75mg to Propranolol slow-release 160mg due to ventricular arrhythmias associated with increased QTc. The patient was monitored by continuous telemetry during the second treatment, and no ventricular arrhythmias were observed. The course of neoadjuvant therapy was interrupted, and the patient underwent surgical resection. Post-operative, the patient received adjuvant treatment with four pulses of docetaxel 80mg/m2 under telemetry monitoring, and no arrhythmias were observed. 

One year after the diagnosis, the patient is doing well, and the QTc has been recorded at 496 ms. No clinical arrhythmias have occurred, and Holter recording 8 months after the first cytostatic treatment showed no premature ventricular complexes. There has been no reoccurrence of ventricular arrhythmias post-switching back to Metoprolol, according to the patient's own wish. 

The patient displayed no complications throughout the admission and was discharged in a stable condition. Follow-ups were scheduled, and the patient was educated regarding managing medications and monitoring of ventricular arrhythmias and QTc intervals.

Hospital Course Summary:
This summary describes a 40-year-old woman admitted for irregular heartbeats during chemotherapy for left breast cancer. She had a long-standing heart condition called LQTS type 2, a genetic change in the KCNH2 gene. A defibrillator was placed in her chest in 2005 to treat dangerous heart rhythms over time. For more than 15 years she took slow-release metoprolol, and her QTc interval was about 480 ms. She said she never felt any symptoms from the irregular beats during that time, and she reported feeling well. During chemotherapy, her doctor changed her medicine from metoprolol 75 mg to slow-release propranolol 160 mg to help control her heart rhythm. The change was made because the chemotherapy was making her QTc interval longer and increasing the risk of dangerous beats. She was continuously monitored with a heart monitor during the second chemotherapy cycle, and no irregular beats were seen. Because of the arrhythmia risk, the chemotherapy course was stopped and she underwent surgery to remove the tumor. After surgery, she received four cycles of docetaxel 80 mg/m2 while being watched by a heart monitor, and no arrhythmias occurred. One year after her diagnosis, she is doing well and her QTc interval is about 496 ms. She has not had any symptomatic irregular beats since her treatment, and she feels fine. A 24-hour Holter monitor worn eight months after her first chemotherapy showed no early beats. She has not experienced a return of ventricular arrhythmias after choosing to go back to metoprolol on her own. During her hospital stay she had no complications and was discharged in stable condition for follow-up care. Follow-up appointments were scheduled, and she was taught how to manage her medicines and watch for irregular heartbeats and QTc.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [patient name]

Gender: [patient gender]

Date of Admission: [date of admission]

Reason for Hospitalization:

The patient was admitted at 22 weeks’ gestation to the Emergency Department due to miscarriage. Upon admission, the patient presented shaking chills, fever, stomatitis, sore throat, abdominal pain, and minimal vaginal bleeding for the previous three days.

Hospital Course:

The laboratory findings upon admission showed a low white blood cell count and high C-reactive protein levels. After induction of labour, the patient delivered a stillborn female fetus. The patient was treated with meropenem, followed by piperacillin/tazobactam for 6 days.

Medical History:

The patient had a complex medical history of monoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis completely resolved at 15 years of age. The patient reported bilateral gonalgia six years before the current hospitalization. Laboratory results showed severe neutropenia, but no ANCA titers. The patient had undergone a bone marrow biopsy, which was reported within normal limits. The patient presented with low neutrophil counts in the past six years but had never contracted opportunistic infections. One year before admission, the patient had delivered a male infant with severe mastitis, followed by two episodes of bilateral knee arthritis.

Postmortem Examination:

The postmortem examination on the nonmacerated female fetus revealed intra-alveolar, gastric, and intestinal neutrophils with oedema, microhemorrhages, and acute tubular necrosis (NTA) of the renal parenchyma. The placenta showed necrotizing AC corresponding to a maternal inflammatory response stage 3/3 and grade 2/2. Funisitis was noted with neutrophilic infiltrate of the umbilical vein and the two arteries with extension to Wharton’s jelly consistent with fetal inflammatory response stage 2/3 and grade 2/2. Initial thrombosis was detected in few spiral arteries of the decidua.

Microbiological Analysis:

Autoptical samples were cultured on different media and identified as K. kingae using MALDI-ToF technology. The microorganism grew in pure culture in all the samples.

Medical Treatment:

The patient was treated with Granulocyte-Colony Stimulating Factor (G-CSF) and cyclosporine (200 mg a day) in addition to hydroxychloroquine due to low neutrophil count and recent intrauterine infection.

Discharge Condition:

The patient fully recovered and was discharged after 10 days.

Follow-Up Plan:

The patient will have regular follow-up appointments with her primary care physician to monitor her medical condition.

Hospital Course:
This 70-year-old female patient presented with active rheumatoid arthritis and was under treatment with salazosulfapyridine 1,000 mg/day. The patient was diagnosed with BRAF wild-type primary mucosal melanoma, which was resected, and adjuvant treatment was administered in the form of 60-Gy/30-Fr radiotherapy. One year after the initial presentation, the patient experienced relapse in her left sixth rib and left iliac fossa, along with duodenal metastasis that resulted in ulceration with gastrointestinal bleeding. The patient required transfusion at least three times per week due to anemia.

Treatment:
The patient underwent treatment with nivolumab (2 mg/kg) and showed no substantial adverse effects. After 19 days, the tumor in the left sixth rib started to decrease in size, and after 26 days, it could no longer be visualized on chest radiography. Computed tomography (CT) performed 1 month after therapy initiation showed the absence of the costal lesion and an acceptable reduction of more than 60 % of the ileal lesion, and the ulcerated duodenal lesion on the endoscopy performed 4 months after treatment showed cicatrization. After the second week, anemia due to bleeding from the tumor was reduced and subsequently blood transfusion was discontinued. The patient received four courses of nivolumab therapy and slight changes to the laboratory data were observed, but no adverse events were noted, and the patient did not experience any worsening of joint pain or DAS28ESR scores. The patient maintained a complete response for 9 months after receiving six courses of nivolumab therapy, without rheumatic exacerbation or drug-related adverse events.

Discharge Condition:
The patient was discharged in stable condition, and there was no evidence of any acute exacerbation of rheumatoid arthritis or adverse effects related to nivolumab therapy.

Discharge Medications:
N/A

Discharge Instructions:
The patient was advised to follow-up with her physicians for routine check-ups and keep a record of any unexpected side effects. The patient was also advised to adhere to a healthy lifestyle and exercise regimen.

Hospital Course:
The 13-year-old Asian girl weighing 24 kg was admitted with a progressive thoracolumbar kyphoscoliosis deformity since 2 years. She underwent tracheostomy 6 years before, related to severe bronchopneumonia management. Since then, she continued to require ventilatory support at night. Genetic study confirmed PD and she was started on ERT.

Physical Exam:
At admission, the patient had thoracolumbar kyphoscoliosis extending from D1 to L4 level, varus deformity of the left foot, bilateral fixed flexor deformity of lower limbs, and wasting of the lower limb and paraspinal muscles with 3/5 motor power. Oxygen saturation was 95% on room air, and chest X-ray showed normal lung fields. Echocardiography showed normal ventricles with ejection fraction of 54% with no evidence of hypertrophy or obstructive cardiomyopathy. Serum creatinine kinase was raised.

Procedure:
General anaesthesia was planned for motor evoked potential (MEP) monitoring during the correction of kyphoscoliosis. The child was induced with dexmedetomidine infusion, ketamine, and morphine, and anaesthesia was maintained with dexmedetomidine infusion, oxygen, and sevoflurane. A total of 450 ml of blood was lost, and 2.3 L of Ringers lactate were infused. The surgery was successful.

Follow-up:
On the 2nd post-operative day, she developed bilateral mild pleural effusion which was treated with diuretics and antibiotics. On the 5th post-operative day, patient was weaned off from ventilator. However, she continued to require nocturnal ventilatory support. Rest of the hospital stay was uneventful, and she was discharged on the 10th day.

Plan:
The patient will continue with ERT and nocturnal ventilatory support. Follow-up appointments will be made with the appropriate specialists.

Hospital Course:

The patient was referred to our pain clinic due to an 8-day history of postural headache, which occurred following acupuncture treatment to manage chronic lower back pain caused by postlaminectomy syndrome. The patient had undergone L4-5 laminectomy 7 years prior. The physical and neurological examinations were normal. The patient was diagnosed with a postdural puncture headache (PDPH) and was placed on bed rest. An epidural blood patch (EBP) was performed, which failed to relieve the symptoms. A brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was unremarkable, while an MRI myelogram showed an abnormal fluid signal intensity in the left lumbar area, along with the left paraspinal muscle, and soft tissues at the L3-4-5 level, probably due to CSF leakage.

After conservative care, which included bed rest, hydration, and taking acetaminophen, the patient's postural headaches persisted. A repeat fluoroscopically guided interlaminar EBP was performed with minor relief. A transforaminal EBP at the L3-4 and L4-5 levels on the left side was performed. After the transforaminal EBP, the patient's headache and other symptoms subsided without complications.

At the 2-week follow-up, the patient reported being headache-free, and the activities had returned to normal.

Diagnosis:

Postdural puncture headache (PDPH)

Treatment:

Conservative care, including bed rest, hydration, and acetaminophen, was recommended. Epidural blood patches were performed, including an interlaminar approach using autologous blood at the L2-3 level with 15ml, and a repeat of this procedure using the same volume of blood at the L4-5 level. Finally, a transforaminal EBP with 3ml autologous blood was given at each level at L3-4 and L4-5 on the left side.

Follow-up Care:

The patient was discharged after 4 days. At the 2-week follow-up, the patient reported being headache-free, and the activities had returned to normal. The patient was advised to follow-up with their primary care physician if there were any changes in the symptoms.

Patient Name: [patient name]
Medical Record Number: [medical record number]

Admission Date: [admission date]
Discharge Date: [discharge date]

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 43-year-old female admitted with acute hypoxic respiratory failure, requiring 15 litres per minute of oxygen. Physical exam was significant for wheezing in lungs bilaterally. Electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm. Troponin and electrolytes were in normal range. She had normocytic anemia with hemoglobin 10.8 g/dl, leukocytes 7.8 X 109/L, serum procalcitonin at 0.10 ng/mL. Arterial blood gases showed respiratory acidosis. Chest X-ray showed extensive bilateral lung infiltrates.

The patient was managed empirically for community acquired pneumonia with broad-spectrum antibiotics. On day 3 of hospital stay, her symptoms and oxygen requirement improved. However, she was noted to have hyperkalemia (potassium: 5.8 mmol/L) and elevated CK at 10,000 U/L. She denied any history of myalgias, muscle weakness, trauma, recent exercise, illicit drug use, and statins. An impression of rhabdomyolysis was made and aggressively hydrated. Surprisingly, the CK level increased despite resuscitation, raising diagnostic curiosity.

Detailed inflammatory workup was negative. Her course of hospitalization was complicated by volume overload requiring aggressive diuresis. A detailed discussion with the patient was held explaining enzyme abnormality and risk versus benefits of invasive workup. She refused further investigations including biopsy and imaging. A CK electrophoresis was ordered and the patient was discharged to follow up as an outpatient. Surprisingly, her isoenzyme panel showed CK MM with type 1 macroCK-macroCKemia.

On post-hospital follow up, subsequent normalization of enzyme levels were seen.

Discharge Diagnosis:

1. Acute hypoxic respiratory failure.
2. Community-acquired pneumonia.
3. Rhabdomyolysis.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient should follow up with her primary care physician. She should monitor for any recurrence of symptoms related to acute hypoxic respiratory failure or pneumonia and report them immediately if they do occur.

The patient should maintain her hydration level, follow a healthy diet and a normal lifestyle.

She should avoid strenuous physical activity until medical clearance is obtained. Emergency medical services should be contacted in case of any emergency issues.

The patient should be advised to go through regular lab tests to address any abnormality issues. 

Follow-up plan:

The patient should be followed up in the outpatient clinic within 2 weeks.

- A second ESP block performed with 20 mL of 0.25% ropivacaine and 40 mg triamcinolone, which produced significant analgesia lasting 2 weeks

To avoid further allergic reactions, switching to a different insulin formulation was recommended. The patient refused treatment with a different insulin regimen despite extensive counseling. She was prescribed oral antihistamines to be taken before her regular insulin injections, and also an EpiPen (epinephrine injection, USP) 0.3 mg, with the instructions to visit the ER if she develops symptoms again.

Outcome:

The patient completely recovered from the COVID-19 infection, but continued having insulin allergies with her humulin 70/30 insulin injections. Eventually, the patient agreed to switch to different insulin formulations after about two weeks of her initial ER presentation. The new insulin formulations brought the glucose levels down to her usual glycemic range without any further allergic reactions.

Low back pain and radicular pain in right leg leading to walking disability.

The patient was admitted with a history of low back pain and radicular pain in her right leg causing difficulty in walking. She underwent posterior spinal fusion from T9 to the sacrum using intrasacral screws and interbody fusion at L3/4, L4/5, and L5/S disc levels. The patient was evaluated by the surgical team preoperatively, and follow-up evaluations were done postoperatively by the same team.

Posterior spinal fusion was performed using intrasacral screws coupled with interbody fusion at L3/4, L4/5, and L5/S levels. The patient received standing rehabilitation on a tilt table from the fifth day after surgery, and walking was allowed with the use of a thoracolumbosacral orthosis beginning on the twentieth postoperative day.

Clinical Progress and Condition:
The patient’s symptoms of low back pain and radicular pain improved after the surgery. The patient could walk for more than 10 minutes with the use of a cane 1 year after the surgery. Spinal fusion was confirmed, but slight loosening of the intrasacral screws was observed by computed tomography at follow-up.

The patient was discharged in stable condition with recommendations for follow-up visits as prescribed by the surgical team.

N/A

The patient was discharged home.

Patient Name: [redacted]

Date of Discharge: [redacted]        

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 47-year-old woman, was admitted to the hospital with bilateral groin pain, inability to urinate, and bloody vaginal discharge. Clinical vaginal examination revealed the presence of a large necrotic mass filling the whole vaginal tract. Transabdominal ultrasound examination showed a cervico-vaginal mass measuring 112 × 114 mm that protruded from the uterine cavity with a distorted view of the uterus. After consultation and an MRI examination, a large heterogeneous signal intensity of a well-defined submucosal fundal fibroid mass was confirmed. Uterine anatomy was distorted as seen as “V shape” fundus in sagittal plane due to traction of the mass. 

Laboratory tests showed a decreased hemoglobin level of 10.1 g/dL, hematocrit of 30.9%, and elevated CRP level of 37.5 mg/L. The patient's fasting glucose level, AST and ALT liver enzymes were within normal range, but the CA125 level was 152 U/mL. 

At laparotomy, a large uterine mass with complete uterine inversion was confirmed. The mass was taken out via transverse uterine incision after depicting the myoma’s pedicle. Total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy was performed due to the patient's request before surgery. The excised specimen revealed a giant mass with extensive necrosis and multiple hemorrhagic foci. Pathology report confirmed 12 × 12 × 10 cm sized leiomyoma including large ischemic necrotic areas. There was no evidence of malignancy. 

The patient was discharged without any complications five days after the surgery.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Uterine inversion with uterine fibroid.

Discharge Condition:
Stable. 

Discharge Medication:
N/A. 

Discharge Instructions:
The patient was instructed to follow up with her gynecologist and primary care physician. She was advised to avoid heavy lifting and intercourse for six weeks to allow for full recovery. She was also instructed to monitor for any signs of vaginal bleeding, pain or fever. If any of these symptoms appeared, she was advised to contact her physician immediately. 

Follow-Up:
The patient was advised to schedule a follow-up appointment with her gynecologist and primary care physician for recovery monitoring.

Hospital Course:

This 60-year-old male patient presented to our outpatient clinic with a 1-year history of generalized yellowish ovoid skin-colored papular eruption located on the trunk, groin, and extremities. The patient reported that he first noticed pruritic papules, and 2–3 months later many yellow and ovoid pruritic papules emerged. On skin physical examination, firm, well-defined ovoid skin-colored to yellow papules were seen on the distal and proximal of upper and lower extremities, trunk, groins, and abdomen.

Diagnostic laboratory tests such as full blood cell count with differential, peripheral blood smear, renal, and liver function tests all were normal. Histopathological examination of the skin biopsy from one of the lesion on the trunk revealed proliferation of mast cells with ovoid and spindle nuclei with distinct cytoplasm borders around capillaries, which was compatible with mastocytosis. Based on concurrent clinical and pathological features, we diagnosed our case as xanthelasmoid mastocytosis.

Treatment with H1 antihistamine, cetirizine 10 mg orally nightly and fexofenadine 120 mg for every morning was prescribed for pruritus control which was successful, but eruptions were persistent without any changes. Treatment with phototherapy also recommended to the patient, but despite a 1-year course, no significant improvement was seen in the lesions.

The patient refused further investigations such as bone marrow biopsy or alternative treatments and decided to end the hospital course. The patient was advised to monitor the lesions and seek medical attention if he noticed any changes or deterioration. The patient was discharged with no complications.

Discharge Summary

Identification: 26-year-old female diagnosed with asthma at the age of 16

Admission Date: October 2018

Discharge Date: July 2019

Chief Complaint: Asthma and nasal polyposis

Hospital Course:

- The patient was admitted with a history of nasal polyposis, which had been surgically treated eight years before but had occurred again in the past two years.
- The patient was treated with inhaled corticosteroids and reported anosmia. Tests for common inhalant allergens were negative.
- The patient displayed sour breath with diffuse obstruction.
- Blood eosinophil count was 1200/mmc; total IgE 126 IU/L; FEV1 by spirometry 70%; ACT 14.
- Treatment with ICS/LABA, combined with LAMA since few months, and daily oral corticosteroids (prednisone 25 mg/die) in the past 3 months.
- In October 2018, benralizumab therapy was started.
- On day 28, no blood eosinophils were detected, IgE value was 38 IU/L and both lung function and symptom control were improved.
- Notably, the use of oral corticosteroids had been reduced.
- At the last follow-up, in July 2019, blood eosinophils were still undetectable, IgE was 26 IU/L and a further clinical and functional improvement was observed.
- Oral corticosteroid therapy had been discontinued three months before.
- The patient did not experience any exacerbation, hospitalization or ER access throughout benralizumab therapy.

Discharge Diagnosis: Asthma with nasal polyposis

Disposition: Stable

Plan: Recommend follow-up with primary care physician. No other specific therapeutic interventions needed.

HOSPITAL COURSE SUMMARY:

Admission Date: [DATE]
Discharge Date: [DATE]

Medical History:
The patient is a 32-year-old woman who presented with a mass in the vulva and intermenstrual bleeding. She had a history of unsuccessful sexual intercourse due to fear of pain, and the mass had gradually enlarged over the past 3 years.

Clinical Findings:
A physical examination revealed a nontender tubular neoplasm outside the intact hymen, with an opening at the distal end. A canal approximately 5 cm long was found in the mass, from which white mucus was secreted. Ultrasonographic evaluation of the pelvis showed a 4.5- × 1-cm stalk originating from the cervix and protruding into the vagina. A mini-hysteroscopy was performed to excise the mass.

Diagnostic Testing:
Hemoglobin level was 9.4 g/dL. The levels of estradiol and progesterone in the luteal phase were 138 pg/mL and 13.77 ng/mL, respectively. Liver and renal functional tests and thyroid hormone levels were all normal.

Treatment:
The patient underwent a mini-hysteroscopy to excise the mass while avoiding damage to the hymen. The mass was found to originate from the squamocolumnar junction at the 3 o’clock position of the left lip of the ectocervix, and it had no communication with the endocervix. The cervical mucosal fold of approximately 0.3 to 0.7 cm in thickness was found inside the canal by mini-hysteroscopy and it had a blind end proximally. The mass was totally excised after suturing of the pedicle. Deep endocervical and endometrial regions were found to be normal.

Condition on Discharge:
The patient's postoperative course was uneventful without bleeding or any other complications. Sexual intercourse was successful for this couple.

Follow-up:
Five weeks after surgery, the patient visited again in the outpatient clinic and was doing well. Written informed consent was obtained from the patient and her husband for publication of this case report and accompanying images. Institutional review board approval was not required for publication of this case report.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 53-year-old male nurse diagnosed with HCV infection 

Hospital Course:
In January 2011, the patient was evaluated at the Outpatient Infectious Diseases clinic for abnormal liver function tests. His HCV RNA was 660,000 IU/mL, genotype 3a. A liver biopsy showed chronic active hepatitis with Metavir A2 necroinflammatory grading and F2 fibrosis. The patient was considered eligible for antiviral treatment and started therapy with PEG-IFN-α-2a and ribavirin in March 2011. Treatment was well tolerated, and HCV RNA became negative by the fourth week and remained undetectable during the entire 24-week treatment regimen. ALT normalized within the first 3 weeks of treatment. The patient underwent post-treatment follow-up until September 2012, and a new biopsy revealed a mild reduction in Metavir grading and staging (A1 and F1, respectively).

Hospitalization:
Nine weeks after finishing the antiviral therapy, the patient developed symmetrical polyarthritis with joint pain and edema in the wrists, knees, shoulders, and metacarpophalangeal joints, associated with prolonged morning stiffness. MRI detected bone erosions with juxta-articular osteopenia in the wrist, knee, and hand joints, revealing a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Rheumatoid factor and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody testing were positive. 

Treatment:
The patient was treated with prednisone and NSAIDs for two months, followed by methotrexate and sulfasalazine with a quick and favorable response to treatment. 

Discharge:
The patient was discharged home in satisfactory condition with a prescription for methotrexate and sulfasalazine. Follow-up with Rheumatologist and Gastroenterologist was advised.

Discharge Summary:

Hospital Course:
The 62-year-old male was admitted to the hospital with a complaint of abdominal pain, vomiting, and ambulatory dysfunction. The initial examination showed no abnormalities. The patient was suspected to have viral gastroenteritis, and hence he was hospitalized for dehydration management. The patient's nausea and vomiting improved after admission, but it was noted that he was leaning backwards and to the right when standing or attempting to ambulate on the first day of hospitalization.

Diagnostic Evaluations:
The neurology service was consulted after assessing the patient's condition on his second day of admission. A CT angiogram of the head and neck showed a congenitally hypoplastic left vertebral artery and no other abnormality was observed in the vertebrobasilar system. MRI of the brain showed acute/subacute infarct in the right cerebellar hemisphere. The echocardiogram showed moderate diastolic dysfunction with trace aortic regurgitation.

Clinical Impression:
The patient was diagnosed with acute/subacute infarct in the right cerebellar hemisphere secondary to chronic atherosclerotic disease that had extended and caused APS. The left-sided dysmetria was observed, which further indicated his neurological impairment.

Hospital Treatment:
The patient was monitored on telemetry for several days without any events or abnormalities noted. He was started on a scheduled antiemetic regimen of metoclopramide 10 mg four times daily and ondansetron 8 mg every eight hours that yielded positive results. Within one day, the patient's nausea and vomiting were controlled, and he was able to eat without difficulty. The patient was successfully discharged from the hospital to rehabilitation.

Follow-up Recommendations:
The patient is recommended to follow up with the neurology service as an outpatient and undergo regular checkups to monitor his neurological function and the progression of his cerebrovascular disease. He is also advised to maintain strict blood glucose control and hypertension management. The family members are recommended to observe the patient's activities, as he is more vulnerable to falls.
