The patient is a 4-year-old girl who was admitted to the hospital with the presentation of snoring, restless sleep, and increasing daytime sleepiness. The patient had no difficulty falling asleep, but she tended to awaken 4-5 times during the nighttime and hardly feel refreshed after sleep. She was diagnosed with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and underwent tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy, which resulted in the elimination of snoring and decreased daytime somnolence. However, her mother was still worried about her persistent hypersomnia and underwent a follow-up sleep test that showed no sleep apnea, with a mean sleep latency of 8 minutes and two sleep onset REM periods (SOREMPs). The diagnosis of OSA and narcolepsy without cataplexy was confirmed, and the patient was started on methylphenidate 10 mg per day, which significantly improved her daytime somnolence and sleep disturbance. She has since been discharged to follow-up with her primary care physician for further management.

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the community hospital with a complaint of syncope. The patient reported experiencing numbness in her arms while kayaking, followed by a loss of consciousness. The patient had a history of dizziness two weeks prior to the current episode. Initial laboratory tests showed low serum potassium and elevated troponin levels. An electrocardiogram revealed sinus tachycardia with monomorphic premature ventricular complexes (PVCs), and a corrected QT (QTc) interval of 520 ms. The QTc interval was normalized with potassium repletion. Echocardiography and cardiac catheterization findings were normal. A treadmill test showed multifocal PVCs and the QT interval shortened with exertion. The patient was discharged on nadolol and a LifeVest® wearable cardioverter-defibrillator.

Later, the patient presented with tachycardia for which the WCD alarmed. The patient pressed the response button to suppress a shock for more than nine minutes but eventually received two shocks. An MRI scan with gadolinium enhancement showed delayed myocardial enhancement in the midmyocardium and epicardium, indicating a nonischemic origin such as myocarditis, amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, or some other form of nonischemic cardiomyopathy. The patient was diagnosed with a phenomenon of residual fibrosis from a past viral myocarditis.

Treatment:

A dual-chamber implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) was placed, and sotalol was initiated at 80 mg twice daily and later increased to 120 mg twice daily. The patient was found to be noninducible via noninvasive programmed stimulation. The patient has been arrhythmia- and symptom-free and is scheduled for further follow-up.

Early blood tests showed low potassium and high troponin, which is a marker of heart injury. An ECG showed a fast heart rhythm with extra beats and a prolonged QT interval of 520 ms. Giving potassium through an IV brought the QT interval back to normal during the hospital stay. Ultrasound of the heart and a heart catheter test showed no problems and were normal. A treadmill test revealed many extra beats from different spots and the QT interval got shorter with exercise. The patient left the hospital taking nadolol and wearing a LifeVest defibrillator vest to protect against dangerous rhythms. Later, she returned with a fast heartbeat that triggered the LifeVest alarm and required her to press the response button. She held the button for over nine minutes to stop a shock, but eventually got two shocks. An MRI with contrast showed scar-like patches in the heart muscle, suggesting myocarditis, amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, or similar disease. Doctors said the scar likely came from a past viral heart infection, also known as myocarditis.
Treatment:
The patient then received a permanent dual-chamber defibrillator implanted in the chest to stop dangerous heart rhythms. She started taking sotalol at 80 mg twice daily, later increased to 120 mg twice daily. Tests showed the device could not trigger a dangerous rhythm, meaning she was not inducible. She has had no arrhythmias or symptoms and will continue with regular follow-up visits to monitor her heart.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with high-grade intermittent fever for three days with spontaneous gum bleeding and mild headache. He subsequently developed gradually worsening drowsiness, and was found to have thrombocytopenia with microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA). A diagnosis of thrombotic thrombocytopenia purpura (TTP) was made. He was promptly commenced on therapeutic plasma exchange and 1 mg/kg of oral prednisolone. 

On the fifth day of illness, the patient developed two episodes of generalized tonic-clonic convulsions which progressed into a non-convulsive status epilepticus, requiring elective ventilation in the intensive care unit. On day 18, he developed flaccid paraparesis with sphincter dysfunction. Magnetic resonance imaging showed haemorrhage at multiple spinal levels.

Despite 16 plasma exchanges and high dose steroids, his platelet count remained persistently low, and he was investigated for alternative etiologies. Polymerase chain reaction of serum revealed clinically significant levels of cytomegalovirus (CMV). He was commenced on oral valganciclovir 450 mg/daily for 21 days. After about 6 days of valganciclovir treatment, his platelet count increased, and the MAHA resolved. 

The patient subsequently had regained normal haematological and biochemical parameters with a negative PCR quantification of CMV. He had regained ambulatory status with support and had normal sphincter function. The patient was transferred to a rehabilitation facility for further care.
nemotron_simplification: Hospital Course: The patient had a high fever that came and went for three days, bleeding gums, and a slight headache. He became increasingly drowsy and had a low platelet count with red blood cell breakdown from small clots. Doctors diagnosed thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, a blood disorder causing clots and low platelets, and started plasma exchange and oral prednisolone. On the fifth day, he had two seizures with whole-body shaking. These seizures turned into ongoing brain seizure activity without shaking, and he needed a breathing machine in the ICU. On day 18, he developed weakness in both legs and lost bladder/bowel control. An MRI showed bleeding in several spots of his spine. Despite 16 plasma exchanges and high-dose steroids, his platelet count stayed low, so doctors looked for other causes. A blood test found a high level of CMV virus. He started taking valganciclovir 450 mg each day for 21 days. After about six days of valganciclovir, his platelet count rose and the red blood cell breakdown stopped. He then returned to normal blood and chemical levels, and a CMV test came back negative. He was able to walk with help and regained normal bladder/bowel control. The patient was transferred to a rehabilitation facility for further care.

Frequent ulcers in the mouth.

Recurrent spontaneous erosions all over the body, healed by hypo- to depigmented scars, hoarseness of voice, and pruritus.

Mild improvement in occurrence of erosions and reduction in scarring was observed. Patient was referred to other departments for further management.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information: Mr. X, 25-year-old male

Reason for Admission: High levels of Hb, management of gout

Hospital Course: Mr. X was admitted to the hospital for evaluation of high levels of Hb and management of gout. A complete blood count showed a Hb value of 20.4 g/dL and hematocrit value of 58%. Bone marrow biopsy indicated no evidence of myeloproliferative features. No abnormalities were found on Hb electrophoresis. Congenital (familial) erythrocytosis was suspected. After mutations were not found in JAK2 V617 or exon 12, MPL W515K/L, CALR exon 9, we performed alpha 1-globin gene (HBA1)/alpha 2-globin gene (HBA2), beta-globin gene (HBB), and Von Hippel Lindau (VHL) gene mutation analysis to identify the cause of congenital erythrocytosis. In HBB gene mutation analysis, we identified a mutation in exon 2 at nucleotide 310, known as Hb Heathrow.

Diagnosis: Hb Heathrow

Medical Management: The patient's case of Hb Heathrow was managed with pharmacological agents. 

Follow-up: Follow-up appointments were scheduled for monitoring and management of the patient's condition. 

Prognosis: The prognosis for Hb Heathrow is favorable, with proper management and monitoring.

Hospital Course:
-The patient was admitted to the cardiac catheterization laboratory with sudden onset chest pain associated with anterior ST-segment elevation on the electrocardiogram. The chest pain occurred during a bowel movement and he was found to be in cardiogenic shock upon arrival.
-Emergency diagnostic coronary angiography was performed, revealing severe proximal stenosis in the left anterior descending (LAD) artery. An extravasation of contrast media from the LAD artery into the pericardium was noted, with no flow in the distal LAD artery, resulting in a suspected dehiscence of the left internal mammary artery (LIMA) graft.
-Injection of contrast media discovered that the LIMA graft's flow of contrast only reached the mid-segment and stopped, while the saphenous vein grafts (SVGs) in the right coronary artery (RCA) and circumflex (LCx) artery were patent.
-After diagnostic coronary angiography, the patient experienced pulseless electrical activity cardiac arrest, but spontaneous circulation was achieved with CPR, and an intra-aortic balloon pump was inserted.
-Urgent echocardiography revealed a large global pericardial effusion with right atrial and right ventricular collapse. Emergency pericardiocentesis was performed to aspirate 700 mL of haemorrhagic fluid that contained an organized thrombus.
-Due to on-going haemodynamic compromise and non-availability of cardiac surgery on-site, it was decided to perform percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) to treat the LAD artery stenosis. Following PCI, thrombolysis in myocardial infarction (TIMI) 3 flow was achieved, and no further extravasation was seen at the dehiscence site.
-Assessment of the LIMA graft showed a sluggish flow with extravasation of contrast media into the pericardium, requiring four coils (Tornado Embolisation Microcoils. Cook Medical, Bloomington, IN, USA) for embolization to halt the flow.
-The patient was then transferred to the local cardiac surgery unit and underwent emergency re-sternotomy and evacuation of the blood clots. His haemoglobin level post CABG (4 weeks prior to this admission) was measured at 100 g/L and dropped to 79 g/L following LIMA avulsion. He received 2 units of blood transfusion.
-The echocardiogram post-PCI revealed residual blood clots in the pericardial space that were difficult to extract percutaneously.
-The patient made a full recovery with no neurological sequelae and was discharged after a few days.
-Outpatient review at 3 months confirmed an excellent recovery without report of cardiovascular symptoms. Control coronary angiography was performed at 5 months, and the patient underwent successful PCI to mid and proximal LAD into the left main (LM) artery with LCx ostium optimization.

- They saw dye leak from the LAD artery into the sac around the heart, with no flow past the blockage.

Hospital Admission: Gastrointestinal complaints

History: A 70-year-old female with a history of asthma, eosinophilic esophagitis, and eosinophilic sinusitis presented with postprandial abdominal pain, bloating, and dyspepsia, which had been ongoing intermittently for 2 years.

Significant Findings: Laboratory results revealed elevated eosinophils, lipase, ALT, AST, and alkaline phosphatase. Initial EGD showed a hypertrophic major papilla, antral gastritis, and superficial gastric ulcers. MRI/MRCP revealed CBD dilatation without choledocholithiasis but with tapering of the distal CBD. ERCP revealed an inflamed major ampulla with benign papillary stenosis.

Treatment: The patient underwent sphincterotomy and insertion of a plastic stent into the bile duct, which was followed by sphincteroplasty and dilation of the papilla and distal CBD. Repeat ERCP was performed with stent removal, and biopsies of the stomach and the ampulla showed benign glandular tissue with no eosinophils. Additionally, the patient was started on prednisone and demonstrated significant improvement with systemic steroid therapy.

Follow-Up: Over six months, the patient was monitored and demonstrated controlled symptoms with normal LFTs. The patient was discharged on 40 mg of pantoprazole twice a day and 2 mg of budesonide daily. 

Prognosis: The patient's prognosis is good at this time, with continued surveillance and management of her gastrointestinal symptoms recommended.

Significant Findings: Blood tests showed high eosinophils, liver enzymes, and pancreas enzyme levels indicating inflammation in the body. An upper endoscopy found a swollen bile duct opening, stomach inflammation, and small stomach ulcers. MRI showed the bile duct was widened but had no stones, with a narrowing at the end. ERCP showed irritation and narrowing of the bile duct opening that was benign and required treatment.

She started taking prednisone and her symptoms improved quickly after a short course of steroid therapy.
Follow-Up: Over six months, the patient was watched and her stomach symptoms stayed under control, and liver tests were normal. She was sent home with pantoprazole 40 mg twice a day and budesonide 2 mg each day.
Prognosis: The patient’s outlook is good, and she should continue regular check-ups and manage her stomach symptoms.

Discharge Summary:

Admitting Diagnosis: Suspected Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP)

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 36-year-old man with a history of bronchial asthma and smoking, presented with sudden onset right upper limb weakness which spread to his lower limb along with slurring of speech and altered consciousness. He was initially admitted to an outside facility where CT scan and carotid ultrasound came out to be normal. His CBC with differential showed low hemoglobin and platelets with elevated bilirubin, and peripheral blood smear (PBS) indicated fragmented red blood cells. TTP was suspected, and fresh frozen plasma (FFP) infusion started. On transfer to our facility, he received PLEX and pulse steroids for 18 sessions which resulted in the stabilization of the patient's LDH and platelet count. During his hospital stay, he was also diagnosed with eosinophilia. A bone marrow aspirate and core biopsy showed trilineage hematopoiesis with 2% blasts and 30% eosinophils. FISH for FIP1L1-PDGFRA (4q12) rearrangement was positive.
After 18 sessions of PLEX, the patient's LDH and platelet counts normalized. However, as weaning off PLEX was attempted, schistocytes re-emerged with a subsequent drop in platelet count. Consequently, a four-dose course of rituximab and Imatinib 100 mg daily were started. Thirty sessions of PLEX were needed to treat the TTP, and the last session was 4 days after the initiation of Imatinib. After more than 28 months of follow-up, the patient's eosinophil count has normalized, and there has been no recurrence of TTP.

Discharge Diagnosis: Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura and Eosinophilia

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient was admitted with suspected TTP, and after receiving 18 sessions of PLEX and methylprednisolone, his platelet count and LDH stabilized. The patient was also found to have eosinophilia with trilineage hematopoiesis, which was treated with a four-dose course of rituximab and Imatinib 100 mg daily. After 30 sessions of PLEX, the TTP was resolved, and the patient's eosinophil count had normalized. After more than 28 months of follow-up, there has been no recurrence of TTP.

When transferred to our center, he received plasma exchange and high-dose steroids for 18 sessions.
These treatments stabilized his LDH enzyme level and platelet count, improving his blood work over time.
During his stay, doctors also found a high eosinophil count, a type of white blood cell.

The patient presented to our hospital with a painful nodular lesion on his left temple which worsened from a month ago. He had a history of chronic rhinosinusitis and was using a fluticasone/salmeterol inhaler for 6 months. Blood tests revealed eosinophilia, and further evaluation confirmed the diagnosis of concurrent JTA and HES. The patient underwent excisional biopsy of bilateral superficial temporal arteries for his JTA and received intravenous steroid for HES.

Diagnostic Findings:
- Physical examination: Tender nodular lesions on both temples and palpable lymph node on the right inguinal area
- Laboratory findings: Elevated total leukocyte, eosinophil, and hemoglobin levels. ESR was slightly elevated
- Imaging studies: CT scan revealed several LN enlargements at bilateral axillary areas, wedge-shaped nonenhancing portion at the spleen, and enlarged LN at right inguinal area. CT angiography and 3-dimensional-brain showed fusiform dilatation in both superficial temporal arteries with wall thickening.
- Histopathological findings: Marked eosinophilic infiltration in arterial wall and perivascular tissue with eosinophilic abscess, focal destruction of vascular wall, and organizing thrombi in the left superficial temporal artery. The right inguinal LN showed reactive follicles and massive eosinophil infiltration, but no evidence of malignancy.

Diagnosis:
Concurrent JTA and HES

Treatment:
- Excisional biopsy of bilateral superficial temporal arteries for JTA
- Intravenous steroid (methylprednisolone) 90 mg per day for HES
- Low-dose steroid (prednisone 10 mg/day) for maintenance after discharge

Outcome:
The patient did not experience a recurrence of JTA after surgical excision during 2 years of follow-up. He was well-maintained without any symptoms due to eosinophilia with low-dose steroid.

Recommendations:
The patient should continue low-dose steroid for maintenance and follow-up with a primary care physician regularly. Further evaluation and management are needed for chronic rhinosinusitis.

Stable and in improved condition.

Reason for Admission: Shortness of breath

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the emergency department with shortness of breath and increasing dyspnea. She was found to have a large goiter that was compressing the trachea and causing respiratory distress. The patient was quickly transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU) where she was intubated using rapid sequence induction to relieve respiratory distress. Subsequent cerebral and thoracic computed tomography (CT) scans revealed a large goiter plunging into the upper mediastinal orifice, which was removed successfully by thyroidectomy 48 hours after admission. Prior to reversal of the neuromuscular blockage, the tube balloon was deflated, and the diagnosis of tracheomalacia was almost confirmed. The endotracheal tube was left in place for 24 hours, and then removed the next day without incident.

Course of Treatment:
The patient received corticotherapy (dexamethasone at 12 mg per day for two days) prior to thyroidectomy to accelerate fetal lung maturation. Surgery was completed without incident, as no intraoperative tracheostomy was necessary. Patient was treated with levothyroxin sodium tablets 75mcg/day post-surgery.

Follow-Up Plan:
Patient was discharged from the hospital on the 5th postoperative day without any complications. Pathology showed multinodular goiter with areas of atypical hyperplasia, but no sign of malignancy. Patient gave birth to a healthy newborn four weeks later.

Recommendations:
Patient should continue taking levothyroxin sodium tablets 75mcg/day as prescribed. She should follow up with her primary care physician for monitoring of her thyroid function and any potential complications related to the goiter removal.

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the emergency room with trouble breathing that got worse over several hours.
She had a large enlarged thyroid in her neck pressing on her windpipe and causing discomfort.
This pressure made it hard for her to breathe and caused anxiety during her stay.
She was moved quickly to the intensive care unit for close monitoring and support by the medical team.
There a breathing tube was placed quickly to help her breathe and keep her airway open.
Head and chest CT scans showed the enlarged thyroid pushing into the chest area and pressing on nearby structures.
The thyroid was removed by surgery 48 hours after she arrived at the hospital, relieving her breathing trouble.
Before the muscle relaxer wore off, the tube cuff was let down and a weak windpipe was suspected.
The breathing tube stayed in for 24 hours then was taken out the next day without problems.
Course of Treatment:
The patient got a steroid medicine dexamethasone 12 mg each day for two days before surgery.
This helped the baby's lungs grow while she was pregnant and prepared her for delivery.
The surgery went well and no hole was made in her windpipe during the operation.
After surgery she started thyroid hormone pills 75 micrograms each day to replace missing hormone.
Follow-Up Plan:
She left the hospital on the fifth day after surgery with no issues and feeling stable.
The removed thyroid showed many nodules with some abnormal cells but no cancer was found.
Four weeks later she gave birth to a healthy baby girl weighing seven pounds and doing well.
Recommendations:
She should keep taking the thyroid hormone pills 75 micrograms each day as directed by her doctor.
She should see her regular doctor to check her thyroid and watch for any surgery-related problems.

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 59-year-old Japanese male with a history of mid-ventricular obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) presented with an asymptomatic thrombus in the apical aneurysm. The patient declined hospital admission and elected to receive treatment at an ambulatory clinic, where anti-coagulation therapy with dabigatran was initiated. The patient showed an approximately two-fold increase in activated partial thromboplastin time and an increased internationalized ratio of the prothrombin time. However, there were no significant alterations in the levels of D-dimer, thrombin-anti-thrombin III complex, and fibrinogen. During the course of treatment, weekly echocardiographic examinations demonstrated a gradual decrease in thrombus size, from 15.0mm×17.0mm to 6.8mm×6.0mm after two weeks. No thrombus was detected after three and four weeks of treatment. No systemic thromboembolic events were reported during the four-week treatment period. Dabigatran administration was continued even after the resolution of the thrombus. 

Diagnosis:

The patient was diagnosed with an asymptomatic thrombus in the apical aneurysm. 

Treatment:

The patient elected to receive treatment at an ambulatory clinic and was initiated on anti-coagulation therapy with dabigatran administration (150mg b.i.d.). Weekly echocardiographic examinations showed a gradual decrease in thrombus size, and after four weeks of treatment, the thrombus appeared to have been resolved. No systemic thromboembolic events were reported during the four-week treatment period. 

Follow-up:

The patient was advised to continue with dabigatran administration. Follow-up appointments were recommended to monitor the patient's condition. 

Discharge Medications:

Dabigatran (150mg b.i.d.) was continued even after the resolution of the thrombus.

The patient was admitted to the hospital with presumptive diagnosis of LVAD pump thrombosis. During his hospital stay, he was managed with argatroban infusion and other medications including bumetanide, carvedilol, digoxin, spironolactone, and milrinone infusion. However, despite being on argatroban therapy, there was a significant increase in LVAD flows and power as well as a steadily increasing LDH. All options were discussed with the patient including LVAD exchange that he declined at that time.

After considering the patient's medical history and current condition, the clinical team decided to start tissue plasminogen activator (tPa) therapy, in which initial dosing included a 10 mg IV bolus followed by 1 mg/min for 20 min and finally 1 mg/h for 24 h. The patient showed an immediate improvement in the device parameters after administration of the initial tPa bolus. Over the following days, the patient's condition continued to improve as evidenced by falling LDH levels.

After 13 days of stabilization and various medical interventions, the patient was discharged from the hospital in stable condition. Subcutaneous enoxaparin and warfarin were instituted to manage the patient's condition while awaiting a suitable transplant donor.

Discharge Diagnosis:
LVAD pump thrombosis

Discharge Instructions:
- Continue taking prescribed medications as directed by your healthcare provider
- Follow a low-sodium diet, and manage fluid intake as recommended
- Continue all outpatient therapies as directed
- Monitor and report any unusual or significant symptoms such as chest pain, shortness of breath, dizziness, or swelling.

Please follow up with your cardiologist and other healthcare providers as recommended.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 44-year-old Hispanic male who was admitted for the evaluation of bilateral ocular inflammation in the setting of treatment with ipilimumab for metastatic cutaneous melanoma. He had received his third infusion two months prior to presentation, which led to systemic inflammatory side effects from therapy including rash, diarrhea, fever, and persistent rectal abscesses.

Physical Exam:
Upon presentation, the patient had central scotoma in the left eye, and both eyes showed pigment on the endothelium without keratic precipitates. Bilateral optic nerve edema with Paton’s lines and macular edema were noted on fundus examination. Cystic intraretinal and subfoveal fluid was also identified during Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT).

Treatment:
The patient was initially treated with topical therapy with prednisolone acetate and was referred to the uveitis service for further evaluation. Bilateral prednisolone acetate 1% was started four times a day with 0.2% brimonidine tartrate-0.5% timolol maleate ophthalmic solution twice a day and increased to 80 mg of oral prednisone daily. The patient was continually monitored and had his medication doses adjusted to promote healing.

Improvement and Discharge:
Over the course of following three weeks, his vision steadily improved with resolution of the optic nerve and retinal edema and subsequent development of a macular star. At the 2-month follow-up, his vision in both eyes improved to 20/25 and his anterior chamber reaction stabilized at 1+ flare and rare cell while taking prednisolone acetate four times a day. The patient was then lost to follow-up.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Hospital Course:
The patient is a 44-year-old Hispanic man with inflamed both eyes while on ipilimumab for spread skin cancer.
He had his third infusion two months before symptoms started, which caused rash, diarrhea, fever, and lasting rectal abscesses.
Physical Exam:
When he arrived, he had a blind spot in the left eye.
Both eyes showed a color change on the inner surface with no white spots.
Swelling of the optic nerves in both eyes was seen, with white lines and swelling in the central retina.
An eye scan also found fluid pockets inside and under the central retina.
Treatment:
First, he received steroid eye drops and was sent to the eye inflammation specialist.
He used steroid eye drops 1% in both eyes four times daily and pressure-lowering eye drops twice daily.
He also took 80 mg of steroid pills each day, and his medicines were adjusted over time to help healing.

Over the next three weeks, his vision improved steadily and the optic nerve and retinal swelling went away.
A star-shaped pattern appeared in the retina, and at the two-month visit, his vision in each eye was 20/25.
The mild eye inflammation stayed low while he used steroid eye drops four times a day.
After that, he was lost to follow-up.

Medical History:
The patient presented with symptoms of poor educational performance at the age of 8 years, followed by gait abnormalities and facial abnormal movements at the age of 12 years. Subsequent symptoms included dysarthria, frequent falls, ataxia and dystonia of right limbs, supranuclear vertical gaze palsy, and swallowing difficulties. Brain MRI at 24 years of age showed a generalized cortical atrophy. A muscle biopsy analyzed by light microscopy showed a nonspecific chronic inflammatory process. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated splenomegaly. The suspicion index for Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC) scored 227 points. Nucleotide sequencing found two heterozygous changes in NPC1, which confirmed the diagnosis of NPC.

Hospital Course:
The patient was initiated on miglustat late in the progression of NPC disease with a modified functional disability scale score of 17 points for a short period (less than 6 months). He had complicated aspiration pneumonia, which required admission to ICU, pulmonary artificial ventilation, and tracheostomy. He is now relatively stable with tracheostomy and GI tube for feeding and restarted very recently treatment with miglustat 200 mg every 8 hours. However, he shows a higher disability score of 21.

Medical Condition at Discharge:
The patient's medical condition at the time of discharge was stable.

Follow-up Care:
The patient will be followed up by the neurology department for treatment and management of his condition.

Recommendations:
The patient was recommended to have regular follow-up with the neurology department. Any significant changes in his condition should be reported immediately.

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 55-year-old woman, was admitted to the hospital due to the sudden onset of severe headache, syncope, left hemiparesis, and aphasia. A computed tomography (CT) scan revealed a right frontal brain hematoma and vasogenic brain edema, while cerebral angiography showed evidence of cerebral vasculitis in branches of the anterior, middle, and posterior right carotid artery system, with a small aneurysm and infundibular dilation of the left posterior communicating artery. A brain biopsy indicated perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate in meninges.

Treatment:

The patient was admitted to the ICU for monitoring and medical management. She was treated with a bolus of methylprednisolone (1 gr each day per three days) and cyclophosphamide (1 gr IV monthly per six doses). She was discharged on a regimen of prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day and phenytoin 300 mg/day.

Follow-up:

The patient is currently under monthly monitoring, receiving cyclophosphamide and prednisolone orally with dose tapering.

Name: [Patient's name]

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient presented with painful, red raised lesions on the right forearm with fever, which gradually coalesced to form larger lesions. The patient had a prior history of upper respiratory tract infection and similar episodes three years back. On examination, a large erythematous plaque was present on the right upper extremity along with small erythematous plaques on both upper limbs, right side of the neck, and chest. Few lesions showed typical “relief of mountain range appearance”. Local temperature was raised in all the lesions. Superficial nerves were not thickened and sensations on the plaques were normal. Histopathology showed a diffuse infiltrate consisting predominantly of mature neutrophils located in the upper dermis without evidence of primary leukocytoclastic vasculitis.

Treatment:
The patient was initially treated with tablet dapsone 100 mg HS with dramatic early improvement, and relapse on discontinuation. The second episode was treated with a combination of dapsone and oral prednisolone started at 30 mg/day and gradually tapered over 4 weeks. The patient is now in remission and discharged. 

Follow-Up Instructions:
The patient is advised to follow-up with their primary care provider for further evaluation and management.

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Age: 46
Sex: Male
Admission Date: [Redacted]
Discharge Date: [Redacted]

Admitting Diagnosis: Peptic perforation

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the emergency department with symptoms of pain in the epigastrium, constipation, nausea, vomiting, fever, and abdominal distension. Physical examination revealed distension, board-like rigidity, marked rebound tenderness, and absent liver dullness. A provisional diagnosis of peptic perforation was made.
Exploratory laparotomy was planned, which revealed a submucosal nodular tumor in the anti-mesenteric border of the jejunum, fifty cm from the duodeno-jejunal flexure. The growth had a central perforation with intestinal contents effusing through the rent. The growth was resected, and an end-to-end, single layer, interrupted anastomosis was performed using 2′0′ polyglycolic suture. The specimen was sent for histopathological examination, which showed a jejunal GIST of intermediate risk. Surgical lines of resection were free.

Post-Operative Course:

The postoperative period was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on the tenth post-op day after stitch removal. The patient is on a six-month follow-up receiving oral imatinib 300 mg twice a day.

Diagnosis at Discharge: None

Instructions on Discharge:

The patient was discharged in a stable condition with instructions to continue taking oral imatinib 300 mg twice a day. No further specific instructions were given.

Follow-up with:

The patient is advised to follow up with the physician for further monitoring and assessment of the condition.

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the emergency department with belly pain, trouble passing stool, feeling sick, and throwing up.
The patient also had a high temperature and a swollen belly, which are signs of infection.
The exam showed a swollen belly, a hard belly, pain when pressing and releasing, and no liver dullness.
The doctors thought the problem was a hole in the stomach or intestine, called a hole in the gut.
Surgery to look inside the abdomen found a lump under the inner lining of the small intestine.
The lump was on the side of the intestine opposite the blood supply, about 20 inches from the start.
The lump had a hole in the middle, and gut contents were leaking out into the belly.
The lump was removed, and the ends of the intestine were sewn together with stitches.
The stitches used were a dissolvable type called polyglycolic suture, which the body absorbs over time.
The lump was sent to the lab and found to be a small intestine tumor with medium risk of returning.
The edges of the removed tissue were checked and had no tumor left, meaning the surgery got all of it.
Post-Operative Course:
Recovery went smoothly and there were no problems after surgery, so the patient healed well.
The patient left the hospital ten days after surgery, once the stitches were taken out.
The patient will take the medicine imatinib 300 mg two times each day for six months.
Diagnosis at Discharge: None
Instructions on Discharge:
The patient left the hospital in good condition and was told to keep taking imatinib 300 mg twice a day.
No other special instructions were given besides continuing the medicine and watching for any problems.

The patient should see the doctor for regular check-ups to watch the condition and make sure the treatment is working.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 23-year-old male with chronic HCV, presented to our care for combination therapy based on the National Committee for Control and Prevention of viral Hepatitis "C" guidelines in Egypt. The therapy regimen included pegylated interferon α 2a 180 ug/week and ribavirin 1000 mg/day. However, at week 12 of therapy, the patient was discontinued due to a lack of early virologic response.

Discharge Summary:
The patient was diagnosed with HCV in a pre-employment checkup 2 years ago. The patient's BMI was 27.5 and had a liver biopsy score of A2 F2 without steatosis. During therapy, the patient's laboratory parameters recorded OBI with HBV DNA values greater than 2000 IU. To treat this activation, lamivudine was administered and continued for 6 months. During this time, the patient continued to be exposed to both HBV and HCV viral load assessment and HBV was undetected, and the HCV RNA level decreased. The patient discontinued lamivudine due to financial constraints and was exposed to HBV and HCV viral load determination 6 months later, where HBV was undetected, and HCV RNA level decreased to 7062 IU/ml.

Overall, the patient's medical history, including HCV and the occurrence of OBI with HBV DNA values over 2000 IU during therapy, was managed effectively with the use of lamivudine. The patient discontinued lamivudine due to financial constraints and was not followed up for HCV RNA levels. No further course of action was taken at the time of the patient's discharge.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
DOB: [REDACTED]
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with hair loss, skin lesions, and itching on their face, trunk, and limbs. Previously diagnosed with folliculitis and eczema, the patient did not respond to treatment with cetirizine, hydrocortisone, and mupirocin. The patient experienced symmetrical pain in their wrist and knee joints after exposure to sunlight. Upon examination, the patient had large alopecia patches on the scalp, erythematous plaques on the scalp and face with slight scales, violaceous lichenoid papules, and blisters on the back of the hands and feet, and papules on their trunk and arms. Laboratory tests revealed WBC count of 3.31 × 109, RBC count of 3.7 × 1012, HGB level of 110 g/L, 24-h urine protein at 248 mg, and ANA at 1:160 (homogeneous spot), 1:80 (cytoplasm), dsDNA (-). The patient's ESR was 58 mm/h, and BP180 was 8 RU/ml. Pathological examination of the scalp indicated hair follicle angle plug and epidermal atrophy. The scalp pathology and laboratory tests were consistent with SLE. Pathological examination of the upper arm, hand, and back supported the diagnosis of bullous lichen planus-systemic lupus erythematosus (LP/LE) overlap syndrome.

Treatment:
The patient was given hydroxychloroquine sulfate, prednisone acetate tablets, topical halometasone cream, and tacrolimus cream. Two weeks later, the patient's symptoms showed significant improvement. The prednisone acetate dosage was decreased to 20 mg daily, acitretin 30 mg daily, and oral methotrexate 10 mg weekly. Three weeks later, the hair loss stopped, joint pain disappeared, and partial lesions regressed. Upon recent follow-up, the patient's symptoms remained stable, skin lesions disappeared, and there was some hair regrowth. The patient was prescribed hydroxychloroquine sulfate 200 mg daily, acitretin 10 mg daily, and oral methotrexate 2.5 mg weekly for continued treatment.

Discharge Condition:
The patient was discharged in stable condition with improved symptoms and prescribed medication for continued treatment. The patient should continue to follow up with their healthcare provider regularly to monitor their condition.

Gender: Female

Discharge Date: XX/XX/XXXX

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the emergency department of our hospital due to iatrogenic acute ascending aortic dissection during coronary angioplasty. Upon arrival, the patient was sedated, afebrile, and diagnosed with atrial fibrillation. An emergent trans-thoracic echography revealed an enlarged ascending aorta. The patient underwent emergency CABG surgery and aortic dissection repair. During the procedure, Stanford type A DeBakey type II ascending aortic dissection with intramural hematoma behind brachiocephalic trunk was found. The aortic valve cusp was decalcified, and a supracoronary aortic tube graft and saphenous vein grafts were successfully placed. The patient was weaned from cardiopulmonary bypass and recovered over the course of 11 days with no reported postoperative complications.

Discharge Diagnosis:

Patient: 61-year-old male with a history of recurrent chest discomfort and palpitations.

Hospital Course:
The patient was referred to our hospital due to frequent ventricular premature contractions, with no positive results found in examinations. RFCA was performed, and the patient experienced dizziness, tightness in the chest, cold sweat, bradycardia, and hypotension afterward. Further examination of the patient showed hydropericardium, and the patient underwent pericardiocentesis drainage to drain off 800 mL blood. The patient's tight chest improved, and their blood pressure increased. However, the patient experienced chest tightness again two hours later, and an additional 750 mL of blood was drained from the indwelling catheter in the pericardium. This time, the patient was given volume expansion and dopamine to sustain normal blood pressure. During the next hour, the patient experienced further circulatory unstability, and a transthoracic echocardiography revealed a left ventricular wall rupture and a hematoma in the left ventricular wall. The patient was then transferred to the operating room for surgical exploration.

Surgical intervention:
The patient underwent median sternotomy, and CPB was established with cannulation of the ascending aorta and right atrium quickly after the pericardium cavity was evacuated. Cardioplegic arrest was used, and further exploration of the heart showed a 6 × 8 cm2 area of contusion in the posterolateral wall with a 5-cm epicardial tear at the center. Teflon-buttressed sutures were used to close the tear, and a pericardium patch with continuous sutures around and bioglue inside was applied to the contusion region. The patient was discontinued from CPB uneventfully with excellent hemodynamic status.

Discharge Summary:
The patient has recovered well from their surgical intervention and was discharged from the hospital on the 15th postoperative day. Final examination showed that the injury region of the left ventricular wall had healed. The patient is advised to maintain a healthy diet and exercise regimen and to follow up with their primary care physician as needed.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to our hospital with a 2-month history of fever, night sweats and fatigue. She had undergone a kidney transplant 5 years ago and was taking tacrolimus and prednisone (2.5 mg daily). A chest magnetic resonance imaging revealed multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules, up to 2.5 cm in diameter. The patient was initially treated empirically for tuberculosis. The serum cryptococcal antigen and Histoplasma immune diffusion tests were negative, and microscopic examination of bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid was negative for fungi. The BAL galactomannan index was 0.3. An open lung biopsy revealed a granulocytic infiltrate, with spherical budding structures suggestive of Histoplasma capsulatum.

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with disseminated histoplasmosis.

Treatment:
The patient received antifungal therapy for the disseminated histoplasmosis. The medical team carefully monitored the patient's response to treatment and the patient was eventually discharged from the hospital.

Follow-Up:
The patient will follow up with her transplant clinic to ensure proper management of her antifungal treatment and overall health. It is important that the patient stays vigilant for any signs of recurrence or other complications following treatment.

Reason for Admission: Fever and Profound Neutropenia

Diagnosis: Metastatic Squamous Cell Carcinoma with Vitamin B6 Deficiency

Hospital Course:

The patient was a 51-year-old woman with relapsed non-Hodgkin lymphoma treated four years earlier with an allogeneic stem cell transplant. She presented with fever and profound neutropenia. A complete blood count showed a normal total leukocyte count with 2% granulocytes together with 84% lymphocytes and 14% monocytes. Red blood cells were normal. The patient had a history of chronic extensive graft-versus-host disease (GvHD) involving the skin and dermal squamous cell carcinoma. Immunosuppression had been discontinued two months earlier due to the development of squamous cell carcinoma. The patient's blood cultures showed a micrococcus species, and her fever resolved with a course of vancomycin.

Histological examination of the patient's marrow demonstrated marked hypocellularity, and biopsy of a cervical lymph node showed poorly differentiated carcinoma consistent with metastatic squamous cell carcinoma. The patient was treated with granulocyte colony stimulating factor (G-CSF) without any improvement in her neutropenia. Following daily supplementation with 150 mg Vitamin B6, blood B6 levels normalized and the neutropenia resolved. The cervical adenopathy completely regressed by clinical examination and became scintographically negative by PET/CT.

The patient's medications were adjusted throughout her hospital course. Valganciclovir, voriconazole, and Soriatane (acitretin) were discontinued, and prophylactic fluconazole and acyclovir were started. The patient was discharged in stable condition.

Instructions at Discharge:

The patient was advised to follow up with her oncologist for continued management of her metastatic squamous cell carcinoma. She was instructed to continue daily Vitamin B6 supplementation, and to avoid exposure to infection. The patient was given a follow-up appointment with her primary care physician in three to four weeks.

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 56-year-old male with a history of dilated cardiomyopathy and atrial fibrillation, presented with epigastralgia and nonsustained VT. The patient was treated with amiodarone, nifekalant hydrochloride, and lidocaine, but the ventricular arrhythmias persisted which led to a decrease in atrial flutter. Severe anemia and blastoid cells were observed in the peripheral blood sample, and the patient was diagnosed with Ph+ ALL. Dasatinib 50 mg twice daily and prednisolone 100 mg daily were initiated to treat the leukemia. The dasatinib was discontinued after five days due to an increase in nonsustained VT although the QTc interval was not significantly prolonged. Bisoprolol was gradually increased to 3.75 mg daily, and dasatinib was rechallenged. The patient showed a complete hematological response and a 2-log reduction in minor bcr-abl mRNA transcripts in the bone marrow. Three weeks after the retreatment with dasatinib, blastoid cells reemerged in the peripheral blood, and the dasatinib was discontinued due to refractoriness of leukemia. The patient received steroid pulse therapy and furosemide, and VT did not recur after. Although, dexamethasone and the short-term use of mercaptopurine were used, the patient expired from leukemia on the 183rd day after admission.

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient was admitted with epigastralgia and nonsustained VT which was treated with amiodarone, nifekalant hydrochloride, and lidocaine. After a diagnosis of Ph+ ALL, the patient was initiated with dasatinib 50 mg twice daily and prednisolone 100 mg daily to manage leukemia. Due to complications, dasatinib and bisoprolol doses were adjusted. After the first retreatment with dasatinib, a complete hematological response was observed and minor bcr-abl mRNA transcripts reduced. The patient expired from leukemia on the 183rd day after admission.

Hospital Course:

An 8-year-old male child was admitted to our hospital with cardiac failure. The patient had a history of TOF repair and left pulmonary arterioplasty two years ago at the referring hospital. Echocardiogram conducted during admission showed the presence of a large residual muscular outlet ventricular septal defect (VSD) likely following VSD patch dehiscence. Cardiac catheterization was performed for further evaluation which confirmed the presence of VSD via angiogram. The right ventricular pressure was high at systole, and angiogram in the main pulmonary artery showed dilated right pulmonary artery while the left pulmonary artery (LPA) was completely occluded.

Intervention:

Radio-frequency (RF) energy was applied to the blind-ending channel of the proximal LPA to recanalize the occluded artery. A 2mm × 10mm coronary balloon was inflated at the atretic segment of LPA and a 6mm × 20mm cutting balloon was used to perform balloon dilatation. A 10mm × 17mm stent was used to address the atretic segment, which was further dilated using an 8mm×40mm Powerflex PTA balloon. The patient was discharged 3 days after the procedure with aspirin at 5mg/kg.

Follow-up:

The patient was readmitted 4 weeks after the procedure for the revision of the VSD patch. Repeat cardiac catheterization conducted three months later shows that the LPA stent is patent and the LPA had increased in size with improved left lung arborization. A localized segment of the left lower lobe artery was stenosed (2.4mm), which was subsequently redilated using an 8mm × 20mm peripheral Flextome cutting balloon.

Outcome:

A Formula 418 Expandable stent was implanted to the stenotic segment distal to the first stent with satisfactory results. The LPA and distal pulmonary arterial tree appear healthy and are of satisfactory size for future growth. Repeat cardiac catheterization conducted four months after the initial intervention showed a reduction of the right ventricular pressure of 41 end-diastolic pressure 8 mmHg (simultaneous aortic pressure: 91/50 mmHg, mean: 66 mmHg).

Conclusion:

The patient was discharged in stable condition with aspirin therapy. The guardian of the patient was instructed to follow-up with their local pediatric cardiologist for routine monitoring and care.
nemotron_simplification:
Hospital Course:
An 8-year-old boy was admitted to the hospital with heart failure.
He had a tetralogy of Fallot repair and left lung artery surgery two years ago at another hospital.
An ultrasound of the heart showed a large hole between the lower chambers.
This hole likely appeared after the patch that covered it came loose.
A heart catheter test with dye confirmed the hole.
It also showed high pressure in the right lower heart chamber when it squeezed.
The dye test in the main lung artery showed the right lung artery was enlarged.
It also showed the left lung artery was completely blocked.
Intervention:
We used radio-frequency energy to open the blocked part of the left lung artery near its start.
A small balloon 2 mm wide and 10 mm long was inflated at the narrowed segment.
A larger balloon 6 mm wide and 20 mm long with a cutting edge was used to widen the artery.
A stent 10 mm wide and 17 mm long was placed to keep the artery open.
The stent was then expanded further using a balloon 8 mm wide and 40 mm long.
The boy left the hospital three days after the procedure and was sent home on aspirin based on his weight.
Follow-up:
Four weeks later the boy returned to the hospital so doctors could fix the patch over the heart hole.
Three months after the procedure a heart catheter test showed the stent in the left lung artery was open.
The test also showed the artery had grown and blood flow to the left lung improved.
A 2.4 mm narrowing in a left lung artery was opened with an 8 mm by 20 mm cutting balloon.
Four months after treatment a heart catheter test showed the pressure in the right lower heart chamber had dropped.
At the same time the aortic pressure was 91 over 50 mmHg with an average of 66 mmHg.
Outcome:
A Formula 418 expandable stent was placed in the narrowed segment just past the first stent and it worked well.
The left lung artery and the lung arteries beyond it look healthy and are the right size for future growth.
Four months after the procedure a heart catheter test showed the pressure in the right lower heart chamber had dropped.
The end-diastolic pressure was 8 mmHg and the aortic pressure was 91 over 50 mmHg (average 66 mmHg).
Conclusion:
The boy left the hospital in stable condition and continued taking aspirin.
His guardian was told to follow up with their local pediatric cardiologist for regular check-ups.

Patient underwent a right parietal craniotomy for evacuation of a subdural hematoma, with good post-operative progress. The patient was then started on unfractionated heparin infusion, given an intravenous bolus of 5000 U and infusion rate of 1000 U/hr with an aPTT goal of 50 to 70 s for 3 days. The patient was admitted to the clinic with a 1 cm round, blackish, ulcerated, and crusted surface lesion on the left upper eyelid that started 5 days ago. Gram(+) bacilli compatible with B. anthracis were observed in Gram staining performed with the wound culture taken from the lesion. The patient had contact with meat bought from a butcher during the regional anthrax endemic period in 2018 and had no direct contact with an infected animal. The patient was started on ciprofloxacin 500 mg every 8 hours and amoxicillin 875 mg + clavulanic acid 125 mg every 12 hours for oral treatment. For topical treatment, chloramphenicol ointment was initiated twice daily. Eyelid edema slightly increased 1 day after the treatment was initiated. A sample was taken from the wound on the second day, and no growth was observed due to antibiotic use. 

On the seventh day of treatment, significant improvement was observed in the lesion, with healing zones seen in the middle of the crust and on the intact skin border. Eyelid edema and redness regressed. The antibiotic treatment was stopped on the 16th day of treatment based on signs of significant improvement in the lesion. All vital signs remained within normal limits throughout the patient's hospital course. 

Discharge Instructions:
The patient was discharged with instructions to follow up with their primary care physician and to continue applying chloramphenicol ointment twice daily on the healed area of the lesion, as directed. The patient was also instructed to practice good hand hygiene and to avoid contact with animals or contaminated products. In case of any additional symptoms or concerns, the patient was advised to contact their healthcare provider.

The initial incision wound did not heal properly and was later reopened after one month. Despite receiving treatment off and on with multiple injectable and oral antibiotics, there was no definitive microbiological diagnosis prior to admission. The patient did not have any history of local trauma/injury, immunosuppressive drugs/corticosteroids, or tuberculosis.

On admission, a previous surgical scar was noticed on the lower anterior abdominal wall in the midline with a large keloid formed over it. Six sinus openings were noted over the lower anterior abdominal wall with a single sinus discharging pus at the time of presentation. Tenderness was noted over and around the sinuses. Gram variable bacilli and numerous acid-fast bacilli were observed in the discharge. Following culture and antibiotic susceptibility testing, the patient was started on a combination of rifampicin, ethambutol, and clarithromycin.

After one month of therapy, there was no pus discharge from the sinus. The patient was advised to continue the therapy and report back to the hospital after another month. After two months of therapy, the patient was found to be completely all right with no such discharge.

Discharge Medications:

The patient was advised to continue taking rifampicin 600 mg once daily, ethambutol 600 mg once daily, and clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily.

Follow-Up:

The patient was advised to continue with periodic follow-up based upon clinical response and microbiological response.

Patient Name: N/A

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to the accident and emergency department with complaints of pain and reduced range of movement in her left shoulder caused by a minimally displaced and impacted fracture of her proximal humerus. She was examined and sent home to attend the next available fracture clinic with a collar and cuff. Upon review in the following fracture clinic, she was diagnosed with thrombophlebitis of her external jugular vein and was prescribed an antibiotic (flucloxacillin 500mg) for five days and placed in a better fitting sling. As the patient was only on holiday in the region, further follow-up was arranged for two weeks in her local hospital. Two days later, the patient returned to the accident and emergency department with pain and gross pitting oedema in her left arm. A Doppler scan demonstrated near complete occlusion of the left subclavian and axillary veins, consistent with a deep vein thrombosis. The patient was started on warfarin and treatment dose enoxaparin (1mg/kg) to be taken once a day until her INR was therapeutic. She was then anticoagulated for 3 months.

Diagnosis:
Left shoulder minimally displaced and impacted fracture, thrombophlebitis of external jugular vein, deep vein thrombosis

Medical History:
The patient had a history of hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and underwent thyroidectomy in 2000 for hyperthyroidism. There was no known history of drug allergies.

Treatment:
The patient was placed in a collar and cuff and later a better fitting sling for nonsurgical management of her left shoulder fracture. She was prescribed antibiotics for five days and anticoagulants for 3 months to manage her thrombophlebitis of external jugular vein and deep vein thrombosis.

Follow-up Care:
The patient made a full recovery and has had no further episodes of thrombosis so far.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 44
Gender: Female
Chief Complaint: Painful oral ulcer

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with a painful oral ulcer, which had developed 6 weeks prior. She had a history of aphthous stomatitis and received systemic steroid treatment. However, her condition worsened with an erythematous maculopapular rash on her body, conjunctival injection, fever, diarrhea, and weight loss. Leukocytosis and eosinophilia were noted. Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) was suspected, and she was treated with systemic steroids, which showed slight improvement in skin condition but unresponsiveness in stomatitis.
A skin biopsy showed interface dermatitis and subepidermal blister formation with basal vacuolization consistent with PNP. Additional tests showed IgG deposition on normal human skin, mouse bladder epithelium, and mouse lung epithelium. The patient was ultimately diagnosed with stage IV follicular lymphoma with BO and invasive pulmonary aspergillosis. 
Chemotherapy resulted in a complete remission of lymphoma, which was confirmed through positron emission tomography. The patient's stomatitis and skin rash were well-maintained with a low-dose steroid therapy of 5mg/day for 8 months. However, she developed BO and invasive pulmonary aspergillosis, which led to respiratory failure. 

Course of Treatment:
Treatment included chemotherapy with rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisolone, which resulted in complete remission of the patient's lymphoma. The patient was also treated with a low-dose steroid therapy of 5mg/day, which maintained the improvement of stomatitis and skin rash. 

Follow-Up Care:
No specific follow-up care is necessary since the patient passed away from respiratory failure. 

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with PNP, which was later associated with stage IV follicular lymphoma with BO and invasive pulmonary aspergillosis.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 53-year-old male, professional chef

Admission Date: January 2017

Discharge Date: N/A

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 53-year-old male professional chef, was admitted due to a severe exacerbation of atopic dermatitis (AD) with involvement of the face, neckline, trunk, and forearms. The patient's medical history was positive for allergic rhino-conjunctivitis and the allergological work-up found the patient to be positive for pollens, foods, and latex. The patient was prescribed oral steroids and anti-histamines, but these did not result in any improvement. Additionally, the patient experienced episodes of diarrhea and frequent severe exacerbations due to exposure to cooking vapors.

The patient followed a pseudo-allergen-free diet and exclusion of grains and tomatoes for six months. A three-day treatment with 6-methyl prednisolone i.v. was administered, which was progressively tapered over the course of three weeks. However, a rapid relapse of the skin legions and severe pruritus was observed.

Treatment with Cyclosporine A (CoA) was started but after three months, the patient saw no significant improvement. An off-label treatment with Omalizumab was proposed and initiated, resulting in clinical improvement after just about two months of treatment as confirmed by a SCORAD of 1 and a clear improvement of quality of life. After one year of Omalizumab treatment, the patient maintains good control for both skin and gastrointestinal symptoms.

Discharge Recommendations:

The patient is advised to implement strict environmental, hygiene, and diet restrictions based on the test results. The patient is discharged from the hospital and may return to work as a chef without complications and eat grains again with no gastrointestinal problems or relapse of dermatitis. The patient should continue reducing steroid doses in anticipation of complete suspension and continue taking CoA at a maintenance dose of 1 mg/kg/day. Follow-up appointments should be scheduled as needed to monitor the patient's condition.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 36-year-old prisoner

Diagnosis: Candida lung abscess

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to our hospital due to fever, asthenia, cough, and hemoptysis, which did not respond to antibiotic therapy. It was revealed that the patient had a history of smoking crack cocaine, injecting heroin, and untreated liver disease related to HCV. Laboratory tests indicated an increase in white blood cell count and inflammation. Further, a 7 cm round and excavated lesion was also detected in the right lower lobe of the lungs. The patient was diagnosed with a Candida lung abscess and started on intravenous fluconazole 400 mg daily followed by its oral formulation, leading to clinical recovery. In addition to the treatment, the patient was monitored under our hepatological unit, and DAAs were prescribed.

Course of Treatment:
The patient was treated with intravenous fluconazole 400 mg followed by an oral formulation until complete clinical recovery and was later discharged. The patient was given an appointment to be followed up with our hepatological unit and to perform the treatment with DAAs. After three months of therapy with sofosbuvir 400 mg/velpatasvir 100 mg once daily, the sustained virological response (SVR) was reached and it’s still active.

Follow-up Care:
The patient was given an appointment to be followed up with our hepatological unit to ensure the continued management of the HCV-related liver disease. The patient was also advised to maintain healthy habits and refrain from drug consumption.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 45 years
Sex: Female
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]
Length of Stay: 7 days

Admitting Diagnosis:
Undifferentiated Spindle Cell Sarcoma Involving the Pancreas

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital urgently due to the acute onset of severe abdominal pain and collapse. Upon examination, she was found to be in class III haemorrhagic shock with distended and diffusely tender abdomen. She was immediately resuscitated with blood transfusions and intravenous crystalloid boluses. Hematological and basic investigations revealed haemoglobin level of 5g/dl and moderate amount of free fluid with mass around the proximal part of the pancreas, respectively. Following which, an emergency exploratory laparotomy was performed, and the source of bleeding was identified as the nidus, which was situated posterior to the body of the pancreas and had ruptured through the inferior border of the pancreas. The histopathological analysis of the biopsy revealed an infiltrating tumour composed of fascicles of spindle cells with oval, vesicular nuclei with scanty eosinophilic cytoplasm that was diagnosed as undifferentiated spindle cell sarcoma, and the tumour was surgically excised.

Treatment:
The patient was managed in the intensive care unit for 4 days and received a course of Ifosfamide and Doxorubicin for 6 months as adjuvant chemotherapy. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography was performed before the commencement of chemotherapy, which showed a 7 × 4.8 × 4.9 cm mass lesion with a thin wall containing hypodense material, attached to the inferior border of the pancreas. There were no other metastatic lesions identified.

Outcome:
The patient recovered following surgery and was discharged 7 days after admission. She was referred to the oncologist and offered a pancreatectomy with excision of the tumour, which was refused. The patient received six months of chemotherapy and finally succumbed to the disease 18 months after the presentation.

Summary:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with undifferentiated spindle cell sarcoma involving the pancreas that was treated with surgery and adjuvant chemotherapy. The patient was discharged following a 7-day hospitalization but eventually succumbed to the disease after 18 months.

The patient, a 46-year-old male, with a history of mild depressive episode treated with medication, was admitted to the isolated COVID-19 ward with symptoms of COVID-19 infection, including cough, fever, sore throat, and fatigue. The patient's Electrocardiogram (ECG) was monitored regularly, and the QT interval was normal to prolonged (corrected QT max: 490ms). On the ninth day of treatment, the patient developed symptoms of distress and insomnia.

On the evening of the same day, the patient showed abrupt onset of psychotic symptoms such as visual hallucinations and incoherent speech, with the outburst of odd behavior and repeated attempts to run away from hospital. The patient's insight was preserved. The cerebral CT scan was normal. Standard laboratory tests were performed and revealed normal results.

Interventions:
COVID-19 medication protocol along with the pre-existing medication vortioxetine was discontinued. Amilsulpride was initiated at a dose of 100 mg per day. Psychotic symptoms disappeared totally after 48 hours. Amilsulpride was tapered off and then stopped within a week.

Follow-up:
The patient remained asymptomatic, and the case was monitored once every two weeks. On the latest psychiatric assessment (May 20), the patient showed no psychotic symptoms.

Impression:
The patient developed psychotic symptoms after nine days of COVID-19 treatment. Clinical diagnosis suggests drug-induced psychosis. The patient responded well to the discontinuation of medication and treatment with amilsulpride. There were no further symptoms observed, and on the latest psychiatric assessment (May 20), the patient showed no psychotic symptoms.

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Medical Record Number: [Redacted]
Date of Admission: 22 July 2013
Date of Discharge: [Redacted]

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 14-year-old female, was admitted to our center due to recurrent palpitation and tremor. She was diagnosed with hyperthyroidism in another hospital, for which she had been prescribed methimazole primarily followed by propylthiouracil. Her thyroid function remained abnormal over the subsequent three years. All antithyroid drugs were discontinued for five months prior to her admission to our center.

Physical examination on admission revealed an increased heart rate, accentuation of the first heart sound, and tremor. Thyroid enlargement without any discernible nodule was also observed. Diagnostic workup included thyroid function testing, measurements of TSH receptor antibody (TRAb), a small dose of 131iodine and a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan that revealed a slightly enlarged pituitary gland not occupied by a lesion. A FT3 concentration exceeding the normal range, along with an elevated FT4 concentration, and suppressed TSH concentration were noted during both thyroid function tests. Elevated TRAb levels were also detected. A point mutation in the TR β gene was identified in the patient and her father, indicating THR syndrome.

The patient's case was complicated by Graves' disease, and propranolol and methimazole were prescribed for treatment. The patient was discharged in stable condition and has since been followed up regularly. 

Discharge Diagnoses: 
- Toxic multinodular goiter complicated by Graves' disease

Discharge Medications: 
- Methimazole 30 mg/day
- Propranolol 60 mg/day

Follow-Up Plans:
The patient is advised to continue taking prescribed medications and attend regular follow-up appointments.

Repeat MRA and BPAS-MRI showed the narrowing had lessened a little compared to the first test. The patient's headache went away by the eighth day in the hospital, and he was discharged without problems.

Discharge Summary:

This is a summary of admission details for a 20-year-old female with a medical history of post-traumatic stress syndrome and facial acne. The patient was admitted to the emergency department after ingesting seven pills of paroxetine.

Course of Hospitalization:

Initial evaluation in the emergency department yielded minimal symptoms, stable vital signs, and no arrhythmia on ECG. The patient was observed for six hours and complained of flushing and became agitated. The patient sustained witnessed spontaneous aborted tonic clinic seizure activity of 90 seconds. She exhibited tachycardia, tachypnea, hypertension, and hyperreflexia. Blood workup, CT of the head without contrast, urine drug screen, and ethanol level were normal. ECG showed a prolonged corrected QT interval of >540. SS was suspected, and the patient was given IV fluids and lorazepam. Cyproheptadine was given 12 mg orally as a single dose and 4 mg every eight hours as needed. The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit for close monitoring with serial ECG. QT interval normalization was observed 16 hours later, and no visual seizures were noted during hospitalization.

Discharge Diagnosis:

Suspected serotonin syndrome 

Treatment:

The patient was given IV fluids and lorazepam. Cyproheptadine was given 12 mg orally as a single dose and 4 mg every eight hours as needed.

Follow-up:

The patient was discharged in stable condition.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]
Admitting Diagnosis: Purpuric rash, fever, shortness of breath

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 10-year-old Caucasian girl, was admitted with complaints of progressively worsening rash, fever, and shortness of breath. Prior to admission, she had a normal complete blood count, electrolyte panel, liver function tests, urinalysis, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). C-reactive protein (CRP) was 1.2 mg/dL, serum IgA 310 mg/dL, and anti-streptolysin O (ASO) titer was elevated. The patient was suspected to have HSP. On admission, she had a purpuric rash on her upper and lower extremities, buttocks, and back. She also presented with oxygen desaturation, shortness of breath, and a dry cough. Her hemoglobin had decreased, and a chest radiograph showed patchy bibasilar opacities. The patient was started on intravenous ampicillin and azithromycin. However, shortly after admission, the patient developed worsening respiratory distress, grunting, and worsening chest imaging. The patient was found to have severe SVV and vasculitis and was started on intravenous methylprednisolone and gammaglobulin. Echocardiogram showed mitral regurgitation, and the patient was started on intravenous furosemide, milrinone, and intravenous epinephrine. After five days of mechanical ventilation, the patient steadily improved and was extubated. The patient continued treatment with oral prednisone taper and enalapril and was discharged after completing 10 days of intravenous ceftriaxone and 7 days of intravenous azithromycin.

Summary of Events:
The patient was admitted with symptoms of rash, fever, and shortness of breath. The medical team suspected HSP, but further analysis revealed severe SVV and vasculitis. The patient was started on intravenous methylprednisolone and gammaglobulin. Treatment with intravenous furosemide, milrinone, and intravenous epinephrine was initiated to treat the patient's worsening respiratory distress, while oral prednisone taper and enalapril were used for afterload reduction. After mechanical ventilation, the patient steadily improved and was discharged with a moderately dilated left atrium, moderate mitral regurgitation, and mild mitral valve prolapse. Follow-up echocardiogram indicated mild to moderate mitral regurgitation.

Hospital Course:
The patient, an 80-year-old non-smoker woman with a history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus was admitted to the Emergency Department with a one-week history of dry cough and high fever. The chest computed tomography showed bilateral peripheral ground-glass opacities, and the real-time reverse transcriptase-polymerase chain reaction test for severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) returned positive.

Treatment and Response:
The patient was started on supplemental oxygen, favipiravir, and dexamethasone. Three days later, she was admitted to the ICU due to respiratory failure and was put on mechanical ventilation. She continued to receive dexamethasone and was also given antibiotics and remdesivir. The respiratory condition and chest infiltration improved, and she was extubated after seven days of mechanical ventilation. Dexamethasone was later discontinued after 10 days.

Relapse and Co-infection:
The patient developed a fever and quickly progressive hypoxaemia two days after the extubation and was reintubated. Cultures and laboratory tests were performed with no evidence of co-infection. She was then given dexamethasone again with a subsequent improvement in the chest shadows and was tapered weekly. However, her chest shadows worsened again, and her serum β-d-glucan was found to be elevated. She was given antifungal treatment, and the CMV antigenemia assay was elevated. Ganciclovir was immediately initiated, but the patient died four days after the positive CMV antigenemia test result.

Autopsy:
A needle autopsy was performed approximately 3 h after her death, and CMV-infected cells were found. This confirmed the diagnosis of CMV pneumonia as the cause of her respiratory failure and bilateral chest infiltrations.

Follow-up:
The patient's family was informed about her condition and treatment. The discharge summary along with instructions for follow-up care, including any medication changes, and any scheduled appointments were explained to the family.

Condition:
The patient's condition had initially improved but worsened due to CMV pneumonia, leading to her death.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Chief Complaint:
The patient presented to the department of Oral Medicine and Oral Surgery for the removal of fibrous hyperplasia in the mandibular vestibule caused by ill-fitting prostheses resulting in epulis fissuratum and vestibular deepening.

Hospital Course Summary:
During the extra-oral examination, a decrease in the vertical dimension of occlusion was noted. Intra-oral examination revealed hyperplastic mandibular lesion of the anterior alveolar mucosa, extending to the vestibular sulcus. Topical mouthwashes with Fungizone and chlorhexidine were prescribed to treat denture-induced hyperplasia and prosthetic candidiasis. After 3 weeks, no symptomatology was noted. Surgical resection combined with gingival graft was carried out to excise fibrous hyperplasia. The resultant lower boundary of the incision was sutured in position. Free gingival graft was carried out from the palate. The final total prosthesis was delivered to the patient 2 months later resulting in perfect integration of the prosthetic volume.

Findings:
The anatomopathological examination confirmed the clinical diagnosis of epulis fissuratum. Favorable postoperative healing was observed 2 weeks later during the removal of sutures.

Treatment:
Topical mouthwashes with Fungizone and chlorhexidine were prescribed to treat denture-induced hyperplasia and prosthetic candidiasis. Antibiotics and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs were administered for 5 days. Chlorhexidine mouth rinse was prescribed twice a day for 2 weeks. The patient was asked to have a soft diet, limited facial movement for 14 days, no brushing around the surgical site for 3 days after the procedure, and to place an ice pack on the lower lip.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient should continue to follow the prescribed soft diet, use chlorhexidine mouth rinse twice a day, and avoid brushing around the surgical site for 3 days after the procedure. The patient should also place an ice pack on the lower lip as needed. In case of discomfort, the patient is advised to contact the hospital. 

Follow-Up:
The patient should have regular follow-up sessions with the oral medicine and oral surgery department to ensure there is no recurrence of the fibrous hyperplasia and that the total prosthesis remains stable and well-extended. 

Signed, 
[REDACTED]
Oral Surgeon
