Hospital Course:
This 7-month-old boy was admitted to our hospital for treatment of respiratory syncytial viral pneumonia, with a history of tracheoesophageal fistula and esophageal atresia surgery performed at 1 day of age. The patient showed recurrent cough and sputum, and was afebrile. The chest radiograph showed increased peribronchial infiltration and air bronchogram. Due to the risk of aspiration pneumonia, oral feeding was discontinued and the patient was given parenteral nutrition via the peripheral venous route.

Extravasation Event:
On day 6 of admission, while the patient was receiving total parenteral nutrition, a 24-gauge intravenous catheter was newly inserted into the dorsal cephalic vein at the dorsum of the patient's right hand. The patient showed signs of irritability, and the obstruction alarm of the infusion pump was triggered. Without any alarm sign, approximately 9 hours after the repositioning of the intravenous catheter, the patient's right hand and arm appeared severely swollen, and capillary refill was absent. There were several blisters observed under the catheter, and an emergency fasciotomy was performed under the suspicion of compartment syndrome.

Treatment and Care:
The patient received orthopedic surgery and fascia suturing, followed by irrigation of the area several times with saline solution. Delayed primary skin closure was performed 8 days after the fasciotomy. A skin graft was scheduled for treatment of the skin necrosis after debriding the necrotic tissue with a moist dressing. Rehabilitation treatment consisting of wrist articulation exercises was started due to the high chance of wrist joint contracture. Skin graft surgery was delayed due to pneumonia, which was diagnosed during the patient's regular wound dressing and rehabilitation treatment. It was performed 4 months after the extravasation event. At the time of this report, skin engraftment had been successfully completed, and the patient was receiving continued rehabilitation treatment.
nemotron_simplification:
Hospital Course: The patient is a 7-month-old boy admitted for RSV pneumonia. He has a history of tracheoesophageal fistula and esophageal atresia repaired at one day old. He had recurrent cough and sputum but no fever during his hospital stay for observation. The chest X-ray showed increased peribronchial infiltration and an air bronchogram, indicating lung inflammation and airway obstruction. Because of the risk of aspiration pneumonia, oral feeding was stopped to prevent food from entering his lungs. He received parenteral nutrition through a vein in his arm to provide calories and nutrients while he could not eat.
Extravasation Event: On day six, a 24-gauge IV catheter was placed in the vein on the back of his right hand. He was receiving total parenteral nutrition at the time to give him calories and nutrients while he could not eat. He became irritable and the infusion pump alarm sounded due to obstruction, indicating a problem with the IV line. About nine hours after the catheter was repositioned, his right hand and arm became swollen and capillary refill was absent. Several blisters were seen under the catheter, signs of tissue damage from the leaking fluid. An emergency fasciotomy was performed because doctors suspected compartment syndrome to relieve pressure and prevent muscle injury.
Treatment and Care: He had orthopedic surgery to repair the fascia and the area was washed several times with saline. Eight days later, the skin was closed loosely in a delayed primary closure to allow healing before grafting. Dead tissue was removed with a wet dressing, and a skin graft was planned to cover the wound. Wrist exercises were started to prevent stiffness because joint contracture was likely during his recovery period. The skin graft was delayed because he developed pneumonia during wound care and rehabilitation that required treatment. Four months after the extravasation injury, the skin graft surgery was performed to replace the damaged skin. At this time, the graft has taken successfully and he continues rehabilitation to improve hand function and strength.

Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Admitting Diagnosis: Achalasia

Hospital Course:

The patient was a 29-year-old female with a history of mild progressive dysphagia who presented with severe dysphagia. The patient had been diagnosed with achalasia three years ago but refused any treatment options. She was given ferrous sulfate capsules for iron therapy by her general practitioner about a month earlier, which led to the development of severe dysphagia after three weeks. She was referred to a gastroenterologist for further evaluation.

On admission, the patient had no odynophagia, nausea, or vomiting. Physical examination was unremarkable.

A barium swallow esophagography showed a dilated esophagus with a bird's beak appearance of the lower esophageal sphincter and a filling defect in the distal part of the esophagus. An EGD revealed a dilated esophagus and an elliptical-shaped, black-colored bezoar in the distal part of the esophagus. There were no ulcers or erosions in the esophagus. The lower esophageal sphincter was severely spastic.

Attempts were made to fragment and push the bezoar into the stomach, but it was discontinued due to high LES pressure and resistance and the risk of aspiration. Finally, the bezoar was retrieved with a basket.

An esophageal manometer was carried out and the results were compatible with the diagnosis of achalasia. In the next endoscopic session, achalasia balloon dilation (size 30 mm) was successfully applied.

The patient was asymptomatic during the 3-year follow-up.

Discharge Condition:

The patient's condition improved after treatment with achalasia balloon dilation. The patient was discharged in good condition and was advised to follow up with her gastroenterologist as scheduled.

Discharge Medications:

N/A

Follow-up:

The patient was advised to follow up with her gastroenterologist as scheduled.

Hospital Course:

The patient presented with necrosis of the right first and second toes and a soft tissue defect on the plantar forefoot after suffering a crushing injury in a traffic accident.

Medical Management:

The necrotized toes were amputated from the metatarsophalangeal joint and the recipient sites were prepared by debridement. To reconstruct the affected area, a medial plantar sensory free flap was elevated on the contralateral side of the plantar region, and the medial plantar artery was anastomosed to the dorsal pedis artery of the recipient site. Furthermore, two venae comitantes were anastomosed end-to-end to the great saphenous vein and the vena comitante of the dorsalis pedis artery. The medial plantar nerve innervating the flap was anastomosed to the deep peroneal nerve of the recipient site. A full-thickness skin graft was performed at the donor sites.

The patient recovered without any complications and was discharged home in stable condition. It is recommended that he receives follow-up care to ensure proper wound healing and mobility rehabilitation.

Follow-up Care:

It is recommended that the patient schedule a follow-up appointment with his healthcare provider to monitor his progress and to address any concerns, if any. The patient should continue to take any prescribed medication as directed and avoid placing excessive pressure on the affected foot. It is also advised that the patient follow up with a physical therapist to improve his gait and regain mobility.

Discharge Diagnosis:

Necrosis of the right first and second toes after a crushing injury and a plantar forefoot soft tissue defect.

Discharged home in stable condition.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Identification:
Patient Name: Not Provided
Gender: Female
Age: 7 years
Medical Record Number: Not Provided

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with various clinical symptoms including lethargy, muscle weakness, skin issues, abdominal distension, polyuria, and polydipsia. Blood work and urinalysis showed increased blood glucose levels, hypercholesterolemia, and glycosuria. After the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus was confirmed, the patient was treated with insulin glargine and a commercial diet for diabetic cats. The insulin dosage was adjusted, and the patient showed considerable improvement in clinical symptoms. An abdominal ultrasound revealed bilateral adrenal hyperplasia and hepatic steatosis. Further tests ruled out spontaneous hypersomatotropism, hyperthyroidism, and feline immunodeficiency virus and feline leukemia virus. However, spontaneous hyperadrenocorticism (HAC) was suspected and diagnosed based on clinical signs, increased urinary cortisol:creatinine ratio, and lack of suppression on the low-dose dexamethasone suppression test. A dosage of cabergoline was prescribed to address the HAC. After the second dose, the patient experienced clinical hypoglycemia that required emergency veterinary assistance. The symptoms of hypoglycemia were managed via appropriate treatment, and the patient was kept under medical observation for several hours. Following successful treatment and management of clinical symptoms, the patient was discharged.

Diagnosis:
1. Diabetes Mellitus
2. Spontaneous Hyperadrenocorticism (HAC)

Treatment:
1. Insulin glargine
2. Commercial diet for diabetic cats
3. Cabergoline

Condition at Discharge:
The patient had stable blood glucose levels and no clinical signs of diabetes mellitus or hypoglycemia. The HAC was treated with cabergoline and patient symptoms showed marked improvement. However, the patient experienced acute decompensation after seven months, and euthanasia was carried out upon the owner's request. 

Recommendations:
None provided due to the patient's clinical outcome.

Blood tests and urine showed high blood sugar, high cholesterol, and sugar in the urine.
After diabetes was confirmed, the patient was given insulin glargine and a special diet for diabetic cats.
The insulin dose was adjusted and the patient showed considerable improvement in clinical symptoms over the next few days.
An ultrasound showed enlarged adrenal glands and fatty liver, indicating possible adrenal overactivity and liver fat.
Other tests ruled out excess growth hormone, overactive thyroid, and feline immunodeficiency and leukemia viruses.
Spontaneous hyperadrenocorticism was suspected and diagnosed based on signs, high urine cortisol, and no suppression on a low-dose dexamethasone test.
Cabergoline was prescribed to treat the hyperadrenocorticism and manage cortisol levels, with dosing adjusted as needed.
After the second dose, the patient had low blood sugar that needed emergency vet help.
The low blood sugar was treated and the patient was watched for several hours to ensure stability.
After treatment and observation, the patient was discharged with stable blood sugar and no immediate symptoms.
Diagnosis:
1. Diabetes Mellitus
2. Spontaneous Hyperadrenocorticism (HAC)
Treatment:
1. Insulin glargine
2. Commercial diet for diabetic cats
3. Cabergoline
Condition at Discharge:
The patient had stable blood sugar and no signs of diabetes or low blood sugar.
The hyperadrenocorticism was treated with cabergoline and symptoms improved, showing better health and reduced signs.
However, the patient worsened after seven months and euthanasia was done at the owner's request.
Recommendations:
No recommendations were provided because the patient's clinical outcome was euthanasia at the owner's request.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: II-13

Date of Admission: November 2018

Date of Discharge: N/A

Hospital Course: 

This discharge summary outlines the case of a 47-year-old Vietnamese woman, who was diagnosed with left breast cancer in November 2018. The patient's diagnostic process involved an x-ray analysis, pathology interpretation, and breast ultrasound. The patient detected a lump in her left breast by herself and underwent a lumpectomy in a private clinic. Post-surgery, the patient had a total removal of the breast with revision PATEY protocol and was treated with adjuvant chemotherapy, including paclitaxel and trastuzumab. Hereditary cancer-predisposing syndrome was suspected in the patient's family after it was found that cancer was present in several family members across different generations.

Findings: 

The patient's pathological features were consistent with invasive carcinoma with the molecular subtype HER2. Postoperative stage was pT1cN0Mx, and no malignancy was found in the 20 lymph nodes removed during surgery. Immunohistochemical stains revealed estrogen receptor (ER) and progesterone receptor (PR) negative, Her2/neu positive 3 plus, and Ki67 index 75%.

Family History:

The patient's mother died of an unknown cause while her father remained healthy. Among nine siblings, two older brothers died of unknown cancers. Her younger sister was diagnosed with left breast cancer in March 2015, and her daughter had left breast cancer at the age of 22 years. Moreover, a genetic factor related to breast cancer was hypothesized, leading to a screening mutation test with her blood by applying targeted next-generation sequencing. Her blood showed a novel mutation of BRCA1 gene while the BRCA2 gene was not mutated. 

Conclusion:

The screening test detected that the patient inherited a mutant allele from her father. Both the patient's daughter and several siblings had the same mutation of BRCA1 gene, including one of the children of the deceased brothers. The BRCA1 gene mutation was identified as a novel heterogenous genetic mutation, named NM_007294.3 (BRCA1): c.4998insA (p. Tyr1666Terfs), according to ClinVar Database of the US National Institutes of Health. The sequencing output was verified via Sanger sequencing and gave the same result.

Recommendations:

The patient's clinical features and family medical history indicate that there may be a hereditary risk for cancer within her family. The discharge summary recommendation is to follow up with the patient and her family members to discuss genetic counseling and determine the best plan of action for future screenings or other medical interventions.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 5-year-old Chinese woman, presented to the emergency department with complaints of cough, fever, headache, vomiting, and altered interactions with her parents. She was admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit and diagnosed with sepsis and pneumonia. Empiric antibiotic therapy, immunoglobulin supply, and restricted fluid administration were given. The patient's condition deteriorated, and she became comatose, hypotensive, and suffered from arrhythmia and hypoxia. Electrocardiogram confirmed prolonged Q–T interval while the thyroid test results were received, indicating untreated hypothyroidism secondary to autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto's thyroiditis). Hormone replacement was immediately started, and the patient was administered levothyroxine via nasogastric tube. She also received vasopressor, mechanical ventilation, and continuous renal replacement treatment. Two days after starting levothyroxine, her consciousness was restored, and temperature returned to normal. She was extubated on the fifth day after the initial hormone administration. The dosage of oral levothyroxine was reduced, and she was discharged on a regimen of 3 μg/kg/d once daily.

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Hospital Course: 

The patient, a 45-year-old male, was admitted to the hospital with symptoms of left flank pain, hypoesthesia, and weakness at both lower extremities. Upon examination, the patient had motor weakness in both lower extremities and elevated deep tendon reflex of the right knee. Diagnostic tests indicated fracture of T8, T9 vertebral body by bone tumor, pathologic fracture of T9 vertebral body by bone tumor, T8–10 myelopathy, and cord compression.

The patient underwent T9 corpectomy and mesh cage insertion with T8–10 posterior screw fixation. Pathological examination confirmed a diagnosis of Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH). The patient underwent radiotherapy at T8–10 spine and showed remarkable improvement in motor weaknesses and hypoesthesia.

The patient has been followed for almost 6 years without any recurrence. Discharge instructions included follow-up care with the primary care physician and regular imaging surveillance to ensure no recurrence of the bone tumor. 

Overall, the patient received excellent medical care from the healthcare team and responded well to treatment.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS: Giant cell variant of GBM

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient, a 51-year-old woman, was admitted with complaints of headache, vomiting, and gait ataxia of 1 month duration. She also noted diminution of her vision during the course of illness. The patient was evaluated and found to have 6/36 visual acuity and mild papilledema bilaterally. Her gait was ataxic in nature and had positive cerebellar signs. Magnetic resonance imaging scan showed a left cerebellar intra-axial mass lesion near cerebellopontine angle with T1-weighted hypointensity and T2-weighted hyperintensity with mild perifocal edema and mass effect. On contrast study, the lesion was enhancing homogeneously with area of unenhanced cystic component in it. Magnetic resonance (MR) spectroscopy showed choline peak with reduced N-acetyl aspartate (NAA) and choline: NAA ratio of 5.74. Lactate peak was also observed at some places. Metastatic tumor, malignant lymphoma, and GBM were considered for radiological differential diagnosis. Workups for common metastatic lesions from breast, lung, colon, and secondary central nervous system lymphoma were found to be negative.

Through a left retromastoid suboccipital craniectomy, a greyish-pink, soft, non-capsulated, vascular tumor in the left cerebellar hemisphere was excised in piecemeal near totally. The diagnosis of giant cell variant of GBM was made on the histopathological section. The patient was referred for radiotherapy. At follow up after 2 months, the patient has been doing well without any cranial nerve deficit.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
1. Follow-up with your primary physician for any further evaluation.
2. Continue to take medications as prescribed.
3. Do not hesitate to contact your physician if any new symptoms appear.
4. Take care of your health.
5. Follow a healthy lifestyle and diet.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: Confidential
Medical Record Number: Confidential
Date of Admission: Confidential
Date of Discharge: Confidential

Hospital Course:
The patient is an 82-year-old female who was admitted to the hospital as an emergency with gross abdominal distension and lower abdominal pain. She had a six-week history of nonspecific malaise, loss of appetite, and dizziness, along with a longstanding history of constipation. Her past medical history included hypertension and impaired glucose tolerance, while her past surgical history included a previous caesarean section.

On examination, the patient had a nontender, grossly distended abdomen with an indentable mass in the lower left quadrant. Blood tests revealed acute renal failure and microcytic anaemia. A CT scan revealed massive dilatation of the sigmoid colon with faecal material within, resulting in bilateral renal tract obstruction. Following a clinical decision, she underwent a laparotomy, during which she was found to have massive colonic dilatation of the sigmoid and descending colon, with dense perirectal fibrosis throughout the length of the rectum. The rectum was resected at the mid rectum, and a Hartman's procedure was performed. Her renal function normalised, and she made an uneventful recovery. 

On histology from the resected specimen, it was observed that the longitudinal muscle layer was degenerate and absent in many areas of the specimen. The myenteric and submucosal plexuses were degenerate where longitudinal muscle was absent, while polyglucosan inclusion bodies were present throughout the longitudinal and circular layers of the muscularis propria, with almost total degeneration of the longitudinal layer, suggesting a myopathic process. The occurrence of longitudinal loss was in areas where the overlying muscle and mucosa were intact indicating that this was likely to be a primary myopathy. There was also a replacement of myocytes in both muscularis layers with elastosis and fibrosis, along with additional areas of elastosis in the submucosa and widespread smooth muscle metaplasia.

Discharge Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with acute renal failure and massive colonic dilatation of the sigmoid and descending colon, with dense perirectal fibrosis throughout the length of the rectum. Histology from the resected specimen revealed a primary myopathy with elastosis and fibrosis.

Follow-Up Care:
The patient is advised to follow a healthy diet and exercise regimen and to attend regular follow-up appointments with the healthcare provider. She is also advised to take appropriate measures to prevent constipation, such as increasing fibre intake and staying hydrated.

Discharge Medications:
None.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient is advised to avoid strenuous physical activity and to take adequate rest for at least two weeks following the surgery. She is also advised to attend regular follow-up appointments with the healthcare provider to monitor her renal and colonic function and to ensure that her postoperative recovery is proceeding smoothly. In case of any unwanted side effects or complications, the patient is advised to immediately contact the healthcare provider.

This surgery created a new opening for stool to exit the body, so waste could leave safely.
After the operation, her kidney function returned to normal and she recovered without problems over the following days.

The patient was found to have sudden kidney failure and a greatly swollen sigmoid and descending colon.
There was thick scar tissue all around the rectum that made the rectal area stiff.

Lumbar puncture was performed, which showed an increased opening pressure, elevated white blood cell count, elevated protein level, and decreased glucose level. Next-generation sequencing of the cerebrospinal fluid identified T. solium DNA sequences. Serum and CSF were positive for C. cellulosae IgG antibodies. The patient was diagnosed with basal subarachnoid NCC and was treated with albendazole, dexamethasone, and ETV. Significant improvement was observed in the patient's symptoms and CSF findings after treatment.

Basal subarachnoid NCC.

Albendazole, Dexamethasone, and ETV were administered.

Hospital Course Summary:

Patient Information:
34-year-old male with an injury to the right hand sustained while grinding sugarcane pulp. Presented within 3 hours of injury.

Clinical Findings:
Injury involved four fingers of the non-dominant hand, with macerations along the margins of the skin. There were longitudinal lacerations over the fingers, both on the dorsal and volar sides, with the extensor expansion having vertical slits running along its length till the metacarpophalangeal joints. The proximal interphalangeal joints were exposed with the avulsion of the central slips and loss of continuity of the covering capsules, whereas, the flexor tendons were in continuity with loss of the flexor tendon sheath in the region of the volar skin laceration. Two of the three patients suffered from bone continuity loss.

Treatment:
Wounds were washed and covered with sterile dressings, with broad-spectrum antibiotics being initiated. Within the operation room, wound debridement and lavage with 6 liters of normal saline were carried out under regional block. The vertical midline slits in the extensor expansion were stitched using interrupted 4-0 nylon sutures. The skin was approximated over tendons to provide them with a biological coverage using sutures i.e. nylon 3-0.

Two of these patients required split thickness skin grafting over the dorsum of hand, which was undertaken after three days of sustaining the injury. The hand was immobilized using a dorsal plaster slab for pain relief, and the patients were allowed to flex their fingers within the slab. The slab was removed in the second week and the K-wires in case 2 were removed after confirming union at three weeks. Patients underwent rehabilitation under the supervision of a physiotherapist, where they practiced passive, active-assisted, and active stretching of the involved joint.

Outcomes:
The patient was assessed for post-traumatic stiffness, which is clinically apparent in inter-phalyngeal, meta-phalyngeal, and wrist joints. The aim is to restore the function to normal or near-normal dexterity. The patients were assessed using mini-dash score at the end of 6 months. The score was 0 in two patients, and one patient (case 3) was lost to follow-up. The hand function was restored to normal in the two patients who were evaluated.

Patient Information:

Long cuts ran along both the back and palm sides of those fingers of the hand.
The top tendon sheath had vertical slits that went down to the knuckle joints of the fingers.
The middle finger joints were opened, the central slips were pulled away, and the joint capsules were lost.
The flexor tendons stayed intact, but their sheath was lost where the palm skin was cut.
Two of the three patients had a break in the bone continuity of the hand.

In the operating room, the wounds were cleaned and flushed with six liters of saline while the arm was numbed.
The vertical slits in the tendon sheath were sewn shut with thin nylon stitches to repair them.
The skin was pulled together over the tendons to give them a natural cover using nylon stitches.
Two patients needed a thin skin graft on the back of the hand, done three days after injury.
The hand was placed in a dorsal plaster splint to ease pain, and the fingers could move inside the splint.
The splint was taken off in the second week to allow further healing of the hand.
The metal pins in case two were removed after bone healing was confirmed at three weeks.
Patients then did rehabilitation with a physiotherapist, practicing passive, active-assisted, and active movements of the injured joint.
Outcomes:
The patient was checked for stiffness after the injury, which can appear in the finger and wrist joints.
The goal is to restore hand function to normal or near-normal levels so the patient can use the hand well.
At six months, the patients were scored using the mini-dash questionnaire to measure hand ability.
Two patients scored zero, meaning no disability, while the third patient could not be reached for follow-up.
Hand function returned to normal in the two patients who were evaluated, showing good recovery.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [Redacted]
Age: 50 years
Sex: Female
Race: South Indian

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to the outpatient department with a productive cough with hemoptysis for the past 2 months. She had a history of pulmonary tuberculosis, which was discontinued within 3 weeks of starting the treatment. She also suffered from diabetes mellitus with peripheral neuropathy for the past 8 years and was taking oral hypoglycemic agents for the same. The patient was diagnosed with an indwelling aspergilloma and was treated with an oral loading dose of Voriconazole followed by an oral maintenance dose. The patient responded well to the treatment, and the hemoptysis resolved after a lobectomy. After 3 weeks, the sputum became negative for acid-fast bacilli. The patient is currently in the 4th month of treatment and is doing well.

Laboratory Results:
Admission baseline investigations showed anemia, and the renal and liver function tests were within normal limits.

Diagnostic Study:
Computed tomogram of the thorax revealed a thick-walled cavity in the right lung upper lobe with an indwelling aspergilloma. 3 sputum samples were tested positive for acid-fast bacilli by Ziehl Neelsen's staining technique. Conventional method of culture on Lowenstein Jensen's medium yielded growth of M. tuberculosis. The anti-tuberculosis drug susceptibility test showed resistance to Isoniazid and Rifampicin but sensitive to Ethambutol, Pyrazinamide, and Streptomycin in their critical concentrations.

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis and an indwelling aspergilloma.

Treatment:
The patient was initially started on a daily dose of Isoniazid, Ethambutol, Pyrazinamide, and Streptomycin. However, after culture demonstrated MDR-TB, Isoniazid was stopped, and oral Levofloxacin and Ethionamide were included in the treatment regimen. Rifampicin was not included due to its interactions with Voriconazole. The patient was given an oral loading dose of Voriconazole 400 mg 12th hourly for 2 doses, which was followed by an oral maintenance dose of 200 mg 12th hourly for 6 weeks.

Follow-up:
After the treatment, the patient was counseled on the importance of adhering to medication and follow-up visits. She was advised to return to the hospital for follow-up visits and monitoring of symptoms.

Summary:
The 50-year-old South Indian woman presented with complaints of productive cough with hemoptysis for the past 2 months. She suffered from diabetes mellitus with peripheral neuropathy and had a history of pulmonary tuberculosis. The patient was diagnosed with an indwelling aspergilloma and treated with an oral loading dose of Voriconazole followed by an oral maintenance dose. Hemoptysis resolved after lobectomy, and the sputum became negative for acid-fast bacilli after 3 weeks. The patient responded well to the treatment and is currently in the 4th month of treatment. The patient was advised to adhere to medication and follow-up visits.

Brief Hospitalization Summary:
The patient, a 32-year-old lady presented with a pathological fracture of the right humerus, previously treated with interlocked, intramedullary nail at an outside facility, with subsequent development of significant pain and nonunion. Biopsy at our institution revealed diagnosis of high-grade fibroblastic osteosarcoma, leading to resection of the entire right humerus with extra-articular glenohumeral excision (modified Tikhoff-Linberg).

Pertinent findings in the admission note:
The patient presented with significant shoulder pain that worsened with motion, with disuse atrophy of the deltoid muscle and an unsightly prominence of the proximal end cap of the prosthesis.

Management Course:
The patient was managed with revision surgery in the form of a reduction in length of the prosthesis by removal of the end cap and reattachment through drill holes to the scapula with mersilene tape. The patient remained relatively pain-free until her 12th annual follow-up, during which identical symptoms recurred. Revision surgery was performed again, involving a reduction in prosthetic length by an additional two centimeters, which resulted in satisfactory pain control that was maintained till her latest follow-up.

Summary:
The patient presented with a pathological fracture of the right humerus, which was diagnosed as high-grade fibroblastic osteosarcoma and treated with the resection of the entire right humerus with extra-articular glenohumeral excision (modified Tikhoff-Linberg). The patient experienced significant complaints of pain and nonunion after the initial treatment. Revision surgeries were performed, including a reduction in length of the prosthesis by removal of the end cap and reattachment through drill holes to the scapula with mersilene tape, and ultimately, a reduction in prosthetic length by an additional two centimeters. The patient is currently maintaining satisfactory pain control.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: N/A
Gender: Male
Age: 6 years old

Chief Complaint: Painful intumescence of the left inguinal area

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient, a 6-year-old Greek boy, was admitted to our hospital with a painful intumescence of the left inguinal area. Prior to admission, the patient was referred to a general hospital where he was diagnosed with an incarcerated left inguinal hernia. The hernia was subsequently reduced by a local surgeon, but the patient continued to experience discomfort and pain. Upon physical examination, the left inguinal area appeared normal, with only subcutaneous edema and a hematoma due to the reduction manipulations observed. Mild discomfort and pain was present in the left testicle without clinical evidence of testicular torsion. These symptoms persisted for three days before the decision was made to operate on the patient.

During the operation, a lower Spigelian hernia was identified. The hernia sac penetrated from a small defect in the Spigelian fascia within Hesselbach's triangle. The orifice diameter was about 1.5 cm, and the sac extended up to 7 cm and contained a small part of the large omentum which was successfully reduced. Reconstruction of the hernia was performed with non-absorbable sutures.

The patient remained in stable condition throughout his hospital stay and was discharged without any complications. The patient was instructed to rest and was prescribed appropriate follow-up care.

Follow-Up Care:

The patient remains free of symptoms and recurrence for eight years after the operation.

Poor feeding, repeated upper respiratory infections, and inability to verbalize due to a wide cleft palate.

An 8-year-old male child with Seckel syndrome and intrauterine growth retardation was admitted to our outpatient department with complaints of a wide cleft palate. After careful examination and investigation, it was decided to perform pushback palatoplasty under general anesthesia.

GA was administered using inhalational induction with sevoflurane in titrated doses. Anesthesia was maintained with oxygen and air along with titrated doses of sevoflurane and intermittent doses of atracurium. Pushback palatoplasty was done for incomplete cleft palate. The intraoperative period was uneventful, with no complications. The operation took approximately 75 minutes.

Postoperatively, the patient was monitored in the intensive care unit for any apneic spells, respiratory failure, or oral bleed. The postoperative period was uneventful, and the patient's vital signs remained stable. 

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS:
Wide cleft palate in a patient with Seckel syndrome and intrauterine growth retardation.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
The patient was discharged home in stable condition. It is recommended to continue feeding the patient with soft and pureed foods that are easy to swallow. The patient should avoid foods that are hard, crunchy, or require significant chewing. Additionally, patients with Seckel syndrome should be monitored for potential developmental delays and co-morbidities. Follow-up with a pediatrician and a specialist for further evaluation and management is recommended.

FOLLOW-UP:
The patient should schedule follow-up appointments with their pediatrician and specialists for further evaluation and management.

None.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSES AND PROCEDURES:
Wide cleft palate and pushback palatoplasty.

ROM exercises were initiated after the removal of the K-wire, and the patient had returned to playing rugby within three months of the initial injury. Hospital Course Summary:

Patient was a 71-year-old female who presented to our clinic with an abnormal ECG finding during a scheduled appointment. She had a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, essential hypertension, and dyslipidemia. During the consultation, the ECG reading showed premature ventricular contraction at a 1:1 ratio (ventricular bigeminy) with a heart rate of 46/min. Therefore, various blood investigations were ordered to rule out secondary causes that could have led to the changes in the ECG. An urgent appointment was scheduled a week later to review these results. The patient was also advised to seek urgent medical attention if she felt palpitations or giddiness.

During the second consultation, a week later, the repeat ECG showed atrial flutter with a 3:1 atrioventricular block. All the results of the blood investigations were normal, except for an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) levels. Urgent transthoracic echocardiography revealed a dilated left atrium and ventricle without any myocardial hypokinetic changes. A large echogenic mass measuring 3.1×4.1 cm was identified at the left atrium. The mass was solid and appeared pedunculated, arising from a stalk at the endocardium. The patient had a left ventricular ejection fraction of 54%.

The patient was immediately referred to a tertiary care cardiology clinic where a second transthoracic echocardiography was performed. An imaging diagnosis of left atrial myxoma was confirmed. The tumor measured approximately 2.9×3.1 cm. A paroxysmal atrial fibrillation pattern was observed on the ECG. Warfarin treatment was initiated while aiming for a target international normalized ratio between 2 and 3. Currently, the patient is jointly cared for by the primary care physician and a multidisciplinary team that is helping to manage the anticoagulation therapy. The patient is unwilling to undergo surgery to remove the tumor.

The patient has been advised to continue with the recommended medical management and to seek medical attention immediately in case of any symptoms suggestive of cardiac compromise. The patient has been provided with educational resources to manage their condition and follow up with the healthcare team.

Admission Diagnosis:  Stage IV poorly differentiated ovarian carcinoma on palliative carboplatin-based chemotherapy.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission:
The patient was admitted due to a brief syncopal episode with associated lethargy, nausea, light-headedness and increased watery ileostomal output following chemotherapy one week earlier. Clinical examination including central nervous system was unremarkable, and the patient was haemodynamically stable and afebrile.

Medical History:
The patient has a history of hypertension, multiple pulmonary emboli on enoxaparin and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. In the past, the patient had undergone bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and hysterectomy, and had an ileostomy due to small bowel obstruction with subsequent fistulae formation and bilateral nephrostomy drainage after radiation-induced ureteric obstruction. She had previously experienced recurrent urinary tract infections, which led to colonisation of her nephrostomies with methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), Staphylococcus epidermidis and Candida albicans. The patient had never received anti-fungal prophylaxis.

Initial Assessment:
Laboratory investigations revealed abnormal levels of sodium, creatinine, haemoglobin, white blood cells and lymphocytes. On day 2 of admission, the patient developed fevers of 38.5°C and was empirically commenced on piperacillin-tazobactam and vancomycin. The isolation of Staphylococcus epidermidis from the nephrostomy fluid was considered colonisation and the nephrostomies were changed. Initial septic screen was non-contributory, including negative faecal microscopy.

Diagnostic Assessment:
Persisting fever during her third week of admission prompted assessment for metastatic disease progression with FDG-PET scan. There was no evidence of metastatic malignant disease detected, but an area of abnormal avidity was identified on the aortic valve. Subsequent transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) revealed a small mobile echo-density superior to the aortic valve. Transoesophageal echocardiogram (TOE) revealed a pedunculated mass within the ascending aorta arising from the commissure of the right & non-coronary cusp of the aortic valve with a calcified base. Brain MRI identified a contrast-enhancing right parasagittal frontal lobe lesion consistent with an embolic lesion.

Treatment:
Fungi were isolated from repeat blood cultures on day 22 of admission and subsequently identified as Lomentospora prolificans with high MIC to amphotericin (>32 mg/l) and itraconazole (>32 mg/L), and in-vitro sensitivity to voriconazole (0.5 mg/L). The patient was commenced on therapy with voriconazole (loading dose 600 mg IV 12 hourly). Unfortunately, due to her underlying advanced malignancy, disseminated fungal infection and poor clinical status, the patient was considered unsuitable for surgical management. She was managed with palliative intent.

Outcome:
The patient passed away five days after the fungus was isolated on day 27 of her admission.

Initial infection screening, including stool exam and blood cultures, did not identify a source of infection.

The scan showed no cancer spread but spotted unusual activity on the heart's aortic valve.
A heart ultrasound through the chest found a small moving spot above the aortic valve.
An ultrasound via the esophagus showed a stalk-like growth on the aortic valve area with a calcium base.
A brain MRI revealed a bright spot in the right front side of the brain, likely from a clot.
Treatment: On day 22, fungus in the blood was identified as Lomentospora prolificans, resistant to two drugs but sensitive to voriconazole.
Treatment began with high-dose voriconazole given intravenously every 12 hours as a loading dose to fight the infection.
Because of widespread cancer, spreading fungus, and her poor overall condition, surgery was not an option.
Care focused on comfort and symptom relief, aiming to improve quality of life without attempting curative treatment.
Outcome: The patient died five days after the fungus was found, which occurred on day 27 of her hospital stay.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [patient name]
Medical Record Number: [medical record number]

Admission Date: [admission date]
Discharge Date: [discharge date]

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 43-year-old female admitted with acute hypoxic respiratory failure, requiring 15 litres per minute of oxygen. Physical exam was significant for wheezing in lungs bilaterally. Electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm. Troponin and electrolytes were in normal range. She had normocytic anemia with hemoglobin 10.8 g/dl, leukocytes 7.8 X 109/L, serum procalcitonin at 0.10 ng/mL. Arterial blood gases showed respiratory acidosis. Chest X-ray showed extensive bilateral lung infiltrates.

The patient was managed empirically for community acquired pneumonia with broad-spectrum antibiotics. On day 3 of hospital stay, her symptoms and oxygen requirement improved. However, she was noted to have hyperkalemia (potassium: 5.8 mmol/L) and elevated CK at 10,000 U/L. She denied any history of myalgias, muscle weakness, trauma, recent exercise, illicit drug use, and statins. An impression of rhabdomyolysis was made and aggressively hydrated. Surprisingly, the CK level increased despite resuscitation, raising diagnostic curiosity.

Detailed inflammatory workup was negative. Her course of hospitalization was complicated by volume overload requiring aggressive diuresis. A detailed discussion with the patient was held explaining enzyme abnormality and risk versus benefits of invasive workup. She refused further investigations including biopsy and imaging. A CK electrophoresis was ordered and the patient was discharged to follow up as an outpatient. Surprisingly, her isoenzyme panel showed CK MM with type 1 macroCK-macroCKemia.

On post-hospital follow up, subsequent normalization of enzyme levels were seen.

Discharge Diagnosis:

1. Acute hypoxic respiratory failure.
2. Community-acquired pneumonia.
3. Rhabdomyolysis.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient should follow up with her primary care physician. She should monitor for any recurrence of symptoms related to acute hypoxic respiratory failure or pneumonia and report them immediately if they do occur.

The patient should maintain her hydration level, follow a healthy diet and a normal lifestyle.

She should avoid strenuous physical activity until medical clearance is obtained. Emergency medical services should be contacted in case of any emergency issues.

The patient should be advised to go through regular lab tests to address any abnormality issues. 

Follow-up plan:

The patient should be followed up in the outpatient clinic within 2 weeks.

Discharge Summary:

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 43-year-old woman who came in with sudden trouble breathing from low oxygen and needed oxygen therapy.
Physical exam showed wheezing in both lungs, indicating airway narrowing and possible inflammation in the airways.
The electrocardiogram showed a normal heart rhythm with no abnormal beats during the hospital stay.
Blood tests for heart damage and electrolyte levels were normal, showing no signs of injury.
She had mild anemia with low red blood cells, normal white blood cells, and low infection marker.
Arterial blood showed excess acid, indicating respiratory acidosis due to breathing trouble and required treatment.
Chest X-ray showed patchy spots in both lungs, suggesting areas of infection and inflammation that needed antibiotics.
She was treated for a common lung infection caught outside the hospital with strong antibiotics.
By day three of her hospital stay, her breathing improved and her oxygen requirement decreased.
But she developed high potassium levels and a very high muscle enzyme level, suggesting possible muscle breakdown.
She had no muscle pain, weakness, injury, exercise, drug use, or statin use during this time.
Doctors thought muscle breakdown was happening and gave aggressive fluid resuscitation to protect the kidneys.
Surprisingly the muscle enzyme kept rising despite fluids, which was puzzling and prompted further investigation.
Further tests for inflammation and infection were negative, ruling out common causes and did not show autoimmune markers.
Her hospital stay was also complicated by extra fluid in the body needing strong water pills.
The team talked with her about the enzyme abnormality and the pros and cons of more invasive tests.
She declined further tests like biopsy and scans, preferring to avoid invasive procedures at this time.
A special enzyme test was ordered and she was sent home to see her doctor as an outpatient.
Surprisingly the test showed a specific muscle enzyme pattern called CK MM with type 1 macroCK.
At her follow-up visit, the muscle enzyme levels returned to normal, indicating resolution and no further concerns.
Discharge Diagnosis:
1. Sudden trouble breathing from low oxygen, also called acute hypoxic respiratory failure requiring extra oxygen support.
2. Lung infection caught outside the hospital, also known as community-acquired pneumonia, treated with antibiotics.
3. Muscle breakdown, also called rhabdomyolysis, which was identified by high enzyme levels and required fluid treatment.
Discharge Instructions:
The patient should see her primary care doctor for follow-up within two weeks of discharge.
She should watch for any return of breathing or infection symptoms and tell her doctor right away if they happen.
She should keep drinking enough fluids, eat a balanced diet, and keep a normal daily routine.

Hospital Course:
The patient, an 89-year-old female with a past medical history of vascular dementia, hypertension, and B12 deficiency secondary to pernicious anemia, was admitted with a 3-month history of a left-sided neck lump that had been constantly increasing in size. On physical examination, a large firm, irregular mass was noted in the upper pole of the left thyroid lobe with a background of multinodular goiter. There was no evidence of lymphadenopathy and the trachea was central with no signs of stridor.

The patient underwent a needle core biopsy to increase diagnostic accuracy. TFTs results showed hypothyroidism due to Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Two core biopsies were obtained, which showed a heavy plasma cell infiltrate and admixed B- and T-lymphocytes. The histological findings were consistent with a plasma cell granuloma of the thyroid with underlying Hashimoto's thyroiditis.

Operative intervention was deemed inappropriate due to the patient's frailty and comorbidities. The patient was started on Thyroxine and regularly reviewed in the clinic. TSH levels improved with modification of T4 dosage. The neck lump remained stable for several months until it showed signs of regression. The patient remained asymptomatic with respect to breathing and swallowing.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Plasma cell granuloma of the thyroid with underlying Hashimoto's thyroiditis.

Follow-up Plans:
The patient will continue to be followed-up in the clinic and thyroid function tests will be performed periodically to ensure appropriate TSH levels.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]                                                   

MR#: [REDACTED]                                                           

Date of Admission: [REDACTED]                                     

Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]                                       

Admitting Diagnosis: Extensive stage small cell lung cancer

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient, a 43-year-old non-smoking woman, was admitted with a six-month history of deteriorating dyspnea on exertion. The patient underwent various diagnostic tests, including a chest X-ray, chest computed tomography, bronchoscopic washing, biopsies, magnetic resonance imaging, and positron emission tomography-computed tomography, which led to the diagnosis of extensive stage small cell lung cancer. The patient was started on first-line chemotherapy with cisplatin and etoposide, which resulted in a significant improvement of the tumor. However, after six cycles, the patient developed progressive disease, and second-line chemotherapy with carboplatin and irinotecan was initiated. Unfortunately, the patient developed obstructive pneumonia after two cycles, and the regimen was changed. The patient was placed in the refractory relapse group and started on third-line chemotherapy using CAV (Adriamycin, vincristine, and cyclophosphamide), which was maintained for 11 cycles. The patient developed progressive disease after the 11th cycle and the regimen was unable to be continued. The patient was then started on fourth-line therapy with ICE (ifosfamide, carboplatin, and etoposide), but had to discontinue due to intolerable toxicity. Later, an ICE regimen without etoposide was commenced as a fourth-line therapy, resulting in a partial response to therapy. The patient’s pain gradually disappeared during this regimen, and she refused further treatment. Eight months after completing the fifth cycle of carboplatin and ifosfamide, the patient presented to the emergency department for dyspnea and rib pain, and a chest CT showed an increase in the size of her mass. Palliative treatment with a sixth cycle of carboplatin and ifosfamide was initiated, and her symptoms improved. However, the patient expired due to aspiration pneumonia 11 days later. The patient survived for approximately 27 months after beginning chemotherapy.

Discharge Diagnosis: Extensive stage small cell lung cancer

Discharge Medications: [REDACTED]

Summary of Hospitalization:

The patient was admitted with extensive stage small cell lung cancer and treated with various chemotherapy regimens, including cisplatin and etoposide, carboplatin and irinotecan, CAV, and ICE. A partial response to therapy was achieved with ICE without etoposide, which resulted in the reduction of the size and uptake of the tumor. The patient was later admitted to the hospital for palliation of symptoms, and dyspnea and chest pain improved after treatment with a sixth cycle of carboplatin and ifosfamide. However, the patient later died from aspiration pneumonia.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
- Name: [REDACTED]
- Age: 15 years old
- Gender: Female
- Medical History: No previous surgeries

Hospital Course:
- The patient presented with a first episode of medial patellar dislocation of the left knee due to a skiing accident.
- Over a period of 9 months, the patient experienced 8 more spontaneous luxation episodes, which resolved after auto repositioning.
- The patient underwent pre-operative imaging assessment, which included weight-bearing anteroposterior and lateral views of both knees, as well as a magnetic resonance imaging and computed tomography-scan of the left knee.
- Pathological MRI findings revealed substantial hypertrophy of both the medial patellar retinaculum and the tendon of the oblique medial vastus muscle.
- Following the initial conservative treatment with the use of a brace during sports activities and muscular imbalance correction, the patient underwent an open medial retinacular release with complete dissection of the hypertrophic MPFL and a transfer of the vastus medialis oblique (VMO) to the superior border of the patella.
- The post-operative protocol included partial weight bearing for the first 4 weeks, with flexion limited at 45° within the first 2 weeks and at 90° within the first 4 weeks. Recovery to a full weight bearing was permitted 4 weeks after surgery, and range of motion was gradually increased.
- At the 6 and 12-week post-operative follow-up, the patient showed no pain or sensation of instability.
- Eight months after surgery on the left knee, the patient experienced a medial patellar dislocation in the right knee, which was surgically addressed with the same procedure performed on the left knee.
- The patient was reassessed 7 years after the surgical operation on the left knee and 6 years after surgical correction of the right one, and has had no further episodes of dislocation.
- The patient reported being highly satisfied with the procedure, with the only complaint being slight difficulty in squatting, jumping, and running.

Assessment and Plan:
- The patient's left and right knees were treated with an open medial retinacular release with complete dissection of the hypertrophic MPFL and a transfer of the vastus medialis oblique (VMO) to the superior border of the patella.
- The post-operative protocol included partial weight bearing for the first 4 weeks, with flexion limited at 45° within the first 2 weeks and at 90° within the first 4 weeks. Recovery to a full weight bearing was permitted 4 weeks after surgery, and range of motion was gradually increased.
- The patient reported no further episodes of dislocation and was highly satisfied with the procedure. The only complaint was slight difficulty in squatting, jumping, and running.

After trying a brace and exercises to balance her muscles, she had surgery to release the tight inner tissue.
The surgery also moved a thigh muscle to the top of her kneecap to help keep it in place.
After surgery, she could put only some weight on the leg for the first four weeks.
She could bend the knee no more than 45 degrees for the first two weeks.
She could bend the knee up to 90 degrees for the first four weeks.
After four weeks, she could bear full weight and gradually increase knee movement over time.
At six weeks and twelve weeks after surgery, she had no pain and felt her knee was stable.
Eight months after left knee surgery, her right kneecap slipped out of place.
She then had the same surgery on the right knee to fix it.
She was checked again seven years after the left knee surgery and six years after the right knee surgery.
Since those checks, she has reported no further kneecap slips or instability at any time.
She said she was very happy with the surgery, noting only mild trouble with squatting, jumping, and running.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: [Name], [Age]-year-old male

Discharge Date: [Date]

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to our pediatric neurology clinic for hyperactivity, speech delay, and behavioral problems. A detailed evaluation by the child psychiatrist revealed that the patient was suffering from attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. The patient was initiated on treatment with antipsychotic drugs (risperidone); however, no significant improvement was noted after 6 months. The patient also had a history of recurrent upper respiratory tract infections.

On physical examination, the patient had mildly coarse facial features, slightly depressed nasal bridge with frontal bossing, and stocky hands with short fingers. Neurological examination showed normal tone, power, and deep tendon reflexes with bilateral flexor plantar response. Laboratory investigations showed normal blood counts, chemistry, electrolytes, urine organic acids, tandem mass, plasma lactate, pyruvate, thyroid function tests, and karyotype, and fragile X tests. In light of these findings, the diagnostic possibility of MPS was suspected, but subsequent laboratory examination revealed normal urine glycosaminoglycans (GAGs). Skeletal survey was not suggestive of the characteristic dysostosis complex. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed J-shaped sella turcica, mild widening of the lateral ventricles with thinning of the corpus callosum.

Further enzyme analysis for MPS IIIA showed null activity of the enzyme sulfamidase activity in leukocytes, confirming the diagnosis. The patient was initiated on rehabilitation and behavior therapy for hyperactivity.

Discharge Diagnosis:

Mucopolysaccharidosis type IIIA

Discharge Condition:

Stable

Discharge Instructions:

The patient's parents were advised to follow up on the rehabilitation and behavior therapy. They were advised to monitor the patient's language development, behavior, and overall growth and development. The patient's parents were also advised to ensure that the patient received appropriate medical care for recurrent upper respiratory tract infections. Finally, the patient's parents were advised to follow up with the pediatric neurology clinic and seek help if any new symptoms or problems appear.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with complaints of enlarged abdominal volume. Physical examination revealed hepatomegaly and liver steatosis, and laboratory tests showed elevated levels of ALT, AST, cholesterol, HDL, and triglycerides. The patient was diagnosed with a possible glycogen storage disease and underwent a liver biopsy, which showed diffuse enlargement of hepatocyte volume with intense microvesicular steatosis and ballooning, as well as deposits of triglycerides in Kupffer cells and portal macrophages, consistent with Wolman Disease/CESD. Acid lipase activity in leukocytes tested low, consistent with a biochemical diagnosis of LAL deficiency. Electron microscopy revealed massive distension of hepatocytes due to a large amount of round triglyceride deposits, consistent with the previous morphological diagnosis. 

Discharge Diagnosis:
The patient is diagnosed with Wolman Disease/CESD.

Consults:
The patient was seen by a hepatologist and a medical geneticist.

Condition at Discharge:
The patient's general health was good, and liver function was preserved at the time of discharge.

Discharge Medications:
None specified in case report.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient's parents were informed of the diagnosis and provided with appropriate genetic counseling. Follow-up care with a hepatologist and medical geneticist was arranged.

Patient: 32-year-old Caucasian Scottish female

Admission Date: [Date]

Discharge Date: [Date]

Admission Diagnosis: Dermographism

Summary of Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted for rest and expedited investigations due to reported symptoms of generalized itch and elevated muscle enzymes. Dermatomyositis was suspected after the patient exhibited associated muscle symptoms, and a muscle biopsy and electromyography confirmed inflammatory myositis consistent with dermatomyositis. Treatment with systemic corticosteroids and high-dose human intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) therapy was initiated. 

The patient responded well to treatment, and symptoms and biochemical features started to improve quickly after the first IVIG infusion. After a few months of regular IVIG infusions, the patient's skin and muscle symptoms and signs resolved, and her CK levels reached near normal population values. The IVIG infusion frequency was gradually reduced and then stopped, and the patient was maintained on a low dose of prednisolone during a subsequent pregnancy. 

At discharge, the patient was stable, and her dermatomyositis had resolved. The patient is to follow up with her primary care physician for ongoing management. 

Discharge Diagnosis: Dermatomyositis

Discharge Instructions:

1. Follow up with your primary care physician for ongoing management of your condition.
2. Continue taking any prescribed medications as directed.
3. Avoid excessive exercise and other strenuous activities until cleared by your doctor.
4. Report any new or worsening symptoms to your doctor immediately.
5. Adhere to a healthy diet and lifestyle to help manage your condition.

The 68-year-old female patient presented with sudden onset of skin rash, redness, and itching all over her body, along with shortness of breath and a generalized uncomfortable feeling. The symptoms occurred after administering her daily subcutaneous humulin 70/30 insulin injection. The patient was found to have an erythematous, pruritic urticarial rash spread over the body and mild dyspnea, consistent with a type-1 hypersensitivity reaction. The patient was treated with antihistamines and the symptoms were resolved without complications.

Past Medical History:

The patient had a past medical history of T2DM, hypertension, and grade-2 diastolic dysfunction. She was compliant with her prescribed medications until she started developing severe allergic reactions to insulin a week after acquiring the COVID-19 infection.

Course of Treatment:

The patient was diagnosed with COVID-19 infection eight days ago, after which she was self-quarantined in her home. To avoid further allergic reactions, switching to a different insulin formulation was recommended. The patient refused treatment with a different insulin regimen despite extensive counseling. She was prescribed oral antihistamines to be taken before her regular insulin injections, and also an EpiPen (epinephrine injection, USP) 0.3 mg, with the instructions to visit the ER if she develops symptoms again.

Outcome:

The patient completely recovered from the COVID-19 infection, but continued having insulin allergies with her humulin 70/30 insulin injections. Eventually, the patient agreed to switch to different insulin formulations after about two weeks of her initial ER presentation. The new insulin formulations brought the glucose levels down to her usual glycemic range without any further allergic reactions.

Hospital Course:

Patient is a 77-year-old female who presented with right L2-3 radiculopathy that was refractory to maximum medical management. This was secondary to foraminal compression at L2-3 and L3-4 due to degenerative disc disease, levoscoliosis, as well as grade 1 spondylolisthesis at both levels.

Treatment:

Given the patient’s prior history of posterior decompressive laminectomy, it was felt that the best approach would be a minimally invasive lateral approach to obtain indirect decompression of the foramina as well as correct her spinal deformity. This will achieve the goals of decompression and fusion as well as deformity correction while avoiding the risk of operating through scar tissue. A retroperitoneal transpsoas approach was used to expose the disc spaces from the patient’s left side.

Complete discectomy was performed with the release of the contralateral annulus fibrosis followed by the interbody fusion. A lordotic PEEK graft was used at each level, 50 mm length x 18 mm width x 9 mm height, packed with demineralized bone matrix (DBM).

Outcome:

Postoperative anteroposterior and lateral x-ray imaging confirmed good position of interbody grafts, correction of scoliosis as well as spondylolisthesis, and restoration of disc height achieving satisfactory foraminal indirect decompression. A routine postoperative x-ray at three months demonstrated lateral cage migration on the left side at the L2-3 level with evidence of arthrodesis in the disc space.

The patient remained asymptomatic and follow-up imaging at one year demonstrated completed fusion without further migration of the interbody graft at L2-3.

Conclusion:

Informed patient consent was obtained prior to treatment and with the patient’s permission, we report on this case of successful minimally invasive lateral approach to obtain indirect decompression of the foramina as well as correct spinal deformity. The patient had significant improvement and remained asymptomatic.
nemotron_simplification:
Hospital Course:
The patient is a 77-year-old woman with right lower-back and leg pain that did not improve with medicines.
This pain was caused by narrowing of the nerve openings at L2-3 and L3-4 due to disc wear-and-tear.
A left curve of the spine and mild slippage of the vertebrae also contributed at those levels.
Treatment:
Because she had earlier surgery to remove bone from the back of the spine, doctors chose a small side incision.
This approach allowed them to reach the discs from the left side to open the nerve spaces.
It opened the nerve spaces, straightened the spine curve, and avoided cutting through scar tissue.
The surgeon went through the area behind the abdomen and through the psoas muscle to expose the disc spaces.
Disc material was removed, outer ring on opposite side loosened, and curved plastic spacer placed.
Each spacer was about 2 inches long, 0.7 inches wide, 0.35 inches tall and filled with bone-growth material.
Outcome:
Front and side x-rays taken after surgery showed the spacers were in the correct place.
The images also showed the spine curve and slippage were improved and disc height was restored.
A routine x-ray three months later showed the spacer had shifted slightly to the left at L2-3.
However, the bone was beginning to fuse in the disc space, indicating early healing.
The patient felt no symptoms and a one-year x-ray showed the bones had fully fused.
The spacer had not moved further, indicating the fusion remained stable and solid over time.
Conclusion:
We obtained the patient’s agreement before treatment and she allowed us to report this case.
The report shows the side-approach successfully relieved nerve pressure, straightened the spine, and improved overall function.
The patient improved greatly, experienced less pain, and remained without symptoms long-term after the procedure.

Chief Complaint: Infertility

History of Present Illness:
The patient was a 37-year-old Korean woman with a history of oligomenorrhea and infertility. She was referred to the Reproductive Medicine and Infertility Clinic at our institution for treatment. The patient had a history of delivering a baby with androgen insensitivity syndrome, who had undergone herniorrhaphy due to bilateral inguinal hernias. She had no growth or developmental abnormalities or any family history of diabetes or cardiovascular disease.

Past Medical History:
The patient had a history of oligomenorrhea and infertility. She had a body mass index of 22.1 and hirsutism with a Ferriman-Gallwey index score of 5.

On physical examination, the patient had no growth or developmental abnormalities and no abnormal gynecological symptoms were noted.

The patient underwent a scrotal ultrasonography and an abdomino-pelvic computed tomography scan, which revealed the presence of both testes in both inguinal canals. The uterus, vagina, and ovaries were not identified in the scan. The patient was diagnosed with complete androgen insensitivity syndrome. Genotyping for the AR gene polymorphism was performed, and it was consistent with carrier of AIS. Routine hormone assay revealed elevated antimullerian hormone and increased testosterone and free testosterone concentrations. Transvaginal USG showed polycystic ovary morphology, and the patient was diagnosed with polycystic ovary syndrome.

Hospital Course:
The patient received in vitro fertilization treatment for preimplantation genetic diagnosis.

N/A

The patient was advised to follow up with her provider for further management and regular check-ups.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 57-year-old woman with a history of high myopia, retinal tear in the left eye treated with focal laser photocoagulation and pneumatic retinopexy and cryotherapy for a retinal tear in the right eye. Past medical history includes osteoarthritis and breast cancer treated with bilateral mastectomy 6 years prior to presentation.

Hospital Course:

The patient was referred to our facility for sudden onset of decreased vision in the right eye, 32 days after a recent procedure. On examination, 2+ anterior chamber and vitreous cells were noted without hypopyon. The patient was started on topical steroid therapy with prednisolone acetate 1 %, which resulted in improvement of inflammation and vision.

However, after 2 weeks, the inflammation worsened, and her vision declined to 2/200. A systemic workup was initiated which was negative for infectious, inflammatory, and vasculitic processes known to cause intermediate and pan-uveitis. Topical steroid therapy was increased, and the patient returned 4 weeks later with no inflammation and 20/30 vision.

Two months later, the patient returned with 2+ cell and flare in the anterior chamber and vitreous cell, again without hypopyon, and a vitreous biopsy was performed, yielding results consistent with intraocular inflammation without evidence of malignancy. Over the next 3 months, despite treatment, there was no resolution of a persistent anterior and intermediate uveitis.

The patient eventually underwent retinal detachment repair with pars plana vitrectomy, air–fluid exchange, 360° of endolaser, and a 12 % C3F8 gas injection, with vitreous biopsy results similar to prior studies. The patient's clinical course progressed to recurrent retinal detachment, requiring repair with scleral buckling and silicone oil tamponade.

Six months after this procedure, the patient was no longer able to perceive light, and given her chronic discomfort, she opted to undergo enucleation of the right eye. Histology of the enucleated globe showed a granulomatous inflammatory membrane, with giant cells, blanketing the angle structures and iris, and forming a pupillary/cyclitic membrane, which was fused to a totally detached, gliotic retina.

Diagnosis:

Granulomatous anterior and intermediate uveitis.

Follow-Up:

The patient's case is an example of the rare and complex nature of this subtype of uveitis, which is often refractory to treatment and can result in severe visual loss. The patient's overall prognosis was poor, and despite multiple interventions, there was no successful resolution of the uveitis. Close monitoring and vigilant follow-up is recommended for patients presenting with similar symptoms.

Discharge Summary:
Patient: 57-year-old woman with severe nearsightedness and a history of retinal tears in both eyes. The left tear was treated with laser and a gas bubble; the right tear was treated with freezing. She also has joint wear and a history of breast cancer treated by removal of both breasts six years ago.
Hospital Course: The patient was referred for sudden vision loss in the right eye 32 days after a recent procedure. Exam showed cells in the front of the eye and in the gel, but no pus. She started steroid eye drops (prednisolone 1%) which reduced swelling and improved her vision and comfort. After two weeks of treatment, the inflammation worsened and her vision decreased to only 2/200. A full body workup found no infection, inflammation, or blood vessel disease that could cause the eye inflammation. Steroid eye drops were increased, and four weeks later she had no swelling and vision of 20/30. Two months later she returned with mild cells and flare in the eye front and gel, no pus. A sample of the eye gel showed inflammation inside the eye and no signs of cancer. Over the next three months, despite treatment, the inflammation in the front and middle eye did not go away. She then had surgery to fix a detached retina, which included removing eye gel and exchanging fluid for air. The surgery also used laser all around the eye and placed a gas bubble to hold the retina. The eye gel sample taken during this surgery showed the same inflammation as before, with no cancer. Her condition worsened and she needed another surgery with a silicone band and silicone oil to keep the retina attached. Six months after that surgery she could not see light and, due to pain, chose to remove her right eye. Exam of the removed eye showed inflamed scar tissue with large cells covering the drainage area and colored part. It also formed a membrane over the pupil that was attached to a completely detached, scarred retina.
Diagnosis: The patient has inflammation with lumps in the front and middle parts of the eye.
Follow-Up: The patient's case shows a rare and severe form of eye inflammation that is hard to treat. This inflammation can lead to major vision loss, and despite many treatments, the patient's eye inflammation did not improve. The patient's overall outlook was poor, and close monitoring is advised for anyone with similar eye symptoms.

Admitting Diagnosis: Ischemic Stroke

Hospital Course:

The patient presented to the emergency room with slurred speech, dizziness, and left-sided weakness which started about two hours before presentation. The patient did not report any cough, fever, shortness of breath, loss of smell, or body aches. On examination, she was hemodynamically stable. In neurological examination, she had slurred speech and weakness in the left upper and lower extremity but normal sensations. The rest of the neurological examination as well as chest, cardiovascular, abdominal, and musculoskeletal examination was normal. 

The emergency CT scan did not show any evidence of major territorial infarction, intracranial hemorrhage, or focal mass lesions. The patient was within the window of tissue plasminogen activator (TPA) for acute stroke and was treated with it. The patient was also screened for COVID-19 on admission as per hospital protocol and the result came back later as positive.

The patient was admitted to the ICU for monitoring and did not have any abnormal electrocardiogram (EKG) rhythm while in ICU. She had full recovery of her neurological symptoms within few hours without any bleeding complications. The patient was subsequently discharged in good health and advised home isolation.

Discharge Diagnosis: Ischemic Stroke with COVID-19

Discharge Instructions: 

The patient is advised to follow safe sleep and nutrition practices and to avoid stress. The patient should be advised not to engage in driving or other actions that require quick reflex. The patient should be advised to follow home isolation and avoid close contact with family members or friends. The patient should also be advised to monitor for any symptoms of COVID-19 and seek medical attention if needed.

Follow-up: The patient should be advised to follow up with the primary care provider or neurologist within one week of discharge.

Hospital Course:
Josh, an 18 year-old male with a history of alcohol and substance abuse, identity problems, and parent-child relational problems, was admitted for 9 weeks to a mental health care institution in 2013 following a suicide attempt. He was diagnosed with dysthymic disorder, personality disorder not otherwise specified, and histrionic, borderline, and narcissistic features. His global assessment of functioning score was 41–50. 

Discharge Summary:
Josh was discharged from the mental health care institution with ongoing support. He continues to experience mood changes and has had limited peer contact but has had some short relationships with other young men. Primary support group problems, social environment problems, and educational difficulties were identified. His parents, who are musicians, have their own psychiatric problems which have affected their involvement in the treatment. 

Follow-up: 
Josh will continue to receive ongoing support and counseling to address his mental health and substance abuse issues. Close monitoring of mood changes will be necessary. Referrals to educational resources and social support groups will be made.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [patient name]

Gender: [patient gender]

Date of Admission: [date of admission]

Reason for Hospitalization:

The patient was admitted at 22 weeks’ gestation to the Emergency Department due to miscarriage. Upon admission, the patient presented shaking chills, fever, stomatitis, sore throat, abdominal pain, and minimal vaginal bleeding for the previous three days.

Hospital Course:

The laboratory findings upon admission showed a low white blood cell count and high C-reactive protein levels. After induction of labour, the patient delivered a stillborn female fetus. The patient was treated with meropenem, followed by piperacillin/tazobactam for 6 days.

Medical History:

The patient had a complex medical history of monoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis completely resolved at 15 years of age. The patient reported bilateral gonalgia six years before the current hospitalization. Laboratory results showed severe neutropenia, but no ANCA titers. The patient had undergone a bone marrow biopsy, which was reported within normal limits. The patient presented with low neutrophil counts in the past six years but had never contracted opportunistic infections. One year before admission, the patient had delivered a male infant with severe mastitis, followed by two episodes of bilateral knee arthritis.

Postmortem Examination:

The postmortem examination on the nonmacerated female fetus revealed intra-alveolar, gastric, and intestinal neutrophils with oedema, microhemorrhages, and acute tubular necrosis (NTA) of the renal parenchyma. The placenta showed necrotizing AC corresponding to a maternal inflammatory response stage 3/3 and grade 2/2. Funisitis was noted with neutrophilic infiltrate of the umbilical vein and the two arteries with extension to Wharton’s jelly consistent with fetal inflammatory response stage 2/3 and grade 2/2. Initial thrombosis was detected in few spiral arteries of the decidua.

Microbiological Analysis:

Autoptical samples were cultured on different media and identified as K. kingae using MALDI-ToF technology. The microorganism grew in pure culture in all the samples.

Medical Treatment:

The patient was treated with Granulocyte-Colony Stimulating Factor (G-CSF) and cyclosporine (200 mg a day) in addition to hydroxychloroquine due to low neutrophil count and recent intrauterine infection.

Discharge Condition:

The patient fully recovered and was discharged after 10 days.

Follow-Up Plan:

The patient will have regular follow-up appointments with her primary care physician to monitor her medical condition.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 75-year-old female with hypertension, presented to the emergency department complaining of odynophagia and neck pain following consumption of chicken porridge. No fever or dyspnea was reported upon admission. Simple radiography suspected esophageal foreign body (FB), which was later confirmed by neck CT. POCUS was utilized to detect the esophageal FB and reveal dilatation with pooling of secretions. The patient underwent urgent esophagogastroduodenoscopy during which the chicken bone was removed after self-vomiting during forceps retrieval. The patient was discharged from the ED two hours post-procedure without complications. 

Impressions:
- Esophageal FB, suspected foreign body ingestion 
- Odynophagia 
- Neck pain 

Procedures:
- Neck CT 
- POCUS 
- Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) 
- Foreign body retrieval 

Follow-Up:
The patient was discharged from the emergency department with no further follow-up required.
