Admission Date: [Date]

Discharge Date: [Date]

Patient Name: [Name]

Medical Record Number: [Number]

Age: 32

Sex: Female

Date of Birth: [Date]

Admitting Diagnosis: Second-stage uterine prolapse

Chief Complaint: Intermittent vaginal blood spotting

Hospital Course: 

The patient was admitted at 28+0 weeks of gestation with complaints of intermittent vaginal blood spotting and diagnosed with second-stage uterine prolapse. Pelvic examination revealed point C as the leading edge according to the pelvic organ prolapse quantification staging system. Sonographic examination revealed a short cervix with 17 mm length and a T-shape. A progesterone capsule was administered vaginally daily.

Two weeks later, at 30+0 weeks of gestation, the patient was admitted again because of regular uterine contractions. She was diagnosed with second-degree uterine prolapse. A more shortened cervix with 10-mm length and a T-shape was noted on sonographic examination. To control preterm uterine contractions, tocolytic therapy was initiated with a favorable outcome. Corticosteroids were also administered. The patient was advised to rest in bed with a suggestion of a slight Trendelenburg position. Vaginal culture revealed mycoplasma infection, which was treated with a single dose of azithromycin 1,000 mg.

At 34+0 weeks of gestation, uterine contractions disappeared without tocolytics, and the patient was discharged. However, she was readmitted at 37+0 weeks of gestation due to regular uterine contractions. The cervix was still prolapsed at the same level and the cervical orifice was opened to about 3 cm width. After a latency period, a healthy male neonate was delivered with an estimated blood loss of about 400 mL, which was not different from that of a normal pregnancy. Apgar scores were 10 at 1 minute and 10 at 5 minutes. 

The prolapsed uterus was manually reduced, and the postnatal period was uneventful. Two days after delivery, the patient was discharged in good health with complete resolution of the cervical prolapse. Follow-up examination 1 and 6 months postpartum revealed no evidence of uterine prolapse.

Discharge Diagnosis: Second-stage uterine prolapse

Condition at Discharge: Good

Discharge Instructions:

- Follow up with obstetrician as recommended for postpartum care.
- Avoid heavy lifting for at least 6 weeks.
- Resume normal activities gradually as tolerated.
- Review vaginal hygiene practices with a healthcare provider.
- Seek medical attention immediately if vaginal bleeding or abnormal discharge occurs.
- Take prescribed medications as directed.
- Follow a healthy diet and maintain a regular exercise routine.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY 

Patient: 44-year-old woman 

Admission Date: [Date] Discharge Date: [Date] 

Diagnosis: Dilated common bile duct, cholecystectomy history, and splenic heterogeneous subcapsular hematoma 

Hospital Course: The patient was admitted to the hospital with intractable nausea and vomiting associated with severe epigastric pain. Physical examination was only notable for mild epigastric tenderness. Laboratory tests showed mildly elevated liver enzymes, and a right upper quadrant ultrasound showed dilation of the common bile duct, which was later confirmed on magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography as well as a 7-mm common bile duct stone. The patient underwent ERCP with sphincterotomy, which demonstrated a dilated common bile duct with no obvious cause. She subsequently experienced severe epigastric and left upper quadrant abdominal pain with hypotension after the procedure. Repeat laboratory testing at the time showed elevated lipase as well as a decline in hemoglobin. A CT scan of the abdomen illustrated a large splenic heterogeneous subcapsular hematoma and peripancreatic stranding. The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit and managed conservatively with fluids and blood transfusions. The hematoma regressed, and her hemoglobin remained stable. With clinical improvement, she was discharged home. 

Follow-up Care: The patient was advised to follow up with her primary care provider for further management and was instructed to return to the emergency department if she experiences any further symptoms. 

Discharge Medications: N/A 

Discharge Instructions: 

1. Rest and avoid strenuous activities 
2. Keep the incision areas clean and dry 
3. Take prescribed medications as directed by your healthcare provider
4. Follow up with your primary care provider for further management of your condition 
5. Return to the emergency department if you experience any further symptoms.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: [Name]
Date of Admission: [Admission Date]
Date of Discharge: [Discharge Date]
Admitting Diagnosis: AKI, Lower Extremity Edema, Resting Dyspnea, Afebrile, Jaundice, Ulcero-Necrotic Lesions

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 58-year-old male, was admitted with complaints of oliguria, lower extremity edema, and resting dyspnea. The physical examination showed an afebrile, jaundiced patient with ulcero-necrotic lesions on the inner aspect of the thighs. Elevated creatinine and urea levels confirmed AKI, and transaminases with conjugated bilirubin were moderately elevated. The patient's lab results showed elevated IgM and decreased complement (C3/C4). Rheumatoid factor, cryoglobulins, and serum viscosity were increased, while antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies and antinuclear antibodies were negative.

Abdominal ultrasound revealed no calcifications in the kidneys, which were of normal size. Hepatic ultrasound revealed two hypoechogenic masses with absent Doppler signs, located in the right and left hepatic lobes.

A suspected hematologic neoplasia with monoclonal gammopathy was suspected as the cause of the patient's neuropathy and cutaneous vasculitis. The patient's renal function and cutaneous lesions improved under therapy with loop diuretics and high-dose glucocorticoids.

Histopathologic and immunohistochemical findings from the hepatic biopsy done on day three indicated a primary hepatic MALT lymphoma in the absence of lymphoproliferative disease outside the liver.

The patient was referred to oncology and began the R-CHOP regimen for treatment. Three months after discharge, the patient was re-admitted with fulminant hepatitis that was ultimately fatal. The viral load of HBV and hepatitis D virus was high despite negative serology for the surface antigen.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient is advised to seek medical attention in case of appearance of new or worsening jaundice, fever, abdominal pain, or other concerning symptoms. The patient should avoid consuming alcohol, taking acetaminophen-containing products, or taking any medications without consulting their physician. The patient's medical records and biopsy results should be shared with any future healthcare providers.

The patient is a 58-year-old man who came in with very little urine, leg swelling, and trouble breathing while resting.
On exam he had no fever, yellow skin, and open sores with dead tissue on the inner thighs.
Blood tests showed high waste levels in the blood, indicating a sudden kidney problem that needed attention.

Other blood markers showed increased rheumatoid factor, cold-sensitive proteins, and thicker blood, but autoimmune tests were negative.
Kidney ultrasound showed no calcium deposits and confirmed that both kidneys were of normal size and appearance.
Liver ultrasound revealed two dark spots with no blood flow, one in each liver lobe.
Doctors suspected a blood cancer with an abnormal protein as the cause of nerve pain and skin blood vessel inflammation.

A liver biopsy on day three showed a MALT lymphoma starting in the liver with no similar disease elsewhere.
He was sent to a cancer doctor who started him on chemotherapy known as the R-CHOP regimen.
Three months after leaving the hospital he returned with sudden severe liver infection that led to his death.
Blood tests showed high levels of hepatitis B and D viruses even though the usual hepatitis B test was negative.

Patient Name: Anonymous

Medical Record Number: XXXXXX

Date of Admission: XXXXXXX           
Date of Discharge: XXXXXXX

Admitting Diagnosis: Incomplete spinal cord injury 

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the Spinal Cord Injury Center at Balgrist University Hospital, Switzerland, with an incomplete spinal cord injury. Clinical examination revealed the patient was suffering from central cord syndrome, at-level neuropathic pain, and mechanical allodynia (brush allodynia) on both forearms. Light touch was normal within the cervical segments, and sharp dull discrimination was preserved while the intensity of the pinprick stimulus was only mildly attenuated. The upper extremity motor score (left: 11/25, right: 11/25) showed a profound weakness of elbow extensors, and no voluntary muscle activity in the finger flexors and abductors bilaterally. The lower extremity motor score was normal (left: 25/25, right: 25/25). Biceps and brachioradialis reflexes, as well as knee-jerk and ankle-jerk reflexes were bilaterally exaggerated. The Babinski sign was negative. Muscle tone was normal without signs of spasticity. Coordination and gait showed discrete signs of ataxia.

Noxious mechanical stimuli were applied with a 256 mN pinprick stimulator, and CHEPs were recorded, which appeared to be normal at C4 and T4 with high pain ratings to the heat stimulation, but almost complete loss of painful heat sensation and absent CHEPs at the level of C6.

The patient was treated for the duration of their stay in the hospital. Written informed consent was obtained from the patient before conducting any study, and the study was approved by the “Kantonale Ethikkommission Zürich”.

The patient was discharged from the hospital in stable condition. The patient was instructed to follow up with their primary care physician or specialist for ongoing management of their condition. Any changes in the patient's condition should be reported immediately to their healthcare provider.

Patient Discharge Summary

Patient Name: Not disclosed
Date of admission: Not disclosed
Date of discharge: Not disclosed

Admission Diagnoses: Hypertension, High cholesterol, Diabetes mellitus, ACS (non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction)

Medical History: The patient had a medical history of hypertension, high cholesterol, and diabetes mellitus.

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient was admitted to the Coronary Care Unit because of sudden onset of chest pain at rest. ECG abnormalities associated with an increase of cardiac enzymes (hs troponin 70 pg/ml and CK-MB 8 ng/ml) were suggestive of an ACS (non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction). Echocardiogram showed left ventricular hypertrophy, end-diastolic diameter, and mild hypokinesia of the basal segment of the inferior wall with normal systolic function. In the parasternal short axis view, there was an abnormal diastolic flow inside the ventricular inferior wall. This flow was directed from the basal segment of the inferior wall into the left ventricular cavity. In the apical two-chamber view, there was the entire intramural course under the mitral valve posterior leaflet, where it was thrown into the ventricular cavity during diastole.

Treatment: According to ESC guidelines, the GRACE (Global Registry of Acute Coronary Events) risk score of the patient was 146 and early invasive strategy of myocardial revascularization (within the first 24 hours from admission) was indicated. The patient underwent coronary angiography, which revealed 90% stenosis in the middle portion and 70% stenosis in the distal portion of the left anterior descending artery, a double 70% stenosis in the proximal and the middle portion of the circumflex artery and the right coronary artery, dominant, with stenosis of 50% at the end of the proximal portion. Angiography confirmed the presence of a tortuous voluminous coronary fistula: it originated from the interventricular posterior artery and coursed along the posterior interventricular sulcus from the apex to the base of the left ventricle. The patient underwent percutaneous coronary angioplasty with the placement of two drug-eluting stents in the left anterior descending artery and a single drug-eluting stent in the circumflex artery.

Follow up: To complete evaluation, cardiac CT was performed to detect coronary fistula anatomy, its relationships with cardiac structures and its course. CT images documented that coronary fistula originated from the distal portion of the right coronary artery, ran into the left ventricular inferior wall, and drained into the left ventricular chamber under the mitral valve, with a final tract with an intramyocardial course. The patient was asymptomatic at 24-month follow-up.

Disposition: The patient was discharged in good condition.

It also showed two 70% blockages in proximal and middle parts of the circumflex and the dominant right coronary artery.

They received two medicine-coated stents in the LAD and one in the circumflex artery to keep the arteries open.

A heart CT scan was done to look at the fistula and its path in the heart.
The CT showed the fistula starts from the lower part of the right coronary artery.
It runs into the lower left heart wall and drains into the heart chamber under the mitral valve.
The fistula has a tract inside the heart muscle that allows blood flow during heart relaxation.
At the 2-year follow-up, the patient had no symptoms and felt well during the check.

The 16-year-old Bangladeshi girl presented to our hospital with hoarseness of voice, which had been gradually worsening over the last 4 months. She was treated with antibiotics by her local physician. Evaluation with a fiberoptic endoscopy revealed a polyp in the anterior 2/3 of the right vocal cord with impaired right vocal cord mobility. The patient had no history of using tobacco or consuming alcohol, and no exposure to radiation/carcinogenic agents. There was no family history of malignancy. Computed tomography scan of the neck showed an irregularity of the right vocal cord, and no neck nodes were observed. Her biopsy slides confirmed the diagnosis of carcinoma, which was staged as T2N0M0 well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma of the larynx.

The patient was planned for radical radiotherapy. The treatment fields were as per the standard guidelines, as described previously. Neck nodes were not prophylactically treated, as the incidence of nodal positivity is <2% in T2 lesions. The patient was treated with radical radiotherapy using 6 MV photons in a linear accelerator. The patient tolerated the radiotherapy well and is on regular follow-up.

N/A

The patient is advised to continue 6-month follow-up visits for appropriate monitoring.

Discharge Summary:

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with complaints of a white mass on the lower conjunctiva, associated with pain and redness in the right eye, and a right eye vision of 20/100. The patient was diagnosed with a circumscribed area of scleral abscess with engorged episcleral and conjunctival vessel around it caused by Nocardia species.

Treatment:
The patient was treated with topical amikacin 2.5% every half hour, oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole twice daily, and topical gatifloxacin every hour was added to the previous treatment postoperatively. Systemic antibiotics were continued for 2 months.

Progress:
After four months of treatment, the patient reported improved vision of 20/60. A slit lamp examination revealed that he had nuclear sclerosis, and there was granulation tissue at the lesion site.

Follow-up Care:
The patient was discharged with instructions for continued follow-up care with his ophthalmologist. No further hospitalization was necessary.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 25-year-old male from Iraq, presented with painful cutaneous swellings, abnormal gait, and recurrent high-grade fever. He had a history of chronic glomerulonephritis and was on hemodialysis twice a week. His renal allograft had failed due to acute rejection, leading to graft nephrectomy. He had previously been treated for pulmonary tuberculosis and chronic active hepatitis C with interferon, which was discontinued due to pancytopenia.

Diagnostic Assessment:
Physical examination revealed subcutaneous masses with reduced joint movements and painful indurated ulcers. Tests showed anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, elevated BUN and creatinine, and altered calcium and phosphorus levels. Intact PTH was significantly elevated, while 25-hydroxy-vitamin D3 was within normal limits. Alkaline phosphatase was elevated, and urine aluminum levels were elevated. A radioisotope bone-scan revealed ectopic calcification, and a CT scan showed heterotopic soft tissue calcification.

Diagnosis and Management:
The patient was diagnosed with tumoral calcinosis and treated with low-calcium dialysate, Sevelemer phosphate binder, and desferal chelation for aluminum toxicity. His fever and painful joints improved after eight sessions of dialysis, after which he was discharged to continue further treatment in his hometown.

Follow-Up and Recommendations:
The patient was advised to continue low-calcium dialysate and phosphate-binder treatment and to seek regular follow-up with his nephrologist. He was advised to maintain adequate hydration, adhere to a low-calcium and low-phosphorus diet, and avoid aluminum-containing antacids and medications. He was also advised to avoid activities that could lead to trauma or pressure on the affected areas and to seek medical attention promptly if he developed any new symptoms.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admitted to the emergency department (ED) with altered mental status, a 66-year-old man with hypertension and high cholesterol was found to have nystagmus, dysarthria, discoordination, and ataxia. While in the ED, the patient's condition worsened and concerned about a posterior circulation stroke, a head computed tomography angiogram was obtained, which was negative for any abnormality. An electrocardiogram showed a normal sinus rhythm. The patient was evaluated by the neurology consultant team, who determined the patient had a National Institute of Health Stroke Scale of 11, and tissue plasminogen activator was administered for thrombolysis. He was subsequently intubated for airway protection and admitted to the ICU.

While intubated in the ICU, the patient developed status epilepticus and was treated with multiple doses of benzodiazepine and phenytoin, resulting in cessation of seizure activity. A comprehensive urine drug screen by gas chromatography and mass spectrometry was positive for clozapine and clozapine metabolites, in addition to caffeine and bupropion, a home medication. It was concluded that the patient must have accidently ingested the family member's clozapine, as the patient's blood work showed no evidence of abuse or other medications. The patient had never been prescribed clozapine but managed the family member's medication and often took their respective medications at the same time. The patient was extubated on hospital day three and discharged with a normal neurologic exam and no further seizure activity on hospital day five.

In summary, the patient presented with altered mental status and exhibited symptoms of nystagmus, dysarthria, discoordination, and ataxia. Concerned about a potential stroke, a head CT angiogram was performed, and the patient was evaluated by the neurology team. After admission to the ICU, the patient developed status epilepticus, and a comprehensive urine drug screen was performed, which identified the presence of clozapine that the patient had entered. Ultimately, the patient was extubated and, after determining there was no further seizure activity, discharged with normal neurologic exam results.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with lower extremity edema and proteinuria on urinalysis. A renal biopsy established the diagnosis of lambda light chain amyloidosis. Treatment included melphalan- and dexamethasone-based chemotherapy followed by autologous stem cell transplantation. Unfortunately, despite therapy, total serum-free light chain levels and massive nephrotic syndrome persisted. Nine months later, the patient underwent hand-assisted laparoscopic ligation of both native ureters to decrease daily urinary protein loss and restore plasma oncotic pressure. Post-operative renal ultrasound confirmed mild hydronephrosis. During the 12-day hospitalization, nutritional and functional status improved, and he was dismissed home on long-term hemodialysis requiring minimal assistance for ambulation.

Final Diagnoses:
Lambda light chain amyloidosis with massive nephrotic syndrome and autonomic dysfunction with disabling orthostatic hypotension.

Procedures:
Hand-assisted laparoscopic ligation of both native ureters.

Follow-Up Plans:
The patient will follow up with the nephrologist for long-term management of his renal disease. Hemodialysis will be continued as needed. Further imaging studies may be considered to evaluate the patient's renal function.

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the hospital following a stab wound to the left chest. He was transferred to the emergency department with hypotension, tachycardia, tachypnea, and Glasgow Coma Scale score of 14. The initial FAST revealed a pleural effusion in the left thorax. A chest drain was inserted, and more than 700 mL of blood was drained. Subsequent FAST had revealed a pericardial effusion.

A Clamshell thoracotomy was started due to the patient's unstable hemodynamic status, and surgical exploration showed a massive hemothorax in the left thorax, left lung posterior lobe injury, pericardial injury, and hemopericardium with blood clots. A 10-mm defect was found in the right ventricle near the left anterior descending coronary artery. Chemical cardiac arrest was induced using ATP, and the cardiac wall was repaired surgically using a horizontal mattress suture. The patient recovered after the surgery and received intensive care in the hospital for 13 days.

Discharge Summary:

The patient was discharged after a 13-day hospital stay without complications. The postoperative echocardiographic check-ups showed a septal injury, but the patient did not exhibit any symptoms of heart failure.

The patient should avoid strenuous activities and get plenty of rest for at least two weeks. It is essential to monitor for signs of infection, such as fever, inflammation, and excessive wound discharge. The patient should report chest pain, shortness of breath, or lightheadedness immediately.

Follow-up care should include a visit with a primary care provider or specialist, depending on the patient's condition, within one week. They should return to the hospital immediately if new symptoms appear or existing symptoms worsen.

The patient's condition is stable currently, and they have been discharged home with follow-up treatment as suggested above.

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Date of Discharge: [REDACTED] 

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 27-year-old female with a history significant for CREST syndrome, limited scleroderma, interstitial lung disease, mild pulmonary hypertension, and chronic kidney disease (CKD) from scleroderma renal crises. She presented with intermittent atypical chest pain that remained consistent despite physical activity. Her chest pain was relieved with nitroglycerin. During one episode of chest pain, the patient showed elevated troponin levels. Further testing was done which included a nuclear stress test. Her condition showed improvement upon use of nifedipine.

The patient underwent a coronary angiography which revealed severe stenosis of the proximal left anterior descending (LAD) artery, as well as collaterals from the right coronary artery and slow flow. The right coronary artery and left circumflex were normal. She was initially managed conservatively due to her CKD and equivocal nuclear stress test findings.

Using an XB 3.5 guide catheter, a pressure wire was advanced across the LAD lesion and the resting Pd/Pa ratio was found to be ischemic. The lesion was pre-dilated and then a coronary stent was placed, followed by post-dilatation. Intravascular imaging with OCT was performed, and showed stent malapposition and insufficient expansion of the distal portion of the stent. The stent was post-dilated with a noncompliant balloon with excellent results.

The patient's condition showed marked improvement after stenting. The patient's pain went away and she was discharged in stable condition.

Discharge Diagnoses:

1. CREST syndrome 
2. Limited scleroderma 
3. Interstitial lung disease 
4. Mild pulmonary hypertension 
5. Chronic kidney disease 

Discharge Medications:

N/A

Discharge Instructions:

1. Follow-up with cardiology in 2 weeks.
2. Continue taking all current prescribed medications.
3. Return to the emergency department immediately if chest pain or any other concerning symptoms occur.
4. Avoid any strenuous physical activity for the next week.

The patient's condition improved rapidly with targeted antibiotic therapy and he was discharged after 6 days of treatment. The patient presented with complaints of constipation, intermittent episodes of pain, and distension of the abdomen for a year associated with poor weight gain.

The patient was evaluated with X-rays and CT scans of the abdomen that showed multiple air fluid levels, dilation of small bowel loops, and was managed as subacute intestinal obstruction. High-resolution esophageal manometry showed weak peristalsis with small peristaltic breaks; anorectal manometry was normal. A whole bowel transit study revealed normal gastric emptying with delayed colonic transit time. 

Treatment:

The patient received medical therapy (polyethylene glycol and itopride) with only a partial response.

Diagnosis:

Due to familial occurrence, a possibility of primary CIPO was suspected and next-generation sequencing performed in the index patient revealed a homozygous missense variation in exon 2 of SGOL1 gene (chr3; c67A>G; p.Lys23Glu; ).

Condition at Discharge:

The patient was discharged in stable condition with a recommendation for an age-appropriate protein-calorie diet with supplemented vitamins and micronutrients.

Follow-up:

The patient was advised to follow up with their primary care physician for further management.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: [Patient's Name]

Gender: Male

Age: 76 years

Medical Record Number: [Medical Record Number]

Admission Date: [Admission Date]

Discharge Date: [Discharge Date]

Admitting Diagnosis: Elevated creatinine levels, elevated IgE level, proteinuria, and glucosuria

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the rheumatology clinic with severe fatigue, unintentional weight loss, memory loss, and ambulatory dysfunction. The patient had a 120 pack-year smoking history and also smoked marijuana. The patient had a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, COPD, and diabetes mellitus.

The labs showed an elevated creatinine level, elevated IgE level, proteinuria, and glucosuria. An ultrasound image of the Kidneys showed echogenic foci in the right kidney. The CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast showed a scar in the interpolar region of the right kidney. CT scan of the chest with contrast showed a 10 mm low-density area in the right thyroid lobe. Thyroid ultrasound showed bilateral thyroid nodules, including a 3.5 cm hypoechoic nodule in the lower pole. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the nodule showed benign follicular nodule.

The patient had a repeat CT chest with contrast, which showed a 1.4 cm right lower lobe lung nodule, bilateral interlobular septal thickening with lower lobe predominance, multiple bilateral ground-glass opacities, cystic changes, and multiple enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes. PET scanning was done, which showed right lower lobe hypermetabolic nodule, highly suspicious for malignancy with extensive smoking history and significant weight loss.

The patient underwent right lower lobe basilar segmentectomy and mediastinal lymph node dissection. Histology was negative for malignancy and showed numerous positive IgG4 plasma cells, along with obliterative phlebitis, significant fibrosis, and arteritis as lymphoplasmacytic infiltration. IgG4:IgG ratio on the lung biopsy was greater than 40%. The lung biopsy was highly suggestive of IgG4-related disease. The lymph node also showed lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, IgG4-positive cells, irregular fibrous bands, but no obliterative phlebitis or arteritis.

Treatment and Procedures:

The patient was started on 40 mg of prednisone, which resolved his fatigue and had significant weight gain, and his prednisone was tapered down and stopped in 4 months. He was not placed on any immunosuppression and was monitored for any further relapse. He is in remission for the last one year off any medications without any relapses.

Diagnosis on Discharge:

IgG4-related disease.

Condition at Discharge:

The patient is asymptomatic with no need for further follow-up.

Follow-up Recommendations:

The patient is advised follow-up with the rheumatology clinic.

Discharge Date: [insert date]

Patient Name: [insert name]               Medical Record Number: [insert number]

Reason for Admission:
The patient was admitted due to suspicion of a mycotic aortic aneurysm and severe infection.

Hospital Course:
The patient underwent intravenous antibiotic therapy for four weeks and was started on tazobactam/piperacillin hydrate. Computed tomography angiography showed a descending aortic aneurysm measuring 70 × 70 mm, which extended 20 mm in only 2 weeks. Transcatheter endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) was performed under local anesthesia using two 37 × 200 mm Conformable stent grafts (W. L. Gore & Associates, Inc., Newark, DE, USA) to prevent aortic rupture.

Upon discharge, the patient was afebrile with a normal white blood cell count and C-reactive protein level. Oral antibiotics were continued for 18 months. The patient underwent monitoring by computed tomography 15 months after the TEVAR, and the aneurysm had regressed significantly, measuring 53 × 53 mm. The patient had no further signs of infection at the time of writing.

Diagnosis:
Descending aortic aneurysm

Procedures:
Transcatheter endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR)

Condition at Discharge:
The patient was discharged without serious complications.

Follow-Up:
The patient was monitored via computed tomography 15 months after TEVAR repair, at which point there was significant regression of the aneurysm. The patient was free from antibiotics at the time of writing.

The patient presented to the Accident and Emergency Department with a history of fall and sustaining a trivial laceration to the right olecranon region. The wound was cleaned and closed with adhesive skin strips and the patient was discharged with analgesia without any radiological evaluation.

Five to six hours later, the patient returned with extensive swelling of the right forearm. Radiograph of the right forearm revealed subcutaneous emphysema from distal arm to the dorsum of wrist. The patient was then referred to the tertiary hospital for further evaluation and management.

On examination at the tertiary hospital, the patient had localised redness at the wound site over the olecranon region. Crepitus was palpable throughout the forearm on both flexor and extensor compartments extending proximally into the distal arm and distally onto the dorsal aspect of wrist. Radiographs of the forearm and arm revealed air in the subcutaneous tissues of the right lower arm, whole forearm and dorsal aspect of the wrist. The patient was afebrile with stable vital signs. There was no evidence of infection on the blood tests with normal white cell count and C-reactive protein.

A dressing was applied over the laceration and the arm rested in a sling. The patient was admitted for observation and prophylactic antibiotics. Swab taken from the wound was negative for any microorganisms and the patient was discharged after 48 hours.

At the last review, three weeks after discharge, there was complete healing of the laceration with resolution of the subcutaneous emphysema.

Patient: 32-year-old female with chief complaint of pain in upper anterior tooth.

The patient reported to the Department of Conservative Dentistry and Endodontics and was diagnosed with an impacted permanent canine and a palatally placed upper permanent right lateral incisor. A radiograph showed loss of lamina dura and slight radiolucency in relation to the periapical area of the upper right central incisor. Gender: Female

Date of Discharge: [redacted]

Reason for Admission:
The patient presented with a history of scalp scaling and itching accompanied by hair loss for 2 years, and scaly plaques on both feet associated with fissuring for 8 years.

Hospital Course:
Physical examination of the scalp revealed diffuse white scales, while the soles showed thick and diffuse scaling. Oral cavity and nails were clinically normal.

Dermatoscopic examination of the scalp revealed peripilar tubular casts with miniaturized vellus hairs, granular grey dots, white dots, and crystalline structures predominantly around hair follicles. Furthermore, histopathological examination of the scalp exhibited basket weave hyperkeratosis, follicular plugging, basal cell vacuolization in the epidermis, and band-like lymphohistiocytic infiltrate in the superficial dermis extending around the infundibulum till the proximal part of the isthmus of the hair follicle with pigment incontinence. Biopsy features were consistent with LPP, and direct immunofluorescence was negative. Histopathology of the sole showed compact hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and vertical streaking of collagen in the papillary dermis without interface changes.

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with Lichen Planopilaris (LPP), which is indicated by basket weave hyperkeratosis, follicular plugging, and band-like lymphohistiocytic infiltrate observed in the histopathological examination.

Treatment:
The discharge summary does not contain any information about the patient's treatment plan.

Follow-up:
The patient will follow up with her healthcare provider for proper management of her LPP. 

Disposition:
The patient was discharged and was advised to continue her follow-up with her healthcare provider.

Patient 4, an 8-month-old female, was admitted due to episodic binocular upward gaze for 7 months. She also had delayed growth development and was unable to sit alone steadily until the present. Discharge Summary:

Patient: 47-year-old edentulous female with maxillary complete denture

Chief Complaint: Dysfunctional maxillary complete denture

History of Present Illness: The patient presented with an unuseful maxillary complete denture, resulting from cervical radiotherapy. She had a limited oral opening and insufficient saliva quantity and flowability.

Hospital Course: The patient's treatment plan consisted of fabricating complete dentures with proper extension of the flanges. Flexible impression trays were used to obtain preliminary impressions for both arches. Custom trays for the final impressions were fabricated with autopolimerized acrylic resin. Final maxillary impressions were made by using polysulfide material alternately for the first and second halves of the sectional trays. Record bases were fabricated and occlusion rims were prepared. A centric relation record was made, and the record was transferred from the patient to a semiadjustable articulator. The try-in was evaluated to verify jaw relations and teeth arrangement. After patient acceptance, final festooning and flasking of the dentures were completed. The final dentures were manufactured using similar designs to that of the record bases. The prostheses were deflasked, finished, and polished. The patient was provided with instructions for cleaning, inserting, and removing the prostheses. She was recalled for follow-up visits to check for the maintenance and her adaptability with the new dentures.

Outcome: The patient reported difficulty in the insertion and removal of denture initially, but progressively, she became used to it.

Follow-up: The patient will continue to be monitored during follow-up visits to check the maintenance and adaptability of her new dentures.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission:
A 43-year-old male with primary hypothyroidism was admitted for evaluation of progressive fatigue, weakness, muscle and joint pain in the setting of recurrent fractures.

History of Present Illness:
The patient had been experiencing musculoskeletal pain in several locations including bilateral knees, ankles, left shoulder, left arm, and lower back which affected his overall functional status. He struggled to climb a flight of stairs, often grabbing the railing to pull himself up. A nuclear medicine bone scan showed abnormal uptake in bilateral ribs, vertebrae, right knee, hips, ankles, and feet. A lower extremity MRI showed stress fractures in left fibula, fifth metatarsal, and right tibia.

Course in Hospital:
The patient was started on calcitriol and phosphate supplements which significantly improved muscle weakness. Due to concern for TIO, a positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) scan with 68Gallium (68Ga)-DOTATATE was performed which showed multiple lytic osseous lesions with increased somatostatin positive uptake seen throughout pelvis, ribs, ankles, and feet. However, after re-review with radiology, multiple areas of increased uptake were considered to be secondary to fractures, and left posterior acetabular lesion was presumed to be the tumor of interest given a remarkably higher standard uptake values (SUVmax) in this lesion compared to other lesions (SUVmax 20 vs. 4–5).

Procedure:
The left acetabular lesion was biopsied and pathology demonstrated a 1.4 cm phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor of the left acetabulum with uninvolved margins. The patient underwent radical resection of the tumor of the posterior left acetabulum with reconstruction of the posterior wall and posterior column of the acetabulum through a Kocher-Langenbach approach. His hip joint was able to be spared utilizing a 3D-printed custom bone cutting guide (CG) and intra-operative O-arm guided surgical navigation (Medtronic© Stealth) utilizing a navigated Sonopet Ultrasonic Bone Cutting Bovie (Stryker). The posterior wall and column of his acetabulum were constructed with a tantalum augment (Zimmer) and a pelvic reconstruction plate and screw construct (Synthes) after tumor removal.

Discharge Summary:
The patient was discharged with normal phosphorus and FGF23 levels, pain-free left hip, no evidence of hardware complication, back to hiking, and walking on the treadmill. Clinical and radiographic follow-up at 6 months postoperatively found him to be pain-free in his left hip, with almost complete resolution of bone pain, and no recurrence of fractures. Phosphorus level also remained normal at 3.4 mg/dL 6 months after surgery.

Hospital Course Summary:
Admission: A 43-year-old man with low thyroid function was admitted for worsening tiredness, weakness, muscle and joint pain, and repeated fractures.

This pain limited his ability to climb stairs, so he often grabbed the railing to pull himself up.

An MRI of the legs revealed stress fractures in the left fibula, left fifth metatarsal, and right tibia.

The doctors started calcitriol and phosphate supplements after admission, which significantly improved his muscle weakness.
Because doctors suspected tumor-induced osteomalacia, they did a PET/CT scan using 68Ga-DOTATATE to look for abnormal bone activity.
The scan showed many lytic bone lesions with increased somatostatin uptake in the pelvis, ribs, ankles, and feet.
After a second review, most of the increased uptake was attributed to healing fractures, leaving one suspicious area.
The suspicious spot in the left posterior acetabulum showed much higher activity (SUVmax 20) than other areas (SUVmax 4-5).
Procedure:
A biopsy of the left hip socket showed a 1.4 cm phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor with clear margins.
The tumor was removed completely, and the back wall and column of the socket were rebuilt using the Kocher-Langenbach approach.
To save the hip joint, surgeons used a 3D-printed custom cutting guide and O-arm navigation (Medtronic Stealth).
They also used a Sonopet ultrasonic bone cutter (Stryker) during the operation to remove bone precisely.
The rebuilt socket used a tantalum implant (Zimmer) and a metal plate with screws (Synthes).
Discharge Summary:
At discharge, his phosphorus and FGF23 levels were normal, and his left hip was pain-free.
There were no complications with the plates or screws used in the surgery, and he could walk without pain.
He was able to return to hiking and to walk on a treadmill as part of his daily activity.
Six months later, follow-up visits showed his left hip remained pain-free and most bone pain had gone away.
No new fractures occurred during follow-up, and his phosphorus level stayed normal at 3.4 mg/dL.

Electronic Health Record Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Age: 50

Gender: Female

Date of Admission: [REDACTED]

Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Reason for Admission: Right Pancoast tumor

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to our institution with a presentation of right arm pain due to a right Pancoast tumor diagnosed as adenocarcinoma by fine needle aspiration cytology. A thorough evaluation using chest computed tomography (CT), brain CT, positron emission tomography (PET), and subsequent thoracoscopy showed N0 status diagnosed by CT and PET; the involvement of the right brachiocephalic and subclavian veins was also highly suspected at the pleural inspection (stage cT4N0M0). The patient underwent four cycles of cisplatin and Pemetrexed plus 60 Gy irradiation with partial tumor regression seen on CT while PET scan became negative.

Surgical Intervention:

The patient underwent successful Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery (VATS) lobectomy for the right upper lobe of the lung. The surgery was preceded by thoracoscopy to evaluate the resectability of the tumor. The procedure was judged feasible and a V-shaped contra-incision was made along the anterior border of the right sternocleidomastoid muscle, extended parallel to the second intercostal space. Through VATS accesses, sections of the right superior bronchus and the remaining fissure were completed, and the “en bloc” specimen was extracted through the apical incision. After lymphadenectomy, the sternum was sutured with metallic stitches and the anterior defect of the thoracic wall was repaired with a synthetic patch.

Outcome:

Postoperative pain remained under control and never exceeded four on the visual analog scale. Neither intraoperative nor postoperative complications were observed and the patient was discharged after nine days. The patient's pathological result was ypT0N0M0. At the twelve-month follow-up, the patient was free from disease and post-thoracotomy syndrome.

Diagnosis: Allergy to ketamine and morphine

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to our hospital with a diagnosis of chronic rhinosinusitis. He had a history of multiple anaphylactic reactions during surgical procedures and eye examinations performed under general anesthesia at various hospitals, since he was 11 years old. The patient and his relatives had been reluctant to come to the hospital due to extreme fear and discouragement for 10 years after his last episode of anaphylaxis during eye enucleation at the age of 29.

Following his evaluation by the allergist, skin testing was performed for morphine and ketamine, using standard concentrations according to the EAACI recommendation. The first test results were negative but due to his history of severe reactions, further testing was recommended 6 weeks later. The second round of skin tests was positive for ketamine and morphine. Hence, we provided a recommendation for the patient to avoid ketamine and morphine for future anesthetic procedures. The ADR card was updated accordingly, and alternative drugs were suggested, tested negative and were used for the patient's sinus surgery, which was performed without any adverse reactions.

The patient was advised to maintain close observation for allergic symptoms in the case of future anesthetic procedures with alternative drugs. The patient expressed full understanding of the recommendations and was discharged home in good condition. A comprehensive discharge report was provided to the patient and his carers.

Discharge Medications:

None recommended.

Follow-up:

The patient is advised to follow-up with the allergist as needed.

Hospital Course:
The patient was referred to the Endocrinology Department for follow-up of an abdominal PGL that had been operated during childhood and subsequently relapsed. He had undergone two surgical interventions that were unsuccessful in completely removing the tumor mass. The patient had a 123I-MIBG scintigraphy which was negative and a 68GaDOTATATE-PET that revealed the tumor to express somatostatin receptors. Due to this, he underwent therapy with somatostatin analogs and a radiometabolic treatment with 90Y-DOTATATE. At the time of referral to our Endocrinology Department, the patient had local relapse of the disease, associated with multiple bone metastases. The biochemical evaluation showed high chromogranin-A levels, urinary catecholamines, and urinary vanilmandelic acid. Radiological assessment revealed evidence of progressive abdominal disease. Therapy with somatostatin analogs was continued and therapy with sunitinib was started.

Current Condition:
Patient's condition has been stable since initiation of therapy with somatostatin analogs, which has been continued along with sunitinib.

Discharge Condition:
The patient has not been discharged and will continue as an outpatient in the Endocrinology Department.

Follow-up:
The patient will continue therapy with somatostatin analogs and sunitinib as an outpatient. Due to the presence of a mutation in the SDHB gene, the patient's family members have undergone genetic testing. The patient's mother and sister resulted negative, and further genetic workup of the father will be pursued. The patient will continue to be closely monitored by the Endocrinology Department.

Discharge Summary:

Hospital Course:
The 62-year-old male was admitted to the hospital with a complaint of abdominal pain, vomiting, and ambulatory dysfunction. The initial examination showed no abnormalities. The patient was suspected to have viral gastroenteritis, and hence he was hospitalized for dehydration management. The patient's nausea and vomiting improved after admission, but it was noted that he was leaning backwards and to the right when standing or attempting to ambulate on the first day of hospitalization.

Diagnostic Evaluations:
The neurology service was consulted after assessing the patient's condition on his second day of admission. A CT angiogram of the head and neck showed a congenitally hypoplastic left vertebral artery and no other abnormality was observed in the vertebrobasilar system. MRI of the brain showed acute/subacute infarct in the right cerebellar hemisphere. The echocardiogram showed moderate diastolic dysfunction with trace aortic regurgitation.

Clinical Impression:
The patient was diagnosed with acute/subacute infarct in the right cerebellar hemisphere secondary to chronic atherosclerotic disease that had extended and caused APS. The left-sided dysmetria was observed, which further indicated his neurological impairment.

Hospital Treatment:
The patient was monitored on telemetry for several days without any events or abnormalities noted. He was started on a scheduled antiemetic regimen of metoclopramide 10 mg four times daily and ondansetron 8 mg every eight hours that yielded positive results. Within one day, the patient's nausea and vomiting were controlled, and he was able to eat without difficulty. The patient was successfully discharged from the hospital to rehabilitation.

Follow-up Recommendations:
The patient is recommended to follow up with the neurology service as an outpatient and undergo regular checkups to monitor his neurological function and the progression of his cerebrovascular disease. He is also advised to maintain strict blood glucose control and hypertension management. The family members are recommended to observe the patient's activities, as he is more vulnerable to falls.

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 20-year-old female diagnosed with pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) and von Willebrand Disease (vWD) who presented to the clinic at 13 weeks of gestation. The patient underwent a caesarian section at 26 weeks of gestation due to decompensated PAH and fetal bradycardia. Post-procedure, the patient went into cardiac arrest and was placed on femoral-femoral venoarterial (VA) ECMO for life support. She remained in the ICU for an extended period of time and required continuous inotropes and vasopressors support. After a prolonged stay in the hospital, she was discharged on postoperative day 101.

Discharge Diagnosis:

1. Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH)
2. Von Willebrand Disease (vWD)

Procedures:

1. emergent caesarian section
2. femoral-femoral venoarterial (VA) ECMO
3. pericardial window

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient was diagnosed with PAH and vWD, and presented at 13 weeks of gestation. Despite counseling sessions, the patient decided to continue her pregnancy, and all teratogenic medications were stopped while tadalafil and treprostinil were continued. The patient was admitted and transitioned from SC treprostinil to intravenous epoprostenol. The patient did well on this regimen until 25 weeks of gestation when she presented to the emergency department with complaints of recurrent hemoptysis and acute respiratory distress. Due to concerns of further decompensation, an emergent caesarian section was performed, and a healthy infant was delivered. However, during the closure of the hysterotomy, the patient went into cardiac arrest and was placed on VA ECMO for life support. The patient remained in the ICU for a prolonged period and required continuous inotropes and vasopressors support. After successful management, the patient was weaned off ECMO support and had a prolonged stay in the hospital. The patient was subsequently discharged on postoperative day 101.

Hospital Course:
A 66-year-old female patient was admitted to the Department of Periodontics, M. S. Ramaiah Dental College and Hospital, Bangalore, with the complaint of burning sensation in the gums and bleeding gums for the past one month.

Medical History:
The patient had no relevant drug history or significant medical history. She had not received any dental treatment before.

Examination Findings:
On extra oral examination, the patient had some obvious skin lesions on the scalp and a hyperkeratotic plaque behind her left ear. Intra oral examination of gingiva revealed reddish marginal, attached gingiva and interdental papilla in both maxillary and mandibular anterior region with desquamation of epithelium present in certain regions.

Diagnosis:
Based on the clinical and histopathologic features, the lesion was suggestive of discoid lupus erythematosus.

Treatment:
Hand scaling was performed as gently as possible in order to minimize tissue disruption. Soft tooth brush and mouth rise (chlorhexidine 0.12%) was recommended. Triamcinolone acteonide oral paste was advised to apply two to three times per day.

Follow-up:
The patient was recalled for follow-up and maintenance.

Hospital Course: The patient, a 50-year-old male, presented at Dankook University Dental Hospital with complaints of pain and swelling at his left TMJ and numerous radiopaque masses around the joint on panoramic radiography. Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [redacted]
Medical Record Number: [redacted]
Sex: Male
Age: 44

Admission Date: [redacted]
Discharge Date: [redacted]

Diagnosis: Severe maxillary atrophy and previous mandibular all-on-6 rehabilitation with current peri-implantitis

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to our department due to complaints of mobility on the inferior implant-supported prosthesis and the superior prosthetic bridge, causing difficulty in chewing and speech. The patient reported a history of congenital dental agenesis, with complete mandibular rehabilitation with six implants and a superior bilateral canine to central incisor prosthetic bridge.
Clinical examination and orthopantomography indicated a combined horizontal and vertical osseous deficiency and active peri-implantitis in all six implants previously placed in the inferior arch, confirmed through cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT). Maxillary vertical and alveolar ridge deficiency was also noted. Bimaxillary custom-made implants were proposed, using an innovative design in the mandible including areas of endosseous support for adequate osseointegration.

The patient underwent surgery under general anesthesia. On the maxilla, a crestal incision was performed, exposing the anterior nasal spine, the pyriform apertures, the canine fossae, the zygomatic buttresses, and the posterolateral maxillae. The implant was tested and fixed with osteosynthesis screws. On the mandible, a crestal incision was performed around the arch to the contralateral side. The implant was tested, fixed with osteosynthesis screws, and bone grafting was carried out in the endosseous zone.

Abutments were placed, and flaps were closed. Prosthetic impressions were taken immediately after closure, and a provisional prosthesis was successfully adapted 12 h later, before patient discharge.

Follow-Up:

Over 1 year and 3 months of follow-up time, there were no complications. The patient reported excellent implant stability, adequate masticatory function, no implant exposure, and absence of pain.

Summary:

The patient with severe maxillary atrophy and previous mandibular all-on-6 rehabilitation with current peri-implantitis underwent bimaxillary custom-made implants. The surgery was successful with no complications, and the patient reported significant improvement in implant stability, masticatory function, and absence of pain after 1 year and 3 months of follow-up time.

Diagnosis: Severe upper jaw bone loss and a previous lower jaw six-implant treatment with infection around the implants
Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted because the lower bridge and the upper prosthetic bridge felt loose, making chewing and speaking hard.
The patient had a history of missing teeth from birth, which is called congenital dental agenesis.
There were six implants in the lower jaw and a bridge from canine to central incisor in the upper jaw.
Exam and X-ray showed bone loss in both horizontal and vertical directions of the jaw.
The images also revealed active infection around all six lower implants, confirmed by a 3-D scan.
The upper jaw also showed vertical bone loss and a thin alveolar ridge, which is the bone that holds teeth.
A custom-made implant set for both jaws was planned to replace the missing bone and improve function.
The design in the lower jaw includes bone-anchored areas to help the implants fuse with the bone.
The patient had surgery under general anesthesia to place the new implants in both jaws.
In the upper jaw, a gum cut exposed the front nasal spine, nasal opening, cheek areas, and rear jaw bone.
The implant was checked and secured with small screws to hold it firmly in place.
In the lower jaw, a similar cut was made around the arch to the opposite side.
The implant was checked, secured with screws, and bone graft was placed in the bone-anchored area.
After that, the abutments were attached, the gum flaps were closed, and impressions were taken right away.
A temporary prosthesis was fitted 12 hours later, before the patient left the hospital for testing.
Follow-Up:
Over one year and three months of follow-up, there were no problems such as infection or implant failure.
The patient said the implants felt stable, chewing worked well, there was no implant exposure, and there was no pain.
Summary:
The patient had severe upper jaw bone loss and a previous lower jaw six-implant treatment with infection around the implants.
The patient received custom-made implants for both jaws to replace the missing bone and restore function.
The surgery went well with no complications, and the patient recovered without issues during the hospital stay.
After one year and three months, the patient reported much better implant stability, better chewing ability, and no pain.

The patient was advised to avoid smoking, alcohol, and any activities that could lead to excessive stress on the neck and to maintain proper oral hygiene. She was advised to watch for any signs of infection, such as fever, chills, and redness or swelling around the incision site. If any of these symptoms occur, she should seek medical attention immediately.

Follow-Up:
The patient was advised to follow up with her primary care physician within the next seven days for a review of her medical condition and to manage her medications. The patient should continue to be monitored closely for any potential complications relating to the abscess and internal jugular vein ligation.

Discharge Summary:

Hospital Course: The patient underwent a simple orthodontic preprosthetic treatment to address a scissor-bite between the upper and lower second molars on the right side. A buccal orthodontic button was placed on the crown of the upper second molar and another button on the lingual surface of the lower second molar. An orthodontic elastic was worn all day, except during meals and oral hygiene. The patient was recalled monthly to monitor tooth movements. After a few months, the patient experienced discomfort in the gum at the level of the second lower molar, where the rubber band was applied. A clinical examination showed slight mobility of the lower molar and a periapical radiograph revealed a small periodontal angular defect mesial to the molar. Elastic use was suspended, and the lingual button removed. Further treatment included subgingival root planning under anesthesia, chlorhexidine gel insertion, and a systemic antibiotic therapy. A week later, rather than an improvement, significant mobility of the lower molar was observed and the worsening of the mesial angular defect affecting the root length was noted. Intraoral elastic around the root was discovered during the extraction procedure, which was not visible in the radiological examination.

Condition at Discharge: The patient was discharged after extraction of the second lower molar.

Discharge Medications: None prescribed.

Discharge Instructions: The patient was advised to maintain a good oral hygiene routine, including regular brushing and flossing. The patient was instructed to avoid hard and sticky foods for a few days after the extraction and to avoid using a straw for about a week. The patient was asked to contact the dentist if any signs of infection, such as swelling, fever, or pain, were observed.

Follow-Up Care: The patient is advised to schedule regular dental check-ups to ensure the good health of the remaining teeth and implant success.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission Date: [Date of admission]
Discharge Date: [Date of discharge]

Chief Complaint: Fracture of jaw and missing central incisors

History of Present Illness: A 12-year-old female with a history of road side accident was brought to the Department of Oral Surgery with the chief complaint of fracture of lower jaw in parasymphysis region and missing both central incisors. She had no history of orthodontic treatment. On examination, the patient was found to have impacted both lower canine and crowding in both jaws.

Hospital Course: Nonextraction treatment was planned, and the treatment objective was to repair the jaw fracture, regain space for prosthetic replacement of central incisors, relieve crowding, and maintain the existing class I molar relationship. After wiring of the arch to hold the fracture segment on the same day, bone plating was done when the patient was fit for surgery. Once the fracture segment was healed, fixed mechanotherapy was started with Roth, 0.022'' appliances in both maxillary and mandibular arches to align, level and create space for the central incisors. The mandibular canines were kept in place as they were close to the screw and disimpaction was challenging due to their location on the fracture line. Riding pontics were prepared, assessed, and adjusted to the rectangular archwire by stainless steel ligature. The esthetic and smile of the patient was improved after ligating riding pontics.

Summary: The 12-year-old female patient with a history of fracture of lower jaw in parasymphysis region and missing both central incisors due to a road side accident successfully underwent the nonextraction treatment plan. After fixing the fracture segment, the patient's malocclusion was treated with fixed mechanotherapy which aligned and leveled both maxillary and mandibular arches and created space for the central incisors, while keeping the mandibular canines in place due to their location on the fracture line. The final step of the treatment was the preparation and ligating of riding pontics that significantly improved the patient's esthetic and smile.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [Redacted]
Age: 41
Sex: Female
Admission Date: [Redacted]
Discharge Date: [Redacted]
Admission Diagnosis: Suspected COVID-19 infection

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with symptoms of a dry cough, shortness of breath, chest tightness, fever, chills, myalgias, mild sore throat, and watery diarrhea. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) tests ruled out several respiratory infections, but a COVID-19 test came back positive after intubation. A computed tomography scan of the chest showed bilateral infiltrates. The patient was then started on empiric treatment with IV vancomycin, piperacillin-tazobactam, azithromycin, and hydroxychloroquine.

Over time, her condition worsened, and she developed severe acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), requiring higher mechanical ventilation settings and continuous prone positioning. Liver enzymes continually increased, and acute kidney injury occurred due to decreased organ perfusion. 

The patient was given high-dose vitamin C, zinc sulfate, and tocilizumab to control her cytokine storm. Despite initial management, her condition still declined, and continuous venovenous hemodialysis (CVVHD) was started for renal failure, along with venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO).

During the VV-ECMO treatment, the patient developed HIT and ischemia in her fingers and toes bilaterally. Although the HIT panel returned negative, Argatroban was administered as anticoagulation due to the significant drop in her platelet count on heparin products. Despite ongoing hemodynamic stability, the patient ultimately passed away four days after the initiation of VV-ECMO due to an asystole rhythm.

Discharge Plan:
The patient passed away during her VV-ECMO treatment. Hospice and supportive care were provided to the family. The next of kin was advised to follow up with her primary care provider for any further concerns.  No further treatment or diagnostic evaluations were scheduled.

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 6-year-old female with mosaic Turner syndrome who was referred for cardiac evaluation secondary to her genetic condition. Physical exam revealed short stature, nevi on skin, and a broad-based gait. An echocardiogram was remarkable for severe apical and posterior wall left ventricular hypertrophy with a spongy appearance. The patient is being managed conservatively since she is clinically asymptomatic. Her follow-up visits with cardiology show preserved cardiac function (ejection fraction of 54% on the right side and 53% on the left side). She is receiving multidisciplinary care as an outpatient.

The patient is recommended to receive continuous follow-up visits with cardiology to monitor her cardiac function. She is advised to continue with multidisciplinary care as an outpatient.

Medical History:
The patient is a 24-year-old male with severe Hemophilia A. He has been receiving Factor VIII replacement therapy three times a week but reported missing the last three doses.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with left medial elbow pain and swelling, along with pain and paresthesias in the ring and small fingers. On examination, there was moderate swelling and tenderness to palpation over the medial epicondyle. Sensation was decreased over the small and ring fingers in the ulnar nerve distribution with intrinsic strength decreased to 4/5 on the MRC grading scale. There was a positive Tinel’s sign at the elbow. The patient was administered Factor VIII and admitted for observation. Following day, the symptoms worsened, and he was taken to the operating room for surgical decompression. The procedure involved decompression of the ulnar nerve at several sites around the elbow. There were no neuroma noted or obvious constriction deformity as seen with chronic compression. 

Discharge Condition: 
The patient was discharged from the hospital and followed up by hematology for maintenance of his Factor VIII levels.

Follow-up Plan: 
At the 6-week follow-up, the patient subjectively reported doing well without activity restrictions, with his paresthesias having completely resolved, and grip strength returned to full 5/5. 

Additional Information:
Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for which identifying information is included in this article.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Date of admission: [REDACTED]
Date of discharge: [REDACTED]
Admitting Diagnosis: Basilar Artery Aneurysm
Discharge Diagnosis: Basilar Artery Aneurysm treated with flow diverting Pipeline stent

Hospital Course:
A 60-year-old male was admitted for investigation of headaches, and a contrast enhanced computed tomography scan of his brain revealed a 20 mm × 10 mm basilar artery aneurysm that was not surgically operable. His past medical history included coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, a metallic mitral valve, a prior ischaemic stroke, hypertension and a previous provoked deep vein thrombosis.

The patient underwent a right CCVAB to allow endovascular access to the aneurysm. The mid portion of the right common carotid artery was exposed in the neck above the omohyoid muscle via a longitudinal incision anterior to the medial border of the sternocleidomastoid. The long saphenous vein was harvested from the left thigh, anastomosed in an end to side fashion to the CCA and to the vertebral artery. A contrast enhanced computed tomography scan confirmed patency of the graft on the Day 1 post procedure.

In the early post-operative period, the patient had ongoing hypotension that was likely secondary to cerebral autoregulation of blood pressure post CCVAB. The patient also suffered from a line sepsis, which delayed the second stage of the operation. Six weeks after the bypass procedure, the patient underwent an angiogram from the right common femoral artery. Access to the basilar artery aneurysm was achieved via a coaxial system consisting of a 6F long sheath to the origin of the anastomosis, a 5F intermediate guide within the graft and a 025 microcatheter to deliver a 3 × 35 mm flow diverting Pipeline stent to exclude the basilar artery aneurysm. There were no significant complications, and the patient recovered well.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient is advised to follow-up with their primary care physician and to continue taking any prescribed medications. They are also advised to monitor for any signs of fever, swelling, or redness at the site of the surgery. Additionally, they are advised to avoid any strenuous activities or heavy lifting for at least 4-6 weeks.

Follow-up:
The patient is advised to follow-up with their primary care physician within 2-4 weeks for a routine check-up. The patient should also schedule a follow-up appointment with their surgeon to monitor their condition and to ensure appropriate care.

Discharge Summary:

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
The patient, a 43-year-old man with gluten intolerance and bullous dermatosis, presented with progressive vision loss, photosensitivity, foreign body sensation, and burning sensation in both eyes. He had a previous diagnosis of dermatitis herpetiformis and was undergoing treatment with dapsone and prednisolone.

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient underwent a keratolimbal allograft transplantation and cryopreserved amniotic membrane implant in his right eye due to the presence of corneal melt. Unfortunately, he persisted with severe ocular surface disease, leading to retinal and choroidal detachments in both eyes. Despite undergoing IVIG therapy, the patient's dermatologic lesions were the only ones that improved significantly. The left eye slightly improved to hand motion but the right eye displayed LP without color discrimination.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS:
Severe ocular surface disease with retinal and choroidal detachments in both eyes.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
The patient has been advised to follow up regularly with the ophthalmologist for monitoring and management of his ocular condition. Additionally, he has been advised to avoid any activities that may cause further damage to his eyes, including prolonged computer and smartphone use, UV exposure, and dusty environments. The patient has been informed about artificial tears and other lubricants that can provide relief for his eye symptoms.

FOLLOW-UP:
The patient will follow up with the ophthalmologist per the provider's recommendations.

Discharge Summary for Patient with Achalasia Cardia

Demographics:
- Patient is a 43-year-old Indian man

Reason for Admission:
- Patient was referred to the gastroenterology department because of dysphagia for both solids and liquids, recurrent vomiting, regurgitating undigested food, and considerable weight loss.

Medical History:
- No significant medical history was reported.

Hospital Course:
- Ultrasound scan of the abdomen showed normal findings.
- Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed a dilated esophageal body and no peristalsis was seen, while the lower esophageal sphincter was tightly closed.
- Retroflexion of the endoscope revealed no mass lesion in the esophagogastric junction or in the cardia.
- Chest X-ray showed an air bubble below the left hemi-diaphragm in the gastric region.
- Barium swallow showed dilated esophagus, "bird beak" appearance of the distal esophagus, and an esophageal air fluid level.
- Diagnosis of primary achalasia cardia was made based on clinical history, examination, upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, and barium swallow X-ray.
- Pneumatic balloon dilatation of the lower esophageal sphincter was performed successfully under sedation with no complications.
- Chest X-ray after the procedure showed two air bubbles under the left hemi-diaphragm in the gastric region, the first of which was confirmed as a colonic air bubble and the second as a gastric air bubble.

Discharge Status:
- Patient was discharged after a successful pneumatic balloon dilatation of the lower esophageal sphincter with no complications.

Instructions:
- Follow up with the primary care physician for further management of achalasia cardia.
- Provide a detailed report of this hospital course to the primary care physician.

A balloon dilatation of the valve at the bottom of the food pipe was performed successfully under sedation.

Hospital Course:
The 45-year-old female with a history of asthma and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) presented to our clinic with a chronic productive cough. She had previously been treated with levofloxacin, which improved her symptoms but they recurred after discontinuing the antibiotic. Chest X-ray and CT scan revealed infiltrates in both lungs, along with bronchiectatic changes in the lower lobes. Her autoimmune screen came back negative for rheumatoid arthritis and Sjogren's syndrome. Immunoglobulins were elevated; however, alpha one antitrypsin and immunoglobulin E (IgE) were normal. Chronic recurrent aspiration was suspected, and esophageal pH monitoring with manometry confirmed the suspicion of chronic aspiration from severe acid reflux with an elevated DeMeester score. Bronchoscopy was performed to rule out obstructive disease and obtain samples to rule out mycobacterial disease, which were positive for heavy growth of Achromobacter xylosoxidans, subspecies denitrificans. The bacteria was responsive to levofloxacin and other antibiotics such as amikacin, cefepime, ceftazidime, gentamicin, meropenem, piperacillin/tazobactam, tobramycin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, but resistant to ciprofloxacin, cefotaxime, and aztreonam.

Management:
Airway clearance techniques with percussion and flutter valve and bronchodilator therapy with hypertonic saline nebulizers were initiated, and the patient was started on a 3-week course of levofloxacin. One month after stopping antibiotics, her symptoms recurred, and again, levofloxacin was initiated for two more weeks with good clinical response. She was referred for surgical intervention to address ongoing injury to the airways and prevent aspiration insult.

Discharge Condition:
The patient was discharged in stable condition.

Follow-Up:
The patient was advised to continue airway clearance techniques with percussion, flutter valve, and bronchodilator therapy with hypertonic saline nebulizers.

Other Notes:
This discharge summary does not contain any clinical information or details such as medication names, dosages, treatment plans, diagnoses, procedures, or test results that are not explicitly mentioned within the given case report.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 9-year-old male

Date of Admission: [Date]

Date of Discharge: [Date]

Admission Diagnosis: Continuous pain in the lower left back tooth region for 1 week

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient presented with a chief complaint of continuous pain in the lower left back tooth region for 1 week. Clinical examination revealed large disto-occlusal caries on tooth 36, with exaggerated response to vitality tests (sensibility) with lingering pain. Intraoral periapical (IOPA) radiograph revealed blunderbuss canals for both mesial and distal roots. A diagnosis of irreversible pulpitis was formulated.

Following administration of local anesthesia (2% Lignox with adrenaline, 2% Lignox with adrenaline, Indoco Remedies Ltd, Mumbai, India) and rubber dam application, access cavity was made, and three canals were located. Mesial canal orifices were slit-shape and the distal orifice was large oval-shaped. In the mesial canals, #30 k-file (Mani Inc., Tochigi, Japan) was snugly fit in the middle third. Working length for the distal canal was determined using the bent file technique, and confirmed radiographically. In the distal canal, #80 k-file was loose and going beyond the apex without any resistance. Circumferential filing was done in the distal root, and the mesial root was minimally prepared till #30 k-file. 5 mL of 3% sodium hypochlorite solution (Parcan, Septodont Healthcare India Pvt. Ltd, Maharashtra, India) was used as an irrigant for each canal along with normal saline. Triple antibiotic paste (TAP) (metronidazole, ciprofloxacin, and minocycline) was made as paste slurry and placed inside the canal using lentulospiral (Mani Inc., Tochigi, Japan) and k files.

After 3 weeks, TAP was removed, and irrigation was performed using 10 mL of 3% sodium hypochlorite (Dentwash, Prime Dental Products Pvt Ltd; Thane, Mumbai, India), followed by 10 mL of saline and a final flush of 10 mL of ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) (Dentwash, Prime, Bhiwandi, Maharashtra, India). Bleeding was induced in the mesial root canals using a #15 k file by taking it beyond the apex. Platelet-rich fibrin (PRF) was separated from the blood corpuscles and squeezed between sterile gauze pieces to remove the trapped fluids. Following which, the PRF membrane was separated into small fragments using sterile scissors. A metal plugger (Manipal instruments, Parkala, India) with a rubber stopper set at 1 mm short of working length was used to pack the first increment inside the distal root. On reaching the desired length, a 0.5 mm diameter metal plugger was used in circumferential tapping manner to pack the PRF, and a flat surface was achieved. Following which, the butt end of sterile No. 80 paper point (DiaDent, Chungcheongbuk-do, Korea) was used to compact the PRF further and to remove any remaining entrapped fluid. Next increment was placed in a similar way after shortening the length. Once the entire canal was filled till the orifice with the PRF, MTA was packed inside the pulp chamber to a thickness of 3 mm. Before temporizing, a moist cotton pellet was placed, and the patient was recalled the next day for the placement of Glass Ionomer Cement (GC type 2, GC Corporation, Tokyo, Japan) seal and Composite restoration (3M Z350 XT, 3M ESPE Dental Products, MN, USA).

The patient received follow-up visits at 6 months, 1 year, 2 years, 3 years and 5 years, during which pulp sensibility tests done using Endofrost (Coltène/Whaledent Private Ltd, Raigad, Maharashtra) were negative for the tooth at all recall visits. Follow-up radiographs at the 2-year recall showed complete closure of the root end along with increased root length. The 5-year recall radiograph showed no signs of pathology, and canals were patent and not obliterated. The patient was completely asymptomatic during all the follow-up visits.

Discharge Diagnosis: Irreversible pulpitis, treated with maturogenesis technique using triple antibiotic paste and platelet-rich fibrin.

Management Plan: None. The patient was discharged in good condition and advised to continue oral hygiene practices.

The patient came in with ongoing pain in the lower left back tooth for one week.

X-ray showed wide-open canals in both roots of the infected tooth, confirming the diagnosis before treatment.

A small metal file size 30 fit snugly in the middle of the side canals.
The length of the back canal was measured with a bent-file method and confirmed by X-ray.
In the back canal, a size 80 file moved freely past the tip with no resistance.
The canals were cleaned with a bleach-like fluid and normal saline to remove debris and bacteria.
A paste made from three antibiotics (metronidazole, ciprofloxacin, minocycline) was placed inside the canals to kill infection.
After three weeks, the antibiotic paste was removed and the canals were flushed with more bleach-like fluid, saline, and EDTA.
Bleeding was started in the side canals by moving a small file past the tip.
The blood clot material (PRF) was separated, squeezed to remove extra fluid, and cut into tiny pieces.
A metal plugger with a rubber stop was used to pack the first piece of clot into the back canal.
A smaller metal plugger tapped around to pack more clot and make a flat surface.
A sterile paper point pressed the clot further and removed remaining fluid to ensure a clean fill.
Additional clot pieces were added the same way, shortening the length each time until the canals were full.
When the canals were full to the opening, a filling material (MTA) was placed 3 mm thick in the pulp chamber.
A cotton pellet was placed, and the patient returned the next day for a white filling and a tooth-colored filling.
The patient was checked at 6 months, 1 year, 2 years, 3 years and 5 years to monitor healing of the treated tooth.
At each visit, nerve feeling tests were negative, meaning no pain response and the tooth felt normal.
