Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Date of Admission: [Redacted]
Date of Discharge: [Redacted]

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 68-year-old Japanese man, underwent resection surgery for a leiomyosarcoma at the mediastinum. Due to dissemination in the pleura, the patient received radiation therapy and a second operation. Ten months post-surgery, the patient developed pain and numbness in the left upper limb, and an enhanced solid lesion and a non-enhanced cystic lesion were observed in the apex of the left lung using contrast enhanced CT scan. Ablation using radiofrequency ablation (RFA) was performed after radiation and chemotherapy were deemed ineffective, and surgery was thought to carry a high risk of bleeding. The patient underwent RFA with a LeVeen electrode, with retractable hooks opened for ablation. A total of three ablations were performed, with the output started at 20 W and increased by 10 W every 2 minutes in each session. The procedure was performed under local anesthesia to monitor the appearance of sharp pain of the left upper limb. A maximum output of 80 W and total ablation time of 57 minutes and 14 seconds were achieved. Contrast enhanced CT performed two days after RFA showed that the enhanced solid lesion in the tumor was smaller in size compared to pre-RFA CT. The patient's pain disappeared for approximately 3 months, accompanied by an improvement in motor function disorder. However, the pain of the left upper limb reappeared due to growth of the tumor, three months after RFA.

Condition at Discharge:

The patient's pain had reappeared, and thus, he was discharged from the hospital with instructions to follow up with his healthcare provider.

Instructions:

The patient is advised to follow up with his healthcare provider regarding his condition.

Reason for Admission:
The patient was admitted with a complaint of painless hematuria with clots of 2 month's duration.

History:
At 3 years of age, the patient was diagnosed with retinoblastoma in both eyes and was treated with 18 cycles of radiation to both the orbits.

Hospital Course:
On examination, the patient had enlarged inguinal lymph nodes that were found to be inflammatory on biopsy. Ultrasonography and computed tomographic urography showed a large (6 cm × 6 cm) mass arising from the right anterolateral wall of the urinary bladder. The upper tract was normal. Cystoscopy revealed a large nodular lesion arising from the right anterolateral wall and hence only transurethral biopsy was performed. On histopathology, a high-grade sarcoma with only spindle cells and no epithelial cells was noted with possible differential diagnosis of high-grade sarcoma (leiomyosarcoma/malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor) and sarcomatoid variant of urothelial carcinoma (carcinosarcoma).

Diagnosis:
On immunohistochemistry (IHC), the tumor was strongly positive for cytoplasmic smooth muscle actin and cytoplasmic vimentin, and focally positive for cytoplasmic desmin and cytokeratin, suggesting leiomyosarcoma. Further, negative IHC for epithelial membrane antigen and S100 ruled out carcinosarcoma and malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor, respectively, thus confirming urinary bladder leiomyosarcoma.

Treatment and Follow-up:
The patient refused further genetic analysis and was not willing for radical surgery. He was referred to the oncologist for further management and subsequently lost to follow-up.

Final Diagnosis:
Urinary bladder leiomyosarcoma with enlarged inguinal lymph nodes.

Discharge Condition:
The patient is lost to follow-up.

HOSPITAL COURSE:
A 62-year-old male, a smoker, with a history of non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI), was admitted to the hospital. A loading dose of ticagrelor was administered, and the patient was transferred to the Cath lab. Coronary angioplasty with DES implantation was performed, and the patient showed no adverse reaction initially.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS:
Acute Bronchial Obstruction due to Ticagrelor

HOSPITAL COURSE SUMMARY:
Two hours after administration of ticagrelor, the patient developed strong anxiety followed by heavy dyspnea and generalised sweating. On auscultation, heavy bronchial obstruction was observed, and there was a significant drop in blood oxygen saturation. The patient was administered inhalation of beta-mimetics, cholinolytics, and corticosteroids, followed by corticosteroids intravenously. This treatment provided only partial relief for a short time and the respiratory attacks were recurrent and numerous, each time starting with a panic and anxiety. Finally, intravenous infusion of theophylline 200mg provided relief, and dyspnea episodes ceased to occur.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
The patient has been advised to stop the use of ticagrelor and switch to clopidogrel upon discharge from the hospital. The patient is requested to remain vigilant and inform the medical professional immediately if any adverse respiratory reaction recurs. Further pulmonary therapy is not required.

DISCHARGE CONDITION:
The patient has been discharged in a stable condition.

The patient is a 39-year-old Vietnamese male with no significant past medical history.

Chief Complaint:

The patient was admitted with an increased anion gap, an acute kidney injury, alkaline phosphatase, AST, ALT, ferritin, and a white blood cell count.

CT scan with contrast of the chest and abdomen showed a large, complex mass in the right lobe of the liver with multiple septations. Ultrasound of the abdomen showed a heterogeneous, hypoechoic, multiseptated hepatic mass with internal vascularity.

The patient was started on vancomycin and piperacillin/tazobactam with fluid resuscitation consisting of crystalloids.

The patient was transferred to the medical intensive care unit (MICU) due to tachypnea, tachycardia, and hypoxia.

ABG showed a pH of 7.34 and a bicarbonate of 14. The patient was placed on bilevel positive airway pressure ventilation and continued on antibiotics.

Repeat CT:
The repeat CT of the thorax and abdomen showed areas of consolidated infiltrate with some associated atelectatic change in the posterior right lower lobe.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging:
MRI showed a peripherally enhancing mass in the anterior segment of the right hepatic lobe that measured 3.5 cm x 3.3 cm with areas of central septations.

Blood Cultures:
Blood cultures grew Klebsiella pneumonia.

Discharge:
The patient was discharged after 11 days. A repeat CT of the abdomen showed interval improvement of the abscess. The patient was referred to an infectious disease specialist for follow-up.

Diagnosis: Brachial plexopathy

HOSPITAL COURSE

This patient was admitted to our facility for an intense pruritus on her right arm, which had been ongoing for six months. She also complained of right brachial paresis.

COMORBIDITIES

The patient has a known history of multiple myeloma.

DIAGNOSTIC TESTS AND PROCEDURES

Computed tomography of the cervical spine, magnetic resonance imaging, and electromyography of the brachial plexus were performed, which showed right cervical disc herniation with nerve root compression of C6-C7 and right brachial plexus inflammation (Parsonage-Turner syndrome).

DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS

The patient was treated with methylprednisolone aceponate cream 0.1% and oral hydroxyzine 25mg every 8 hours, which resulted in little improvement of the pruritus. Gabapentin was introduced at 900mg/day, which achieved optimal control after three months of follow-up.

FOLLOW-UP INSTRUCTIONS

The patient was referred to neurosurgery and oncology consultation for additional therapeutic orientation.

SUMMARY

The patient presented with brachial plexopathy, which is attributed to neoplastic infiltration of multiple myeloma. The treatment plan included the application of methylprednisolone aceponate cream 0.1% and oral hydroxyzine 25mg every 8 hours, along with the introduction of gabapentin at 900mg/day. The patient was referred to neurosurgery and oncology for further management.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 23-year-old female, presented with paroxysmal hypertension, palpitations, headache, diaphoresis and vomiting for 11 months. After extensive workup, the patient was diagnosed with retroperitoneal PGL and underwent surgical excision. Immunohistochemical staining revealed positive Syn and CgA, negative Melan A, HMB45 and α-inhibin, positive S-100 cells and positive CD31 vascular endothelium marker. Genetic testing showed that the patient carried a likely pathogenic missense mutation in exon 6 of the SDHB gene [c.563 T > C]. The patient was medically managed with doxazosin and metoprolol for 2 weeks as preoperative preparation. Clinical follow-up examinations were performed three times after surgery and showed no recurrence or symptoms of paroxysmal hypertension. The patient is recommended to have long-term follow-up and screening over her lifetime.

Retroperitoneal PGL was diagnosed, and the patient underwent surgical excision. Immunohistochemical staining and genetic testing were performed, which revealed positive Syn and CgA, negative Melan A, HMB45, α-inhibin, and a likely pathogenic missense mutation in exon 6 of the SDHB gene [c.563 T > C]. Preoperative preparation was managed with doxazosin and metoprolol. Clinical follow-up examinations showed no recurrence or symptoms of paroxysmal hypertension, and long-term follow-up and screening are recommended.

Hospital Course:

The 75-year-old male patient was admitted to our tertiary care center due to prolonged aPTT discovered during preoperative laboratory tests. Prior to admission, the patient reported bilateral parotid enlargement and cervical lymphadenopathies.

Medical History:

The patient had no significant medical history.

Diagnostic Findings:

Biological work-up showed normal kidney, liver, pancreas, and thyroid functions. Acute phase reactants and immunological tests were within normal range. The prolonged aPTT was confirmed with normal PT and found decreased FVIII plasma levels associated with positive anti-FVIII IgG4 autoantibodies. An axillary lymph node biopsy was performed, revealing benign follicular hyperplasia with elevated IgG4/IgG ratio and no evidence of lymphoma. Further laboratory tests showed elevated serum IgG4 levels with other IgG subclasses within normal range.

Treatment:

The patient was diagnosed with IgG4-RD-associated AHA and treated with oral prednisone 1mg/kg/day for both diseases. The treatment led to a regression of parotid and lymph node enlargement, a decrease in serum IgG4 levels, a progressive correction of FVIII and aPTT values, and a suppression of anti-FVIII plasma activity. Prednisone was then slowly tapered and discontinued after 9 months.

Follow-up:

Nine months after treatment withdrawal, the patient relapsed with a new increase in IgG4 serum levels without organ involvement and a decrease in FVIII plasma levels with elevated anti-FVIII autoantibodies but without bleeding. The patient was started on a new course of oral corticosteroids associated with 2 infusions of rituximab 1g, which led to a sustained remission. The patient had a total follow-up of 3 years after diagnosis.

Summary:

The patient was admitted to our tertiary care center due to prolonged aPTT. Diagnostic findings revealed IgG4-RD-associated AHA. The patient was treated with oral prednisone and achieved sustained remission with the addition of rituximab. The patient had a total follow-up of 3 years after diagnosis.

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 75-year-old man who came to the hospital because a blood clotting test was long before surgery. He also had swollen glands on both sides of his face and neck, noted before admission.
Medical History:
The patient had no major health problems, such as heart disease or diabetes, before admission.
Diagnostic Findings:
Tests showed normal kidney, liver, pancreas, and thyroid function, and normal inflammation markers, with no abnormal results.
Immune system tests were also normal, with no signs of autoimmune activity or abnormal proteins.
The prolonged clotting test was confirmed with a normal prothrombin time and low factor VIII levels.
Low factor VIII was linked to positive anti-factor VIII IgG4 antibodies, indicating an immune cause.
A lymph node biopsy under the arm showed benign growth with high IgG4/IgG ratio and no lymphoma.
Blood tests showed high IgG4 levels while other IgG subclasses remained within the normal range.
Treatment:
The patient was diagnosed with IgG4-related disease-associated acquired hemophilia A and started oral prednisone 1 mg/kg/day.
Treatment reduced swollen glands, lowered IgG4 levels, improved factor VIII and clotting time, and suppressed the harmful antibody.
Prednisone was slowly decreased and stopped after nine months of therapy to avoid side effects.
Follow-up:
Nine months after stopping prednisone, the patient relapsed with higher IgG4 blood levels but no organ swelling.
Factor VIII levels dropped again and anti-factor VIII antibodies rose, yet there was no bleeding.
The doctor started oral corticosteroids plus two rituximab infusions of 1 gram each to treat the relapse.
This treatment led to lasting remission of both the clotting disorder and the IgG4-related disease.
The patient was followed for a total of three years after diagnosis, with no further relapses.
Summary:
The patient came to the hospital because a prolonged clotting test was found before surgery.
Testing showed IgG4-related disease-associated acquired hemophilia A, a condition where antibodies attack a clotting factor.
The patient was treated with oral prednisone and later added rituximab to achieve lasting remission.
Follow-up continued for three years after diagnosis, with the patient staying in remission and no new symptoms.

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to our hospital with complaints of asymptomatic dark-colored lesions on his hands and feet and light-colored skin lesions involving the trunk for the past three years. Over time, these dark-colored lesions increased in number and involved other parts of his body. Dermatological examination revealed mildly atrophic hyperpigmented macules in a reticulate pattern. In addition, there were multiple hypopigmented macules widely distributed over the trunk and anterior aspect of both legs. The patient also had multiple pits on both palms, with breaks in dermatoglyphics, and multiple nonacne facial scars predominantly on the nose and malar areas. 

Diagnostic Assessment:

Skin biopsy from a hyperpigmented lesion on the dorsum of the hand revealed filiform elongation of rete ridges. Histopathology of the axillary lesion was similar except for features of follicular plugging. Melan-A stain confirmed increased melanocytes. Skin biopsy from the hypopigmented lesion on the left leg revealed decreased melanocytes. 

Treatment:

The patient was provided with medical advice and was advised to follow up for periodic monitoring. No further treatment was offered during the hospital stay. 

Diagnostic Conclusion:

The patient was diagnosed with a rare disorder characterized by hyperpigmented and hypopigmented macules in a reticulate pattern and multiple pits on the palms along with nonacne facial scarring. Clinically, this diagnosis resembles Dowling-Degos disease, which primarily affects people in their twenties and thirties. 

Follow Up:

The patient was advised to follow up for periodic monitoring. No further treatment was offered during the hospital stay.

These spots did not cause any symptoms and had been present for about three years. Over time, the dark spots increased in number and spread to other parts of the body. Skin exam showed slightly thin, dark spots in a net-like pattern on the trunk and limbs. Many light spots were spread over the chest and the front of both legs and body. The patient also had several small pits on both palms, with breaks in the skin lines. Several facial scars not from acne were seen mainly on the nose and both cheeks. Diagnostic Assessment: A biopsy of a dark spot on the back of the hand showed long, thin skin ridges. A biopsy from an underarm spot looked similar but had blocked hair follicles in the skin. A special stain showed more pigment cells in the dark spot biopsy sample taken from the hand. A biopsy of a light spot on the left leg showed fewer pigment cells than normal. Treatment: The patient received medical advice and was told to return for regular check-ups during recovery. No other treatment was given during the hospital stay because the condition was monitored only. Diagnostic Conclusion: The patient was diagnosed with a rare condition that causes dark and light spots in a net-like pattern. The condition also produces several pits on the palms and facial scars not from acne. This condition looks like Dowling-Degos disease, which usually appears in people in their 20s and 30s. Follow Up: The patient was told to return for regular check-ups to monitor the skin condition over time. No other treatment was given during the hospital stay because doctors chose observation only for safety.

The patient was discharged in stable condition.

Discharge Summary:

Patient name: not identified
Gender: Male
Age: 60 years

Medical History:
-15-year history of diabetes, medically controlled

Hospital Course:

The patient was referred to us with severe pain and decreased vision in both eyes two days after undergoing cataract surgery on the left eye and one month ago on the right eye. The patient had undergone phacoemulsification under topical anesthesia in both eyes one month apart with uneventful postoperative period after the first surgery. The patient presented with bilateral flat anterior chambers and high intraocular pressure (IOP) four hours after his cataract surgery. The patient was diagnosed and treated as malignant glaucoma and was given intravenous (IV) mannitol 20% (1-2 g/kg body weight), tab acetazolamide 250 mg thrice daily and timolol maleate 0.5% eye drops twice daily in both eyes (B/E), peripheral iridotomy in the right eye and YAG hyloidotomy in the right eye, and posterior capsulotomy in the left eye.

On further examination, visual acuity was finger counting at half meter in the right eye and one meter in the left eye. There was bilateral lid edema, conjunctival chemosis, corneal edema, shallow ACs, mid-dilated pupils, patent peripheral iridotomy in the right eye, in-the-bag posterior chamber pseudophakos with opening in the posterior capsule. IOP was 72 mmHg in the right eye and 68 mmHg in the left eye. Fundus was unclear. B-scan Ultrasonography revealed annular cilio-choroidal effusion in both eyes.

A possible drug reaction was suspected and the systemic drug list was reviewed. Acetazolamide, a sulphonamide derivative was suspected as the possible cause and was discontinued. Topical antiglaucoma medications along with atropine, topical steroids, and antibiotics were continued. Over the next two weeks, the patient's condition improved. Five weeks following the initial surgery, his vision was 20/20, N6 with correction and IOP 21 mm Hg in the right eye and 20 mm Hg in the left eye without medications. ACs were quiet with clear corneas in both eyes and gonioscopy showed open angles in both eyes. Fundus examination revealed healthy optic discs with 0.5:1 cup and resolved choroidals in both eyes.

Disposition: The patient's vision was stable and his condition had improved over the two weeks. The patient was discharged in good condition with instructions to follow up as an outpatient.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Name]
DOB: [Date of Birth]
Admission Date: [Admission Date]
Discharge Date: [Discharge Date]

Medical History:
The patient had a history of obesity and underwent anterior cervical discectomy and fusion five years prior.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to the emergency room with a persistent headache and was admitted to the hospital. A CT scan and MRI of the brain and spine showed extensive pneumocephalus and potential meningitis. After imaging and consultation with the neurosurgery team, the patient was found to have a CSF leak, and surgery was recommended.

The otolaryngology/rhinology team was consulted for further evaluation of the CSF leak. The patient was taken to the operating room for identification and repair of the CSF leak. The location of the potential defect was confirmed with intraoperative surgical navigation, and an area of mucosal thickening was noted. A small, pinpoint fistula with actively leaking CSF was also found in the posterior oropharynx.

The head and neck surgery team was asked to assist with repair of the fistula. An anterior neck approach to the cervical hardware was performed, and the anterior cervical hardware was removed, revealing a profuse CSF leak. The defect was repaired with DuraSeal followed by rotation of the right omohyoid muscle into the site of the defect between the prevertebral fascia and the oropharyngeal mucosa. The patient was then monitored in the neurosurgery intensive care unit.

Outcome:
The patient's headaches resolved, and repeat imaging showed resolution of the pneumocephalus. He remained in the ICU on bed rest with the lumbar drain open at 10 ml/hr for 5 days. The patient was then allowed to mobilize, and the lumbar drain was removed. He was subsequently discharged and continued to do well with no evidence of CSF leak on follow-up imaging.

Follow-up:
A repeat CT myelogram of the spine at 8 months showed no signs of persistent leak. The patient was advised to follow-up with his primary care provider for routine care.

Diagnosis:
CSF Leak

Procedure:
Repair of CSF Leak with anterior neck approach to cervical hardware and DuraSeal repair, followed by the rotation of right omohyoid muscle into the site of the defect.

Hospital Course:

The patient was a 43-year-old male with a 17-year history of paraplegia who presented with dark purple discoloration of the left second and third toes. He had been experiencing a cold sensation in both feet for the past year. The patient had a history of hypertension and was taking hydrochlorothiazide-valsartan, kallidinogenase, ranitidine, levosulpiride, phloroglucinol, and loxoprofen. Physical examination showed both feet were cold, although the pulse was palpable on ankles and heels bilaterally. A portable Doppler device showed a decrease in pulse signal intensity on the left side and prolonged capillary refilling time on both toes. Despite a vascular function test showing normal leg circulation levels, the skin over the left toes showed dark discoloration with skin necrosis. The patient's antihypertensive medication was switched to a calcium channel blocker, amlodipine besylate, to address suspicion of Raynaud's phenomenon. Within 3 days, the patient saw a decrease in cold sensation and normalization of capillary refilling time. The patient was admitted with complaints of nausea, vomiting, and epigastric pain. On examination, mild epigastric tenderness was noted. The patient had been experiencing intermittent epigastric discomfort for more than 12 months but had not sought medical attention until now. 

The differential diagnosis included peptic ulcer disease, malignancy, and gastritis. Tests revealed the presence of H. pylori infection and the patient underwent endoscopy. The endoscopic findings were consistent with moderate nodular mucosal changes throughout the entire gastric region, with the most prominent changes being in the gastric body and angle. Biopsies revealed increased intraepithelial lymphocytes without gland destruction. Immunohistochemistry showed these cells to be mostly positive for CD3 and CD8 but negative for CD4 or CD20.

Eradication therapy was started, but follow-up tests showed persistence of the H. pylori infection. The patient underwent a second eradication therapy, which was successful in resolving the infection. Clinical symptoms also resolved, and follow-up tests showed no evidence of recurrent infection or mucosal changes.

Summary:

The patient was admitted with complaints of nausea, vomiting, and epigastric pain. Endoscopy and biopsies revealed moderate nodular mucosal changes throughout the entire gastric region, with increased intraepithelial lymphocytes without gland destruction. Immunohistochemistry showed these cells to be mostly positive for CD3 and CD8 but negative for CD4 or CD20, consistent with gastritis. H. pylori infection was present and eradicated with a second course of treatment. The patient's symptoms resolved, and follow-up tests showed no evidence of recurrence or mucosal changes.

Hospital Course Summary:

Chief Complaint:
The patient presented with sudden onset breathlessness and right sided pleuritic chest pain.

History of Present Illness:
The patient had a painful swelling of his right leg while he was being treated in the hospital for recurrent episodes of ENL. On examination, the patient was dyspneic at rest without central cyanosis. He had leonine facies and generalized erythematous skin with multiple nodules. His right leg was swollen with pitting ankle edema while having normal arterial pulses. His respiratory system examination revealed a respiratory rate of 30 per minute and signs of right lower zone pleural effusion.

Past Medical History:
The patient had lepromatous leprosy following a positive slit skin smear for mycobacterium leprae. He was commenced on World Health Organization (WHO) multi-drug therapy (MDT) regimen for multi-bacillary (MB) leprosy, which was complicated by type II lepra reaction (ENL) with right sided panuveitis and treated with oral prednisolone. 

Review of Systems:
There was no history suggestive of past venous or arterial thrombosis and tendency to develop thrombosis in his family. Neurology revealed a glove and stocking sensory peripheral neuropathy. There was no organomegaly noted on abdominal examination.

Diagnostic Testing:
A venous doppler ultrasound of the lower limb confirmed a deep vein thrombosis in the right femoral vein. Subsequently, a computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) confirmed pulmonary emboli in the right and left main pulmonary arteries with right lower lobe lung collapse and a mild pleural effusion.

Treatment:
The patient was started on enoxaparin and warfarin concomitantly. Thalidomide and anti-leprosy therapy were stopped temporarily while low dose corticosteroid was continued. After one week, the patient's dyspnea and general condition improved.

Follow-up:
The patient was discharged and provided with instructions to follow up with his healthcare provider for ongoing treatment and monitoring.

Diagnosis: 
- Aphakic bullous keratopathy 
- Corneal scarring

Hospital Course: 
The patient underwent penetrating keratoplasty for aphakic bullous keratopathy and corneal scarring. The donor cornea was replaced due to a large dendritic-geographic epithelial ulcer noted immediately after placement. Perioperative administration of intravenous aciclovir was given. Postoperatively, the patient was started on systemic and local antiviral therapy, and local antibiotic treatment. The graft was clear and re-epithelialized at 1 week. Long term prophylactic acyclovir 400 mg was started. However, six months later the patient developed a geographic corneal ulcer involving the graft-host interface with keratic precipitates and corneal edema. The patient was treated with acyclovir 400 mg and topical aciclovir both five times a day for 2 weeks with resolution of the ulcer and residual scarring.

Summary: 
The patient who had aphakic bullous keratopathy and corneal scarring underwent a successful penetrating keratoplasty with the use of a donor corneoscleral disc. The initial donor corneoscleral disc was removed and replaced with a second donor corneoscleral disc which was available. The patient was treated with antiviral and antibiotic medications following the surgery. The patient developed a geographic corneal ulcer, which was treated successfully with antiviral medications. The patient was discharged with instructions for a follow-up within a week.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with various clinical symptoms including lethargy, muscle weakness, skin issues, abdominal distension, polyuria, and polydipsia. Blood work and urinalysis showed increased blood glucose levels, hypercholesterolemia, and glycosuria. After the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus was confirmed, the patient was treated with insulin glargine and a commercial diet for diabetic cats. The insulin dosage was adjusted, and the patient showed considerable improvement in clinical symptoms. An abdominal ultrasound revealed bilateral adrenal hyperplasia and hepatic steatosis. Further tests ruled out spontaneous hypersomatotropism, hyperthyroidism, and feline immunodeficiency virus and feline leukemia virus. However, spontaneous hyperadrenocorticism (HAC) was suspected and diagnosed based on clinical signs, increased urinary cortisol:creatinine ratio, and lack of suppression on the low-dose dexamethasone suppression test. A dosage of cabergoline was prescribed to address the HAC. After the second dose, the patient experienced clinical hypoglycemia that required emergency veterinary assistance. The symptoms of hypoglycemia were managed via appropriate treatment, and the patient was kept under medical observation for several hours. Following successful treatment and management of clinical symptoms, the patient was discharged.

Diagnosis:
1. Diabetes Mellitus
2. Spontaneous Hyperadrenocorticism (HAC)

Treatment:
1. Insulin glargine
2. Commercial diet for diabetic cats
3. Cabergoline

Condition at Discharge:
The patient had stable blood glucose levels and no clinical signs of diabetes mellitus or hypoglycemia. The HAC was treated with cabergoline and patient symptoms showed marked improvement. However, the patient experienced acute decompensation after seven months, and euthanasia was carried out upon the owner's request. 

Recommendations:
None provided due to the patient's clinical outcome.

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Hospital Course: 

The patient, a 45-year-old male, was admitted to the hospital with symptoms of left flank pain, hypoesthesia, and weakness at both lower extremities. Upon examination, the patient had motor weakness in both lower extremities and elevated deep tendon reflex of the right knee. Diagnostic tests indicated fracture of T8, T9 vertebral body by bone tumor, pathologic fracture of T9 vertebral body by bone tumor, T8–10 myelopathy, and cord compression.

The patient underwent T9 corpectomy and mesh cage insertion with T8–10 posterior screw fixation. Pathological examination confirmed a diagnosis of Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH). The patient underwent radiotherapy at T8–10 spine and showed remarkable improvement in motor weaknesses and hypoesthesia.

The patient has been followed for almost 6 years without any recurrence. Discharge instructions included follow-up care with the primary care physician and regular imaging surveillance to ensure no recurrence of the bone tumor. 

Overall, the patient received excellent medical care from the healthcare team and responded well to treatment.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:
A 75-year-old male patient was admitted to the hospital due to the development of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) following surgery to drain a peritonsillar abscess that had extended down to the hypopharynx. Upon admission, the patient exhibited decreased peripheral oxygen saturation and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, which were treated with noninvasive ventilation with a positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP). However, the patient's respiratory insufficiency continued to deteriorate, and after three days, the patient was intubated and treated with invasive ventilation. Two days later, the patient was tracheostomized, and CT scans of the lungs showed bilateral patchy infiltrates and dorsal consolidation extending from the cranial to caudal lung regions.

After six days of ARDS and three days of invasive continuous positive pressure ventilation (CPPV), a decision was made to apply continuous end-expiratory negative pressure ventilation (CENPV). During the first application, the patient's PaO2/FiO2 value increased significantly, and alveolar infiltrates showed impressive reduction. During the second application, the patient's PaO2/FiO2 value increased to more than 500 mmHg, indicating significant recruitment of lung volume without the use of any recruitment maneuvers. After five days of CENPV, the patient was weaned from the ventilator and discharged to the normal ward.

Summary of Treatment:
Upon admission, the patient received noninvasive ventilation with a positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) to improve their respiratory insufficiency. However, after the condition continued to deteriorate, the patient was treated with invasive continuous positive pressure ventilation (CPPV) followed by continuous end-expiratory negative pressure ventilation (CENPV), which improved the patient's respiratory status significantly. Following five days of CENPV, the patient was weaned from the ventilator and discharged to the normal ward.

Discharge Condition:
The patient's respiratory condition has significantly improved, and they have been discharged in stable condition. It is recommended that the patient continue to follow up with their primary care provider for further evaluation and monitoring. 

Follow-up Care:
The patient is recommended to maintain close follow-up care with their primary care provider. No further follow-up care is required from this hospital.

Admitting Diagnosis: Progressive Neuropathy

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient was admitted with complaints of involuntary facial twitching and weakness, loose skin, and a deep furrowed tongue which had been progressively worsening for four years. The symptoms resulted in paresthesia of the right hand, intermittent cramps on the right calf, and decreased sweating on both hands. Neurological exam revealed mild weakness in the orbicularis oculi and orbicularis oris muscles without any motor weakness or sensory changes observed in the four extremities. A family history of the same symptoms was found in his mother, maternal uncle, and two sisters but no non-Korean relatives. Electrophysiological studies, including nerve conduction study (NCS), electromyography (EMG), and autonomic function tests (AFTs), were performed which demonstrated signs of bilateral facial nerve dysfunction, chronic denervation of the cervical and lumbar regions, and sudomotor dysfunction. To identify the etiology of the undiagnosed neuropathy, whole-exome sequencing (WES) was performed following informed consent and it revealed the presence of a p.D214Y mutation in GSN.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS:
Progressive neuropathy with associated mutation in GSN

DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS:
[No medication information was provided in the case report]

FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS:
Follow-up with primary care physician recommended.

Patient: [Name]
Sex: Female
Age: 61 years old
Date of admission: [Date]
Date of discharge: [Date]
Diagnosis: Papillary Fibroelastoma (PF)

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted with recurrent paroxysmal pleuritic chest pain and severe dyspnea. Pulmonary CT angiography did not reveal any emboli, and cardiac tests showed a mobile mass attached to the septal tricuspid valve (TV) leaflet, measuring 1.3 × 0.9 × 1.1 cm with tricuspid regurgitation. A differential diagnosis of papillary fibroelastoma (PF) versus cardiac myxoma was entertained. Cardiac surgery was advised due to the established recurrent embolic potential of the tumor and size (>1 cm).

Surgery:

Shave excision of the sessile mass and TV repair using a 30-mm Medtronic Contour ring was performed in this patient.

Postoperative Procedures:

The patient's condition was monitored postoperatively with adequate treatment. Postoperatively, the patient continued anticoagulation for 8 weeks. To date, the patient remains asymptomatic at rest and exercise.

Follow-Up:

The patient is advised to follow a healthy lifestyle and to ensure adequate follow-up with the treating physician.

Addendum:

The patient did not experience any complications and remains stable during the hospital course and at the time of discharge.

Patient Name: [Redacted]

Admission Date: [Redacted]
Discharge Date: [Redacted]
Diagnosis: Incomplete pancreatic duct (PD) with pancreatic pseudocyst, acute recurrent pancreatitis

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the Department of Hepatopancreatobiliary Surgery with complaints of abdominal pain, abdominal distension, fatigue, and anorexia lasting for 8 days. The patient had a significant medical history of recurrent pancreatitis with one episode of acute pancreatitis. Diagnostic tests revealed pseudocyst lesions of the pancreas, indicating incomplete PD and pancreatic pseudocyst. Laboratory test results showed increased levels of amylase, lipase, and cholestatic indexes, leading to a diagnosis of acute recurrent pancreatitis.

Further investigation showed pancreatic duct stenosis, which led to endoscopic pancreatic duct drainage, papillotomy, and stent insertion to successfully excise the pancreatic pseudocyst. The patient was observed to be stable, and the stent was replaced after four months without any complications.

After a few days of observation, the patient was discharged in stable condition. The patient recovered uneventfully without any evidence of pseudocyst recurrence. During the follow-up period of eight months, follow-up CT and ERCP revealed no signs of pseudocyst recurrence, and the stent was removed.

Discharge Condition:
The patient was discharged in a stable condition without any complications.

Discharge Medications:
Not applicable as no medications were prescribed at discharge.

Discharge Diagnoses:
- Incomplete pancreatic duct (PD)
- Pancreatic pseudocyst
- Acute recurrent pancreatitis

Discharge Instructions:
- Eat a healthy and balanced diet.
- Avoid foods that are high in fat and cholesterol.
- Take prescribed medications according to the instructions.
- Follow up with the treating physician as recommended.

Hospital Course:
The 13-year-old Asian girl weighing 24 kg was admitted with a progressive thoracolumbar kyphoscoliosis deformity since 2 years. She underwent tracheostomy 6 years before, related to severe bronchopneumonia management. Since then, she continued to require ventilatory support at night. Genetic study confirmed PD and she was started on ERT.

Physical Exam:
At admission, the patient had thoracolumbar kyphoscoliosis extending from D1 to L4 level, varus deformity of the left foot, bilateral fixed flexor deformity of lower limbs, and wasting of the lower limb and paraspinal muscles with 3/5 motor power. Oxygen saturation was 95% on room air, and chest X-ray showed normal lung fields. Echocardiography showed normal ventricles with ejection fraction of 54% with no evidence of hypertrophy or obstructive cardiomyopathy. Serum creatinine kinase was raised.

Procedure:
General anaesthesia was planned for motor evoked potential (MEP) monitoring during the correction of kyphoscoliosis. The child was induced with dexmedetomidine infusion, ketamine, and morphine, and anaesthesia was maintained with dexmedetomidine infusion, oxygen, and sevoflurane. A total of 450 ml of blood was lost, and 2.3 L of Ringers lactate were infused. The surgery was successful.

Follow-up:
On the 2nd post-operative day, she developed bilateral mild pleural effusion which was treated with diuretics and antibiotics. On the 5th post-operative day, patient was weaned off from ventilator. However, she continued to require nocturnal ventilatory support. Rest of the hospital stay was uneventful, and she was discharged on the 10th day.

Plan:
The patient will continue with ERT and nocturnal ventilatory support. Follow-up appointments will be made with the appropriate specialists.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: Not Provided
Gender: Female
Age: 31 years
Admission Date: Not Provided
Discharge Date: Not Provided
Admitting Diagnosis: Not Provided
Discharge Diagnosis: Hydatid cysts of the bone

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient presented with a history of increasing pain in the right hip and pelvis for the last 3 years, radiating to the right lower limb and back, progressively increasing in intensity, and associated with tingling sensation since last 3 months. She had become quite incapacitated due to painful restricted movements. Her past history showed that at 22 years of age, she had presented with a large abdominal mass. Her CT at that time showed a multicystic lesion measuring 18.0×9.8×7.6 cm in the right abdomen, which appeared to be arising from the right ovary. She underwent surgery which showed a hydatid cyst which was confirmed on histopathology. After remaining asymptomatic for 3 years, in 2007, she again gradually developed pain in the right pelvic region. This time MRI showed a large solid cystic mass measuring 10×6.3 cm in the right iliac fossa and right gluteal region. She underwent a diagnostic laparatomy where multiple cysts in the iliac bone with osteolysis were seen. Two cystic pieces were removed which were diagnosed as hydatid cyst. The patient continued with the pelvic pain although postoperative MRI showed reduction in size of the lesion along the right iliac bone and sacroiliac joint. The x-ray of the pelvis and hips revealed cortical irregularity with ill defined lytic defects and linear areas of patchy sclerosis along the right iliac blade. She continued with pain and follow-up CT revealed extension of the disease. Resection of the hydatid cyst of sacroiliac region with allograft and autograft with lumbosacroiliac fixation was done. Histopathology results revealed hydatid cysts of the bone. The patient was also put on a medical treatment with albendazole for 1 month. The postoperative period was uneventful and patient was discharged on the 10th day of surgery. The follow-up of the patient at 6 months showed no detectable abnormality on radiology, and she was doing well.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
The patient is advised to follow up with the treating physician for regular check-ups and medication management. The patient should continue taking the prescribed medication as per the treatment plan. She should follow a healthy diet and lifestyle to maintain optimal health. The patient is also advised to rest and avoid physical activity until further notice from the treating physician. Any new or worsening symptoms should be reported promptly to the physician.

Discharge Summary:

Admission Date: 

Discharge Date: 

Patient Name: 

Medical Record Number: 

Principal Diagnosis: Prostatic TB with Intracranial TB 

Hospital Course:

The patient was a 54-year old man who was admitted to the hospital due to persistent fever and weight loss. Upon admission, various tests were conducted, including blood counts, liver and renal function tests, and blood culture for common pathogens. However, no significant abnormality was discovered. 

As a result, the patient underwent a whole body F-18 FDG PET-CECT, which revealed intense FDG uptake in the right lobe of the prostate gland and asymmetric heterogeneous FDG uptake in the left frontal lobe peripherally. Following this finding, an MRI scan of the pelvic region was advised. 

Subsequently, a TRUS-guided biopsy was carried out, which ultimately revealed multiple caseous epithelioid granulomas containing giant cells. This validated the diagnosis of prostatic TB, and the patient was prescribed anti-tubercular therapy (ATT) immediately. 

However, before the patient was scheduled to undergo an MRI brain, the patient developed sudden altered mental state, which lasted for a brief period. The provisional diagnosis for this episode was Ethambutol and Isoniazid induced psychosis. Later, an MRI brain with gadolinium contrast demonstrated asymmetrical exaggerated irregular leptomeningeal enhancement in the left frontal region with enhancing granulomas in the supra and infratentorial brain parenchyma, which represented intracranial TB. 

Overall, the patient responded favorably to the ATT treatment, with a subsided fever and normalized ESR within 2 months. The patient did not experience any other neurological episodes. Serum PSA was observed to be normal after the first three months. 

Discharge Medications:

N/A

Follow-up:

The patient is advised to remain aware of the symptoms of TB and seek help if such symptoms reoccur in the future.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

Patient Information:
Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 67 years
Sex: Female

Chief Complaint:
Moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon. Right hemicolectomy was performed, and the pathology confirmed stage III (pT3N1) adenocarcinoma. Adjuvant chemotherapy was initiated but was discontinued after four of eight cycles due to severe neuropathy. After completion of adjuvant treatment, the patient underwent active surveillance. In November 2012, a recurrence near the right psoas muscle was identified and excised in December. Immunohistochemical workup showed an abnormal mismatch repair profile with loss of MLH1 protein. The patient underwent radiotherapy concurrent with capecitabine, but again, significant neutropenia necessitated a capecitabine dose reduction. In October 2013, the patient relapsed with disease in the L3 spinous process and received 42 Gy of stereotactic radiotherapy in 10 fractions. In June 2014, the tumor recurred at the same site, and the patient underwent palliative resection of the mass.

Enter Personalized OncoGenomics (POG) initiative:
The patient consented to genomic analysis of the tumor resected from the L3 spinous process by the POG initiative at the BC Cancer Agency. The genomic analysis revealed overexpression of FOS and JUN genes that encode the AP-1 transcriptional complex. Immunohistochemical workup confirmed robust expression of c-JUN protein. It was suggested that irbesartan could be a potential option due to the blockade of the renin–angiotensin pathway.

Treatment:
The patient had a pretreatment baseline PET/CT scan and started irbesartan at a dose of 150 mg daily in December 2014. After 5 weeks of therapy, a follow-up PET/CT was performed, and there was virtually a complete functional radiological resolution of her disease. CEA levels decreased from 18 to 3.1.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon.

Discharge Condition:
The patient has been discharged, and her condition is stable. Follow-up visits have been scheduled, and medication and dietary instructions have been provided.

Medications:
Irbesartan 150 mg daily.

Follow-up:
Follow-up appointments have been scheduled. The patient has been advised to adhere to a healthy diet and lifestyle and continue medication as prescribed.

The patient, a 78-year-old woman with a history of Parkinson's disease, cerebral lacunar infarction, and high cholesterol, was admitted to the hospital with a complaint of fever and general weakness. Upon examination, the patient was found to have acute gastric dilatation in the presence of pneumonia. The initial treatment included intravenous fluid replacement, antibiotics, and vasopressor administration. A nasogastric tube was inserted, which drained 4 L of liquid. An esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) was performed 24 hours after admission, which revealed acute gastric mucosal erosion and multiple gastric superficial ulcers. The patient's vital signs stabilized, and her mental status improved after initial treatment.

However, approximately 36 hours after admission, the patient suddenly complained of severe dyspnea, chest pain, and aggravated abdominal pain. Follow-up imaging revealed free air in both subphrenic spaces and pulmonary edema in both lung fields. Despite aggressive intervention, the patient's condition worsened rapidly with a dramatic decrease in mental condition and blood pressure, resulting in her demise.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Identification:
This is the discharge summary for a 69-year-old woman with a history of coronary artery disease, hypertension, and dyslipidemia who was admitted for rapidly progressive muscle weakness.

Hospital Course:
Upon admission, the patient presented with predominantly proximal muscle weakness, mild back pain, poor appetite, and dysgeusia. Physical examination showed marked hepatosplenomegaly, and laboratory studies revealed severely elevated serum total calcium and creatinine levels indicative of acute renal injury. Subsequent testing revealed suppressed parathyroid hormone levels, negative PTH-related peptide, mildly elevated lactate dehydrogenase, and almost 5 times the upper range of normal for serum angiotensin-converting enzyme activity along with elevated levels of vitamin D metabolites.

Diagnostic Assessment:
Given strong suspicion for multiple myeloma, a skeletal survey was conducted, which revealed a 1.7-cm punched-out lytic lesion of the vertex of the skull. Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofluorescence failed to demonstrate a monoclonal spike or clonal light chains. Serum free light chains demonstrated an elevated serum Kappa free light chain concentration and a normal Lambda free light chain concentration along with an imbalanced Kappa/Lambda free light chain ratio. A bone marrow biopsy with flow cytometry studies were performed and showed a low-grade B-cell lymphoma with a prominent histiocytic reaction. Subsequently, she underwent a lymph node biopsy, which revealed grade 3B follicular lymphoma. Further staging was performed with positron emission tomography, which showed diffuse patchy uptake within the proximal appendicular and axial skeleton in addition to increased uptake of the large lytic lesion of the skull.

Treatment:
The patient was treated with aggressive hydration and Zoledronate, which resulted in resolution of her hypercalcemia and acute renal injury. R-CHOP chemotherapy was later initiated with significant improvement of her other presenting symptoms.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient is advised to follow-up with her oncologist for further treatment and management of her lymphoma. She should continue to manage her other comorbid conditions including coronary artery disease, hypertension, and dyslipidemia. She should be mindful of her diet and stay active to promote optimal health. She should report any new symptoms or concerns to her healthcare provider.

Hospital Course:

47-year-old male was admitted following a car accident. The patient presented with forehead abrasion and confusion. A brain CT scan and cervical X-rays showed no hematoma or cerebral edema, but cervical instability at C6-7. The patient was immobilized with a neck collar and closely monitored. Two weeks after admission, the patient complained of severe posterior neck pain (VAS > 9) and bilateral upper extremity numbness. Subsequent surgical stabilization was performed. An anterior cervical plate was positioned, and pilot holes were tapped. The upper left pilot hole was stripped due to repeated drilling, and PMMA augmentation was performed, which resulted in a mass lesion at the spinal canal. C6 corpectomy was promptly performed to remove the mass. Anterior reconstruction with an anterior cervical plate and mesh cage from C5 through C7 was done. Postoperatively, the patient had left side weakness and impairment of the left 4th and 5th digit extension, but he improved without intervention.

Discharge Diagnosis:

Cervical injury with spinal cord compression leading to cervical corpectomy.

Hospital course:

The patient was admitted to the hospital following a car accident. During his hospital stay, he underwent surgical stabilization for cervical instability at C6-7. There were some complications during the procedure, which led to a mass lesion at the spinal canal and cervical corpectomy. The patient had some postoperative weakness and impairment of the left hand digits, but he improved without intervention. The patient was discharged in good condition with a follow-up appointment with a spinal specialist.

He wore a neck brace and was watched closely by the medical team during his stay.
Two weeks later, he reported very bad neck pain over nine out of ten and numbness in both arms.
Doctors did surgery to steady his neck by placing a plate in the front and drilling small guide holes.
The left guide hole was damaged from drilling, and bone cement was added, creating a lump in the spinal canal.
Doctors quickly removed the C6 bone to take out the lump and relieve pressure on the spinal cord.
They rebuilt the front of the neck using a plate and a spacer from C5 to C7.
After surgery, he had weakness on his left side and trouble straightening his left ring and little fingers.
But he got better without any extra treatment and his symptoms improved on their own.
Discharge Diagnosis:
He had a neck injury that squeezed his spinal cord, which led to removal of the C6 bone.

Admitting Diagnosis: Relapsing episodes of progressive swelling in the patellar region in both knees.


Hospital Course:

The patient, a 12-year-old boy diagnosed with Globoid cell leukodystrophy, was admitted to the Department of Pediatric Rheumatology with progressive swelling in the patellar region of both knees. Diagnostic arthroscopy revealed severe synovitis in the joint space of the right knee. Synovial tissue and fluid analysis revealed foamy macrophages consistent with the previous diagnosis of Globoid cell leukodystrophy.

Treatment consisted of aspiration of excessive joint fluid and subsequent intra-articular injection of triamcinolonhexacetonide, which was highly effective in all episodes. The duration of clinical remission after injection of corticosteroids was approximately 1 year.

He was discharged in a stable condition.

The patient was advised to follow up with the treating physician.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 75-year-old male, was admitted to the hospital with upper abdominal pain. The blood tests showed elevated levels of total and direct bilirubin, γ-GTP, ALP, AST, and ALT, along with radiological evidence of dilation of hepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts and wall thickening of the common bile duct. Subsequent ERCP revealed defects in intrahepatic and common bile ducts, leading to a diagnosis of perihilar cholangiocarcinoma. The patient underwent left hepatectomy, caudate lobectomy, extrahepatic bile duct resection, and right hepaticojejunostomy. The patient was discharged 23 days after surgery in stable condition.

Follow-up:
Two years and 9 months after the first operation, follow-up CT showed a liver metastasis. The patient underwent a limited liver resection of segment 8. During surgery, another liver metastasis was detected intraoperatively. Two limited liver resections were performed for these two lesions, which were later diagnosed as NET G2. Five years and 4 months after the first operation, four liver metastases were detected, for which the patient received monthly octreotide LAR followed by lanreotide depot/autogel 120 mg. Six years and 3 months after the first operation, the patient underwent a third hepatectomy that revealed seven liver metastases with NET G2 recurrence. In the fourth surgery, the patient had no newly detected tumor and was discharged in stable condition.

Medical Management:
Seven months after the initiation of the third hepatectomy, the patient's follow-up showed four liver metastases. After 6 months of everolimus (10 mg/day) administration, all tumors shrank, but the chemotherapy was discontinued due to its side effects.

Clinical Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with perihilar cholangiocarcinoma based on clinical, radiological, and pathological findings. Later, the patient developed liver metastases that were diagnosed as NET G2, leading to multiple surgical resections followed by chemotherapy with everolimus. The patient was discharged in stable condition after each surgery with no recurrence on follow-up. 

Impressions:
This is a case of perihilar cholangiocarcinoma with NET G2 liver metastases. The patient has undergone multiple surgical resections and chemotherapy with everolimus with no recurrence on follow-up.

This case involves bile duct cancer near the liver with NET G2 liver tumors that were treated.
The patient had many liver surgeries and everolimus chemotherapy, and no cancer has returned on follow-up.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [INSERT NAME]
Sex: Female
Age: 65 years
Medical record number: [INSERT NUMBER]

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with complaints of pain and swelling of the left hand along the thenar eminence and the proximal aspect of the thumb. She also had cervical lymphadenopathy. A plain radiograph showed pathological fracture of the base of 1st metacarpal along with lytic lesion at the base of the 1st metacarpal with haziness of the surrounding soft tissue. An ultrasound revealed presence of an abscess. The MRI scan suggested an abscess like picture most likely due to infective etiology and less likely to be neoplastic lesion. 

The patient underwent drainage of abscess and debridement with stabilization of the fracture fragment. Intra-operatively we found thick caseous material within the soft tissue and the fragment at base of the 1st metacarpal was freely mobile similar to a loose body. The fragment was removed and sent for biopsy and culture sensitivity along with the surrounding soft-tissue. A kirschner wire was passed through the 1st carpo-metacarpal joint to stabilize it. 

The biopsy report came back positive for tuberculous osteomyelitis which suggested fibro-collagenous tissue and few bony fragments showing large caseous necrosis with few epitheloidid cell granuloma. The patient was then started on anti-tuberculous treatment emprerically while awaiting the culture report. A Combination of Isoniazid, Rifampicin, Pyrazinamide and ethambutol was started. 

At the end of 5 weeks the kirschner wire backed out partially which was then removed and range of movement exercises were started. The cervical lymphadenopathy regressed by the end of 3 months. The patient had 1 episode of recurrence of cervical lymphandenopathy at the end of 7 months of treatment which eventually regressed on the continuous phase of AKT. 

At the end of one year, the patient had almost complete range of movement with no sequel due to tuberculosis as compared to the opposite hand. Plain radiographs showed some degree of joint remodelling at one year. 

Discharge Medications:
The patient is dispensed her usual home medications.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient is advised to follow up with the orthopedic surgeon regularly and continue taking the prescribed medication. The patient is counselled to adopt a healthy lifestyle and a balanced diet. Any symptoms of recurrence or deterioration should be reported to the physician immediately. Additionally, the patient is advised regarding the importance and significance of regular follow-up, which is critical to the management of her condition.

Follow-up:
The patient is referred to the orthopedic surgeon for follow-up to assess progress and discuss the patient's ongoing management.

Hospital Course:

The patient was a 68-year-old male who was admitted with weakness and aggravation. He had a past history of gastric stromal tumors and type-B hepatitis. On admission, he had mild yellowing of the skin and sclera. Laboratory examination showed liver dysfunction. Abdominal CT showed pelvic and peritoneal cavity fluids, occupation of the left lateral lobe of the liver, and an unclear margin of the pancreas. PET-CT suggested swelling of the pancreas and metastases in the liver. The patient received comprehensive internal treatment combined with artificial liver treatment, but his condition deteriorated, and he became unconscious and developed hepatic encephalopathy. He was put on the transplant waiting list and received a liver transplant from a deceased donor on day 4 due to his critical condition. After the transplantation, the patient was sent to the ICU for further treatment.

Postoperative Course:

The patient's condition improved after the transplant, and he was started on immunosuppressive agents. Abdominal CT showed pancreatic swelling with massive exudation and effusion, indicating acute pancreatitis on postoperative day 8. His pathogen culture of various body fluids suggested multiple bacterial infections. An arrow tube was placed around the liver and tail of the pancreas under B-mode ultrasound guidance instead of operative treatment on postoperative day 11, and coffee-like turbid liquids flowed from the arrow tube. 

On postoperative day 20, the patient experienced a sudden increase in heart rate, decrease in blood pressure, increase in blood gas lactate, blurred consciousness, and poor light reflex. He received emergency trachea cannula, continuous renal replacement therapy for anuria, and norepinephrine to maintain blood pressure. On postoperative day 21, he was unconscious and died of septic shock.

CT scan showed fluid in the belly and pelvis, indicating possible infection or inflammation. It also showed a growth in the left part of the liver and an unclear edge of the pancreas. PET scan showed pancreas swelling and cancer spread to the liver, indicating advanced disease. He received medical treatment and artificial liver support, but his condition continued to worsen. He became confused and unconscious because of liver failure, leading to hepatic encephalopathy. He was placed on the transplant list due to his worsening condition. He received an emergency breathing tube, kidney dialysis because he was not urinating, and medicine to raise his blood pressure. On day twenty-one, he was unconscious and died from septic shock despite intensive treatment.

Admission Diagnosis:  Stage IV poorly differentiated ovarian carcinoma on palliative carboplatin-based chemotherapy.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission:
The patient was admitted due to a brief syncopal episode with associated lethargy, nausea, light-headedness and increased watery ileostomal output following chemotherapy one week earlier. Clinical examination including central nervous system was unremarkable, and the patient was haemodynamically stable and afebrile.

Medical History:
The patient has a history of hypertension, multiple pulmonary emboli on enoxaparin and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. In the past, the patient had undergone bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and hysterectomy, and had an ileostomy due to small bowel obstruction with subsequent fistulae formation and bilateral nephrostomy drainage after radiation-induced ureteric obstruction. She had previously experienced recurrent urinary tract infections, which led to colonisation of her nephrostomies with methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), Staphylococcus epidermidis and Candida albicans. The patient had never received anti-fungal prophylaxis.

Initial Assessment:
Laboratory investigations revealed abnormal levels of sodium, creatinine, haemoglobin, white blood cells and lymphocytes. On day 2 of admission, the patient developed fevers of 38.5°C and was empirically commenced on piperacillin-tazobactam and vancomycin. The isolation of Staphylococcus epidermidis from the nephrostomy fluid was considered colonisation and the nephrostomies were changed. Initial septic screen was non-contributory, including negative faecal microscopy.

Diagnostic Assessment:
Persisting fever during her third week of admission prompted assessment for metastatic disease progression with FDG-PET scan. There was no evidence of metastatic malignant disease detected, but an area of abnormal avidity was identified on the aortic valve. Subsequent transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) revealed a small mobile echo-density superior to the aortic valve. Transoesophageal echocardiogram (TOE) revealed a pedunculated mass within the ascending aorta arising from the commissure of the right & non-coronary cusp of the aortic valve with a calcified base. Brain MRI identified a contrast-enhancing right parasagittal frontal lobe lesion consistent with an embolic lesion.

Treatment:
Fungi were isolated from repeat blood cultures on day 22 of admission and subsequently identified as Lomentospora prolificans with high MIC to amphotericin (>32 mg/l) and itraconazole (>32 mg/L), and in-vitro sensitivity to voriconazole (0.5 mg/L). The patient was commenced on therapy with voriconazole (loading dose 600 mg IV 12 hourly). Unfortunately, due to her underlying advanced malignancy, disseminated fungal infection and poor clinical status, the patient was considered unsuitable for surgical management. She was managed with palliative intent.

Outcome:
The patient passed away five days after the fungus was isolated on day 27 of her admission.
nemotron_simplification:
Admission Diagnosis: Advanced ovarian cancer that has spread widely, treated with carboplatin chemotherapy to relieve symptoms palliatively.
Hospital Course Summary:
Admission: The patient was admitted after a fainting spell with tiredness, nausea, dizziness, and more watery output from the ileostomy.
This happened one week after chemotherapy; the nervous system exam was normal, and vital signs were stable without fever.
Medical History: The patient has high blood pressure, past lung blood clots on blood thinner shots, and occasional irregular heartbeat.
Previously, both ovaries, fallopian tubes, and the uterus were removed, and an ileostomy was created after a bowel blockage.
Abnormal connections formed, and tubes were placed in both kidneys to drain urine because radiation blocked the ureters.
Repeated bladder infections caused germs to live in the kidney tubes, including MRSA, another staph bacteria, and yeast.
The patient never received any medicine to prevent fungal infections during her hospital stay or outpatient care.
Initial Assessment: Blood tests showed abnormal sodium, kidney function, red blood cell count, and white blood cell levels.
On the second day, a fever of 101.3°F appeared, and broad-spectrum antibiotics were started to cover possible infection.
Staphylococcus epidermidis found in the kidney tube fluid was thought to be just colonization, so the tubes were replaced.
Initial infection screening, including stool exam and blood cultures, did not identify a source of infection.
Diagnostic Assessment: Ongoing fever in the third week led to a scan to look for cancer spread.
The scan showed no cancer spread but spotted unusual activity on the heart's aortic valve.
A heart ultrasound through the chest found a small moving spot above the aortic valve.
An ultrasound via the esophagus showed a stalk-like growth on the aortic valve area with a calcium base.
A brain MRI revealed a bright spot in the right front side of the brain, likely from a clot.
Treatment: On day 22, fungus in the blood was identified as Lomentospora prolificans, resistant to two drugs but sensitive to voriconazole.
Treatment began with high-dose voriconazole given intravenously every 12 hours as a loading dose to fight the infection.
Because of widespread cancer, spreading fungus, and her poor overall condition, surgery was not an option.
Care focused on comfort and symptom relief, aiming to improve quality of life without attempting curative treatment.
Outcome: The patient died five days after the fungus was found, which occurred on day 27 of her hospital stay.

A follow-up thyroid ultrasonogram revealed an increase in the size of the previously observed nodule in the right lobe and contralateral lobe atrophy. A 99m-Technetium-pertechnetate thyroid scan demonstrated a functioning toxic nodule. The patient refused surgery or radioactive iodine therapy and was prescribed methimazole.

Outstanding Clinical Issues:
The patient was diagnosed with thyroid disease and had an increase in the size of the previously observed nodule in the right lobe and contralateral lobe atrophy at the time of the follow-up. The patient was prescribed methimazole and TSH levels normalized two weeks later. 

Discharge Medications:
Calcium channel blocker, angiotensin receptor antagonist, diuretic and aspirin.

Follow-up Instructions:
The patient should continue follow-up for thyroid disease and any heart failure symptoms.

Hospital Course:

The patient is an 8-year-old female with tufting enteropathy who presented on three separate occasions with central venous catheter infection due to Bacillus species. The patient had initially presented in the first few months of life with chronic watery diarrhoea and impaired growth, and was found to have tufting enteropathy - a rare congenital enteropathy that requires indefinite dependence on parenteral nutrition from early infancy. 

On each occasion the patient presented with fever after flushing of the central venous catheter. The first episode of infection was treated with 4 weeks of intravenous flucloxacillin because bacteraemia had persisted despite 14 days of treatment.

The patient was transferred to our hospital following the recurrence of fever and rigors, 10 days after stopping the antibiotics. Bacillus species was isolated from central venous catheter cultures both before and whilst on cefotaxime and flucloxacillin, later identified as Bacillus pumilus at the National Reference Laboratory. There were concerns that the patient had previously reacted to systemic vancomycin, so antibiotics were changed to intravenous clindamycin with vancomycin line locks given for 2 weeks. Blood cultures taken both during and after this treatment were negative. Echocardiography showed no evidence of vegetations at the tip of the catheter or in the heart.

Ten days after stopping the intravenous antibiotics the child presented for the third time with fever and rigors. A Bacillus species was again grown from blood taken from the central venous catheter. The central venous catheter was removed after 5 days treatment with intravenous vancomycin and a new central venous catheter was inserted. Subsequent blood cultures were negative and there has been no recurrence of further fever or infections over a 9-month period, suggesting the infection has been eradicated.

Discharge Summary:

The patient is an 8-year-old female with tufting enteropathy on long-term parenteral nutrition, presenting on three separate occasions with central venous catheter infection due to Bacillus species. The patient was treated with multiple courses of antibiotics and required catheter replacement once due to recurrence of fever and rigors.

The patient is being discharged without any active infections or clinical concerns at this time. The patient's care plan will continue to include regular follow-up with the primary care physician and periodic bloodwork to monitor for any potential infections.

The patient and family were counseled on signs and symptoms of catheter-related infections and the importance of prompt reporting to medical professionals if fever or other concerning symptoms develop. The family was also provided with written and verbal information regarding infection prevention measures, such as strict hand hygiene and catheter care, to minimize the risk of future infections.

The patient was discharged home in good condition and was advised to follow up with the primary care physician for routine care and blood work. The patient's parents were instructed to monitor the patient for any signs of infection and to seek prompt medical attention if any concerning symptoms develop.

Hospital Course:
A 27-year-old male with a history of recent COVID-19 infection presented with fever, sore throat, multiple joint pain, and body rash mainly on the forearms. Physical examination revealed tracheal cartilage tenderness and macular rashes on both arms. Laboratory investigations revealed leukocytosis with neutrophilia, elevated serum C-reactive protein, elevated serum ferritin, and abnormal liver function. Nasopharyngeal SARS CoV-2 PCR and serum SARS CoV-2 immunoglobulin G were positive. The patient was admitted under the care of internal medicine as a case of possible cytokines storm syndrome related to COVID-19 versus post viral bacterial infection. Despite treatment with 5 days of antibiotic therapy, the patient showed no improvement. The patient’s clinical presentation and labs met the Yamaguchi criteria for Adult Onset Still’s disease. The patient was cleared by the infectious disease team with an impression of the positive COVID-19 result being most likely due to viral shedding. The patient was started on IV methylprednisolone, resulting in clinical improvement with resolving joint pain and disappearance of the rash. The patient’s fever resolved and he was discharged on oral Prednisolone with follow-up appointments in the rheumatology clinic.

Patient Name: [redacted]

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 47-year-old woman, was admitted to the hospital with bilateral groin pain, inability to urinate, and bloody vaginal discharge. Clinical vaginal examination revealed the presence of a large necrotic mass filling the whole vaginal tract. Transabdominal ultrasound examination showed a cervico-vaginal mass measuring 112 × 114 mm that protruded from the uterine cavity with a distorted view of the uterus. After consultation and an MRI examination, a large heterogeneous signal intensity of a well-defined submucosal fundal fibroid mass was confirmed. Uterine anatomy was distorted as seen as “V shape” fundus in sagittal plane due to traction of the mass. 

Laboratory tests showed a decreased hemoglobin level of 10.1 g/dL, hematocrit of 30.9%, and elevated CRP level of 37.5 mg/L. The patient's fasting glucose level, AST and ALT liver enzymes were within normal range, but the CA125 level was 152 U/mL. 

At laparotomy, a large uterine mass with complete uterine inversion was confirmed. The mass was taken out via transverse uterine incision after depicting the myoma’s pedicle. Total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy was performed due to the patient's request before surgery. The excised specimen revealed a giant mass with extensive necrosis and multiple hemorrhagic foci. Pathology report confirmed 12 × 12 × 10 cm sized leiomyoma including large ischemic necrotic areas. There was no evidence of malignancy. 

The patient was discharged without any complications five days after the surgery.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Uterine inversion with uterine fibroid.

Discharge Condition:
Stable. 

Discharge Medication:
N/A. 

Discharge Instructions:
The patient was instructed to follow up with her gynecologist and primary care physician. She was advised to avoid heavy lifting and intercourse for six weeks to allow for full recovery. She was also instructed to monitor for any signs of vaginal bleeding, pain or fever. If any of these symptoms appeared, she was advised to contact her physician immediately. 

Follow-Up:
The patient was advised to schedule a follow-up appointment with her gynecologist and primary care physician for recovery monitoring.

Discharge Summary:

Patient 1, a 47-year-old man with a history of spinal injury resulting in complete paraplegia, was admitted to the department of physical medicine and rehabilitation at our university hospital due to spasticity. Despite taking baclofen and diazepam, the patient reported experiencing 3-4 beats of knee extension clonus and spasm of adductor thigh muscles. The spasticity was not controlled and was interfering with the patient's sleep.

The patient underwent pulsed radiofrequency (PRF) procedure on both L2 and L3 DRGs with 5 Hz and 5 ms pulsed width for 360 seconds at 45 V under the C-arm fluoroscopy guide. There were no complications after the PRF. Following the procedure, the clonus of both knee extensors disappeared completely, and the spasticity on both hip adductors was reduced from a score of 3 to 1+. The patient reported significant improvement in quality of sleep and a 50% reduction in spasticity on both hip adductors.

The spasticity returned at nearly the same degree six months after the procedure, and a repeat PRF was performed with similar results, which were also sustained for six months.

Overall, the PRF procedure was effective in reducing the spasticity of the patient's adductor thigh muscles and improving his quality of sleep. The patient was discharged in stable condition and advised to follow up with the clinic as needed.

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 27-year-old pregnant female with a history of congenital heart disease, was admitted to the hospital at 34 weeks of gestation due to pain abdomen for 2 days. On examination, the patient was found to be cyanotic with clubbed fingers and raised Jugular venous pressure, and there was a pansystolic murmur and bilateral basal crepitations present. The patient was diagnosed to have a large perimembranous ventricular septal defect (VSD) with bidirectional shunt and severe pulmonary hypertension (PAH), tricuspid regurgitation, and a dilated right atrium seen on echocardiography.

Treatment:

The patient had been on irregular treatment with sildenafil 25 mg twice a day since 4 months, and given her previous obstetric history, lower segment cesarean section (LSCS) was planned. All risks were explained, and written informed consent was obtained. Prophylaxis against bacterial endocarditis was provided, and an epidural catheter was inserted for pain management during the surgery. Ampicillin and gentamicin were administered as per standard prophylaxis guidelines.

Procedure:

Over a period of 30 min, a total of 7cc of lignocaine with adrenaline solution and 8 cc of bupivacaine with 25 μg of fentanyl produced a block height of T8 tested to touch with blunt forceps. CVP was maintained between10-12 mm throughout surgery. The procedure was uneventful, and after delivery of the baby, furosemide 10 mg was given intravenously. A total of 450 cc of colloid was given.

Postoperative:

After surgery, the patient was shifted to the intensive care unit (ICU) for monitoring and was discharged on the 10th day. Epidural analgesia was maintained with 0.125% bupivacaine and 20 μg of fentanyl every 8 hourly for 72 h.

Summary:

The patient was diagnosed to have a large perimembranous ventricular septal defect (VSD) with bidirectional shunt and severe pulmonary hypertension (PAH), tricuspid regurgitation, and a dilated right atrium seen on echocardiography. She had a history of a stillborn delivery in her previous pregnancy and was advised against conceiving again, but she refused. She had been on irregular treatment with sildenafil, and given her previous obstetric history, LSCS was planned. The procedure was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on the 10th day. Epidural analgesia was maintained for pain management after surgery.
