Discharge Summary:

This is a summary of admission details for a 20-year-old female with a medical history of post-traumatic stress syndrome and facial acne. The patient was admitted to the emergency department after ingesting seven pills of paroxetine.

Course of Hospitalization:

Initial evaluation in the emergency department yielded minimal symptoms, stable vital signs, and no arrhythmia on ECG. The patient was observed for six hours and complained of flushing and became agitated. The patient sustained witnessed spontaneous aborted tonic clinic seizure activity of 90 seconds. She exhibited tachycardia, tachypnea, hypertension, and hyperreflexia. Blood workup, CT of the head without contrast, urine drug screen, and ethanol level were normal. ECG showed a prolonged corrected QT interval of >540. SS was suspected, and the patient was given IV fluids and lorazepam. Cyproheptadine was given 12 mg orally as a single dose and 4 mg every eight hours as needed. The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit for close monitoring with serial ECG. QT interval normalization was observed 16 hours later, and no visual seizures were noted during hospitalization.

Discharge Diagnosis:

Suspected serotonin syndrome 

Treatment:

The patient was given IV fluids and lorazepam. Cyproheptadine was given 12 mg orally as a single dose and 4 mg every eight hours as needed.

Follow-up:

The patient was discharged in stable condition.

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient was a 50-year-old Chinese male who presented with cough and expectoration of black phlegm for about 2 weeks, sometimes accompanied by bloody sputum and breathlessness. A computed tomography (CT) scan of his chest revealed a rough-edged shadow measuring nearly 32×22×10 mm in the right upper lobe of his lung. The patient was diagnosed with a giant cell carcinoma-like tumor (GCCL) of the lung after undergoing a right-sided upper lobectomy and systematic mediastinal lymphadenectomy. Histopathologic examination of the tumor cells revealed a positive reaction for cytokeratin (CK) and vimentin, while immunostaining for chromogranin A (CgA) and synaptophysin (Syn) was negative.

The patient had several chronic disorders, including a 10-year history of bronchitis and emphysema, and was a smoker with a 30-pack-year history, but had no family history of lung cancer. He underwent combined chemotherapy using gemcitabine and cisplatin for four cycles and was followed up with whole-body radiography examinations every year in a local hospital. As of 7 years after surgery, he remained alive and free from disease progression.

The patient's hospital course was notable for his successful treatment of GCCL, good response to treatment, and his long-term follow-up. The patient was able to communicate clearly and effectively with the healthcare team during his stay. He was compliant with his treatment regimen and was actively involved in discharge planning. The healthcare team discussed the importance of smoking cessation and provided resources for smoking cessation for the patient.

Diagnoses:

1. Giant cell carcinoma-like tumor (GCCL) of the lung.

Discharge Medications:

None.

Follow-Up Care:

The patient is advised to continue yearly follow-up visits with a local hospital to monitor his condition. He is also encouraged to continue smoking cessation efforts.

Discharge Summary:

Hospital Course:
The 62-year-old male was admitted to the hospital with a complaint of abdominal pain, vomiting, and ambulatory dysfunction. The initial examination showed no abnormalities. The patient was suspected to have viral gastroenteritis, and hence he was hospitalized for dehydration management. The patient's nausea and vomiting improved after admission, but it was noted that he was leaning backwards and to the right when standing or attempting to ambulate on the first day of hospitalization.

Diagnostic Evaluations:
The neurology service was consulted after assessing the patient's condition on his second day of admission. A CT angiogram of the head and neck showed a congenitally hypoplastic left vertebral artery and no other abnormality was observed in the vertebrobasilar system. MRI of the brain showed acute/subacute infarct in the right cerebellar hemisphere. The echocardiogram showed moderate diastolic dysfunction with trace aortic regurgitation.

Clinical Impression:
The patient was diagnosed with acute/subacute infarct in the right cerebellar hemisphere secondary to chronic atherosclerotic disease that had extended and caused APS. The left-sided dysmetria was observed, which further indicated his neurological impairment.

Hospital Treatment:
The patient was monitored on telemetry for several days without any events or abnormalities noted. He was started on a scheduled antiemetic regimen of metoclopramide 10 mg four times daily and ondansetron 8 mg every eight hours that yielded positive results. Within one day, the patient's nausea and vomiting were controlled, and he was able to eat without difficulty. The patient was successfully discharged from the hospital to rehabilitation.

Follow-up Recommendations:
The patient is recommended to follow up with the neurology service as an outpatient and undergo regular checkups to monitor his neurological function and the progression of his cerebrovascular disease. He is also advised to maintain strict blood glucose control and hypertension management. The family members are recommended to observe the patient's activities, as he is more vulnerable to falls.

Descending aortic aneurysm

Transcatheter endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR)

The patient was discharged without serious complications.

The patient was monitored via computed tomography 15 months after TEVAR repair, at which point there was significant regression of the aneurysm. The patient was free from antibiotics at the time of writing.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Identification: Baby S P, 6-year-old girl

Hospital Course:
Baby S P was admitted with a complaint of progressive bilateral breast enlargement, cyclical vaginal bleeding, and pubic hair development. She had a recent increase in height, but no neck swelling, pigmented skin marks, bone pain/fractures, or clitoral enlargement. Her birth and neonatal period were normal. 

On examination, her vitals were normal, and she had no thyroid swelling, café au lait spots, or any bony abnormality. Tanners staging revealed B3P3, with no axillary hair or genital ambiguity. There were no abnormalities noted in her cardiac, thoracic, or neurological examinations. Abdominal examination was normal. 

Investigations showed normal hemogram, liver and renal functions, and thyroid functions. However, her hormonal profile revealed low levels of LH and FSH, and high levels of testosterone and DHEAS. CT pelvis showed a bulky left ovary of size 5.4 cm predominantly solid with follicles seen at periphery and pubertal uterus. 

She underwent laparoscopic resection of right tuboovarian mass, which on histopathological examination was found to be mixed germ cell sex cord stromal tumor. The post-operative period was marked by withdrawal vaginal bleeding lasting for 72 hours. A repeat hormonal profile done on the 6th post-operative day showed reduced estradiol levels.

At the 6-month follow-up, there was no vaginal bleeding reported.

Diagnosis: Mixed germ cell sex cord stromal tumor

Treatment: Laparoscopic resection of right tuboovarian mass

Follow-up: 6-months follow-up showed no vaginal bleeding.

Course and Outcome: Baby S P was admitted for evaluation of progressive bilateral breast enlargement, cyclical vaginal bleeding, and pubic hair development. Following laparoscopic resection of right tuboovarian mass, post-operative bleeding was noted, and a repeat hormonal profile showed reduced estradiol levels. On the fourth day of his admission, he underwent an eschar excision procedure in his right upper limb. However, on the seventh day, the patient experienced a burst of heavy bleeding. The nurse and doctors responded quickly, and fluid resuscitation was done immediately. Additionally, a tourniquet cuff was used to prevent further bleeding, and the NPWT material was removed. After the bleeding vessels were blocked, the patient was given a balanced solution, manufactured colloid, plasma, and red cell suspension to replace the volume of blood lost. The patient gradually recovered, and his hemoglobin levels and blood pressure returned to normal.

Course of Treatment:
The patient was given a thorough examination and was given the appropriate treatment for his burns. His wounds were regularly dressed, and he was given enteral nutrition. Due to the sudden burst of heavy bleeding, he required emergency fluid resuscitation and blood transfusion. Upon successful completion of the treatment, the patient's condition improved, and he was ready for discharge.

The patient was discharged from the hospital in a stable condition. Follow-up appointments with a burn specialist were scheduled.

The patient was started on IV maintenance fluids and ampicillin-sulbactam for broad spectrum coverage including oral flora.

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient was admitted for evaluation of an ulcerative lesion on the left side of the lower lip. Biopsies confirmed the diagnosis of well-differentiated infiltrating squamous cell carcinoma, which was staged at T2N0M0 according to TNM guidelines. The patient opted for HDRIB treatment and received five equidistant metallic needles to insert plastic catheters through the tissue. CT image was taken to plan HDRIB treatment. The patient received one fraction of 5.00 Gy on the first day of treatment and two daily fractions of 5.00 Gy for the next 4 days. 

One month post-treatment, the patient had localised acute radiation toxicity with bleeding ulcerative mucositis at the treatment site. The patient was given analgesics, anti-inflammatory drugs, and a mouthwash to treat his symptoms. At the second follow-up, a month later, the ulcer measured 1.5 × 1.5 cm with an indurated area. The LL was epithelialised and tumour-free at his third follow-up, a month later. Finally, a two-year-long evaluation was conducted, which revealed that the patient was asymptomatic and disease-free, albeit mild atrophy and skin hypopigmentation were observed as long-term side effects of the treatment. 

The patient stated that he was pleased with the results and aesthetic outcome of his procedure.

Admitting Diagnosis: Transverse fracture of the left little finger proximal phalanx with ulnar displacement of the phalangeal head and an undisplaced fracture of the basal metaphysis of the middle phalanx

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the emergency department with a history of hyperextension injury to the left little finger while playing football. Radiographs of the hand confirmed a transverse fracture through the neck of the little finger proximal phalanx with ulnar displacement of the proximal phalangeal head and also an undisplaced fracture of the basal metaphysis of the middle phalanx. The fracture was manipulated to a satisfactory alignment under adequate analgesia and digital anaesthetic block. The injury was stabilized with neighbour strapping and a dorsal extension block splinting at 30 degrees flexion.

Post reduction radiographs revealed an improvement in the position of the head of the proximal phalanx with unchanged appearance of the middle phalangeal fracture. The PIPJ alignment was satisfactory. Clinically the injury was stable and there was no change in the neurovascular status. The patient was further followed up in the fracture clinic and reduction was assessed both clinically and radiologically with serial radiographs for 2 weeks since the injury.

At 4 weeks, dorsal extension block splinting was discontinued as clinical healing was confirmed. The patient was discharged to physiotherapy and further assessed at 8 and 12 weeks. By 12 weeks, the injury had fully healed with mild ulnar deviation at the proximal phalanx but with complete restoration of function.

Impression:

The patient presented to the emergency department with a transverse fracture of left little finger proximal phalanx with ulnar displacement of the phalangeal head and an undisplaced fracture of basal metaphysis of middle phalanx. The fracture was manipulated and stabilized with neighbour strapping and a dorsal extension block splinting at 30 degrees flexion. The patient was further followed up in the fracture clinic and reduction was assessed both clinically and radiologically. By 12 weeks, the injury had fully healed with complete restoration of function despite mild ulnar deviation at the proximal phalanx. The patient was discharged to physiotherapy.

Patient Information:
Name: Not provided
Age: 57
Sex: Male

Admission Date: Not provided
Discharge Date: Not provided

Reason for Admission:
Decreased vision in the left eye of 1-month duration

Hospital Course:
The patient was diagnosed with primary intraocular lymphoma (PIOL) based on the results of his diagnostic vitrectomy. As a PCNSL was not detected by magnetic resonance imaging, the patient was treated with weekly intravitreal injections of methotrexate (MTX) for 1 month, followed by monthly maintenance injections for seven more months.

Assessment:
The patient showed significant improvement in his best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA), from 20/25 to 20/16 after 9 months. Fundus examination showed regression of the yellowish lesions in the posterior fundus, changing gradually to atrophy of the RPE. Fundus autofluorescence (FAF) and spectral domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) showed significant improvement in the degree of hyperreflective infiltration in the inner retina, restoration of the RPE and IS/OS junction, and recovery of foveal thickness. Enhanced depth imaging OCT (EDI-OCT) showed a gradual decrease in the subfoveal choroidal thickness during the treatment. The total macular volume reduced significantly after the treatment.

The mean deviation (MD) on standard automated perimetry increased from -13.95 dB before treatment to -7.23 dB after treatment. The mean retinal sensitivity within the central 10° measured with a fundus-related microperimeter increased from 0.3 dB before treatment to 4.1 dB after treatment. Full-field electroretinograms (ERGs) and multifocal ERGs (mfERGs) showed decreased amplitudes.

Final Diagnosis:
Primary intraocular lymphoma (PIOL)

Discharge Instructions:
The patient is advised to follow up with his ophthalmologist regularly for monitoring of his visual acuity and ocular health. Any new or worsening symptoms should be reported to his healthcare provider immediately.

Admitting Diagnosis: HTLV-I associated myelopathy (HAM) following renal transplantation

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 65-year-old man with a history of diabetic nephropathy, underwent renal transplantation using his HTLV-I seropositive wife as the donor. Eight months after the transplant, he presented with weakness of his legs, which progressed rapidly, leaving him wheelchair-bound 12 days later. Despite receiving pulsed steroid therapy, he did not regain his leg muscle strength, and was transferred to our hospital.

At our facility, the patient underwent neurological examinations which showed flaccid paraparesis of his legs with diminished deep tendon reflexes. Nerve conduction studies did not reveal any evidence of peripheral neuropathy. His serum anti-HTLV-I antibody titer was elevated, and the CSF protein content was elevated with an increased cell count. Western blotting identified HTLV-I antibodies in his spinal cord fluid.

MRI scans of the thoracic spinal cord displayed T2 high signal intensities with slight swelling. A diagnosis of HAM was made based on these findings. The patient was started on interferon-α treatment, but showed little improvement. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) therapy was added along with interferon-α, following which the patient showed improvement and was able to move his legs more easily. MRI examinations showed spinal cord atrophy. His OMSD improved during his inpatient stay.

Discharge Condition:

The patient was discharged in stable condition with recommendation for continued outpatient follow-up by his primary care physician and neurologist. Instructions were given to continue with interferon-α and IVIg therapy at his follow-up appointment. It was recommended that the patient continue to participate in physical therapy and rehabilitation programs to improve his mobility.

Summary:

A 65-year-old man with a history of diabetic nephropathy and renal transplantation, presented with flaccid paraparesis of the legs. A diagnosis of HTLV-I associated myelopathy (HAM) was made. The patient was treated with interferon-α and IVIg therapy, and showed improvement. The patient was discharged in stable condition with recommendation for continued outpatient follow-up.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with symptoms of fever, nonproductive cough, shortness of breath, and audible wheezing. The initial diagnosis was community-acquired pneumonia, which was treated with IV antibiotics, oral steroids, and nebulized bronchodilators. Despite treatment, the patient's shortness of breath progressed and she was readmitted to the hospital. Workup revealed eosinophilia, and a biopsy confirmed a diagnosis of eosinophilic pneumonitis. The patient was discharged home with oral steroids and was counseled on the possibility of the black mold in her home causing her symptoms. However, she was readmitted to the hospital 2 weeks later with profound shortness of breath and hypoxia. Imaging studies showed worsening lung infiltrates and liver lesions. Despite continued treatment with antibiotics, steroids, and ventilator support, the patient eventually died before a liver biopsy could be performed. The autopsy revealed diffuse eosinophils in all organs, and immunohistochemistry staining showed positive staining for T-cell markers, which confirmed the diagnosis of aggressive diffuse PTCL.

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient was admitted with symptoms of pneumonia and was treated with IV antibiotics, oral steroids, and nebulized bronchodilators. Following discharge, she was readmitted with worsening symptoms of eosinophilic pneumonitis. Despite treatment, the patient's condition deteriorated and she eventually developed aggressive diffuse PTCL. Unfortunately, the patient passed away before further testing could be performed.

Deceased. The patient passed away during hospitalization.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [redacted]

Gender: Male

Age: 40 years

Date of Admission: [redacted]

Date of Discharge: [redacted]

Admission Diagnosis: Painless swelling over the left side of the face

Discharge Diagnosis: Schwannoma, most likely arising from the terminal branch of the infra-orbital nerve

Hospital Course Summary: 

The patient was admitted with the chief complaint of painless swelling over the left side of the face. On examination, a localized, nontender, firm, round swelling of around 4 cm was evident over the left side of the mid-face, extending from below the infra-orbital margin to the upper lip. The overlying skin appeared stretched and tense. The skin was pinch-able over the lesion, except at the center of the lesion. The naso-labial fold was obliterated. Intra-oral examination showed no swelling over the anterior maxilla. The maxillary anterior teeth were firm and nontender on percussion. There was no proptosis, and vision was normal. The cervical lymph nodes were not palpable. 

Ultrasonography was advised to study the size and extent of the lesion. The ultrasonogram showed a well-defined, heterogeneous oval mass of 45mm x 30mm x 23mm within the buccal sub-cutaneous tissue with no orbital, maxillary sinus, or underlying bone involvement. 

Aspiration biopsy of the lesion showed spindle-shaped cells predominantly arranged in Antoni A pattern around verocay bodies, with less organized Antoni B tissue in a few places. A diagnosis of schwannoma, probably arising from the terminal branch of the infra-orbital nerve, was established.

Surgical excision of the lesion was planned and executed under local anesthesia. After attaining adequate anesthesia, a linear incision of about 3 cm was placed over the skin along the natural skin crease of naso-labial fold. The lesion was well-encapsulated and freed from surrounding tissue by blunt dissection. The portion of skin overlying the center of the lesion appeared thinned and was included in the excised nodule. At the time of exploration, the lesion was found to emanate from the nerve trunk of the peripheral branch of the infra-orbital nerve, which was dissected and preserved. Histopathological examination of the excised lesion confirmed diagnosis of schwannoma.

The patient has had an uneventful recovery post-surgery and is advised to follow up with their primary care physician for routine check-ups.

Condition at Discharge: Stable

Discharge Medications: Please refer to the medication summary provided to the patient

Discharge Instructions: The patient is advised to rest and avoid any strenuous activities. They are encouraged to follow up with their primary care physician for routine check-ups as advised. 

Follow-up / Appointments: Follow-up appointments are to be scheduled with the primary care physician.

Diagnosis:
Transverse fracture of the patella with a lytic lesion, suggestive of chondroblastoma.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 24-year-old male, was admitted with complaints of inability to walk after a trivial fall. He had pain and noticed mild swelling in the right knee for the past one year. On clinical examination, the patient had tense swelling and tenderness over the right patella, with painful movements and straight leg raising test not possible. X-ray showed a transverse fracture of the patella with a lytic lesion occupying most of the two halves of the patella. 

After considering clinicoradiological differential diagnoses including solitary bone cysts, aneurysmal bone cyst, giant cell tumor, chondroblastoma, a fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) was performed, which revealed a few osteoclastic giant cells and occasional osteoblasts against a hemorrhagic background. Subsequently, patellectomy was performed, and histopathology was suggestive of chondroblastoma. 

The patient had an uneventful recovery and was discharged with a full range of movements after two years.

Follow-up:
The patient will be advised to follow up with regular orthopedic consultations, with specific emphasis on keeping the surgical site clean and free of infection. 

Keywords:
Transverse fracture, patella, lytic lesion, chondroblastoma, patellectomy.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission Date: [date]
Discharge Date: [date]

Patient Name: [name]
Age: 68 years
Sex: Male

Medical History:
- Prostate cancer treated with radiation therapy, 3 years ago
- Endoscopic polypectomy for colonic polyps, 1 year ago
- Chronic constipation

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with sudden-onset upper abdominal pain and was found to have a fist-sized mass lesion located between the stomach and pancreas on computed tomography (CT) without contrast. He was initially diagnosed with a malignant tumor with peritonitis carcinomatosa and hospitalized for further examinations and observation. However, the next day, he was found to have intra-abdominal hemorrhage and was transferred to our hospital, a tertiary emergency center, for further diagnosis and treatments.

On arrival at our hospital, the patient was alert and well oriented. A physical examination revealed moderate tenderness in his left upper abdomen with a peritoneal sign. His laboratory data showed mild leukocytosis, moderate anemia, elevated urea nitrogen level, and high serum amylase. The results of a CT with contrast demonstrated an unenhanced, high-density, homogeneous, mass-like lesion located to the ventral side of the pancreatic tail, and a large amount of ascites, which suggested a hematoma and massive intraabdominal hemorrhage. 

An emergency exploratory laparotomy was performed and a 5 cm laceration was found in the mesentery of transverse colon, which arose from the left margin of Treitz's ligament extending in the left direction. Hemostasis was achieved by suture ligations and absorbable hemostat materials were applied on the oozing points. Intraoperative blood transfusion was performed, and the operation was uncomplicated except for temporary paralytic ileus. The patient was discharged in a good postoperative condition on the postoperative day 20.

During the patient's hospital stay, we discovered that he had a history of intractable constipation and had a habit of massaging his abdomen to facilitate defecation, which likely caused the laceration. We advised the patient to avoid massaging his abdomen in the future and to seek medical attention if he experiences any abdominal symptoms.

In summary, the patient with a medical history of prostate cancer, endoscopic polypectomy, and chronic constipation presented with sudden-onset upper abdominal pain and was found to have intra-abdominal hemorrhage due to a mesenteric laceration caused by self-massage for defecation. An emergency exploratory laparotomy was performed to achieve hemostasis, and the operation was uncomplicated except for temporary paralytic ileus. The patient was discharged on the postoperative day 20 with instructions to avoid abdominal self-massage and seek medical attention for abdominal symptoms in the future.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to the fast-track ENT clinic with persistent left-sided throat discomfort and pain. The patient reported positive reflux symptoms with heartburn. Medical management was implemented, but it yielded no symptomatic relief. The patient underwent flexible nasendoscopy and a contrast-enhanced MRI scan, which revealed post-cricoid oedema consistent with laryngopharyngeal reflux. As the symptoms continued to persist, a transnasal oesophagoscopy was performed, and a proximal oesophageal lesion was identified. Multiple punch biopsies were taken.

The histological examination of the specimen revealed squamous cell papilloma, which tested positive for human papilloma virus (HPV). Oesophageal manometry and 24-hour oesophageal pH monitoring indicated borderline pathological reflux with some proximal penetration. The patient then underwent complete endoscopic excision of the lesion. Histology confirmed HPV-positive squamous papilloma.

The patient's symptoms resolved after the excision, and the patient received continued anti-reflux treatment, including lifestyle changes. A yearly follow-up confirmed complete remission of symptoms.

Diagnosis:

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [redacted]

Diagnoses:
1. Sarcoidosis
2. Pseudopapillary tumor (Frantz tumor) of the pancreas

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with complaints of right flank pain, low-grade fever, nausea, anorexia, and unintentional weight loss. Upon physical examination, she was found to have tenderness to palpation in the right upper quadrant and epigastric regions. Ultrasound of the abdomen showed a well-defined complex solid-cystic mass in the neck of the pancreas. Additionally, a routine chest X-ray revealed suspicious mediastinal lymphadenopathy. CT scans of the chest and abdomen were subsequently sought that revealed mediastinal lymphadenopathy, bilateral pleural effusions, and a 4.5 x 5.5 cm mass in the neck of the pancreas with mixed solid and cystic features.

Further investigations revealed multiple non-caseating granulomas, negative flow cytometry and special stains for microorganisms, and elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme level. These findings eventually led to the diagnosis of sarcoidosis in this patient. A CT-guided biopsy of the pancreatic mass revealed polygonal epithelial cells with characteristic pseudopapillary changes, leading to the diagnosis of pseudopapillary tumor (Frantz tumor) of the pancreas. Special stains including vimentin and beta-catenin were positive, thus confirming our diagnosis.

The patient underwent a Whipple pancreaticoduodenectomy for her pancreatic mass and she recovered well post-operatively. On discharge, she was in a stable hemodynamic condition.

Instructions upon Discharge:
1. Continue taking prescribed medications as directed by your healthcare provider.
2. Follow-up with your healthcare provider for routine monitoring and management of your medical condition.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with a 2-year history of progressive left greater than the right-hand weakness/myelopathy. On physical examination, left greater than the right-sided atrophy of the thenar/hypothenar eminences, and interosseous muscles were observed. Motor nerve conduction/electromyographic studies showed left greater than the right-sided C7-T1 denervation, while sensory conduction studies were normal.

The patient underwent both neutral and flexion MRI scans, revealing diffuse lower cervical spinal cord swelling most severely at C5-C6. A cervical laminectomy with durotomy was performed to obtain an intramedullary cord biopsy to exclude an intrinsic cord tumor. The biopsy showed focal cord ischemia consistent with intrinsic HD.

A C5-C6 ACDF was performed for anterior decompression. Postoperative cervical MRI showed a reduction of the ischemic C5-C6 cord focus, and the patient exhibited no clinical changes. Follow-up MRI scans over the next two years showed a mild progressive focal atrophy of the cord at the C5-C6 level with selective involvement of the anterior horns.

Discharge Diagnosis:
1. Intrinsic HD with cord ischemia.

Discharge Medications:
N/A

Follow-up:
The patient is advised to follow up with the treating neurologist for regular check-ups and further management of his medical condition. Further scans assessing the disease progression may also be ordered. 

Discharge Condition:
The patient's condition has not improved, but the hospitalization resulted in the successful exclusion of an intrinsic cord tumor and confirmation of the diagnosis of Intrinsic HD. The patient is now able to continue his treatment under the guidance of his neurologist as an outpatient.

Admitting Diagnosis: Hypocalcemia and generalized tonic-clonic seizure

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to the hospital with a new-onset generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Physical examination revealed short stature, hypertelorism, hooded upper eyelids, prominent forehead, hypernasal speech, and fullness of the nose over the bridge. Laboratory tests showed marked hypocalcemia, with further work-up revealing hypoparathyroidism. Genetic testing was performed due to the presence of subtle dysmorphic facial features, revealing a deletion of the DiGeorge/velocardiofacial syndrome critical region (TUPLE1) at 22q11.2 locus. The patient received treatment with calcium citrate and calcitriol and remained asymptomatic with normalization of serum calcium levels. Echocardiogram, abdominal ultrasound, and electroencephalogram were normal, and a computer tomography of the brain showed basal ganglia calcification.

Treatment was administered with calcium citrate and calcitriol, resulting in normalization of serum calcium levels. Patient's condition has been stable since initiation of therapy with somatostatin analogs, which has been continued along with sunitinib.

The patient has not been discharged and will continue as an outpatient in the Endocrinology Department.

During the patient’s second hospitalization for aspiration pneumonia, the spasms and dystonia were aggravated, leading to severe respiratory distress that required admission to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) and tracheal intubation. Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) was placed for the patient to facilitate her difficulty feeding.

At the age of 36 months, the patient’s problems with limb spasticity and dystonia were still present, but her feeding problem had been ameliorated. Unfortunately, she died 1 month later due to cardiorespiratory arrest at home.

The patient was discharged home with instructions for the family to return if symptoms should worsen. The patient’s parents were counselled about the nature of the underlying neurodegenerative disease.

Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

HOSPITAL COURSE:

The patient presented to the Emergency Department with pain in their right hand after punching a locker. The patient had significant soft tissue swelling over the dorsum of the right hand with tenderness over the third through fifth metacarpals. The patient had significantly limited range of motion at the metacarpophalangeal joints and interphalangeal joints and was diagnosed with comminuted intra-articular fractures through the radial aspect of the base of the third metacarpal with dorsal carpometacarpal dislocations of the third through fifth metacarpals.

The patient received a hematoma block and CMC dislocation was reduced by applying axial traction at the metacarpal phalangeal joints with pressure at the dorsum of the proximal CMC joints. The reduction was successful and the patient's hand was immobilized. The patient was advised to follow up with Orthopedic Surgery and ultimately underwent closed reduction with percutaneous placement of Kirschner wires and was immobilized for six weeks.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS:

Comminuted intra-articular fractures through the radial aspect of the base of the third metacarpal, with dorsal carpometacarpal dislocations of the third through fifth metacarpals.

TREATMENT:

Hematoma block, closed reduction, percutaneous placement of Kirschner wires, and immobilization for six weeks.

FOLLOW-UP:

The patient was advised to follow up with Orthopedic Surgery.

Diagnosis: Esophageal fistula with massive hematemesis; 6 cm saccular thoracic aortic aneurysm distal to the left subclavian artery

Hospital Course:

The patient was a 48-year-old male with a history of hypertension and a percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stents three years ago. He presented to the emergency with one episode of massive hematemesis. An urgent UGI endoscopy revealed a large depressed ulcer with a red spot located in the middle third of the esophagus along with a diverticulum located in the lower end of the ulcer. Imaging studies revealed a 6 cm saccular thoracic aortic aneurysm eroding into the esophagus.

Surgery was performed through a posterolateral thoracotomy. The aneurysmal segment of the aorta was replaced with a Dacron graft while taking care to preserve as many intercostal arteries as possible while suture ligating the others. The esophageal opening of the fistula was debrided and repaired with interrupted polypropylene sutures, superimposed with a vascularized intercostal muscle pedicle. The patient was placed on broad-spectrum antibiotics postoperatively.

Postoperatively, the patient recovered well and had an uneventful course. He was successfully separated from the partial bypass, and a gastrostomy and jejunostomy were created. He was discharged and advised to follow up with his primary care physician and the treating surgeon as part of a long-term management plan. 

Discharge Medications: None

Instructions: No heavy lifting, straining or strenuous activity for the next 6-8 weeks. Follow-up appointments were scheduled with the primary care physician and surgeon.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 32-year-old female with chief complaint of pain in upper anterior tooth.

Hospital Course:
The patient reported to the Department of Conservative Dentistry and Endodontics and was diagnosed with an impacted permanent canine and a palatally placed upper permanent right lateral incisor. A radiograph showed loss of lamina dura and slight radiolucency in relation to the periapical area of the upper right central incisor. A CBCT revealed a periapical lesion related to both roots of the central incisor and an additional root positioned more facially than expected. A nonsurgical endodontic therapy was decided after a discussion with the patient. The root canals were cleaned and shaped, copiously irrigated, and obturated with corresponding Protaper gutta-percha and AH Plus sealer. The patient refused restoration of the facial groove with composite resin.

Outcome:
The patient was asymptomatic after 2 weeks and at a one-year follow-up. The patient was satisfied with the treatment outcome and would continue to be monitored by her dentist. 

Impression:
The patient presented with a rare case of an additional root present with the central incisor, which was successfully treated with nonsurgical endodontic therapy.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]   Date of Admission: [REDACTED]    Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Admitting Diagnosis: Poorly controlled type 1 diabetes (T1D) and marked hepatomegaly.

Hospital Course:
The patient, an 11-year old boy with a history of T1D, was hospitalized in the Emergency Department due to symptoms of polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, and weakness. He presented with diabetic ketoacidosis, for which he received insulin therapy according to the International Society of Pediatric and Adolescent Diabetes guidelines. Following this treatment, he was prescribed multiple daily insulin injections and discharged after a week. However, the patient did not attend the follow-up visit at the Diabetes Centre, resulting in poor glycometabolic control and recurrent episodes of diabetic ketoacidosis.

At the age of 10, the patient moved to Southern Italy with his family and was eventually admitted to our Paediatric Diabetes Clinic after an episode of severe diabetic ketoacidosis, accompanied by marked hepatomegaly and short stature. Secondary sexual characteristics were absent, and the patient's hormonal levels were evaluated.

Laboratory tests were performed to determine the differential diagnosis of his hepatomegaly, but autoimmune hepatitis and infectious causes were excluded and no inflammation or fibrosis was noted in the liver biopsy. A diagnosis of hepatic glycogenosis was confirmed.

While in the hospital, the patient received education on diabetes management, and his daily insulin dosage was titrated to achieve good metabolic control. A follow-up examination three months later, however, showed poor metabolic control, severe hepatomegaly, and abnormal lipid levels, leading to another hospitalization.

During this second hospitalization, the patient received intravenous continuous insulin treatment for normalization of aminotransferases and to achieve good glycaemic control, which was reached after eight days. The patient maintained good glycemic control at the last follow-up visit, with complete remission of biochemical, clinical signs, and hepatomegaly resolution.

Diagnostic Impression:
The patient is diagnosed with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes, marked hepatomegaly, and hepatic glycogenosis.

Follow-Up Recommendations:
The patient is advised to continue managing his diabetes as planned and maintain regular follow-ups with his healthcare provider. The patient should also continue monitoring his lipid levels periodically.

Hospital Course:
The patient, an 89-year-old male, was admitted with complaints of cough and haemoptysis. The patient had a history of bronchiectasis in the right middle lobe bronchus for 30 years. One month before admission, the patient suffered a massive haemoptysis, which was controlled through bronchial artery embolization. However, haemoptysis recurred, and the patient was admitted to our hospital. Bronchoscopy performed on the patient showed active bleeding from the right middle lobe bronchus, which was temporarily controlled through haemostatic medications and cryotherapy.

Management:
On the next day, an 8 mm x 3 cm silicon stent was deployed using biopsy forceps after multiple attempts. Another customized stent with a diameter of about 6 mm was placed from the right intermediate bronchus to the right lower lobe bronchus, to avoid stent migration. Bleeding stopped promptly after the placement of stents. The patient received successive antibiotic therapy, and no obvious complication of obstructive pneumonia developed.

Outcome:
One month after the operation of stents implantation, the patient experienced complete atelectasis of the right middle and lower lobe with the complication of right pleural effusion. The patient received further surgery to remove the silicon stent inside the right intermediate bronchus. Thoracic puncture and drainage were done after stent extraction for relieving pleural effusion. Post-operation CT scan reviewed the patient's chest and revealed the right lower lobe recruitment. The patient did not experience any more haemoptysis during the three-month follow-up time and left the hospital ten days after stent extraction.

The bleeding returned, leading to his admission to the hospital for further care.
A lung exam with a scope showed active bleeding from the right middle lobe, briefly stopped with medicines and freezing.
Management:
The next day, doctors placed an 8 mm by 3 cm silicone tube in the airway using a special tool after several tries.
They also put a custom-made 6 mm tube from the middle airway to the lower lung airway to keep it from moving.
Bleeding stopped quickly after the tubes were placed, and the patient’s condition stabilized.
He received antibiotics over several days, and no lung infection from blockage developed.
Outcome:
One month after the tube placement, the right middle and lower lung parts collapsed and fluid built up around the lung.
He had surgery to remove the silicone tube from the middle airway, and the procedure was successful.
After the tube was taken out, a needle was used to drain the fluid around the lung.
A chest scan after the procedure showed the lower lung had reopened and was working better.
He did not cough up blood again during the three-month check-up and left the hospital ten days after the tube removal.

Admission Diagnosis:
Fetal perianal mass detected at 23 weeks' gestation

Hospital Course:
The patient was evaluated for a fetal perianal mass that was detected during routine antenatal care. At the initial visit, an echogenic perivaginal mass was visible on 2D transabdominal ultrasound. Further evaluation with 3D ultrasound revealed that the mass was originated from the skin apart from anus or vagina. Amniocentesis was performed which revealed normal fetal karyotype and no acetylcholinesterase level was detected. As the gestational age progressed, the size of the mass increased. A female neonate was delivered at GA 41 weeks and a pedunculated soft mass was visible on the right posterior labium major of the neonate. A complete physical and laboratory evaluation was performed preoperatively, including routine postnatal cardiac echo which showed a patent foramen ovale with a flow from left to right. There was no significant congenital anomaly identified in vertebral body, both kidney, and anus on MRI. Simple surgical excision was planned for the lesion but during the operation, the right anal external muscle complex was displaced due to the original mass and perineal groove type anorectal malformation was found. Posterior sagittal anorectoplasty (PSARP) was performed with complete mass excision. The histopathological result was lipoblastoma with free resection margin. The neonate was discharged from the hospital without any complication on the postoperative seventh day.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Fetal perianal mass and lipoblastoma

Discharge Condition:
Stable

Discharge Medications:
N/A

Discharge Instructions:
The care team discussed the details of the operation and postoperative care with the patient and their family. The patient is advised to return to the follow-up clinic as scheduled for further evaluation. They were also advised to avoid any strenuous physical activity or heavy lifting for several weeks after surgery. If any signs of infection, such as fever or drainage at the surgical site, develop, the patient should contact their health care provider immediately. It is also recommended to maintain routine postnatal care and follow-up evaluations to monitor neonate's health.

Follow-up:
The patient is scheduled for regular follow-up appointments to monitor their recovery and evaluate any potential complications.

The patient, a 30-year-old male, was admitted to the orthopedic outpatient department (OPD) with complaints of lower back pain radiating to the left lower limb and difficulty in walking associated with low-grade fever. The physical examination revealed tenderness in the lumbosacral area of the spine, reduced power, and sensory changes in the left lower limb. Laboratory investigations showed decreased hemoglobin levels, total leucocyte count of 14800/cumm, and platelet count of 688000/cumm. Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine revealed T2 hyperintense and T1 iso to hyperintense moderately enhancing soft tissue in the spinal cord, extending within neural foramina with obliteration of neural foraminal fat. The impression of diffuse Kochs involvement of the spine was given along with suspicion of neoplastic etiology like lymphoma. Vertebral bone biopsy from left L3 and L4 region was performed and sent for histopathological examination which revealed actinomycosis of the lumbosacral spine. The patient was started on penicillin group antibiotics and tolerated the therapy well.

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the community hospital with a complaint of syncope. The patient reported experiencing numbness in her arms while kayaking, followed by a loss of consciousness. The patient had a history of dizziness two weeks prior to the current episode. Initial laboratory tests showed low serum potassium and elevated troponin levels. An electrocardiogram revealed sinus tachycardia with monomorphic premature ventricular complexes (PVCs), and a corrected QT (QTc) interval of 520 ms. The QTc interval was normalized with potassium repletion. Echocardiography and cardiac catheterization findings were normal. A treadmill test showed multifocal PVCs and the QT interval shortened with exertion. The patient was discharged on nadolol and a LifeVest® wearable cardioverter-defibrillator.

Later, the patient presented with tachycardia for which the WCD alarmed. The patient pressed the response button to suppress a shock for more than nine minutes but eventually received two shocks. An MRI scan with gadolinium enhancement showed delayed myocardial enhancement in the midmyocardium and epicardium, indicating a nonischemic origin such as myocarditis, amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, or some other form of nonischemic cardiomyopathy. The patient was diagnosed with a phenomenon of residual fibrosis from a past viral myocarditis.

Treatment:

A dual-chamber implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) was placed, and sotalol was initiated at 80 mg twice daily and later increased to 120 mg twice daily. The patient was found to be noninducible via noninvasive programmed stimulation. The patient has been arrhythmia- and symptom-free and is scheduled for further follow-up.

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the hospital after fainting, with arm numbness while kayaking before losing consciousness. She also had felt dizzy two weeks before this episode, as she reported during the visit. Early blood tests showed low potassium and high troponin, which is a marker of heart injury. An ECG showed a fast heart rhythm with extra beats and a prolonged QT interval of 520 ms. Giving potassium through an IV brought the QT interval back to normal during the hospital stay. Ultrasound of the heart and a heart catheter test showed no problems and were normal. A treadmill test revealed many extra beats from different spots and the QT interval got shorter with exercise. The patient left the hospital taking nadolol and wearing a LifeVest defibrillator vest to protect against dangerous rhythms. Later, she returned with a fast heartbeat that triggered the LifeVest alarm and required her to press the response button. She held the button for over nine minutes to stop a shock, but eventually got two shocks. An MRI with contrast showed scar-like patches in the heart muscle, suggesting myocarditis, amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, or similar disease. Doctors said the scar likely came from a past viral heart infection, also known as myocarditis.
Treatment:
The patient then received a permanent dual-chamber defibrillator implanted in the chest to stop dangerous heart rhythms. She started taking sotalol at 80 mg twice daily, later increased to 120 mg twice daily. Tests showed the device could not trigger a dangerous rhythm, meaning she was not inducible. She has had no arrhythmias or symptoms and will continue with regular follow-up visits to monitor her heart.

Patient Name: [redacted]
Medical Record Number: [redacted]
Gender: Female
Age: 67 years

Hospital Course:
The 67-year-old female patient with a stage 3 macular hole was admitted on [redacted] with a complaint of decreased vision in the left eye for the past one month. The patient underwent pars plana vitrectomy, triamcinolone acetonide-assisted internal limiting membrane peeling, and fluid-gas exchange. The postoperative OCT scans obtained at four weeks demonstrated the photoreceptor layer with 1820 µm wide disorganization. The patient had a visual acuity of 20/100. At six weeks, a macula spared retinal detachment with multiple breaks was found. She underwent pars plana vitrectomy, laser photocoagulation, and fluid-gas exchange. Her visual acuity was 20/40 at six months, and the OCT studies disclosed reorganization of the photoreceptor layer at multiple locations along the macula. Slight disorganization of the photoreceptor layer was noted under the center of the fovea. By 1 year, the patient's visual acuity had improved further to 20/25, and the photoreceptor layer of the fovea had been reorganized on the OCT images.

Diagnosis:
Stage 3 macular hole, macula-spared retinal detachment with multiple breaks.

Treatment:
Pars plana vitrectomy, triamcinolone acetonide-assisted internal limiting membrane peeling, fluid-gas exchange, laser photocoagulation.

Condition on Discharge:
The patient's condition has improved significantly, with visual acuity improving to 20/25, and there being a complete reorganization of the photoreceptor layer of the fovea.

Follow-up Care:
The patient will require regular follow-up to monitor her vision and retina health.

Summary:
The 67-year-old female patient with a stage 3 macular hole who presented with decreased vision in the left eye underwent successful pars plana vitrectomy, triamcinolone acetonide-assisted internal limiting membrane peeling, fluid-gas exchange, and laser photocoagulation. The postoperative follow-up scans showed a reorganization of the photoreceptor layer at multiple locations along the macula, and a slight disorganization was noted under the center of the fovea. The patient's condition steadily improved over the course of one year, with visual acuity improving to 20/25, and the photoreceptor layer of the fovea being reorganized on the OCT images. Regular follow-up care will be required to monitor vision and retina health.

Discharge Summary:

This is a summary of the hospital course of a 62-year-old male with Kearns-Sayre syndrome (KSS) who presented to the emergency department (ED) after two syncopal episodes. He has a past medical history of multi-system involvement including skeletal muscle myopathy, pigmentary retinopathy, heart failure, non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, pulmonary hypertension, chronic heart block, chronic kidney disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and mitral valve prolapse.

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted for syncope secondary to VT, and 150 mg of IV amiodarone bolus was administered. He was started on amiodarone drip at 0.5 mg/min. Follow-up AICD interrogation yielded sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia to the 140s during both syncopal episodes. Chest X-ray revealed right pleural effusion. On day two, the patient was noted to have non-sustained VT with increasing oxygen requirements. A plan was in place to transition the patient from IV to PO amiodarone, but instead, he developed VT storm and was thus continued on amiodarone drip. He was transferred to the critical care unit (CCU) for further monitoring and started on lidocaine drip (1 mg/min) with continued amiodarone and milrinone drips. In the CCU, he continued to have non-sustained VT with symptoms of palpitations despite the AICD reprogramming and medical management. He also continued to have shortness of breath with minimal improvement on bilevel positive airway pressure (BIPAP). Unfortunately, recurrent VT progressed to a VT storm, requiring multiple boluses of IV amiodarone, IV lidocaine, and multiple shocks from his AICD which were futile. The VT storm was refractory to his current medical management. The patient eventually passed away after the withdrawal of care.

Final Diagnosis:

The final diagnosis of the patient was VT storm in the setting of KSS with multi-system involvement including heart failure.

Follow-Up:

The patient was not discharged due to his unfortunate clinical outcome.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: N/A
Medical Record Number: N/A
Discharge Date: N/A

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 56-year-old male with a history of dilated cardiomyopathy and atrial fibrillation, presented with epigastralgia and nonsustained VT. The patient was treated with amiodarone, nifekalant hydrochloride, and lidocaine, but the ventricular arrhythmias persisted which led to a decrease in atrial flutter. Severe anemia and blastoid cells were observed in the peripheral blood sample, and the patient was diagnosed with Ph+ ALL. Dasatinib 50 mg twice daily and prednisolone 100 mg daily were initiated to treat the leukemia. The dasatinib was discontinued after five days due to an increase in nonsustained VT although the QTc interval was not significantly prolonged. Bisoprolol was gradually increased to 3.75 mg daily, and dasatinib was rechallenged. The patient showed a complete hematological response and a 2-log reduction in minor bcr-abl mRNA transcripts in the bone marrow. Three weeks after the retreatment with dasatinib, blastoid cells reemerged in the peripheral blood, and the dasatinib was discontinued due to refractoriness of leukemia. The patient received steroid pulse therapy and furosemide, and VT did not recur after. Although, dexamethasone and the short-term use of mercaptopurine were used, the patient expired from leukemia on the 183rd day after admission.

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient was admitted with epigastralgia and nonsustained VT which was treated with amiodarone, nifekalant hydrochloride, and lidocaine. After a diagnosis of Ph+ ALL, the patient was initiated with dasatinib 50 mg twice daily and prednisolone 100 mg daily to manage leukemia. Due to complications, dasatinib and bisoprolol doses were adjusted. After the first retreatment with dasatinib, a complete hematological response was observed and minor bcr-abl mRNA transcripts reduced. The patient expired from leukemia on the 183rd day after admission.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Age: 8
Gender: Male
Date of Admission: [Redacted]
Date of Discharge: [Redacted]

HOSPITAL COURSE:

The patient was admitted to our hospital due to abdominal pain, which was relieved by conservative management. He had been diagnosed with congenital IPSVS six years prior and was under medication for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder.

Laboratory tests revealed elevated ammonia levels and a prolonged coagulation profile. Imaging studies confirmed the presence of IPSVS and the hepatic mass.

The patient's parents opted for close follow-up rather than invasive treatment for the IPSVS. However, at the six-month follow-up, the patient's blood ammonia level had risen significantly, and the shunt ratio indicated the potential progression of hepatic encephalopathy. Hence, endovascular treatment was performed to close the shunt.

During the procedure, the patient experienced bleeding from the sheath's tract, which was managed promptly using US-guided compression. Within six days of the procedure, the patient's serum ammonia levels had decreased to within normal range, and he was discharged after nine days.

FOLLOW-UP:

Two weeks post-embolization, an abdominal US showed occluded shunts with a decrease in the size of the hepatic mass. The right portal vein's blood flow had increased markedly, and the spleen size had minimally increased. A follow-up CT scan a month later showed complete embolization of the IPSVS, improved portal flow to the right lobe, and nearly complete disappearance of the hepatic mass.

On discharge, the patient was stable, alert and oriented. His physical exam and vital signs were normal. His medications were reviewed, and he was instructed to follow up with his referring physician.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS:

1. Congenital IPSVS
2. Hepatic mass.

DISCHARGE PLAN:

1. Follow up with the referring physician for routine care and monitoring.
2. Medications to be continued as before.
3. No dietary restrictions.
4. No strenuous physical activity for two weeks.
5. Report back to the hospital if there are any concerns or adverse events.

Hospital Course:
A 31-year-old female presented with flu-like symptoms and a positive COVID-19 PCR test result. She was transferred to ICU with acute onset respiratory distress and maintained satisfactory oxygenation on nasal prongs. The patient was found to be positive for HIV with a CD4+ count of 3 cells/uL and a viral load of 53 781 copies/mL. Treatment with 1 g meropenem 8-hourly, 60 mg subcutaneous enoxaparin twice daily, 50 mg hydrocortisone 6-hourly, as well as zinc supplementation was given. ART was commenced as well as Pneumocystis prophylaxis. The patient was transferred to the general ward after 3 days and ultimately discharged 4 days later after a negative COVID-19 PCR test result.

Discharge Medications:
1. ART medications as prescribed
2. Pneumocystis prophylaxis

Follow-up:
1. The patient was instructed to continue taking medications as prescribed and to schedule follow-up appointments with her primary care physician.
2. The patient was also counseled on the importance of regular HIV viral load testing and maintaining an appropriate medication regimen for her HIV diagnosis.

Discharge Condition:
The patient was discharged in stable condition.

Discharge Destination:
The patient was discharged to home.

Hospital Course:

The patient presented with sudden onset and severe occipital headache accompanied by bending his neck downwards. He was given loxoprofen sodium hydrate which momentarily relieved the headache but it persisted. Neurological examination shows no abnormalities. Brain CT and MRI were normal, but MRA showed multisegmental narrowing of the basilar artery, identified via BPAS-MRI agreement. After ruling out inflammation or infection by CSF investigation, a diagnosis of RCVS was presumed, and the patient was put on lomerizine hydrochloride (10 mg/day). Repeat MRA and BPAS-MRI were done, which showed a mild resolution of vasoconstriction. The symptoms resolved by post-admission day 8, and the patient was discharged uneventfully.

Hospitalization Summary:

A 41-year-old man presented with sudden onset and severe occipital headache, accompanied by bending his neck downwards. Nothing seen in the neurological examination, brain CT and MRI were normal, but MRA showed multisegmental narrowing of the basilar artery, in agreement with BPAS-MRI. CSF investigation was conducted, which ruled out inflammation or infection. RCVS was presumed, and the patient was treated with lomerizine hydrochloride (10 mg/day). Repeat MRA and BPAS-MRI showed a mild resolution of vasoconstriction, with symptoms resolving by post-admission day 8. The patient was then discharged.

Hospital Course:

This 60-year-old male patient presented to our outpatient clinic with a 1-year history of generalized yellowish ovoid skin-colored papular eruption located on the trunk, groin, and extremities. The patient reported that he first noticed pruritic papules, and 2–3 months later many yellow and ovoid pruritic papules emerged. On skin physical examination, firm, well-defined ovoid skin-colored to yellow papules were seen on the distal and proximal of upper and lower extremities, trunk, groins, and abdomen.

Diagnostic laboratory tests such as full blood cell count with differential, peripheral blood smear, renal, and liver function tests all were normal. Histopathological examination of the skin biopsy from one of the lesion on the trunk revealed proliferation of mast cells with ovoid and spindle nuclei with distinct cytoplasm borders around capillaries, which was compatible with mastocytosis. Based on concurrent clinical and pathological features, we diagnosed our case as xanthelasmoid mastocytosis.

Treatment with H1 antihistamine, cetirizine 10 mg orally nightly and fexofenadine 120 mg for every morning was prescribed for pruritus control which was successful, but eruptions were persistent without any changes. Treatment with phototherapy also recommended to the patient, but despite a 1-year course, no significant improvement was seen in the lesions.

The patient refused further investigations such as bone marrow biopsy or alternative treatments and decided to end the hospital course. The patient was advised to monitor the lesions and seek medical attention if he noticed any changes or deterioration. The patient was discharged with no complications.

Exam showed firm, oval skin-colored to yellow papules on the arms, legs, trunk, and groin. Blood tests, including complete blood count, peripheral smear, kidney and liver tests, were all normal. The biopsy showed many mast cells with oval and spindle shapes, which is consistent with mastocytosis. Based on the clinical exam and biopsy results, we diagnosed the patient with xanthelasmoid mastocytosis. The patient took cetirizine 10 mg at night and fexofenadine 120 mg each morning to control itching. Although the antihistamine treatment reduced the itching, the skin bumps stayed the same over time. Phototherapy was also recommended, but after one year of treatment the lesions showed no significant improvement. The patient declined further tests such as a bone marrow biopsy and other alternative treatments. He chose to stop the hospital care and end his hospital course at that point. He was told to watch the lesions and call his doctor if they change or get worse. He was discharged from the hospital and sent home without any complications or new health issues.

Patient Name: [Name]

Sex: Female
Date of Admission: [Admission Date]
Date of Discharge: [Discharge Date]
Admitting Physician: [Physician Name]
Primary Diagnosis: Urticaria

Hospital Course:

The patient presented to the outpatient allergy clinic with a complaint of recurrent generalized urticaria, rash, and facial angioedema, worsened by high-seasoned, spicy or Chinese foods. Previously, she had been treated for allergic rhinitis and experienced severe urticaria with a generalized rash after taking non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Peripheral eosinophil counts and serum total IgE in her blood were elevated, and a skin prick test showed weakly positive reactions to silk worm pupa, herring, cabbage, celery, and walnut. However, none of them induced urticaria in her history.

The patient underwent basophil activation test (BAT), in which a total of 18.7% of basophils were activated after stimulation with monosodium glutamate (MSG). No other additives induced significant basophil activation compared to the negative control. T4 and thyroid stimulating hormone levels were within normal range.

The patient was diagnosed with urticaria and was advised to avoid foods that tend to trigger her symptoms. No medications were prescribed.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient was provided with instructions on how to manage her symptoms at home and advised to avoid the foods that tend to trigger urticaria. She was also advised to return to the clinic if her symptoms persist or worsen.

Follow-up:

The patient was advised to follow-up with the clinic for further evaluation and management.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Name]
Medical Record Number: [Number]

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 29-year-old male of Syrian origin, was admitted for evaluation of a painless right-sided testicular swelling that had been present for 12 months. Upon clinical examination, he had a nontender enlarged right testis. Further evaluation with alpha-fetoprotein (α-FP) and beta human chorionic gonadotropin (β-HCG) tumor markers revealed negative results. An ultrasound scan of the scrotum showed a 7-cm hypoechoic, hypervascular, and cystic mass replacing the right testis. A right radical inguinal orchidectomy was performed, and a staging computed tomography scan was negative for lymphatic or metastatic disease.

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient was diagnosed with Sertoli cell sarcoma (SCS) with undifferentiated sarcoma confined to the testis. The tumor was composed of small, intermediate, and large epithelioid cells arranged in sheets with broad areas of necrosis. Microscopic features of these cells were consistent with SCS. Additionally, there were ill-defined areas of undifferentiated sarcoma composed of highly pleomorphic, epithelioid, and spindle-shaped cells with high mitotic activity invested in fibrous and fibromyxoid stroma. The tumor did not extend beyond the tunica albuginea. The spermatic cord and epididymis were uninvolved, and no lymphovascular invasion was identified.

Treatment:
The histological diagnosis was SCS with undifferentiated sarcoma confined to the testis. Further oncological treatment with adjuvant chemotherapy was strongly advised, but the patient declined and moved to a different locality.

Follow-up:
The patient should be advised to receive regular follow-up consultations for potential recurrence of the tumor, and to notify his healthcare provider if he develops any symptoms concerning for the same.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [redacted]
Age: 35
Gender: Male
Admission Date: [redacted]
Discharge Date: [redacted]
Admitting Diagnosis: Acute transverse myelitis
Discharge Diagnosis: HIV infection

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to the Emergency Room with urinary retention and diminished strength in the lower limbs. He had recently returned from Angola where he had been working. He had been vaccinated for yellow fever, poliomyelitis, typhoid fever, and meningococcal disease in advance. He was initially treated for a possible spider bite and later presented with fever, cough, dyspnea, myalgia, and thoracic pain. After undergoing several tests, he was diagnosed with acute transverse myelitis and started on treatment with ceftriaxone, ganciclovir, and methylprednisolone.

However, there were some deteriorations in his condition, including intensifying upper thoracic pain, progressing hypoaesthesia, dysaesthesia, numbness, and ice cold sensation. A second lumbar puncture was performed which was negative. Doxycycline and human immunoglobulin were added to his medication. The treatment resulted in significant improvement, and he was able to walk unassisted and all symptoms fully resolved within three weeks. His HIV testing was positive and repeated before discharge.

Outcome:
The patient was discharged after completing 21 days of ceftriaxone, 7 days of methylprednisolone, 7 days of doxycycline, and 5 days of human immunoglobulin. He was asymptomatic at his first follow-up appointment and his CD4 count was above 400/mm3. But after a year of follow-up, the count went down to below 400/mm3, and his viral load was stabilized around 130,000 cp/mL. He started his HAART with abacavir/lamivudine and efavirenz six months later, which led to an increase in the CD4+ cell count and undetectable viral load.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Overview:
The patient is a 58-year-old male who presented with a painless, asymptomatic lesion on the right upper lid that he has had for 15 years. He had also been diagnosed with right lower lid senile entropion for which an entropion repair was scheduled. 

History and Physical:
On examination, the eyelid nodule was found to be firm, and not adherent to the overlying skin. The size of the nodule was 5mm x 5mm and was mobile. The patient did not show any evidence of skin ulceration, but the eyelid skin had an extra fold due to dermatochalasis. Apart from these findings, the rest of the ocular examination was unremarkable.

Hospital Course:
The patient underwent an entropion repair procedure as well as an excision of the eyelid nodule which the patient had requested. The postoperative period was uneventful. 

Outpatient Follow-up:
At the last follow-up appointment, 3 months later, the patient did not show any evidence of recurrence.

Diagnosis:
As per the case report, there is no formal diagnosis mentioned. 

Treatment:
The patient underwent an entropion repair along with an excision of the eyelid nodule. 

Prognosis:
The patient has a good prognosis with no evidence of recurrence at his last follow-up.

Discharge Summary:

Patient was diagnosed with annular alopecia areata (AA) based on clinical examination and histopathological findings. The patient presented with asymptomatic loss of hair in an annular pattern at multiple sites over the scalp for 2 months. Hair loss was more pronounced at the periphery compared to the center of the patch. The patient had no history of similar illness in family members and no history of drug intake or trauma.

On examination, there were multiple well-defined annular patches of non-scarring alopecia ranging in size from 2 cm x 3 cm to 4 cm x 4 cm present at the parietal and occipital region of the scalp. The area was smooth with no associated skin changes. Systemic examination was within normal limits. Potassium hydroxide (KOH) examination of hair showed no fungal elements, and fungal culture with Sabouraud's media at 4 weeks revealed no growth.

Histopathological examination from the hairless region showed a few vellus follicles in mid dermis with a sparse perifollicular lymphocytic infiltrate. The dermis and subcutis also showed several follicular stellae representing former follicular papillae. The total number of follicles was substantially reduced, with no terminal follicles.

The patient was treated with intralesional injections of trimacinolone acetonide (5mg/ml) every 4 weeks, with remarkable improvement in the lesions after 3 months (3 intralesional injections) of follow-up.

The patient was discharged with recommendations for follow-up care and to continue treatment with intralesional injections of trimacinolone acetonide. The patient was advised to schedule appointments with their healthcare provider every 4 weeks for follow-up care and to monitor for any signs of recurrent alopecia.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 44
Gender: Female
Chief Complaint: Painful oral ulcer

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with a painful oral ulcer, which had developed 6 weeks prior. She had a history of aphthous stomatitis and received systemic steroid treatment. However, her condition worsened with an erythematous maculopapular rash on her body, conjunctival injection, fever, diarrhea, and weight loss. Leukocytosis and eosinophilia were noted. Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) was suspected, and she was treated with systemic steroids, which showed slight improvement in skin condition but unresponsiveness in stomatitis.
A skin biopsy showed interface dermatitis and subepidermal blister formation with basal vacuolization consistent with PNP. Additional tests showed IgG deposition on normal human skin, mouse bladder epithelium, and mouse lung epithelium. The patient was ultimately diagnosed with stage IV follicular lymphoma with BO and invasive pulmonary aspergillosis. 
Chemotherapy resulted in a complete remission of lymphoma, which was confirmed through positron emission tomography. The patient's stomatitis and skin rash were well-maintained with a low-dose steroid therapy of 5mg/day for 8 months. However, she developed BO and invasive pulmonary aspergillosis, which led to respiratory failure. 

Course of Treatment:
Treatment included chemotherapy with rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisolone, which resulted in complete remission of the patient's lymphoma. The patient was also treated with a low-dose steroid therapy of 5mg/day, which maintained the improvement of stomatitis and skin rash. 

Follow-Up Care:
No specific follow-up care is necessary since the patient passed away from respiratory failure. 

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with PNP, which was later associated with stage IV follicular lymphoma with BO and invasive pulmonary aspergillosis.

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 22-year-old female with no significant past medical history who presented with altered mental status, acute psychosis with suicidal ideation, decreased oral intake, and reduced urine output. On admission, she was placed on an involuntary hold by a psychiatrist and was noted to be delirious, uncooperative, agitated, demanding, and impulsive. Initial imaging did not show acute intracranial abnormalities, and she was started on sodium valproate for a presumed bipolar disorder with psychotic features in addition to olanzapine and clonazepam.

Diagnosis and Treatment:
The working diagnosis at this time was considered to be encephalopathy, sepsis vs systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) from aspiration and acute hypoxic respiratory failure. She had an extensive infectious, metabolic, autoimmune, and neurologic workup. The initial panels have returned negative. However, her CSF differential showed a high WBC count with lymphocytic pleocytosis. Further investigation showed elevated titers of anti-NMDA antibodies evaluated by Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay. Anti-NMDA antibodies were detected in both serum and CSF. She was started on IV steroids, IV immunoglobulin (IVIG), and plasma exchange.

Hospital Course Post-Surgery:
Following surgical intervention, the patient was started on high dose steroids, IVIG 2 rounds (with one month interval) of 10% IVIG 17.5 g, and repeated cycles of plasma exchange with gradual improvement in symptoms three weeks post-surgery as evidenced by restoration of sleep-wake cycles, increased frequency of alertness, ability to more consistently follow commands, decreased frequency of fevers, improvement of blood pressure, and tachycardia.

Discharge:
After two and a half months post-surgery, the patient was discharged with full return of function. She returned for follow-up six months after surgery, before returning to college, this time she reported feeling that her memory and movement had improved, and she felt more like her normal self. Her neurological and psychiatric workup was completely within normal. It was considered that she did not need future treatment or follow-up as she was completely recovered.

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 22-year-old woman with no prior health problems, came in confused and had thoughts of harming herself.
She also was not eating or drinking enough and was urinating less than usual during her hospital stay.
On admission, she was held without her consent for safety and appeared confused, uncooperative, restless, pushy, and impulsive.
A brain scan showed no sudden problems, so doctors looked for other causes and began treatment.
She was given a seizure medicine because doctors suspected a mood disorder with loss of touch with reality.
She also received two calming medicines to help control her agitation and prevent seizures during her stay.
Diagnosis and Treatment:
Doctors thought she might have brain dysfunction caused by infection or body inflammation from inhaling stomach contents.
This was also linked to low oxygen levels in her lungs, which made her breathing difficult.
She underwent many tests to check for infection, body chemistry, immune system, and nerve problems.
All of the initial test results came back normal, so doctors continued searching for the cause.
A spinal fluid test showed many white blood cells, most of which were lymphocytes, indicating inflammation.
Further testing found high levels of antibodies that attack brain receptors in both her blood and spinal fluid.
Treatment began with steroid medicine given through a vein, antibody treatment through a vein, and blood cleaning procedures.
Hospital Course Post-Surgery:
After surgery, she received strong steroid medicine, two doses of antibody medicine one month apart, and several blood cleaning sessions.
About three weeks later, her symptoms started to improve noticeably as she began to regain normal function.
She began sleeping normally, felt more alert, and followed directions more consistently than before during her recovery.
She experienced fewer fevers, her blood pressure improved, and her fast heart rate slowed over the following weeks.
Discharge:
About two and a half months after surgery, she was discharged with full return of her normal function.
Six months after surgery, before returning to college, she came back for a follow-up visit.
At that visit, she said her memory and movement had improved and she felt like herself again.
All neurological and psychiatric tests were completely normal, showing no remaining problems and indicating full recovery.
Doctors decided she no longer needs treatment or follow-up because she has fully recovered at this time.

The patient is diagnosed with Wolman Disease/CESD.

The patient was seen by a hepatologist and a medical geneticist.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital due to acute onset of hoarseness, voice fatigue, and effort dyspnea. The patient was diagnosed with HHT and presented with characteristic vascular lesions in the oral cavity. A fiberolaryngoscopy and a phoniatric examination were performed, which revealed unchanged mobility and morphology of the right vocal fold and paresis of the left vocal fold. CT and MRI of head, neck, and chest showed no pathologic findings.

The patient was treated for 12 months for unilateral paresis of the vocal fold as idiopathic by means of extensive rehabilitation, but no improvement was observed. Due to persistent symptoms, the patient underwent type I thyroplasty (medialization) under local anesthesia. The surgical procedure was successful, and the patient was advised to avoid vocal effort or extensive physical activity for about 2 weeks post-surgery.

After surgery, the patient's voice quality improved significantly, with most parameters defining amplitude and frequency normalizing. The Voice Handicap Index (VHI) also improved significantly.

The patient is on regular follow-up in the outpatient setting, and during 1-year follow-up, there was no recurrence of symptoms.

Summary:
The patient presented with hoarseness, voice fatigue, and effort dyspnea. Due to persistent symptoms, the patient underwent type I thyroplasty (medialization) after extensive rehabilitation failed to improve the vocal fold paresis. The surgery was successful, and after two weeks of recovery, the patient was discharged with significant improvement in voice quality and the VHI.
