The patient has HHT, a condition that causes abnormal blood vessels, and showed typical blood vessel spots in the mouth.
A throat scope exam and a voice exam showed the right vocal cord moved normally and looked normal.
The left vocal cord was weak and did not move well.
CT and MRI scans of the head, neck, and chest showed no problems.
The patient had 12 months of voice therapy for a weak vocal cord with unknown cause, but saw no improvement.
The patient had thyroplasty (type I, medialization) with local anesthesia after voice therapy did not help the weak vocal cord.
The surgery went well, and the patient was told to rest the voice and avoid heavy activity for two weeks.
After surgery, the patient's voice got much better.
Most voice measures returned to normal and the Voice Handicap Index score also got much better.
The patient continues regular outpatient check-ups, and at the one-year visit, symptoms did not come back.
Summary:
The patient had hoarseness, a tired voice, and shortness of breath when exerting, leading to hospital admission.
Because symptoms continued, the patient had type I thyroplasty (medialization) after voice therapy did not help the weak vocal cord.
The surgery went well, and after two weeks rest, the patient left with better voice and Voice Handicap Index score.

Admitting Diagnosis: Hepatitis B virus-related liver cirrhosis with portal vein thrombosis and portal systemic encephalopathy.

Hospital Course:
The patient underwent donor liver transplantation and was admitted to the surgical intensive care unit for postoperative care. Medications included aspirin and nafamostat mesilate to prevent thrombosis, prostaglandin E1 to vasodilate the anastomosed vessels, tacrolimus and prednisolone for immunosuppression, and ampicillin/sulbactam, fluconazole, and nystatin for prophylaxis against infection.

On postoperative day 6, the patient showed deteriorated mental status and decreased motor power on both upper extremities (grade III) and lower extremities (grade I). A neurologic examination was performed by a neurologist. Over the next 6 days, the patient experienced seizures with abnormal mouth chewing movements, which were controlled by the administration of antiepileptic drugs (AED). A brain computed tomography (CT) scan on pod 15 showed that the existing intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) had decreased slightly.

Disposition: The patient was discharged two weeks later and demonstrated movement in blinking his eyes and shaking his head. Follow-up brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a 50% decrease in the size of the ICH three months after liver transplantation. 

Diagnosis at discharge: Hepatitis B virus-related liver cirrhosis with portal vein thrombosis, portal systemic encephalopathy, and intracerebral hemorrhage.

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 46-year-old woman with a history of appendectomy and mass lesion excision from her right breast, was admitted to our hospital due to pain in the neck region and numbness in her right arm. Physical examination revealed pain at the cervical region, trigger points bilaterally on upper parts of the trapezius muscle on palpation, and restricted movements in all directions. The Spurling test on the right side was considered positive, while upper extremity muscle strength was complete, and no pathology was detected during sensory examination. Deep tendon reflexes were bilaterally normoactive, and no pathological reflex was found.

Diagnostic Assessment:

The patient was referred to our clinic for cervical magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) based on the findings of the present complaints and physical examination. Cervical MRI showed vascular structures with signal void areas that obliterated the right neural foramen at the level of C2-C3 articular disc, compressed the right C3 nerve root, and attracted our attention with curves appearance. Although signal loss consistent with degenerative changes in cervical intervertebral articular discs was observed, no pathological findings were found on both sides occupying other neural foraminal areas. Contrast-enhanced lesion was not observed after contrast injection. Contrast-enhanced MR angiography of the cervical region revealed a significant loop formation in the distal extracranial segment of the right VA. No pathological findings were found in the radius health strikes (RDUS) examination performed following MRI.

Discharge:

The patient was discharged after completion of diagnostic evaluation. The treatment plan was discussed with the patient for pain management and physical therapy. Close follow-up and monitoring of symptoms were recommended. Further evaluation was advised for any recurrence or progression of symptoms. The patient was advised to maintain good posture and avoid repetitive stress in the neck region.

Diagnosis: Central giant cell tumor (CGCT)

Hospital Course: 
The patient was admitted to our department's consultation for specialized care due to painless slow-growing swelling of the jaw that had persisted for 3 years with dental loss. Clinical examination revealed large tender swelling with a protruding lower lip. Intra-oral examination showed hard swelling of about 50 mm with displacement of teeth leading to malocclusion. Further imaging revealed an iso-dense large destructive cystic mass that was confirmed as a central giant cell tumor (CGCT) through a biopsy. 

The patient underwent a surgical intervention by the chief professor of our department. A unilocular cystic mass without liquid content was excised, and there was a rupture of the external wall of the mandible cortical without iatrogenic fracture. The patient received antibiotics and antalgics daily for 8 days and recovered well postoperatively. 

Recommendations:
The patient was advised for oral rehabilitation and entered into routine follow-up 3, 6, and 12 months later with no signs of recurrence. 

Summary: 
The 8-year-old girl presenting with central giant cell tumor (CGCT) underwent surgical intervention and exhibited no signs of recurrence during routine follow-up 3, 6, and 12 months later. She was advised for oral rehabilitation following the surgery.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to our facility with swelling in his right cheek, which had been present for two weeks. A malignant lesion of the oral cavity was suspected. However, a thorough examination revealed an oval, firm swelling measuring 2.5 × 2 cm in size, located 2 cm above and medial to the right angle of the mandible. An ultrasound of the cheek revealed that the swelling was a cystic lesion in the bucco-masseteric region with perilesional edema.

Further testing, including an MRI of the face and neck, was performed, and a hyperechoic intralesional structure consistent with the scolex was identified. Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) was performed but showed no evidence of malignancy. Radiographs of the chest, bilateral arms and thighs were taken, and an MRI of the head and orbit was performed, revealing no additional lesions.

The patient was advised to take analgesics and steroids for seven days, and the swelling gradually reduced in size. Deworming therapy with albendazole was also prescribed.

Discharge Medications:
Albendazole

Discharge Diagnosis:
Involvement of the facial musculature manifesting as a cystic swelling in the bucco-masseteric region consistent with cysticercosis.

Follow-Up:
The patient should follow up with his primary healthcare provider for continued monitoring.

Discharge Condition:
The patient's condition has improved since admission. He is stable and ready for discharge.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient is advised to continue taking his albendazole medication as prescribed. He should avoid tobacco use as it has been associated with cysticercosis. He is encouraged to follow up with his primary healthcare provider for continued monitoring and to report any new or concerning symptoms.

The patient presented with abdominal pain and distention, elevated white blood cell count and eosinophilia, elevated serum IgE levels, and showed moderate ascites on imaging. Biopsies revealed eosinophilic infiltration of the gastrointestinal tract, suggestive of eosinophilic gastroenteritis. Upon completion of the steroids, the patient remained asymptomatic and has not required any further treatment.

A 28-year-old Saudi female with no significant past medical history presented with a two-week history of abdominal pain and distention. Upon physical examination, there was diffuse tenderness and moderate ascites. Blood work showed an elevated white blood count with eosinophilia and elevated serum IgE levels. Imaging studies revealed moderate ascites with gastrointestinal thickening and mesenteric lymphadenopathy. Biopsies from an esophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy confirmed eosinophilic infiltration of the gastrointestinal tract, consistent with eosinophilic gastroenteritis. 

Treatment was initiated with oral prednisone, resulting in symptomatic improvement and complete resolution of the ascites and gastrointestinal thickening. Upon completion of the steroid regimen, the patient remained asymptomatic without further treatment required. Follow-up peripheral blood count and imaging studies confirmed sustained improvement. The patient was discharged with instructions to follow up with their primary care physician as needed.

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the hospital with pleuritic right chest pain, high fever (40ºC), and severe dyspnea. The laboratory results showed an elevated CRP, hypoxemia, and hyperlactatemia. The chest x-ray showed the presence of a right lower lung field infiltrate. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed hepatic steatosis. The patient was diagnosed with sepsis caused by right lower lung pneumonia, and started on piperacillin/tazobactam. On the third day of antibiotic treatment, the patient developed right upper quadrant pain and was diagnosed with subhepatic appendicitis with perforation and local abscess.

Treatment:

Exploratory laparoscopic surgery was performed, which revealed subhepatic appendicitis with perforation and local abscess. Infection source control was implemented, and the patient was treated with multidrug-resistant Escherichia coli, which was isolated from the drainage fluid. The antibiotic therapy was switched to meropenem, and the patient's condition rapidly improved. The patient was discharged after 6 days of targeted antibiotic therapy.

Follow-up:

The patient was advised to follow-up with the Internal Medicine Department and continue taking the prescribed antibiotics for the recommended duration. The patient was also advised to take necessary precautions to avoid any future infections.

Diagnosis:

The patient was diagnosed with sepsis caused by right lower lung pneumonia which was later complicated by subhepatic appendicitis with perforation and local abscess.

Summary:

The patient, a 55-year-old male with hypertension and dyslipidemia, presented to the Emergency Department with pleuritic right chest pain and was eventually diagnosed with sepsis caused by right lower lung pneumonia. The patient later developed subhepatic appendicitis with perforation and local abscess and underwent exploratory laparoscopic surgery. The patient's condition improved rapidly with targeted antibiotic therapy and he was discharged after 6 days of treatment. The patient was advised to follow-up with the Internal Medicine Department and continue taking prescribed antibiotics.

Date of Discharge: [Redacted]

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 4-month-old female, was admitted to the hospital due to poor eye contact. She was delivered at 35 weeks of gestation and had an unremarkable family history. The patient was diagnosed with Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA) due to the presence of esotropia and nystagmus, and the extinguished electroretinogram (ERG) in both eyes. Cycloplegic refractive errors were also noted, which were subsequently addressed. A slit lamp examination, fundus examination, and systemic evaluation for any metabolic and organ abnormalities were conducted, but no significant findings were observed except for the aforementioned ocular symptoms.

Diagnostic evaluations were performed, which included genetic testing for CRX, CRB1, GUCY2D, AIPL1, RDH12, RPE65, LRAT, RPGRIP1, and TULP1. However, the results were unremarkable. A brain MRI revealed the presence of a prominent enlargement in the subarachnoid space of both frontal convexities, and absence of the septum pellucidum. However, no focal lesions were found, and the size of the corpus callosum and white matter myelination were normal. Follow-up MRI scans showed the absence of the septum pellucidum, but with stable external hydrocephalus. A diagnosis of septo-optic dysplasia was considered, however, the normal appearance of the optic nerve and normal pituitary function left the diagnosis doubtful.

Medical History:
The patient did not have any notable medical history aside from the ocular and neuroimaging findings with LCA and the subarachnoid space abnormalities observed in the brain MRI scans.

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient, a 4-month-old female, was admitted to the hospital for poor eye contact. She was diagnosed with LCA, and further diagnostic evaluations including genetic testing and a brain MRI were conducted. Follow-up MRI scans showed the absence of the septum pellucidum, but with stable external hydrocephalus. At the age of 3 years, the patient showed moderate developmental delay. No noteworthy medical history was obtained during her hospital course.

Hospital Course:
The patient, an 8-year-old female child, was admitted to our department due to diminution of vision in the right eye since 5 years, with headache and vomiting since 6 months. On examination, no perception of light was observed in the right eye with normal vision in the left eye. An MRI revealed a cystic lesion at the right temporo-frontal-parietal region measuring 8 × 9 × 6.5 cm. A small rounded nodule was seen on the medial aspect of the cystic lesion at the paraventricular location. The lesion was reported as a cystic astrocytoma/ganglioglioma. Endocrine workup subsequently revealed secondary hypothyroidism.  

Treatment:
The patient underwent right fronto-temporo-parietal craniotomy for drainage and marsupialisation of the cystic lesion. The cystic fluid was yellowish and machine oil-like, containing cholesterol crystals and flecks mostly over the medial side. Histological examination revealed inflamed Rathke's cleft cyst with a cystic wall lined by a flattened to pseudostratified squamous epithelium with congested blood vessels, chronic inflammatory infiltrate in the form of lymphocyte, plasma cells, and lymphoid aggregates.

Outcomes:
Postoperatively, the patient's recovery was uneventful, and the headache and vomiting subsided completely. The patient is in regular follow-up with postoperative MRI at 6 months without any recurrence.

An MRI showed a fluid-filled cyst about 8 by 9 by 6.5 cm in the right front-top-side brain part.
The cyst had a small round bump on its inner side near the ventricles of the brain.
The cyst was diagnosed as either a cystic astrocytoma or a ganglioglioma, both types of brain tumors.

Hospital Admission: Gastrointestinal complaints

History: A 70-year-old female with a history of asthma, eosinophilic esophagitis, and eosinophilic sinusitis presented with postprandial abdominal pain, bloating, and dyspepsia, which had been ongoing intermittently for 2 years.

Significant Findings: Laboratory results revealed elevated eosinophils, lipase, ALT, AST, and alkaline phosphatase. Initial EGD showed a hypertrophic major papilla, antral gastritis, and superficial gastric ulcers. MRI/MRCP revealed CBD dilatation without choledocholithiasis but with tapering of the distal CBD. ERCP revealed an inflamed major ampulla with benign papillary stenosis.

Treatment: The patient underwent sphincterotomy and insertion of a plastic stent into the bile duct, which was followed by sphincteroplasty and dilation of the papilla and distal CBD. Repeat ERCP was performed with stent removal, and biopsies of the stomach and the ampulla showed benign glandular tissue with no eosinophils. Reason for Admission: Shortness of breath

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the emergency department with shortness of breath and increasing dyspnea. She was found to have a large goiter that was compressing the trachea and causing respiratory distress. The patient was quickly transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU) where she was intubated using rapid sequence induction to relieve respiratory distress. Subsequent cerebral and thoracic computed tomography (CT) scans revealed a large goiter plunging into the upper mediastinal orifice, which was removed successfully by thyroidectomy 48 hours after admission. Prior to reversal of the neuromuscular blockage, the tube balloon was deflated, and the diagnosis of tracheomalacia was almost confirmed. The endotracheal tube was left in place for 24 hours, and then removed the next day without incident.

Course of Treatment:
The patient received corticotherapy (dexamethasone at 12 mg per day for two days) prior to thyroidectomy to accelerate fetal lung maturation. Surgery was completed without incident, as no intraoperative tracheostomy was necessary. Patient was treated with levothyroxin sodium tablets 75mcg/day post-surgery.

Follow-Up Plan:
Patient was discharged from the hospital on the 5th postoperative day without any complications. Pathology showed multinodular goiter with areas of atypical hyperplasia, but no sign of malignancy. Patient gave birth to a healthy newborn four weeks later.

Recommendations:
Patient should continue taking levothyroxin sodium tablets 75mcg/day as prescribed. She should follow up with her primary care physician for monitoring of her thyroid function and any potential complications related to the goiter removal.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: ______________

Admission Date: ____________

Discharge Date: ____________

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to our institution with progressive neurological symptoms. He had a history of seropositive Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) that was managed with maintenance methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine and low-dose prednisone. The patient developed fluctuating confusion, word-finding difficulty, right-sided weakness and gait imbalance. An evaluation was done by the neurologist which confirmed the presence of neurological deficits. An MRI scan showed areas of scattered restricted diffusion and enhancement within the cortex and leptomeninges of the left hemisphere near the vertex, suspicious for meningoencephalitis. CSF analysis also demonstrated lymphocytic meningitis with negative, bacterial and fungal cultures. 

The patient was started on antiepileptic medication and a whole-body PET scan was done to rule out underlying malignancy. A bone marrow biopsy was also done to rule out lymphoid neoplasm. An open meningeal biopsy was performed and gross examination revealed thickening and opacification of the meninges. The histopathological findings were consistent with leptomeningeal involvement by nodular rheumatoid meningitis.

Immunosuppressive therapy with monthly cyclophosphamide and high-dose corticosteroids was initiated for 6 months and then the corticosteroids were tapered. The patient's neurological examination improved one month post treatment initiation, although confusion and bilateral postural tremor persisted. Most parkinsonian features also largely resolved following immunosuppressive therapy. 

Repeat MRI 3 months after treatment initiation showed complete resolution of previous findings, and CRP levels also normalized. The patient was eventually transitioned to a long-term care facility due to the persistent behavioral and cognitive deficits with intermittent periods of agitation.

Diagnosis:
Leptomeningeal involvement by nodular rheumatoid meningitis

Course:
The patient was admitted for investigation of progressive neurological symptoms and was treated with immunosuppressive therapy. The patient's neurological examination improved one month post treatment initiation, although confusion and bilateral postural tremor persisted, and most parkinsonian features largely resolved following immunosuppressive therapy. Repeat MRI 3 months after treatment initiation showed complete resolution of previous findings.

Discharge Condition:
The patient has been transitioned to a long-term care facility due to persistent behavioral and cognitive deficits with intermittent periods of agitation.

The patient is advised to follow up with her primary care provider and the gastroenterology clinic for regular check-ups.

The patient had been lost to follow-up for over 4 years prior to this presentation. Biopsy of the lymph nodes revealed metastatic SCC. The patient was enrolled in a trial and treated with carboplatin, 5-FU, and pembrolizumab at a dose of 200 mg. After 4 cycles, the patient showed signs of partial response, but presented with fatigue and hypotension to systolic blood pressure of 70 seconds. The patient was diagnosed with immune-related central adrenal insufficiency and was started on high-dose dexamethasone and later transitioned to hydrocortisone. Brain MRI did not show any inflammation of the pituitary stalk and was without metastatic lesions. The patient's fatigue was resolved ten days later and was restarted on pembrolizumab. The patient continues to take hydrocortisone.

- Discharge Diagnosis: Malaria

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 2-month-old male infant, was admitted to our pediatric antiretroviral clinic with the complaint of fever, which was occurring every 2 to 3 days. The mother of the patient reported that the fever was associated with nonprojectile vomit containing recently ingested milk formula. Upon examination, the patient was found to have hepatic and splenic enlargement of 4 cm each. A diagnosis of sepsis was made and the patient was treated with intravenous cefuroxime before complete blood count investigation. Fever resolved 2 days after commencing antibiotics and the patient was discharged home on oral cefuroxime.

The patient was re-admitted a week later with the complaint of fever recurring every 2 to 3 days. A diagnosis of malaria was made upon detection of trophozoites of Plasmodium falciparum in the peripheral blood film. The patient was treated with oral quinine and showed a remarkable improvement in his condition, with the intermittent fever resolving by crisis within 24 hours of administration. The packed cell volume of 26% at readmission increased to 32% on the fourth day of quinine therapy. The child remained well and was discharged home two days after.

Follow-up Recommendations:
The patient is advised to continue co-trimoxazole prophylaxis as previously prescribed and follow up with the pediatric antiretroviral clinic for routine monitoring.

Patient Education:
The mother of the patient is advised to be vigilant in reporting signs and symptoms of fever and to consider malaria as a potential diagnosis in the event of persistent fever. She is also advised to continue the patient's medication regimen as prescribed and follow up with the pediatric antiretroviral clinic for routine monitoring.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 71-year-old male with a history of heart disease and recent heart surgery.

Admission Date: [Date]

Discharge Date: [Date]

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted for progressive weakness, shortness of breath, and a syncopal episode. On examination, he had peripheral cyanosis, pallor, and elevated jugular venous pressure. Echocardiography showed severe left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction with a reduced stroke volume. CT angiogram of the head and neck showed extensive stenosis of arteries. Coronary angiography indicated severe stenosis of the proximal left subclavian artery.

Management:

A multidisciplinary team placed a bypass graft from the left common carotid artery to the left subclavian artery distal to the stenosis, reperfusing the LAD territory myocardium. This required intra-aortic balloon pump support and the patient remained on dobutamine post-operatively. The patient showed remarkable improvement in his symptoms. The patient was weaned off dobutamine and discharged to cardiac rehabilitation.

Follow-up:

The patient should follow up with the team of cardiologists, interventional cardiologists, and vascular surgeons for further evaluation of the bypass graft. The patient should also continue with cardiac rehabilitation to optimize his physical function and quality of life.

Summary:

The patient with a history of heart disease and recent heart surgery presented with progressive weakness, shortness of breath, and a syncopal episode. He was diagnosed with extensive arterial stenosis, which was managed by placing a bypass graft. The patient showed remarkable improvement in his symptoms and was discharged to cardiac rehabilitation. The patient should follow up with the team of specialists for further evaluation.

HOSPITAL COURSE SUMMARY:

Admission Date: [DATE]
Discharge Date: [DATE]

Medical History:
The patient is a 32-year-old woman who presented with a mass in the vulva and intermenstrual bleeding. She had a history of unsuccessful sexual intercourse due to fear of pain, and the mass had gradually enlarged over the past 3 years.

Clinical Findings:
A physical examination revealed a nontender tubular neoplasm outside the intact hymen, with an opening at the distal end. A canal approximately 5 cm long was found in the mass, from which white mucus was secreted. Ultrasonographic evaluation of the pelvis showed a 4.5- × 1-cm stalk originating from the cervix and protruding into the vagina. A mini-hysteroscopy was performed to excise the mass.

Diagnostic Testing:
Hemoglobin level was 9.4 g/dL. The levels of estradiol and progesterone in the luteal phase were 138 pg/mL and 13.77 ng/mL, respectively. Liver and renal functional tests and thyroid hormone levels were all normal.

Treatment:
The patient underwent a mini-hysteroscopy to excise the mass while avoiding damage to the hymen. The mass was found to originate from the squamocolumnar junction at the 3 o’clock position of the left lip of the ectocervix, and it had no communication with the endocervix. The cervical mucosal fold of approximately 0.3 to 0.7 cm in thickness was found inside the canal by mini-hysteroscopy and it had a blind end proximally. The mass was totally excised after suturing of the pedicle. Deep endocervical and endometrial regions were found to be normal.

Condition on Discharge:
The patient's postoperative course was uneventful without bleeding or any other complications. Sexual intercourse was successful for this couple.

Follow-up:
Five weeks after surgery, the patient visited again in the outpatient clinic and was doing well. Written informed consent was obtained from the patient and her husband for publication of this case report and accompanying images. Institutional review board approval was not required for publication of this case report.

Discharge Summary

Patient name: [Name]
Medical record number: [Number]
Date of admission: [Date]
Date of discharge: [Date]

Hospital Course:
[Name], a 48-year-old female with polycystic liver and kidney diseases, was admitted to our hospital for surgical treatment. She had been followed up for 5 years at another institution and complained of progressive distension of the abdomen and abdominal fullness leading to gradual decrease in body weight without shortness of breath.

Upon admission, the patient was observed regularly without considering palliative surgery or liver transplantation. During the outpatient clinic follow-up for 1 year, the patient's condition worsened with increasing fatigue and dyspnea on exertion. Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status worsened from 2 to 3.

Medical Treatment:
Medical treatment with somatostatin analogue was not considered primarily due to the high medical cost as well as the undetermined therapeutic efficacy. After obtaining consent from the patient on the uncertain effect of fenestration treatment as well as high risk of disease recurrence, the patient underwent surgical fenestration treatment. Multiple cysts in the enlarged liver were opened, and the cyst walls were excised with electrocautery.

At the end of the fenestration procedure, the liver appeared to be markedly shrunken, and three Jackson-Pratt type drains were inserted to evacuate the ascitic fluid. After performing follow-up CT at 1 week, the drains were removed. The total liver volume by using CT volumetry was 3,870 ml before surgery and 3,125 ml at 1 week after surgery, showing a volume reduction of 19.3%.

Clinical Outcome:
After the surgery, ECOG performance status improved to 1 at 1 month and to 0 at 1 year. Gastrointestinal Quality of Life Index (GIQLI) score was significantly increased to 122 after 1 month. During regular follow-up at an interval of 6 months, follow-up CT showed no progression in cyst size and flat abdomen was observed. At 18 months after surgery, the patient is doing well and performing her normal activities with no evidence of disease recurrence.

Conclusion:
In summary, the patient underwent surgical fenestration treatment for polycystic liver and kidney diseases, resulting in significant improvement in clinical outcomes with no evidence of disease recurrence.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [redacted]
DOB: [redacted]
Admission Date: [redacted]
Discharge Date: [redacted]
Attending Physician: [redacted]

Admission Diagnosis: West syndrome

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 2-month-old male who previously underwent surgical correction for intraventricular defect, was admitted to the hospital after presenting frequent episodes of inconsolable crying, associated with neck extension, stiffening of the arms and trunk, sometimes followed by swallowing and vomiting. Symptoms were attributed to GERD, and therapy with PPI started, however, no improvement was noticed.

In the following weeks, episodes became even more frequents with exacerbation of symptoms. His mother video-recorded an attack, which showed the presence of flexion spasms. The child eventually underwent fundoplication, but no improvement was noticed. Persistence of symptoms and occurrence of spasms of the arms during acute episodes finally suggested the diagnosis of West syndrome.

IS was then confirmed by EEG while MRI was negative. Despite starting appropriate therapy at 8 months of age, clinical signs of mental retardation were present. Although IS is a rare disorder, diagnosis was suspected based on age and patient history with a complete neurological evaluation.

To our knowledge, this is the first report of IS misdiagnosed as GERD. The attention towards GERD in children may reduce attention towards other peculiar clinical conditions, like in cases we presented. We would suggest considering GERD only in those patients with high risk rate for developing GERD like children with cerebral palsy, in those with surgery complications after oesophageal atresia and/or in any child with very evocative GERD symptoms, such as hematemesis and or chronic vomiting with growth failure.

Discharge Diagnosis: West syndrome

Final Condition at Discharge:
At the time of discharge, the patient continued to experience symptoms of West syndrome, but appropriate therapy was initiated. The patient's family was instructed to follow up with the pediatricians for medication management and further evaluations.

Discharge Medications:
Not Applicable

Follow-Up:
The parents were advised to follow up with a pediatrician for routine well-child visits and to monitor the patient's condition closely. Additional appointments were scheduled with a neurologist for further evaluation and management.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]   
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]   
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]   

Hospital Course:   
The 45-year-old patient was admitted to the outpatient department with complaints of a right vulvar mass that was painful and tender. She noticed the tumor a few days back and reported an aggravation of pain during menstruation. No other symptoms like fever, erythema, or discharge were identified, and her personal medical history was unremarkable. Physical examination disclosed a mass on her right labia minor, which was superficially located and very mobile. Ultrasonography revealed a hypoechoic lesion that suggests the presence of Bartholin gland cyst or abscess. The uterus and both adnexae were insignificant. Therefore, a mass excision was carried out for definitive diagnosis and treatment. During surgery, the vulvar mass was located in deep dermis and had a tortuous appearance with soft rubbery consistency.   

Diagnosis:   
Microscopic examination revealed a well-demarcated convoluted or multinodular tumor with solid growth pattern. The tumor was composed mainly of uniform epithelioid round or polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and centrally located round nuclei. Extracellular myxoid materials were multifocally identified in stroma. In addition, intracellular vacuolar myxoid changes were also noted. The focal areas were made up of spindle cells with blunt-ended elongated nuclei in part, and in some areas, the tumor originated from the vessel wall. Mitotic activity, cellular atypia, or necrosis pleomorphism were absent. Immunohistochemistry revealed diffuse strong positive and focal positivity for desmin, smooth muscle actin (SMA), smooth muscle myosin heavy chain (Smm-hc), and estrogen receptor (ER). HMB45 was not expressed in the tumor cells. Based on histologic features and immunohistochemistry, the tumor was diagnosed as vulvar epithelioid leiomyoma.

Treatment and Condition on Discharge:   
The patient underwent a mass excision and was discharged without any complications. She was advised periodic follow-up visits. There was no evidence of clinical or radiologic recurrence for 10 months.

Follow-up Plan:   
The patient is advised to visit the hospital periodically as per the follow-up schedule informed by the doctor.   

Summary:   
A 45-year-old female visited the outpatient department with pain and tenderness in a right vulvar mass. Imaging suggested Bartholin gland cyst or abscess, and therefore a mass excision was performed. Histopathological examination revealed the tumor to be vulvar epithelioid leiomyoma. The patient was discharged without any complications and advised periodic follow-up visits. No clinical or radiologic recurrence was observed for 10 months after the surgery.

Treatment: The patient's treatment plan did not change during this hospital admission.

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Gender: Female
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Admission Diagnosis: Insidious onset severe persistent headache with bilateral hypoglossal nerve palsy.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with an insidious onset of severe persistent headache, most prominent in the occipital region lasting for 10 days. Six days after the onset, she experienced dysarthria, difficulty in moving her tongue within the mouth, and difficulty in eating and drinking. On admission, she was found to have a high-grade fever. Neurological examination revealed bilateral hypoglossal nerve palsy with marked tongue atrophy, more prominent in the left side. Her eye movements were saccadic with a broad-based ataxic gait without any other signs of cerebellar involvement. Her blood test revealed a high neutrophil leukocytosis, and her ESR and CRP levels were elevated. Noncontrast CT brain did not reveal any abnormality. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biochemistry revealed significant elevation of protein with 59 polymorphs and 8 lymphocytes per cubic millimetre with reduced CSF glucose.

Treatment:
The patient was initiated on empirical treatment as for pyogenic meningitis with ceftriaxone and vancomycin for which she had a gradual improvement of general status with improvement of fever, meningism, gaze, and gait abnormalities while tongue weakness and atrophy persisted.

Diagnostic Results:
Subsequently, she underwent MRI of brain and brainstem, which revealed a posteromedial infarction in the lower part of the medulla oblongata without leptomeningeal enhancement and did not show a significant cerebral oedema. Her chest radiograph did not reveal any changes suggestive of pulmonary tuberculosis or sarcoidosis. Syphilis (VDRL & THPA), HIV serology, and autoimmune markers for vasculitis (rheumatoid factor, ANA (IF), and p & c-ANCA) were negative.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Pyogenic Meningitis with posteromedial infarction in the lower part of the medulla oblongata without leptomeningeal enhancement.

Discharge Medications:
No medications were prescribed at the time of discharge.

Follow-up:
The patient was reviewed at one month and three & six months and was found to be free of fever with good general condition and had normal inflammatory markers. However, she had persistent tongue atrophy with difficult speech from which she was gradually recovering with the help of physiotherapy.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient was advised to continue physiotherapy for persistent tongue atrophy. Further follow-up appointments were recommended to monitor her condition.

Discharge Summary: Patient 2

Patient 2, a 45-year-old female, was admitted to hospital due to headache and vomiting in February 2016. Imaging examinations showed an intracranial mass, and the patient received neurosurgical resection of the space-occupying. Postoperative pathological examination indicated non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL). In March 2016, she received whole brain radiotherapy. Cranial MRI after radiotherapy revealed a decrease in the left parietal lobe, basal ganglia, and corpus callosum lesions. In May 2016, the patient underwent chemotherapy for 2 cycles. Two weeks after treatment, she experienced right weakness that gradually progressed to right hemiplegia with muscle strength at 0 level. Due to little symptomatic improvement from conventional therapy of mannitol and dexamethasone for dehydration, cranial MRI was performed, which indicated an increase in left parietal lobe edema.

In July 2016, the patient was started on oral apatinib, which showed remarkable improvement in right hemiplegia symptoms, and her muscle strength was restored to normal. Headache, nausea, and vomiting disappeared. Further details regarding the patient's medical history, clinical course, laboratory test results, medications, and imaging studies can be found in the patient's medical record.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Patient Name: N/A
Age: 13
Gender: Female
Complaints: Oligomenorrhoea, masculinizing features of enlarged clitoris, facial hair, deep voice and rapidly growing abdominal lump in left side

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient, a 13-year-old female, presented with complaints of oligomenorrhoea, enlarged clitoris, facial hair, deep voice and rapidly growing abdominal lump in left side since one month. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a 10-cm neoplastic capsulated mass in the left ovary. Hormonal study showed CA 125-37.5 IU/mL, AFP 8.6 ng/mL, HCG-4 IU/L and testosterone 1196 ng/mL.

Unilateral salpingooophorectomy was done and histological examination showed a well-encapsulated mass with proliferation of plumped, ovoid to spindle cells arranged in bundles and fascicles forming nodules, with mild degree of anisonucleosis and hyperchromasia and infrequent mitosis and lacking nuclear grooving. A few interspersed large, polygonal cells with pale cytoplasm (luteinized/steroid cells), lacking Reinke’s crystalloids were also seen. Tiny foci of cuboidal cells (less than 5%) arranged in cords, micro and macrotubules (sertoliform cells of intermediate differentiation) were seen at the periphery. On the basis of histology and immunohistochemistry, final diagnosis of ovarian fibrothecoma with minor sex cord stromal elements was made.

All masculinizing features were significantly reduced in post-operative follow-up of four months. Ostradiol was 100.96 pg/mL and testosterone dropped to 5 ng/dL. The patient hasn’t reported back to the center again.

Summary of Findings:

-The patient presented with oligomenorrhoea, enlarged clitoris, facial hair, deep voice and a rapidly growing abdominal lump in the left side
-Hormonal study showed CA 125-37.5 IU/mL, AFP 8.6 ng/mL, HCG-4 IU/L and testosterone 1196 ng/mL
-The patient underwent unilateral salpingooophorectomy
-The histology showed a well-encapsulated mass with proliferation of plumped, ovoid to spindle cells arranged in bundles and fascicles forming nodules, with mild degree of anisonucleosis and hyperchromasia and infrequent mitosis and lacking nuclear grooving
-The final diagnosis of ovarian fibrothecoma with minor sex cord stromal elements was made
-All masculinizing features were significantly reduced in post-operative follow-up of four months

Recommendations:

-The patient is advised to follow-up with the treating physician for further evaluation and management.

Left renal calculus

Chief Complaint:
Poor effort tolerance

History of Presenting Illness:
A 60-year-old woman was admitted with a history of poor effort tolerance. On further evaluation, the patient was diagnosed with left renal calculus and scheduled for left percutaneous nephrolithotomy. During preanesthetic evaluation, the patient's irregularly irregular pulse and abnormal ECG raised concern for an asymptomatic sinus node dysfunction.

Past Medical History:
The patient reported a past medical history of ischemic heart disease with hypertension since 6 months and was on regular treatment. There was also evidence of an asymptomatic sinus node dysfunction, which was resistant to atropine.

Hospital Course:
The patient was given balanced general anesthesia with endotracheal intubation, induced with propofol and vecuronium, and secured under direct laryngoscopy with size 7.0 endotracheal tube. During the surgery, there were repeated episodes of continuous pacing by the temporary pacemaker, followed by a resumption of normal sinus rhythm. Other vital parameters were stable in the intraoperative period. Neuromuscular blockade was reversed with neostigmine and glycopyrrolate. The patient was shifted to the post anesthesia care unit with stable vitals.

Discharge Condition:
The patient was discharged in stable condition on the 5th postoperative day.

Follow-up Care:
The patient was advised to follow-up with their cardiologist for further evaluation and management of their asymptomatic sinus node dysfunction.

Medications on Discharge:
None

Instructions to Patient:
The patient was advised to rest and follow-up with their cardiologist for further evaluation and management of their asymptomatic sinus node dysfunction.

Hospital Course Summary:

Chief Complaint:
The patient presented with sudden onset breathlessness and right sided pleuritic chest pain.

History of Present Illness:
The patient had a painful swelling of his right leg while he was being treated in the hospital for recurrent episodes of ENL. On examination, the patient was dyspneic at rest without central cyanosis. He had leonine facies and generalized erythematous skin with multiple nodules. His right leg was swollen with pitting ankle edema while having normal arterial pulses. His respiratory system examination revealed a respiratory rate of 30 per minute and signs of right lower zone pleural effusion.

Past Medical History:
The patient had lepromatous leprosy following a positive slit skin smear for mycobacterium leprae. He was commenced on World Health Organization (WHO) multi-drug therapy (MDT) regimen for multi-bacillary (MB) leprosy, which was complicated by type II lepra reaction (ENL) with right sided panuveitis and treated with oral prednisolone. 

Review of Systems:
There was no history suggestive of past venous or arterial thrombosis and tendency to develop thrombosis in his family. Neurology revealed a glove and stocking sensory peripheral neuropathy. There was no organomegaly noted on abdominal examination.

Diagnostic Testing:
A venous doppler ultrasound of the lower limb confirmed a deep vein thrombosis in the right femoral vein. Subsequently, a computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) confirmed pulmonary emboli in the right and left main pulmonary arteries with right lower lobe lung collapse and a mild pleural effusion.

Treatment:
The patient was started on enoxaparin and warfarin concomitantly. Thalidomide and anti-leprosy therapy were stopped temporarily while low dose corticosteroid was continued. After one week, the patient's dyspnea and general condition improved.

Follow-up:
The patient was discharged and provided with instructions to follow up with his healthcare provider for ongoing treatment and monitoring.

Discharge Summary:

Hospital Course:
The 62-year-old male was admitted to the hospital with a complaint of abdominal pain, vomiting, and ambulatory dysfunction. The initial examination showed no abnormalities. The patient was suspected to have viral gastroenteritis, and hence he was hospitalized for dehydration management. The patient's nausea and vomiting improved after admission, but it was noted that he was leaning backwards and to the right when standing or attempting to ambulate on the first day of hospitalization.

Diagnostic Evaluations:
The neurology service was consulted after assessing the patient's condition on his second day of admission. A CT angiogram of the head and neck showed a congenitally hypoplastic left vertebral artery and no other abnormality was observed in the vertebrobasilar system. MRI of the brain showed acute/subacute infarct in the right cerebellar hemisphere. The echocardiogram showed moderate diastolic dysfunction with trace aortic regurgitation.

Clinical Impression:
The patient was diagnosed with acute/subacute infarct in the right cerebellar hemisphere secondary to chronic atherosclerotic disease that had extended and caused APS. The left-sided dysmetria was observed, which further indicated his neurological impairment.

Hospital Treatment:
The patient was monitored on telemetry for several days without any events or abnormalities noted. He was started on a scheduled antiemetic regimen of metoclopramide 10 mg four times daily and ondansetron 8 mg every eight hours that yielded positive results. Within one day, the patient's nausea and vomiting were controlled, and he was able to eat without difficulty. The patient was successfully discharged from the hospital to rehabilitation.

Follow-up Recommendations:
The patient is recommended to follow up with the neurology service as an outpatient and undergo regular checkups to monitor his neurological function and the progression of his cerebrovascular disease. He is also advised to maintain strict blood glucose control and hypertension management. The family members are recommended to observe the patient's activities, as he is more vulnerable to falls.

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 46-year-old woman with a history of appendectomy and mass lesion excision from her right breast, was admitted to our hospital due to pain in the neck region and numbness in her right arm. Physical examination revealed pain at the cervical region, trigger points bilaterally on upper parts of the trapezius muscle on palpation, and restricted movements in all directions. The Spurling test on the right side was considered positive, while upper extremity muscle strength was complete, and no pathology was detected during sensory examination. Deep tendon reflexes were bilaterally normoactive, and no pathological reflex was found.

Diagnostic Assessment:

The patient was referred to our clinic for cervical magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) based on the findings of the present complaints and physical examination. Cervical MRI showed vascular structures with signal void areas that obliterated the right neural foramen at the level of C2-C3 articular disc, compressed the right C3 nerve root, and attracted our attention with curves appearance. Although signal loss consistent with degenerative changes in cervical intervertebral articular discs was observed, no pathological findings were found on both sides occupying other neural foraminal areas. Contrast-enhanced lesion was not observed after contrast injection. Contrast-enhanced MR angiography of the cervical region revealed a significant loop formation in the distal extracranial segment of the right VA. No pathological findings were found in the radius health strikes (RDUS) examination performed following MRI.

Discharge:

The patient was discharged after completion of diagnostic evaluation. The treatment plan was discussed with the patient for pain management and physical therapy. Close follow-up and monitoring of symptoms were recommended. Further evaluation was advised for any recurrence or progression of symptoms. The patient was advised to maintain good posture and avoid repetitive stress in the neck region.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Gender: Female
Age: 60

Admission date: February 2015
Discharge date: [REDACTED]

Summary of Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the emergency department of St. Orsola Hospital in Bologna, Italy with complaints of generalized articular pain, fever, paresthesia of lower limbs and feet soles, resulting into unstable gear, and visual disorders characterized by impaired ability to focus and binocular vision. The patient's clinical history was marked by acute rheumatic pain about 40 years prior. Physical examination revealed the presence of internuclear left ophthalmoplegia with diplopia secondary, right facial-brachial plexus deficit, hypopallesthesia of inferior limbs and superficial weakness of the feet, depressed mood, moderate peripheral edema, basilar wet sounds, and normochromic urine. The laboratory tests revealed nephritic syndrome with normal renal function, positive antinuclear, anti-double-stranded DNA, anti-Ro/SSA, and antiphospholipid antibodies. Serum complement component C3 was slightly reduced, and CD19+ count constituted 38.4% of total lymphocytes (normal range: 7% to 14%). The MRI reported diffuse inflammatory lesions, and EEG was compatible with minimal structural alterations. Lupus anticoagulant antibodies were positive. Renal ultrasound was unremarkable.

The patient's treatment began with prednisone, which led to an increase in proteinuria and admission to the Nephrology Unit of the hospital. Doppler-ultrasound revealed deep vein thrombosis, and sodium enoxheparin treatment was started. As the patient had high percentages of circulating B cells, rituximab was presented as a therapeutic option, and the patient provided written informed consent to the treatment. The patient received 4 weekly infusions of rituximab after premedication with chlorphenamine, hydrocortisone, and paracetamol. 

At the time of discharge, the patient had stable vital signs and was asymptomatic. The patient's symptoms had improved, and she was advised to follow-up with the primary care physician for continued care and treatment.

Diagnosis on Discharge:
SLE with simultaneously manifestations of LN and NPSLE.

Medical History:
The patient is a 30-year-old male with no significant personal or family medical history.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented in November 2006 for diagnosis of a large tumor on the left chest wall that had been growing for 4 years. The patient had a previous diagnosis of myositis ossificans circumscripta, but a biopsy in May 2004 showed an intramuscular tumor with mature bone trabeculae, suggesting a diagnosis of "atypical" myositis ossificans or heterotopic ossification. The patient was proposed for surgical removal, but refused and was lost to follow-up until November 2006.

Upon presentation to our institution, the patient had a frozen left shoulder associated with ipsilateral radial and cubital paralysis and cervical pain. Physical examination revealed a voluminous, plane, hard, and immobile mass extended from the basicervical region to the scapulo-humeral joint and from the left side of the chest wall to the axillary region. Radiological imaging showed a huge calcified heterogeneous mass with cystic and solid elements. The mass had a 25-cm transversal diameter, an 18-cm antero-posterior diameter, and a 30-cm cranio-caudal diameter. It included the left scapula, the periscapular muscles and the chest wall, with intercostal invasion to the pleura and muscular extension to the left arm (triceps).

Diagnostic testing confirmed a diagnosis of low-grade extraskeletal osteosarcoma (ESOS) based on pathological samples collected in May 2004 that were re-examined for molecular analysis of MDM2 and CDK4 oncogenes. The disease was stable after 2 API/AI chemotherapy cycles but progressed after 4 additional cycles, with extension of cutaneous nodules and tumor mass associated with the apparition of left pleuritis. Palliative radiation therapy was not possible technically due to the tumor volume. A thoracoscopic talcage was done, followed by trabectedin-based chemotherapy. However, three weeks after the first cycle, the patient deteriorated rapidly and died of respiratory failure secondary to loco-regional extension, 5 years after the initial symptoms.

Discharge Condition:
The patient died of respiratory failure secondary to loco-regional extension.

Medical History:
In November 2006, the patient sought care for a large left chest wall tumor growing for about four years.
A May 2004 biopsy showed an intramuscular tumor with bone tissue, suggesting atypical myositis ossificans or heterotopic ossification.
Doctors suggested surgery to remove the tumor, but the patient refused and was lost to follow-up until November 2006.
He had a frozen left shoulder, nerve damage causing radial and cubital paralysis, and neck pain.
Exam showed a large, hard, immobile mass from the neck base to the shoulder joint.
It also extended from the chest wall to the armpit, involving nearby tissues.
Imaging showed a huge calcified mass with solid and cystic parts.
It measured 25 cm across, 18 cm front-to-back, and 30 cm top-to-bottom.
The mass included the left shoulder blade, surrounding muscles, and chest wall.
It invaded the pleura and extended into the left arm's triceps muscle.
Tests confirmed low-grade extraskeletal osteosarcoma, based on the May 2004 sample re-examined for MDM2 and CDK4 gene changes.
The disease stayed stable after two cycles of API/AI chemotherapy.
It worsened after four more cycles, with skin nodules, tumor growth, and left pleuritis.
Palliative radiation could not be used because the tumor was too large.
A thoracoscopic talcage was performed, followed by chemotherapy with trabectedin.
Three weeks after the first chemotherapy cycle, the patient's condition declined quickly.
He died of respiratory failure due to local tumor spread, five years after symptoms began.
Discharge Condition:
The patient died of respiratory failure caused by local tumor spread.

Patient Name: [redacted]

Sex: Female

Discharge Date: [redacted]

Diagnosis: Diffuse large B cell lymphoma

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 77-year-old woman, presented to our outpatient clinic with a two-month history of dysphasia. Both thyroid lobes were diffusely enlarged with the right lobe being slightly firmer than the left lobe. Palpable masses were found along the right cervical levels II and III. Thyroid function test was within the normal range. A flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy showed no remarkable findings. 

An ultrasound showed a larger-than-4-cm, irregular shaped, heterogeneously hypoechoic, solid mass occupying the entire right thyroid lobe with suspicious small internal calcifications. The mass directly invaded the right lateral and posterior wall of trachea, and encased the right common carotid artery. A fine needle aspiration was performed revealing suspicious findings for undifferentiated carcinoma. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed a heterogeneously enhancing mass compared to adjacent muscle in the posterior portion of the right thyroid lobe, outgrowing towards the posterior wall of the trachea. Subsequent excisional biopsy of the thyroid lesion was done and it was histopathologically diagnosed as diffuse large B cell lymphoma. 

The patient received three cycles of R-CHOP chemotherapy as well as total 3,816 cGy of intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) which resulted in complete regression on the CT images four months after the initial diagnosis. 

Discharge condition:
The patient has been discharged with significant improvement in her condition.

Follow up care plan:
The appropriate follow-up care plan has been explained to the patient, and she has been advised to return to the outpatient clinic for a follow-up appointment.

Summary:
The patient presented with dysphasia and diffuse thyroid enlargement with suspicious findings of undifferentiated carcinoma. An excisional biopsy was done, and it was histopathologically diagnosed as diffuse large B cell lymphoma. She was treated with R-CHOP chemotherapy and IMRT which resulted in complete regression on the CT images four months after the initial diagnosis. The patient has been discharged with significant improvement in her condition with appropriate follow-up care plan advised.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 19-year-old woman
Medical history: L4/5 lumbar herniation, underwent discectomy at age 15
Admission Reason: Numbness and pain from a recurrent L4/5 lumbar herniation

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the hospital due to recurrent L4/5 lumbar herniation. After undergoing a repeated discectomy, the patient developed hypotension, tachycardia, and marked abdominal distension during the operation. The enhanced computed tomography (CT) showed a right common artery injury and a large retroperitoneal hematoma, including extravasated contrast. The patient was promptly transferred to our hospital, and an angiogram was performed. Hemodynamics stabilized significantly after occlusion of the aorta, and the patient's family was informed. An emergency laparotomy was started and a right common iliac artery laceration was detected and repaired by excision. A 9 mm Dacron graft was interposed between the aorta and the right common iliac artery.

Outcome:

The patient's postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient remained hospitalized due to a high inflammatory response. However, after prolonged medical supervision and complication-free recovery, the patient was discharged on the 45th postoperative day. Currently, the patient remains in good condition one year after the surgery.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Redacted]

Admission Date: [Redacted]

Discharge Date: [Redacted]

Clinical Course:

The patient was admitted to the emergency department with a history of moderate hematemesis associated with dyspnea, hemoptysis, and a non-measured fever for 4 days. On admission, he presented with tachycardia, tachypnea, and pulse oximetry of 70% in room air. Physical exam revealed rales in the left base with hemorrhagic pangastritis without active bleeding, and moderate duodenitis. Blood culture samples and microbiological examination of the broncoalveolar lavage were negative for bacterial, fungi, or acid-fast bacilli. HIV serology was positive, with a viral load >500,000 copies, and CD4 count was 58 cells/mm3. Because of progressive respiratory insufficiency, the patient was transferred to the Intensive Care Unit where orotracheal intubation was performed. Empirical antimicrobial therapy was initiated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, ceftriaxone, and clarithromycin plus prednisone. On the third day of hospitalization, petechiae appeared over the periumbilical area, with refractory shock, fever, cardiac arrest, and death.

Medical History:

The patient denied other gastrointestinal or genitourinary complaints, illicit drug use, and was not taking any medication. He referred to homosexual relations with a single partner for six years.

Hospital Course:

The patient was hospitalized for the treatment of progressive respiratory insufficiency and hemorrhagic gastritis. Despite the empirical antimicrobial therapy, he developed petechiae over the periumbilical area, followed by refractory shock, fever, cardiac arrest, and death. An autopsy was performed, which revealed the presence of a filariform larva of Strongyloides stercoralis in the lungs, liver, stomach, and large intestine.

Summary:

The patient was a 34-year-old, previously healthy male who presented with moderate hematemesis associated with dyspnea, hemoptysis, and a non-measured fever for 4 days. After admission and physical examination, HIV serology was positive with a CD4 count of 58 cells/mm3. The patient was transferred to the Intensive Care Unit, and empirical antimicrobial therapy was initiated. However, the patient developed petechiae over the periumbilical area, refractory shock, fever, cardiac arrest, and eventually died. The autopsy revealed the presence of a filariform larva of Strongyloides stercoralis in the lungs, liver, stomach, and large intestine.

The patient presented with painful, red raised lesions on the right forearm with fever, which gradually coalesced to form larger lesions. On examination, a large erythematous plaque was present on the right upper extremity along with small erythematous plaques on both upper limbs, right side of the neck, and chest. Few lesions showed typical “relief of mountain range appearance”. Local temperature was raised in all the lesions. Superficial nerves were not thickened and sensations on the plaques were normal. Histopathology showed a diffuse infiltrate consisting predominantly of mature neutrophils located in the upper dermis without evidence of primary leukocytoclastic vasculitis.

The second episode was treated with a combination of dapsone and oral prednisolone started at 30 mg/day and gradually tapered over 4 weeks. The patient is now in remission and discharged.

The patient is advised to follow-up with their primary care provider for further evaluation and management.

The patient was a 67-year-old male with essential tremor who underwent an implantation of a Boston Scientific DBS system into the left VIM nucleus of the thalamus. At a follow-up visit 3 months postoperatively, he reported increased tremors in his right hand, and there were difficulties in communicating between his IPG and the programming device at the location. Troubleshooting was done to identify the issue, and radiofrequency interference was noticed during the data download process. The error message "action unsuccessful: communication link (25035)" was found, which led to the evaluation of the RF readings at every corner of the room. A higher RF reading was found at the patient's location. To avoid interference, the patient was moved to a new location, and the computer connected to the IPG with normal programming proceeding. After programming completion, the patient was moved back to the original location where the previous error message reappeared. The problem was resolved by ensuring a lower interference location for the programming.

Summary:
A 67-year-old man with essential tremor underwent implantation of a DBS system. During his follow-up visit, there were difficulties in communicating between the IPG and the programming device because of radiofrequency interference. The issue was evaluated by taking RF readings at every corner of the room, where a higher reading was found at the patient's location and resolved by moving the patient to a new location for programming.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 33-year-old, Malaysian male, presented to the hospital following a nocturnal seizure. Prior to admission, the patient had flu-like symptoms, loss of appetite, and general myalgia. On admission, he was disoriented but had no lateralizing symptoms or signs. The patient experienced post-ictal periods of approximately 30 minutes and had a 21-second asystole during the third seizure. A permanent pacemaker was placed to address this complication.

The patient's neurological exam was unremarkable except for gaze-evoked nystagmus, thought to be a side effect of the administered phenytoin. Despite administration of anticonvulsant medication and subsequent optimization of phenytoin, the patient continued to have recurrent seizures. He developed additional symptoms such as right-sided headache, right ear pain, tenderness, and an unusual sound in the right ear which evolved into a hallucination of music. The patient also developed complex partial seizures, indicating the possibility of HSV encephalitis.

Investigations:
LPs performed on two separate occasions showed no abnormality other than a slightly elevated protein level. CT scans of the head with contrast were normal, and a SPECT scan showed a slight decrease in perfusion of the left side compared to the right. A repeat EEG showed nonspecific abnormality of the right temporal lobe.

Treatment:
The patient was started on a course of acyclovir, and over the first week of therapy, there was significant improvement. Seizures and headaches resolved, but the hallucination of music persisted for several days. The patient was discharged to complete a three-week course of acyclovir. While tapering the anticonvulsants, there were breakthrough seizures, so the patient remains on levetriacetam and phenytoin.

Summary:
The patient was diagnosed with possible HSV encephalitis, which was successfully managed with acyclovir therapy. The patient was discharged with instructions to continue the full course of medication and remain on anticonvulsants.

During the third seizure, his heart stopped for 21 seconds, and doctors placed a permanent pacemaker to fix this problem.
His brain exam was normal except for eye jerking that seemed caused by the phenytoin medicine.
Even after giving seizure drugs and adjusting the phenytoin dose, he kept having seizures and needed further treatment.
He then got a headache on the right side, pain and tenderness in his right ear.
He also heard a strange sound in his ear that later became a music hallucination.
He also started having complex partial seizures, which made doctors think of herpes brain infection.
Investigations:
Doctors did two spinal taps, and the fluid was mostly normal except for a little extra protein.
A CT scan of his head with dye showed no problems and looked completely normal.
A SPECT scan found slightly less blood flow on the left side compared to the right side.
A repeat EEG showed a nonspecific change in the right temporal lobe area of the brain.
Treatment:
The doctors started him on acyclovir medicine to fight a possible virus in the brain.
During the first week, his seizures and headaches got much better, and he felt more alert.
The music hallucination lasted several days and then stopped; it did not happen again after discharge.
He was sent home to finish a three-week course of acyclovir as prescribed by his doctors.
When doctors tried to lower his seizure medicines, his seizures came back, so he stays on two drugs now.
He continues to take levetiracetam and phenytoin to prevent further seizures as directed by his doctor.
Summary:
The doctors believe he had herpes encephalitis, a brain infection caused by a virus that needed antiviral treatment.
He got better with acyclovir and was told to finish the full course and keep taking his seizure medicines.
He will follow up with his doctor as instructed to make sure his recovery continues well.

The patient presented with a non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) and underwent coronary angiography which revealed an occluded mid right coronary artery with brisk collaterals from the left anterior descending artery. The RCA was engaged, and the lesion was crossed easily and distal flow was restored. The RCA was found to be diffusely diseased with stenosis extending from the distal RCA to the ostium. Finally, a GBAT technique was used, and a compliant balloon was inflated and protruded halfway out of the GuideLiner at 8 atm, thus facilitating stent delivery and procedural success. The RCA was stented distal to the ostium with a total of five drug-eluting stents.

Assessment and Plan:
The patient successfully underwent coronary revascularization and was started on antiplatelet therapy, statins, and periprocedural antithrombotic agents. He will require close follow-up with his primary care physician and cardiologist for surveillance and monitoring of his coronary artery disease. Appropriate lifestyle modifications have been advised.

Recommendations:
The patient is advised to follow a healthy diet, maintain a healthy weight, and engage in regular physical activity. The importance of medication adherence and regular follow-up appointments has been emphasized. The patient was discharged in stable condition and advised to seek medical attention should any new symptoms arise.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 40-year-old woman, was admitted to our clinic due to left back pain that lasted 2 months. Physical examination revealed no abnormalities. Laboratory tests showed slightly increased adrenaline and plasma renin activity (recumbent position) levels. Upon further examination by abdominal enhanced computed tomography (CT), the patient was found to have well-defined bilateral adrenal masses and was tentatively diagnosed as having primary adrenal malignancy. The patient underwent left adrenalectomy and ipsilateral nephrectomy, with postoperative pathology showing proliferating lymphocytes, plasma cells, and tissue cells. An immunohistochemical staining and gene rearrangement test resulted in a diagnosis of EBV-associated nasal type extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma. Subsequently, the patient underwent 18F-Fluoro-2-Deoxy-D-Glucose (18F-FDG) positron emission tomography (PET)/CT examination for staging, which showed heterogeneous FDG uptake in the left adrenal gland region, homogeneously increased FDG uptake in the right adrenal gland, and left thigh subcutaneous lesion. 

Discharge Summary:
The patient was diagnosed with EBV-associated nasal type extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, resulting in left adrenalectomy and ipsilateral nephrectomy. The patient underwent 7 cycles of chemotherapy (GLIDE regimen) and autologous stem cell transplantation, and two subsequent follow-up FDG PET/CT scans within 1 year showed complete resolution with no abnormal FDG uptake in the initially involved sites after treatment. The patient was discharged with instructions for follow-up appointments and maintenance. The discharge summary serves as a comprehensive document outlining the patient's medical history, treatment, and prognosis.

Admission Date: [Date of admission]

Diagnosis:
- Retinitis pigmentosa
- Intermittent diplopia

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with complaints of intermittent diplopia that had been present for the past few years, with recent progression. The patient was diagnosed with retinitis pigmentosa after a fundus examination revealed retinal pigmentary changes, narrowing vessels, and relatively pale discs bilaterally. VF examination showed that only the central island remained bilaterally. Prism-cover testing revealed 30 PD left hypertropia and 4 PD XT. Ocular-motility testing demonstrated slight overaction of the inferior oblique muscle and slight underaction of the superior oblique muscle in the left eye. On prism-adaptation testing, the patient reported no diplopia with a 16 PD prism. However, the patient did not prefer prism glasses and requested surgical correction.

The patient underwent an inferior oblique myectomy in the left eye, which resulted in improvement in the hypertropia. One month after surgery, cover testing revealed an 18 PD left hypertropia and 4 PD XT at the primary position. The patient experienced occasional diplopia only with right-up gazing but no diplopia at the primary position or with near work. At the last follow-up visit 3 months later, the prism-cover testing measurements were unchanged, and the patient reported satisfaction with the resolution of diplopia in daily life.

Follow-Up Plan:
The patient will undergo routine follow-up examinations with an ophthalmologist to monitor the progression of retinitis pigmentosa and to evaluate diplopia if it recurs in the future.

During surgery, it was discovered that the tumor was without any dural attachment and primarily intraparenchymal in location. After complete removal of the tumor from the temporal lobe, a portion of it was left attached to the MCA branches to avoid injury to these vessels.

Further evaluation showed that there was a microscopic invasion of the pial surface, which was consistent with the transformation to a WHO grade II meningioma. Fractionated external beam radiation therapy was done instead of further surgery, as it was considered high risk for permanent speech and language deficits.

A repeat MRI showed that the tumor has remained stable in size two years later, but the patient continues to experience occasional seizures despite medication.

Discharge Diagnosis: Partial complex seizures

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to our department with sudden-onset stuporous consciousness. A brain CT scan revealed a subarachnoid hemorrhage with a right temporal lobe intracranial hemorrhage and a right subdural hematoma. Following the CT, angiography demonstrated an aneurysmal sac at the right posterior communicating artery. Emergency decompressive craniectomy (DC) and aneurysmal neck clipping were performed. Following recovery there was some sinking of the scalp flap, and the decision was made to proceed with an autologous cranioplasty 61 days after the initial hemorrhage. There were no complications during the cranioplasty procedure, and there was no evidence of cardiovascular instability or cerebral swelling. Epidural and subdural drains were placed and connected to a suction system during skin closure. Following skin closure the drains were connected to a drainage bag to avoid subgaleal and epidural blood accumulation.

However, the patient had a seizure in the recovery room. Emergency brain CT revealed widespread cerebral edema. Increased intracranial pressure (ICP) and cerebral edema were managed with osmotic diuretics, corticosteroids, and antiepileptic drugs. The edema slowly subsided, but new low-density areas were noted on follow-up brain CT 1 week after the cranioplasty. The decision was made to clamp the drain catheters to control the intracranial pressure.

The patient was monitored closely for any signs of complications, and no further episodes of seizure or cerebral edema were observed. The patient's overall condition improved, and she was discharged in stable condition with instructions for continued follow-up care.

Final Diagnosis:

- Subarachnoid hemorrhage
- Right temporal lobe intracranial hemorrhage
- Right subdural hematoma
- Aneurysmal sac at the right posterior communicating artery
- Widespread cerebral edema

Discharge Instructions:

1. Follow-up appointments with your primary care physician and neurologist are recommended to monitor your recovery and manage any ongoing symptoms.

2. Please continue to take all prescribed medications and follow any instructions provided by your healthcare providers.

3. Adequate rest and nutrition are essential for your continued recovery.

4. Avoid activities that may increase your risk of falls or head injury.

5. In case of any new or worsening symptoms, seek immediate medical attention.

[DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS END]

Discharge Summary:

This is a discharge summary for a 74-year-old woman with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma. The patient was admitted to the hospital due to pain in the right lower chest wall, which was found to be caused by cancer that had spread to multiple areas of the body, including the right lung, mediastinal lymph nodes, liver, and pleural nodules.

The patient was prescribed various medications to manage her cancer, including gefitinib and osimertinib, but after several months of treatment, disease progression was observed.

In September 2017, the patient began receiving a combination of low-dose decitabine and camrelizumab, which resulted in significant improvement in the patient's mediastinal lymph nodes, liver, and pleural nodule metastases. However, after 7 cycles of treatment, the patient's disease progressed again, and she stopped receiving this treatment altogether. 

Throughout the patient's treatment, various markers were measured and showed fluctuations, including an increase in TMB and a decrease in TNB during combined therapy; however, the MSI status and HLA LOH events remained unchanged. 

In May 2019, the patient ultimately passed away from multiple organ failure.

This patient was admitted to our facility for an intense pruritus on her right arm, which had been ongoing for six months. She also complained of right brachial paresis.

The patient has a known history of multiple myeloma.

Computed tomography of the cervical spine, magnetic resonance imaging, and electromyography of the brachial plexus were performed, which showed right cervical disc herniation with nerve root compression of C6-C7 and right brachial plexus inflammation (Parsonage-Turner syndrome).

The patient was treated with methylprednisolone aceponate cream 0.1% and oral hydroxyzine 25mg every 8 hours, which resulted in little improvement of the pruritus. Gabapentin was introduced at 900mg/day, which achieved optimal control after three months of follow-up.

The patient was referred to neurosurgery and oncology consultation for additional therapeutic orientation.

SUMMARY

The patient presented with brachial plexopathy, which is attributed to neoplastic infiltration of multiple myeloma. The treatment plan included the application of methylprednisolone aceponate cream 0.1% and oral hydroxyzine 25mg every 8 hours, along with the introduction of gabapentin at 900mg/day. The patient was referred to neurosurgery and oncology for further management.
