Admission Diagnosis:
Fetal perianal mass detected at 23 weeks' gestation

Hospital Course:
The patient was evaluated for a fetal perianal mass that was detected during routine antenatal care. At the initial visit, an echogenic perivaginal mass was visible on 2D transabdominal ultrasound. Further evaluation with 3D ultrasound revealed that the mass was originated from the skin apart from anus or vagina. Amniocentesis was performed which revealed normal fetal karyotype and no acetylcholinesterase level was detected. As the gestational age progressed, the size of the mass increased. A female neonate was delivered at GA 41 weeks and a pedunculated soft mass was visible on the right posterior labium major of the neonate. A complete physical and laboratory evaluation was performed preoperatively, including routine postnatal cardiac echo which showed a patent foramen ovale with a flow from left to right. There was no significant congenital anomaly identified in vertebral body, both kidney, and anus on MRI. Simple surgical excision was planned for the lesion but during the operation, the right anal external muscle complex was displaced due to the original mass and perineal groove type anorectal malformation was found. Posterior sagittal anorectoplasty (PSARP) was performed with complete mass excision. The histopathological result was lipoblastoma with free resection margin. The neonate was discharged from the hospital without any complication on the postoperative seventh day.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Fetal perianal mass and lipoblastoma

Discharge Condition:
Stable

Discharge Medications:
N/A

Discharge Instructions:
The care team discussed the details of the operation and postoperative care with the patient and their family. The patient is advised to return to the follow-up clinic as scheduled for further evaluation. They were also advised to avoid any strenuous physical activity or heavy lifting for several weeks after surgery. If any signs of infection, such as fever or drainage at the surgical site, develop, the patient should contact their health care provider immediately. It is also recommended to maintain routine postnatal care and follow-up evaluations to monitor neonate's health.

Follow-up:
The patient is scheduled for regular follow-up appointments to monitor their recovery and evaluate any potential complications.

Patient: 61-year-old male with history of controlled type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia and past smoking presented with lumbar pain and weight loss.

He was discharged after 25 days and forwarded to rehabilitation physiotherapy and Tuberculosis Differentiated Ambulatory Unit.

Diagnosis: Chronic granulomatous inflammatory process consistent with tuberculosis.

Condition at discharge: Stable.

Discharge Summary:

The 23-year-old female patient was admitted to the hospital for cardiac workup. The patient presented with negative T waves and cardiac enlargement detected on electrocardiogram and thoracic radiography. She was asymptomatic at presentation and had a history of chronic toxoplasmosis. The patient presented with pallor of skin and mucous membrane, maculo-papular non-itching rash on the forearms and thighs, axillary enlarged lymph nodes, hepatosplenomegaly, blood pressure of 110/60 mmHg, heart rate of 70 b/min, regularly and apexian systolic murmur grade III/VI radiating to the axilla.

Initial laboratory tests showed a discrete inflammatory syndrome and IgG antibodies to Toxoplasma in serum. The echocardiogram confirmed left ventricular enlargement with severe systolic and diastolic dysfunction. A cardiac Magnetic Resonance Imaging was performed and it confirmed dilated cardiomyopathy with excessively prominent trabeculations in left lateral wall and ventricular apex, severe alteration of left ventricular function with diffuse hypokinesia.

The patient was discharged and will be advised to continue antibiotic treatment for the chronic toxoplasmosis. Further follow-up and appropriate care for the dilated cardiomyopathy will be pursued.

MRI and 18F-FDG PET-CT were performed, revealing no significant abnormalities. MRI angiography was also normal.

Diagnosis: Left ventricle tumour, paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to our hospital on [Redacted] with complaints of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia. Further examination revealed a left ventricle tumour, which was confirmed by colour Doppler echocardiography and computed tomographic angiography. The tumour was found to be large relative to the left ventricle, occupying 80% of cavity volume of the left ventricular obstructing mitral valve inflow.

Due to the extensive adhesions of the base of the tumour to the anterior wall and side wall of the left ventricle and its proximity to the mitral valve, chordae tendineae, and other important anatomical structures, the orthotopic cardiac tumour resection was deemed difficult and risky. Therefore, the patient underwent a heart autotransplantation procedure, which involved a median sternotomy incision, instituting cardiopulmonary bypass, isolating the heart, removing the tumour, and returning the heart to its original position.

Histology revealed that the tumour was a rhabdomyoma. The patient was discharged on [Redacted] after 13 days of hospitalization. In 5 months of follow-up, there was no tumour recurrence or arrhythmia observed.

Instructions at Discharge:

The patient was instructed to follow up with his primary care physician for routine assessments and to notify our hospital if any symptoms recurred. A referral to a cardiac rehabilitation program was also made to support the patient's continued recovery. The parents were provided with instructions for symptom management and was advised to seek care immediately if there were any changes in the patient's condition.

Discharge Medications:

N/A

Follow-up Appointments:

The patient was scheduled for follow-up appointments with his primary care physician and the cardiac rehabilitation program.

Hospital Course:
This 7-month-old boy was admitted to our hospital for treatment of respiratory syncytial viral pneumonia, with a history of tracheoesophageal fistula and esophageal atresia surgery performed at 1 day of age. The patient showed recurrent cough and sputum, and was afebrile. The chest radiograph showed increased peribronchial infiltration and air bronchogram. Due to the risk of aspiration pneumonia, oral feeding was discontinued and the patient was given parenteral nutrition via the peripheral venous route.

Extravasation Event:
On day 6 of admission, while the patient was receiving total parenteral nutrition, a 24-gauge intravenous catheter was newly inserted into the dorsal cephalic vein at the dorsum of the patient's right hand. The patient showed signs of irritability, and the obstruction alarm of the infusion pump was triggered. Without any alarm sign, approximately 9 hours after the repositioning of the intravenous catheter, the patient's right hand and arm appeared severely swollen, and capillary refill was absent. There were several blisters observed under the catheter, and an emergency fasciotomy was performed under the suspicion of compartment syndrome.

Treatment and Care:
The patient received orthopedic surgery and fascia suturing, followed by irrigation of the area several times with saline solution. Delayed primary skin closure was performed 8 days after the fasciotomy. A skin graft was scheduled for treatment of the skin necrosis after debriding the necrotic tissue with a moist dressing. Rehabilitation treatment consisting of wrist articulation exercises was started due to the high chance of wrist joint contracture. Skin graft surgery was delayed due to pneumonia, which was diagnosed during the patient's regular wound dressing and rehabilitation treatment. It was performed 4 months after the extravasation event. At the time of this report, skin engraftment had been successfully completed, and the patient was receiving continued rehabilitation treatment.
nemotron_simplification:
Hospital Course: The patient is a 7-month-old boy admitted for RSV pneumonia. He has a history of tracheoesophageal fistula and esophageal atresia repaired at one day old. He had recurrent cough and sputum but no fever during his hospital stay for observation. The chest X-ray showed increased peribronchial infiltration and an air bronchogram, indicating lung inflammation and airway obstruction. Because of the risk of aspiration pneumonia, oral feeding was stopped to prevent food from entering his lungs. He received parenteral nutrition through a vein in his arm to provide calories and nutrients while he could not eat.
Extravasation Event: On day six, a 24-gauge IV catheter was placed in the vein on the back of his right hand. He was receiving total parenteral nutrition at the time to give him calories and nutrients while he could not eat. He became irritable and the infusion pump alarm sounded due to obstruction, indicating a problem with the IV line. About nine hours after the catheter was repositioned, his right hand and arm became swollen and capillary refill was absent. Several blisters were seen under the catheter, signs of tissue damage from the leaking fluid. An emergency fasciotomy was performed because doctors suspected compartment syndrome to relieve pressure and prevent muscle injury.
Treatment and Care: He had orthopedic surgery to repair the fascia and the area was washed several times with saline. Eight days later, the skin was closed loosely in a delayed primary closure to allow healing before grafting. Dead tissue was removed with a wet dressing, and a skin graft was planned to cover the wound. Wrist exercises were started to prevent stiffness because joint contracture was likely during his recovery period. The skin graft was delayed because he developed pneumonia during wound care and rehabilitation that required treatment. Four months after the extravasation injury, the skin graft surgery was performed to replace the damaged skin. At this time, the graft has taken successfully and he continues rehabilitation to improve hand function and strength.

FINAL DIAGNOSIS: 

Right hepatic artery pseudoaneurysm

HOSPITAL COURSE: 

A 58-year-old male was admitted with hilar bile ductal carcinoma and underwent preoperative percutaneous transhepatic portal embolization (PTPE) of the anterior and posterior branches of his right portal vein. Two days later, the patient complained of an acute abdominal pain, and a contrast-enhanced computed tomography scan confirmed the presence of a pseudoaneurysm. Follow-up CT revealed complete pseudoaneurysm occlusion, and liver hypertrophy was observed. The patient subsequently underwent right hepatectomy, which was uneventful.

The patient was discharged in stable condition 30 days post-procedure. The patient was observed for four weeks post-procedure and showed no evidence of pseudoaneurysm recurrence or hepatic infarction.

Discharge Summary:

This is a 48-year-old female patient, who was admitted to our hospital for surgical treatment of a recurrence of squamous cell carcinoma on the left mandible body. She underwent a wide excision and left mandibulectomy followed by a mandible, mouth floor, and tongue reconstruction with a titanium implant and an anterolateral thigh (ALT) free flap. The ALT flap was harvested from the ipsilateral thigh and then anastomosed to the lingual artery and the internal jugular vein. After surgery, the patient was observed to have an acceptable overall facial shape and was capable of mastication.

The patient received adjuvant radiation and chemotherapy due to the recurrence of the disease after previous surgery. The patient did not have any suspicious tumor recurrence on the follow-up CT.

The designed implant was manufactured using an A1 metal 3D printer with a biocompatibility material that was composed of titanium, aluminum, and vanadium. The prosthesis appeared well positioned on the radiograph taken after surgery.

The patient was discharged from the hospital and advised to continue follow-up care with the multidisciplinary team. Further information and recommendations for follow-up care were discussed with the patient and their family.

The patient, a 36-year-old female, was admitted to the hospital after jumping from a four-foot high deck and experiencing extreme pain and inability to bear weight on the right limb. Given the patient's continued symptoms, close follow-up with an orthopedic surgeon is recommended.

The patient presented with a 2-month history of cough and intractable hemoptysis. A bronchoscopic examination performed in another hospital revealed a vascular fleshy growth protruding onto the left main bronchus, and an attempted biopsy resulted in profuse bleeding. The patient was then referred to our center for further management. A repeat bronchoscopy performed at our center confirmed the previous bronchoscopy findings, and a biopsy from the lesion was managed conservatively. Histology with immunohistochemistry (IHC) correlation suggested a diagnosis of a primary pulmonary angiosarcoma, intermediate grade. The tumor was found to completely occlude the left main bronchus. A fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography (18F-FDG PET/CT) done as a part of metastatic workup showed a solitary metabolically active endobronchial lesion in the left main bronchus extending into the left lower bronchus causing complete obstruction and collapse of the entire left lung; further corroborating the diagnosis of a primary pulmonary angiosarcoma.

Treatment:
A formal cardiopulmonary evaluation was done, and the patient was taken up for a definitive surgery. Intraoperatively the tumor was found to originate at the bifurcation of the left main bronchus and a sleeve resection was deemed not possible, the patient, therefore, underwent a left pneumonectomy. Her postoperative recovery was uneventful. The patient received 50 gray of adjuvant radiotherapy.

Follow-up Plan:
The patient is on regular follow-up for the past 7 months.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Primary pulmonary angiosarcoma.

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient presented with a history of increasing pain in the right hip and pelvis for the last 3 years, radiating to the right lower limb and back, progressively increasing in intensity, and associated with tingling sensation since last 3 months. She had become quite incapacitated due to painful restricted movements. Her past history showed that at 22 years of age, she had presented with a large abdominal mass. Her CT at that time showed a multicystic lesion measuring 18.0×9.8×7.6 cm in the right abdomen, which appeared to be arising from the right ovary. She underwent surgery which showed a hydatid cyst which was confirmed on histopathology. After remaining asymptomatic for 3 years, in 2007, she again gradually developed pain in the right pelvic region. This time MRI showed a large solid cystic mass measuring 10×6.3 cm in the right iliac fossa and right gluteal region. She underwent a diagnostic laparatomy where multiple cysts in the iliac bone with osteolysis were seen. Two cystic pieces were removed which were diagnosed as hydatid cyst. The patient continued with the pelvic pain although postoperative MRI showed reduction in size of the lesion along the right iliac bone and sacroiliac joint. The x-ray of the pelvis and hips revealed cortical irregularity with ill defined lytic defects and linear areas of patchy sclerosis along the right iliac blade. She continued with pain and follow-up CT revealed extension of the disease. Resection of the hydatid cyst of sacroiliac region with allograft and autograft with lumbosacroiliac fixation was done. Histopathology results revealed hydatid cysts of the bone. The patient was also put on a medical treatment with albendazole for 1 month. The postoperative period was uneventful and patient was discharged on the 10th day of surgery. The follow-up of the patient at 6 months showed no detectable abnormality on radiology, and she was doing well.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
The patient is advised to follow up with the treating physician for regular check-ups and medication management. The patient should continue taking the prescribed medication as per the treatment plan. She should follow a healthy diet and lifestyle to maintain optimal health. The patient is also advised to rest and avoid physical activity until further notice from the treating physician. Any new or worsening symptoms should be reported promptly to the physician.

Discharge Diagnosis: Hydatid cysts of the bone
HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient is a 31-year-old woman with increasing right hip and pelvis pain for three years.
The pain spread to her right leg and back, and she felt tingling for the last three months.
This pain made her unable to move normally and caused disability and limited her daily activities.
When she was 22, doctors found a large abdominal mass that seemed to come from her right ovary.
A scan showed a cyst about 18 by 10 by 8 centimeters, and surgery confirmed it was a hydatid cyst.
After three years with no symptoms, she again felt pain in her right pelvic area in 2007.
An MRI showed a solid cystic mass about 10 by 6 centimeters in her right hip and buttock area.
Doctors did a laparotomy and saw several cysts in her pelvic bone that had caused bone loss.
They removed two pieces, and laboratory tests confirmed that both pieces were hydatid cysts of bone.
After surgery, her pelvic pain continued, but she remained hopeful that further treatment would help.
A later MRI showed the lesion had shrunk along her right iliac bone and sacroiliac joint.
An X-ray of her pelvis showed uneven bone with unclear dark spots and patchy white areas on the right side.
She still had pain, and a follow-up CT scan showed the disease had spread to nearby bone.
Doctors performed surgery to remove the cyst from the sacroiliac area of her pelvis and stabilize the joint.
They used donor bone and her own bone tissue to fill the gap left after cyst removal.
They fixed the joint with screws and plates to keep it stable while it healed.
Tissue tests confirmed that the removed material was a hydatid cyst of bone, matching the earlier diagnosis.
She also took the medicine albendazole for one month after the operation to kill any remaining parasites.
Her recovery after surgery was smooth, and she left the hospital ten days later with no complications.
A check-up six months later showed no abnormal findings on imaging, and she felt well.

The patient should see her doctor regularly for check-ups and to manage her medicine as needed.

The patient was admitted to our tertiary referral center from a regional hospital with hypercalcaemic hyperparathyroid crisis. He presented with a two-week history of weakness and lethargy and a one-week history of vomiting, polyuria and polydipsia. He became confused 24 hours prior to his admission and registered 12 on the Glasgow Coma Scale. On examination, he had a left-sided mass in the anterior triangle of his neck measuring 3 × 3 cm. The patient remained intubated and ventilated overnight in the intensive care unit. His metabolic laboratory profile resolved quickly following the surgery. A lower respiratory tract infection delayed his initial recovery. 

The patient was discharged home 24 days after surgery on oral calcium supplementation. He has been followed up for 6 months so far without any complications or disease recurrence.

The patient was admitted with hypercalcaemic hyperparathyroid crisis and managed with aggressive fluid resuscitation, cardiac monitoring and the administration of intravenous bisphosphonates. Ruptured proximal splenic artery aneurysm

Angiography with coil embolization of the aneurysm and proximal splenic artery using 2D and 3D mechanically detachable fibered micro coils, and N-butyl-cyanoacrylate (NBCA) glue.

A ruptured proximal splenic artery aneurysm was identified, and angiography with coil embolization was performed with the aim of preserving all collateral vessels for the spleen. The patient was referred to the surgical department for further treatment and monitoring. The patient's condition remained stable, and he was discharged on the 12th day after embolization. After three months of therapy with sofosbuvir 400 mg/velpatasvir 100 mg once daily, the sustained virological response (SVR) was reached and it’s still active.

Follow-up Care:
The patient was given an appointment to be followed up with our hepatological unit to ensure the continued management of the HCV-related liver disease. The patient was also advised to maintain healthy habits and refrain from drug consumption.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission:
A 43-year-old male with primary hypothyroidism was admitted for evaluation of progressive fatigue, weakness, muscle and joint pain in the setting of recurrent fractures.

History of Present Illness:
The patient had been experiencing musculoskeletal pain in several locations including bilateral knees, ankles, left shoulder, left arm, and lower back which affected his overall functional status. He struggled to climb a flight of stairs, often grabbing the railing to pull himself up. A nuclear medicine bone scan showed abnormal uptake in bilateral ribs, vertebrae, right knee, hips, ankles, and feet. A lower extremity MRI showed stress fractures in left fibula, fifth metatarsal, and right tibia.

Course in Hospital:
The patient was started on calcitriol and phosphate supplements which significantly improved muscle weakness. Due to concern for TIO, a positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) scan with 68Gallium (68Ga)-DOTATATE was performed which showed multiple lytic osseous lesions with increased somatostatin positive uptake seen throughout pelvis, ribs, ankles, and feet. However, after re-review with radiology, multiple areas of increased uptake were considered to be secondary to fractures, and left posterior acetabular lesion was presumed to be the tumor of interest given a remarkably higher standard uptake values (SUVmax) in this lesion compared to other lesions (SUVmax 20 vs. 4–5).

Procedure:
The left acetabular lesion was biopsied and pathology demonstrated a 1.4 cm phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor of the left acetabulum with uninvolved margins. The patient underwent radical resection of the tumor of the posterior left acetabulum with reconstruction of the posterior wall and posterior column of the acetabulum through a Kocher-Langenbach approach. His hip joint was able to be spared utilizing a 3D-printed custom bone cutting guide (CG) and intra-operative O-arm guided surgical navigation (Medtronic© Stealth) utilizing a navigated Sonopet Ultrasonic Bone Cutting Bovie (Stryker). The posterior wall and column of his acetabulum were constructed with a tantalum augment (Zimmer) and a pelvic reconstruction plate and screw construct (Synthes) after tumor removal.

Discharge Summary:
The patient was discharged with normal phosphorus and FGF23 levels, pain-free left hip, no evidence of hardware complication, back to hiking, and walking on the treadmill. Clinical and radiographic follow-up at 6 months postoperatively found him to be pain-free in his left hip, with almost complete resolution of bone pain, and no recurrence of fractures. Phosphorus level also remained normal at 3.4 mg/dL 6 months after surgery.

Admission: A 43-year-old man with low thyroid function was admitted for worsening tiredness, weakness, muscle and joint pain, and repeated fractures.

This pain limited his ability to climb stairs, so he often grabbed the railing to pull himself up.
A bone scan showed abnormal activity in both sides of the ribs, spine, right knee, hips, ankles, and feet.
An MRI of the legs revealed stress fractures in the left fibula, left fifth metatarsal, and right tibia.
Course in Hospital:
The doctors started calcitriol and phosphate supplements after admission, which significantly improved his muscle weakness.
Because doctors suspected tumor-induced osteomalacia, they did a PET/CT scan using 68Ga-DOTATATE to look for abnormal bone activity.
The scan showed many lytic bone lesions with increased somatostatin uptake in the pelvis, ribs, ankles, and feet.
After a second review, most of the increased uptake was attributed to healing fractures, leaving one suspicious area.
The suspicious spot in the left posterior acetabulum showed much higher activity (SUVmax 20) than other areas (SUVmax 4-5).
Procedure:
A biopsy of the left hip socket showed a 1.4 cm phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor with clear margins.
The tumor was removed completely, and the back wall and column of the socket were rebuilt using the Kocher-Langenbach approach.
To save the hip joint, surgeons used a 3D-printed custom cutting guide and O-arm navigation (Medtronic Stealth).
They also used a Sonopet ultrasonic bone cutter (Stryker) during the operation to remove bone precisely.
The rebuilt socket used a tantalum implant (Zimmer) and a metal plate with screws (Synthes).
Discharge Summary:
At discharge, his phosphorus and FGF23 levels were normal, and his left hip was pain-free.
There were no complications with the plates or screws used in the surgery, and he could walk without pain.
He was able to return to hiking and to walk on a treadmill as part of his daily activity.
Six months later, follow-up visits showed his left hip remained pain-free and most bone pain had gone away.
No new fractures occurred during follow-up, and his phosphorus level stayed normal at 3.4 mg/dL.

Hospital Course:
Upon examination, a clear inferior altitudinal defect was evident with associated arterial attenuation in the left eye. The patient was diagnosed with superior branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) and was started on Aspirin. The patient was urgently referred to the local stroke team for further evaluation.

The patient underwent trans-thoracic echocardiography, MRI and MR-angiogram of brain and neck, which were all unremarkable. Haematological investigations revealed a raised homocysteine level, vitamin B12 deficiency, and borderline folate deficiency. Subsequent genetic testing revealed a C677T subtype homozygous mutation for the gene encoding methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR).

Treatment:
The patient was started on vitamin B12 and folate replacement, which led to normalization of homocysteine levels. Aspirin therapy was also continued.

Outcome:
Follow-up visual field testing at two months revealed slight improvement in the visual field defect, and no further vaso-occlusive events were noted.

Summary:
The patient presented with acute inferior hemi-field visual loss in the left eye with a diagnosis of superior branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO). Through various diagnostic tests, a C677T subtype homozygous mutation for the gene encoding methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) was identified. The patient was successfully treated with vitamin B12 and folate replacement, and aspirin therapy was continued. Follow-up testing at two months revealed improvement in the visual field defect.

The patient, a 63-year-old woman with typical chest pain, was admitted to the hospital and underwent several tests including a transthoracic echocardiography which showed a 40% ejection fraction, left ventricular dilatation with hypokinesia in the lateral walls and dyskinesia of septal and apical walls. Stenting of proximal lesion with a 3 mm x 19 mm, paclitaxel-eluting coronary stent system (EURoCOR), and mid part of lesion with a 2.5 mm x 32 mm paclitaxel-eluting coronary stent system (EURoCOR) was carried out with success.

After 6 days, the patient referred with a typical chest pain without any response to medication. Coronary angiography was done and showed an optimal extent expansion without any significant residual stenosis. However, the definite fracture of stent that was implanted in the mid part of LAD 6 days before her admission was detected which required further intervention.

During her hospital course, the patient was monitored closely and treated with standard care and preventive measures, including medication administration, diet and exercise counseling and vital signs monitoring.

The patient's condition is improved and stable upon discharge. Home care instructions were provided along with prescribed medications and follow up visits with her Primary Care Physician and Cardiologist were scheduled.

Despite the ongoing medical support, the patient showed no signs of improvement, leading to a mutual decision to withdraw from ventilation. The patient passed away eventually.

- Chronic Hepatopathy
- Portal Hypertension
- Esophageal Varices

Discharge Summary:

Admission Date: November 2018
Discharge Date: [Date not specified]

Hospital Course:
A 53-year-old female patient, with a history of NHL (diffuse large B-cell lymphoma [DLBCL]), presented with a short history of progressively deteriorating pain and weakness in the right lower limb. The patient had completed chemotherapy (8 × R-CHOPP) with a complete metabolic response in January 2018. Further examination revealed mild swelling over the left maxillary region with few palpable nodes in bilateral upper cervical regions. Neurological examination revealed a significant lower motor weakness in the right lower limb (2/5), and sensory examination revealed mild appendicular acral numbness to light touch. There was also evidence of mild motor weakness in both the upper limbs (4/5) without significant abnormality on sensory examination. Biopsy of the left facial swelling revealed DLBCL (CD20 positive with Ki-67 index >90%). Her cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and bone trephine did not reveal lymphomatous infiltration. A low-dose noncontrast 18FDG PET/CT examination was performed, which revealed hypermetabolic soft-tissue deposits and hypermetabolic lymph nodes in various regions, including left Level II, V, and celiac regions. There was also evidence of hypermetabolic uptake (predominantly linear pattern) over the bilateral brachial and right sacral plexuses and bilateral sciatic, right gluteal, and both femoral nerves. Based on the clinical, facial biopsy and 18FDG PET/CT findings, a diagnosis of recurrent lymphoma with NLS was made. The second-line chemotherapy was started, and after four cycles, she became asymptomatic with a resolution of left facial swelling and normalization of sensory and motor deficits too. An interim 18FDG PET/CT revealed a complete metabolic response too.

Hospital Diagnosis:
Recurrent lymphoma with NLS

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with the diagnosis of recurrent lymphoma with NLS. Second-line chemotherapy was administered, resulting in the resolution of left facial swelling and normalization of sensory and motor deficits. An interim 18FDG PET/CT revealed a complete metabolic response. The patient was discharged in stable condition.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Redacted]

Hospital Course:
A 9-year-old male patient was admitted to our hospital with sudden loss of vision in his left eye for the past 10 days, following an episode of vigorous eye rubbing. On examination, corneal ectasia with Vogt's striae was observed in the right eye along with a superficial corneal scar. The left eye exhibited dense stromal edema along with a central corneal ectasia, indicating acute hydrops. A diagnosis of bilateral keratoconus with left eye acute hydrops was made based on the clinical findings.

Treatment and Procedures:
The patient underwent pneumodesmetopexy with C3F8 in the left eye, with AC paracentesis using a 26-gauge needle under aseptic conditions. Air was first added to completely fill the anterior chamber (AC) and then replaced with 14% of C3F8 to fill two-thirds of the AC. Topical antibiotics and steroids were prescribed, and the patient was advised to remain in a supine position postoperatively.

Outcome:
The patient has been followed up for 12 months, and the corneal edema has completely resolved. The patient currently has a nebular grade corneal scar and the best-corrected visual acuity is 6/9 (with contact lens). Intraocular pressure (IOP) has been normal postoperatively.

Impressions and Plan:
The patient was treated for bilateral keratoconus with left eye acute hydrops through pneumodesmetopexy with C3F8. The patient’s corneal edema completely resolved, and the best-corrected visual acuity has improved with contact lens. The patient has been discharged with long term follow-up recommended.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [Redacted]
Age: 26 years
Gender: Female

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with a ten-year history of vomiting that was not relieved by standard antiemetic and behavioral treatments for cyclic vomiting syndrome. After thorough medical examination, a possible diagnosis of epilepsy was considered as the patient experienced cramping of the tongue, clenched her teeth against her will, and had an abnormal EEG showing spike and wave complexes in the left temporal lobe. Clonazepam was administered, which substantially improved background wave activity and decreased vomiting episodes. Psychological treatment, including relaxation techniques, breathing exercises, drawing pictures, and counseling, was also provided as the patient was suspected of having a mental trigger for her epilepsy.

Patient's Social and Family History:
The patient had a noncontributory past and family medical history. Family dynamics were identified as a possible psychological trigger. In her childhood, the patient was well-behaved, but her mother paid little attention to her as she was busy caring for her sick elder sister. When her sister entered college and was seldom at home, the mother began to nag the patient to do things and was overprotective of her. Through therapeutic sessions, the patient discussed her family's history, and psychological interventions were implemented to encourage independence and support her in moving away from her family.

Follow-Up:
After leaving the hospital, the patient experienced some ictal vomiting during periods of high stress. Still, with empathic support and therapy, her condition improved drastically when she obtained job training and subsequently found employment. Her symptoms disappeared entirely within several months, and she has been in good health without medication for over seven years.

Recommendations:
The patient is advised to continue to avoid triggers that may cause stress and has been encouraged to maintain independence and lead a healthy lifestyle. Follow-up clinical and psychological assessments are recommended to monitor her condition and prevent any relapses or complications.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 71-year-old Japanese woman, presented with a 10-year history of left hip pain and 1-year history of left leg edema. Physical examination revealed limitation of the range of motion (ROM) of her left hip, with 80° flexion, 20° abduction, 15° adduction, 45° external rotation, and 5° internal rotation. Plain radiographs revealed advanced osteoarthritis (OA) secondary to developmental dysplasia of the left hip. Computed tomography (CT) images and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed compression of the femoral vessels by a mass that was absent 8 years ago on a previous radiograph. The mass was diagnosed as a capital drop secondary to OA and total hip arthroplasty (THA) with resection of the mass was performed. Following surgery, the left leg edema immediately diminished and the postoperative course was uneventful. At the latest follow-up, that is, 3 years after the surgery, the patient was able to walk without an aid and was independent in all activities of daily living, with no evidence of recurrence. 

Diagnoses:
Advanced osteoarthritis secondary to developmental dysplasia of the left hip

Procedures performed:
Total hip arthroplasty (THA) with resection of the mass, using a short tapered wedge stem with a 32mm ceramic head and a 48mm cementless cup with a polyethylene liner

Histopathological findings:
Peripheral cartilage layer, with mature trabecular bone present in the central zone. No malignant cells were observed

Discharge condition:
Stable

Functional status at discharge:
The patient was able to walk independently and had no evidence of recurrence.

X-rays showed severe wear of the left hip joint because the hip socket never formed properly. CT and MRI scans showed a mass pressing on the leg's blood vessels near the hip. This mass had not been seen on a previous X-ray from eight years before. Doctors diagnosed the mass as a bone piece that had slipped out of place due to joint wear. They performed a total hip replacement and removed the mass. They used a short metal stem with a 32-mm ceramic ball. They also used a 48-mm cup without cement that had a plastic liner. After the operation, the leg swelling went down right away and the recovery was smooth. At the latest check-up, three years after surgery, the patient walked without help. She managed all daily activities on her own and showed no sign the problem returned.

Procedures performed: The doctors replaced the hip joint and removed the mass. They used a short metal stem with a 32-mm ceramic ball. They also used a 48-mm cup without cement that had a plastic liner.
Histopathological findings: The tissue showed a cartilage layer on the outside and normal bone inside, with no cancer cells.
Discharge condition: The patient's condition was stable at discharge.
Functional status at discharge: The patient could walk on her own and showed no sign the problem came back.

The patient was diagnosed with pulmonary embolism along with right lower-limb deep-venous thrombosis, which was confirmed by computed tomography scans of the chest. Warfarin was initiated, but the patient had been taking the drug erratically without proper monitoring. On physical examination, the patient had asymmetry in the girth of the lower limbs with the right limb girth being larger. The chest auscultation revealed bibasilar fine-end inspiratory crepitation with vesicular breath sounds of equal intensity. The initial hemoglobin level was 14.2 gm%, which decreased to 10.6 gm% over the course of 3 days. Moreover, the international normalized ratio (INR) was 7.2, and the patient had bilateral upper-zone infiltrates (right>left) and ground-glass opacities in the upper lobes of the lungs.

The patient was immediately taken off Warfarin, and high-flow oxygen was administered. The patient was also given 10-mg intravenous Vitamin K injection followed by transfusion of four units of fresh frozen plasma. In a couple of days, the patient showed improvement and was weaned off the supplemental oxygen.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Anticoagulant (Warfarin)-induced Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH).

Discharge Condition:
The patient was discharged in stable condition with an advice of strict INR monitoring in further follow-ups.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient was instructed to continue taking the prescribed medications as directed by their primary care physician. The patient was advised to follow-up with their primary care physician for close monitoring of their condition. Moreover, the patient was advised to follow a healthy diet and lifestyle to prevent the recurrence of any possible complications.

The patient is recommended to follow up with their primary care physician for further treatment and monitoring of their condition.

The patient, a 38-year-old male, was admitted to our hospital with complaints of fever and painful swelling in the right proximal leg. He had a history of travel to Malaysia and was suspected to have tuberculosis of the abdomen in a previous hospital, where he was started on antitubercular drugs. He also had an ongoing anorexia with weight loss. On presentation to our hospital, he was in septic shock and was diagnosed with acute osteomyelitis of the right proximal tibia with septic arthritis of the knee joint. He underwent arthrotomy and was found to have a Gram-negative, safety pin-shaped bacteria infection suggestive of B. pseudomallei. He was initiated on six weeks of ceftazidime and levofloxacin, followed by oral eradication therapy with cotrimoxazole and doxycycline for six months. He completed the treatment course without any adverse drug reactions.

Admitting Diagnosis: Acute stroke resulting in dysarthria and left-sided hemiparesis.

Hospital Course:
A 78-year-old female with type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and obesity was admitted to our tertiary care hospital following an acute stroke, which resulted in dysarthria and left-sided hemiparesis. Multiple complications were encountered during the hospital course including a code blue due to aspiration pneumonia and prolonged hospitalization. After failing multiple swallow studies, a decision was made to insert a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube for long-term enteral nutrition. A fluoroscopic evaluation identified an air-distended colonic loop, which caused the procedure to be aborted. The gastrointestinal team recommended holding clopidogrel for 5 days before proceeding with endoscopic PEG placement. The procedure was successful, and the patient tolerated tube feeds without any complications. Post-procedure imaging showed that the gastrostomy tube had traversed the lateral margin of hepatic segment 3 with an adjacent hematoma measuring 2 × 2 × 4 cm. The patient tolerated the PEG tube well and was safely discharged to a nursing home for further care.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Acute stroke resulting in dysarthria and left-sided hemiparesis, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, obesity, aspiration pneumonia, and hematoma in hepatic segment 3.

Discharge Medications:
None specified.

Follow-up:
The patient expired on day 3 in the nursing home, and the cause of death remains un-established as the patient's family denied completion of an autopsy.

A 66-year-old female patient was admitted to the Department of Periodontics, M. S. Ramaiah Dental College and Hospital, Bangalore, with the complaint of burning sensation in the gums and bleeding gums for the past one month.

Medical History:
The patient had no relevant drug history or significant medical history. She had not received any dental treatment before.

Examination Findings:
On extra oral examination, the patient had some obvious skin lesions on the scalp and a hyperkeratotic plaque behind her left ear. Intra oral examination of gingiva revealed reddish marginal, attached gingiva and interdental papilla in both maxillary and mandibular anterior region with desquamation of epithelium present in certain regions.

Diagnosis:
Based on the clinical and histopathologic features, the lesion was suggestive of discoid lupus erythematosus.

Treatment:
Hand scaling was performed as gently as possible in order to minimize tissue disruption. Soft tooth brush and mouth rise (chlorhexidine 0.12%) was recommended. Triamcinolone acteonide oral paste was advised to apply two to three times per day.

Follow-up:
The patient was recalled for follow-up and maintenance.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 39-year-old woman diagnosed with plasmablastic IgA lambda multiple myeloma

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to our facility in January 2011 with a diagnosis of plasmablastic IgA lambda multiple myeloma, stage III (International Staging System). She underwent four cycles of PAD chemotherapy (bortezomib, adriamycin, and dexamethasone) and zoledronic acid before receiving an autologous peripheral blood stem cell transplant, conditioned with melphalan (200 mg/m2), in August 2011. The patient experienced a symptomatic relapse with a T7 vertebral collapse in March 2013, after which treatment with lenalidomide and dexamethasone was initiated. Due to a loss of response after four cycles of treatment, the patient received VCD chemotherapy (bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone), achieving a second complete remission. In December 2013, a fully matched sibling hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, after reduced-intensity conditioning regimen, was performed to consolidate the excellent response. The patient experienced another bone marrow relapse, along with a plasmacytoma of tibia in April 2014, following which she was retreated with VCD. This regimen was stopped after two cycles of treatment due to bortezomib-related peripheral neuropathy. The patient was then placed on VBCMP/VBAD chemotherapy (vincristine, carmustine, cyclophosphamide, melphalan, prednisone/vincristine, carmustine, doxorubicin, and high-dose dexamethasone), achieving a third complete remission.

In April 2015, the patient presented with pericardial effusion and echocardiographic signs of cardiac tamponade, which were resolved through pericardiocentesis. In May 2015, the patient presented with massive left-side pleural effusion. Two thoracocentesis revealed plasmablastic cells. Despite this EMM relapse, multiple myeloma was not detected in blood, urine, or bone marrow. The patient was then started on carfilzomib plus dexamethasone, which resulted in a sudden improvement in her general condition and was discharged without pleural effusion.

Follow-Up Recommendations:

The patient is currently receiving the 18th cycle of treatment and remains in complete remission 19 months after the EMM was detected. Further follow-up appointments will be scheduled to monitor the patient's progress.

Discharge Summary:
Patient: 39-year-old woman with plasmablastic IgA lambda multiple myeloma
Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted in January 2011 with stage III blood cancer, diagnosed as plasmablastic IgA lambda multiple myeloma.
She received four cycles of PAD chemotherapy, which includes bortezomib, adriamycin, and dexamethasone, plus zoledronic acid for bone health.
In August 2011 she had an autologous stem cell transplant using her own blood cells after high-dose melphalan.
In March 2013 the cancer returned with a collapsed T7 vertebra, and she started lenalidomide and dexamethasone.
After four cycles the disease stopped responding, so she switched to VCD chemotherapy (bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, dexamethasone) and achieved complete remission.
In December 2013 she received a transplant from a matched sibling after milder conditioning to keep the remission.
In April 2014 the cancer returned in the bone marrow and a tumor appeared in the tibia.
She was given VCD chemotherapy again, consisting of bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone, to try to control the disease.
Treatment stopped after two cycles because bortezomib caused peripheral neuropathy, a nerve damage in her feet.
She then received VBCMP/VBAD chemotherapy, a mix of vincristine, carmustine, cyclophosphamide, melphalan, prednisone, doxorubicin, and high-dose dexamethasone.
This treatment led to a third complete remission, meaning no signs of cancer were detected.
In April 2015 fluid around the heart caused tamponade, which was relieved by draining the fluid.
In May 2015 a large left pleural effusion appeared, requiring drainage and further testing to check for cancer.
Fluid removal showed cancer cells, but blood, urine, and marrow tests did not detect any cancer.
She started carfilzomib plus dexamethasone, her condition improved quickly, and she left the hospital without pleural effusion.
Follow-Up Recommendations:
The patient is now on her 18th cycle of treatment, continuing the current medication plan.
She remains in complete remission, which has lasted 19 months since the pleural effusion was discovered.
Future visits will be scheduled to check her progress and ensure the cancer stays in remission.

Discharge Summary:

Admitting Diagnosis: Suspected Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP)

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 36-year-old man with a history of bronchial asthma and smoking, presented with sudden onset right upper limb weakness which spread to his lower limb along with slurring of speech and altered consciousness. He was initially admitted to an outside facility where CT scan and carotid ultrasound came out to be normal. His CBC with differential showed low hemoglobin and platelets with elevated bilirubin, and peripheral blood smear (PBS) indicated fragmented red blood cells. TTP was suspected, and fresh frozen plasma (FFP) infusion started. On transfer to our facility, he received PLEX and pulse steroids for 18 sessions which resulted in the stabilization of the patient's LDH and platelet count. During his hospital stay, he was also diagnosed with eosinophilia. A bone marrow aspirate and core biopsy showed trilineage hematopoiesis with 2% blasts and 30% eosinophils. FISH for FIP1L1-PDGFRA (4q12) rearrangement was positive.
After 18 sessions of PLEX, the patient's LDH and platelet counts normalized. However, as weaning off PLEX was attempted, schistocytes re-emerged with a subsequent drop in platelet count. Consequently, a four-dose course of rituximab and Imatinib 100 mg daily were started. Thirty sessions of PLEX were needed to treat the TTP, and the last session was 4 days after the initiation of Imatinib. After more than 28 months of follow-up, the patient's eosinophil count has normalized, and there has been no recurrence of TTP.

Discharge Diagnosis: Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura and Eosinophilia

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient was admitted with suspected TTP, and after receiving 18 sessions of PLEX and methylprednisolone, his platelet count and LDH stabilized. The patient was also found to have eosinophilia with trilineage hematopoiesis, which was treated with a four-dose course of rituximab and Imatinib 100 mg daily. After 30 sessions of PLEX, the TTP was resolved, and the patient's eosinophil count had normalized. After more than 28 months of follow-up, there has been no recurrence of TTP.

Hospital Course Summary:

Chief Complaint: Dyspnea, palpitation, and shortness of breath for two years

Medical History: Pulmonary artery hypertension, received anticoagulation therapy and sildenafil

Assessment and Plan: Upon admission, a physical examination was conducted, revealing grade III systolic murmurs over the left lower sternal border and a wide fixed splitting S2. A thoracic computed tomography scan showed a huge thrombus in the aneurysmal dilatation of the proximal pulmonary arteries. An electrocardiogram revealed a right axis deviation and bi-ventricular hypertrophy with a strain pattern. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed profound pulmonary hypertension with right ventricular hypertrophy and dysfunction. A right heart catheter was also done. Pulmonary thrombosis with an ASD and Eisenmenger syndrome was diagnosed. A heart-lung transplant was arranged for the patient. 

Laboratory Examinations: Normal blood cell counts, with a mildly elevated D-dimer level

Imaging Studies: Chest radiography revealed marked enlargement and a lobulated contour to the hilar shadows of bilateral lungs

Other Risk Assessment Studies: Surveyed possible causes of her pro-coagulant status, including hepatitis serum marker, anti-human immunodeficiency virus antibody, the Venereal Disease Research Laboratory test, anti-double stranded deoxyribonucleic acid antibodies, anti-phospholipid IgG/IgM, anti-beta 2 glycoprotein IgG/IgM, anti-nuclear antibody, lupus anticoagulant, protein C, protein S, anti-thrombin III, and homocysteine level without positive findings. 

Diagnosis: Pulmonary thrombosis with an ASD and Eisenmenger syndrome

Discussion and Follow-Up: Due to the high-risk nature of the recommended surgery (thrombectomy with aneurysm repair), a heart-lung transplant was determined to be the most beneficial course of action. The patient was referred for the transplant.

A heart electrical test showed the axis shifted to the right and both heart chambers were thickened with strain. Hospital Course:
The patient, a 36-year-old male with situs viscerum inversus and dextrocardia, presented to the hospital with endocarditis in May 2016. He had previously undergone permanent VVI pacemaker implantation in 1998 due to complete AV block, with battery replacement in 2006 and dual chamber pacemaker implantation in 2007. The patient had three surgical pocket revisions due to pocket decubitus. In May 2016, he underwent transvenous lead extraction (TLE) of the atrial lead and extraction of the can due to endocarditis. As the patient was pacemaker-dependent, a temporary pacemaker was placed via the left femoral vein before the Micra implantation. Electrical measurements were tested multiple times in different positions before the successful placement of the Micra via the right femoral vein. However, the Micra delivery system was almost completely obstructed by clots after seven attempts, requiring a replacement with a new system. 

Discharge Summary:
The patient with situs viscerum inversus and dextrocardia was admitted to the hospital for transvenous lead extraction and Micra implantation on May 2016. The procedure lasted 119 minutes with a fluoroscopic duration of 35 minutes. After the successful placement of the Micra in the anteroseptal region, the patient experienced no adverse events during a 12-month follow-up period. The electrical measurements were stable, confirmed by chest X-ray, and were within normal range.

The pleural effusion was classified as exudate based on the laboratory findings.

The patient was diagnosed with pleural effusion, chylous effusion and helminth larvae infection.

Not applicable

Patient Name: Not provided

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission: The patient presented with two weeks of flank pain and four days of cola-colored urine. On physical exam, he had a regular rate and rhythm with a crescendo-decrescendo murmur heard best over the left sternal border. He had severe, left CVA tenderness and bilateral, basilar crackles on auscultation. Initial laboratory data showed low white blood cell count, low hemoglobin, low platelet count, high creatinine levels, and abnormal urinalysis.

Diagnosis: The patient was diagnosed with splenic infarct, bicuspid aortic valve with vegetation, and negative culture endocarditis. A renal biopsy revealed immune complex GN.

Treatment: The patient received 6 weeks of antibiotic therapy with doxycycline and rifampin, and underwent a valve replacement surgery. During the course of treatment, the patient showed improvement in flank pain, decreased RBC count in urine, and a decrease in creatinine levels.

Prognosis: The patient's condition improved during the course of treatment. Repeat proteinase-3 antibodies remained elevated despite antibiotic therapy.

Follow-up: Follow-up with a primary care physician and additional testing as needed is recommended.

Discharge Summary:

This is a discharge summary for a 50-year-old female patient who presented to our department with an intraoral swelling at the left mandible for six months. The patient underwent surgical excision and reconstruction using a submental island flap, under general anesthesia.

History of Present Illness: The patient reported to our department with swelling and pain in the left mandible region for six months, which grew rapidly after the extraction of lower left back teeth. The patient had no history of fever or difficulty swallowing.

Physical Examination: On extraoral examination, facial asymmetry was noted in the lower left facial region, but there was no evidence of any regional lymphadenopathy. Intraoral clinical evaluation revealed the presence of an expansile mass with anteroposterior as well as buccolingual expansion, extending from the region of the first premolar up to retromolar area, measuring approximately 6x4 cm. The overlying mucosal colour and texture appeared normal.

Diagnostic Tests: A radiographic orthopantomogram revealed a well-defined radiolucent lesion extending from the lower left first premolar to retromolar area. Computed tomography (CT) scans confirmed the presence of aggressive bony resorption of the lower left jaw starting from the premolar region and extending well into the mandibular ramus. Histopathological analysis of a biopsy specimen confirmed an aggressive CGCG.

Hospital Course: The patient underwent surgical excision and reconstruction using a submental island flap, under general anesthesia. The surgical procedure involved extraoral and intraoral approach to excise the lesion completely and a submental island flap for reconstruction. The patient was discharged without any complications.

Follow-up: In subsequent follow-ups, until one year, no evidence of recurrence was observed clinically as well as radiographically. The donor site healed uneventfully with minimal scars, which was present away from aesthetically visible regions of the face.

Summary: A 50-year-old female patient presented with an intraoral swelling at the left mandible for six months and was diagnosed with an aggressive CGCG. The patient underwent surgical excision and reconstruction using a submental island flap, under general anesthesia. The patient was discharged without any complications, and subsequent follow-ups showed no evidence of recurrence.

Discharge Summary: This is a discharge summary for a 50-year-old female patient seen in our clinic today. She came to our department with a swelling inside the mouth on the left lower jaw that lasted six months. The patient had surgery to remove the swelling and rebuild the area with a chin tissue flap. The surgery was performed while the patient was asleep under general anesthesia in the operating room.
History of Present Illness: The patient reported swelling and pain in the left lower jaw for six months, which grew quickly after tooth extraction. The patient reported no fever, no trouble swallowing, and no other systemic symptoms during this period.
Physical Examination: On external exam, the face looked uneven on the left lower side, but no swollen lymph nodes were seen. Inside the mouth, a growing lump was found from the first premolar tooth area to the back of the mouth. The lump measured about 6 by 4 centimeters, and the overlying tissue looked normal in color and texture.
Diagnostic Tests: A panoramic X-ray showed a dark spot in the bone from the first premolar to the back of the mouth. A CT scan confirmed aggressive bone destruction in the left lower jaw, starting at the premolar. The destruction extended into the ramus of the jaw, as clearly seen on the scan. A biopsy examined under the microscope showed an aggressive central giant cell granuloma, confirming the diagnosis.
Hospital Course: The patient underwent surgery to remove the lump and rebuild the area with a chin tissue flap. The surgery was performed while the patient was asleep under general anesthesia in the operating room. The surgeons used both an outside and an inside approach to take out the lump completely. They used the chin tissue flap to repair the surgical site, and the wound healed well. The patient left the hospital with no complications and was discharged home to continue recovery.
Follow-up: At follow-up visits over the next year, no sign of the lump returning was seen by exam or X-ray. The donor site healed well with only a small scar that is not in a visible part of the face.
Summary: A 50-year-old female patient had a six-month swelling inside the left lower jaw that prompted medical evaluation. The swelling was diagnosed as an aggressive central giant cell granuloma after biopsy and imaging. She had surgery to remove it and rebuild the area with a chin tissue flap while asleep under general anesthesia. She left the hospital without problems and follow-up visits showed no return of the lump.

Discharge Summary:

Patient was admitted with complaints of high-grade fever and left-sided pleuritic chest pain of 3-week duration associated with anorexia and significant weight loss of 6 kg in the last 1 month. The patient's hemogram showed polymorphonuclear leukocytosis and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 70 mm/h. He had a fasting blood sugar value of 236 mg/dL and a postprandial value of 300 mg/dL with a urine sugar of 2%. A chest X-ray showed right upper zone fibrosis, and an ultrasound of the abdomen revealed a collection of heterogeneous echogenicity near the inferior pole of the spleen suggestive of a perisplenic abscess. 

After several diagnostic tests, the patient was diagnosed with melioidosis, a bacterial infection caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei. He was treated with 2 weeks of parenteral ceftazidime (2 g t.i.d.) followed by oral co-trimoxazole (160/800 mg t.i.d.) for 12 weeks. The patient's fever and arthritis subsided, and follow-up ultrasound showed resolution of the abscess. Chest X-ray showed improvement in the right upper lobe lesion. 

The patient's vital signs were stable upon discharge, and there were no further complaints at the time of discharge. His condition has significantly improved, and he was asked to attend regular follow-up appointments with his primary care physician. His medication list was reviewed, and the patient was advised to continue medication for his pre-existing conditions. The patient and family were instructed to monitor the patient's blood sugar level as appropriate diet and exercise guidelines were given. 

The patient was informed of the importance of following medication and lifestyle guidelines for successful management of the disease and advised to seek medical attention if the symptoms worsen. An additional patient education pamphlet was given upon discharge that outlines important lifestyle modifications and risk management practices for the disease.

Hospital Course Summary:

Subjective:

The patient is a 65-year-old female with relapsing oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma who presented to our facility after experiencing a left parapharyngeal relapse. The patient underwent cervical radiotherapy and chemotherapy and was subsequently referred to our Phase I unit for enrollment in an early-phase trial.

Objective:

During the screening procedure, chest CT scans showed GGOs, suggestive of COVID-19. IgG antibodies against SARS-CoV-2 were positive, indicating a prior exposure to the virus. The patient was asymptomatic, and two consecutive nasopharyngeal swabs resulted negative. The patient underwent experimental treatment with an anti-PD-L1 mAb administered intravenously every three weeks and a daily oral TKI. The initial tumor assessment showed overall stable disease with an enlargement of GGOs affecting bilateral lower lobes.

Assessment and Plan:

Further investigation revealed no evidence of malignancy, and the interstitial proliferation, CD8+ lymphocytic infiltration, and alveolar damage were consistent with immune-mediated pneumonitis. The immunotherapy with PD-L1 blockade likely led to worsening GGOs initially detected during the screening procedure, with the COVID-19 lung injury acting as an inflammatory primer for subsequent ICI-related pneumonia development. The TKI assumption was unlikely to have played a role in the development of lung damage as it was deemed safe and did not suggest any involvement in its mechanism.

The patient underwent a CT-guided lung biopsy, and the pathological examination supported the diagnosis of immune-mediated pneumonitis. The lung toxicity was classified as grade 1, but the patient experienced no symptoms. Since there was clinical and radiological benefit on the underlying tumor, the patient restarted experimental immunotherapy and was on-treatment at the time of discharge.

Plan:

The patient's discharge instructions include strict adherence to follow-up visits with the primary care physician and the oncologist regularly, especially as part of on-treatment follow-up. Further screening to monitor any progress of immune-mediated pneumonitis and continued radiological monitoring of lung changes. Measurements to monitor respiratory function and continued reporting of any respiratory symptoms are also critical.

Prognosis:

The patient's prognosis is good, and she is expected to continue receiving experimental immunotherapy for the relapsing oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma.

Hospital Course Summary:
We summarize the hospital stay for a 65-year-old woman with mouth cancer that returned during admission.
Subjective:
The patient is a 65-year-old woman whose mouth cancer came back in the left throat area.
She received neck radiation and chemotherapy, then was sent to an early-phase study unit for a new treatment.
Objective:
A chest CT during screening showed spots that looked like COVID-19 lung changes in her lungs.
Blood tests showed she had COVID-19 before, but two throat swabs were negative and she felt no symptoms.
She started immunotherapy given through a vein every three weeks and took a daily TKI pill.
The first cancer check showed disease stable, but the lung spots increased in both lower lungs.
Assessment and Plan:
Further tests found no cancer, and lung changes matched immune-mediated pneumonitis seen on biopsy in the lungs.
The immunotherapy likely made the lung spots worse, and the earlier COVID-19 lung injury may have helped trigger this inflammation.
The daily TKI pill was considered safe and probably did not cause the lung problem.
A CT-guided lung biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of immune-mediated pneumonitis shown by pathology in the lung tissue.
Lung toxicity was grade 1 (mild) and she had no symptoms at any point during her stay.
Because her cancer still responded, she restarted the immunotherapy and was receiving it when discharged.
Plan:
She must see her primary doctor and her cancer doctor often, especially while on the study treatment.
Regular tests will watch for any worsening of lung inflammation and repeat lung scans will be done.
Breathing tests will check lung function and she should report any new breathing symptoms right away.
Prognosis:
Her outlook is good and she is expected to keep getting the experimental immunotherapy for her mouth cancer.

History of Present Illness:
A 37-year-old male presented with an asymptomatic right renal mass detected by ultrasonography and CT. No apparent cutaneous lesions were found on the skin by careful inspection and palpation. No mutations were found in any other members of the patient’s family.

The patient had a history of spontaneous pneumothorax on both sides and underwent pulmonary bullectomy on the right side at the age of 30. There was no history of any other significant medical conditions.

Patient Name:
Gender: Male
Age: 38
Date of Admission: [Date of admission]
Date of Discharge: [Date of discharge]
Admitting Diagnosis: Painless scrotal mass

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to [Hospital Name] with a chief complaint of a painless left scrotal mass. The patient had no significant past medical history and reported discovering the mass one month prior to admission. Physical examination revealed a 2 cm well-defined mass in the upper pole of the left testis with a firm consistency. Palpation of the right testis and lower pole of the left testis were normal. Routine blood tests were unremarkable. A bioassay of testicular tumor markers was ordered which revealed normal levels of Alpha-fetoprotein, human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). An extratesticular mass was observed on scrotal ultrasound, attached to the upper pole of the patient's testis. The mass was isoechoic to the testis parenchyma and poorly vascularized on Doppler. The patient underwent a radical inguinal orchiectomy. Histological examination of the operative specimen confirmed the presence of regular splenic tissue in the suspect mass without any signs of malignancy. The splenic proliferation had a preserved capsule, demarcating from the testis. Testicular pulp, the albuginea, and the tunica vaginalis had a preserved microscopic architecture. The patient was discharged on the second postoperative day.

Discharge Diagnosis: Painless scrotal mass

Summary:
A 38-year-old North African man presented with a painless left scrotal mass. A scrotal ultrasound showed an extratesticular mass, attached to the upper pole of his testis. The patient underwent a radical inguinal orchiectomy which confirmed the presence of splenic tissue in the suspect mass without any signs of malignancy. The patient was discharged on the second postoperative day and was examined again after 3 weeks and 2 months in our out-patient unit, where his spleen was found to be of habitual location with standard measurements and a regular aspect.

Hospital Course:

The 70-year-old female patient was incidentally found to have left maxillary sinus mass on a computed tomography (CT) scan of the facial bones performed for trauma. The patient was referred to Otolaryngology for further workup. On physical examination, a palpable mass was noted below the left zygoma, and on endoscopy, the left ostiomeatal complex was compromised secondary to adjacent soft tissue fullness. Contrast enhanced CT of the paranasal sinuses demonstrated a large, soft tissue density mass without significant enhancement in the left maxillary sinus. Bony destruction was noted along the anterior, posterior and lateral walls of the left maxillary sinus, as well as the left orbital floor. A left maxillectomy was performed under general anesthesia. Repeat CT 1 month later showed no evidence of recurrence. 

Medical History:

The patient had a medical history notable for Human Immunodeficiency Virus, Diabetes Mellitus, Hypertension, and chronic sinusitis. There was no history of tobacco or alcohol use.

Presenting Symptoms:

The patient reported having intermittent blood-tinged mucus for over 2 years with episodes of epistaxis over the last month. They also reported 1 week of left facial numbness, and one day of drooling from their left oral commissure.

Diagnostic Findings:

Non-contrast magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the paranasal sinuses showed the soft tissue mass was isointense to muscle on T1 weighted images, extending anteriorly into the pre-maxillary soft tissue.

Pathology Results:

Fine needle aspiration of the mass revealed scant groups of cohesive cells with nuclear enlargement, hyperchromasia, and mild cellular crowding, without high-grade features. Special staining further revealed positivity for cytokeratin AE1/AE3, p63, and p40, but was negative for S100, diagnostic for ameloblastoma. 

Plan:

Resection of the lateral and most inferior aspects of the mass was performed with a Caldwell-Luc procedure, achieving near total resection.
nemotron_simplification: Hospital Course: The 70-year-old female patient had a growth in the left cheek sinus seen on a CT scan after an injury. The patient was sent to an ear, nose, and throat doctor for more checks and evaluation. On exam, a lump could be felt below the left cheekbone, and the patient reported tenderness. A scope showed the sinus opening was blocked by tissue, confirming the mass location and need for further imaging. A contrast CT showed a large soft tissue mass in the left maxillary sinus that did not light up much. The scan also showed bone damage in the sinus walls and the eye socket floor. A left maxillectomy was performed while the patient was asleep under general anesthesia to remove the mass. A repeat CT one month later showed no sign of the growth coming back, indicating successful treatment. Medical History: The patient’s past health includes HIV infection, diabetes, high blood pressure, and long-term sinus problems. The patient has never smoked or used alcohol, which helps reduce risk for other diseases. Presenting Symptoms: The patient said they had occasional blood-streaked mucus for more than two years, with nosebleeds in the last month. They also had one week of numbness on the left side of the face, which prompted concern. They also had one day of drooling from the left corner of the mouth, which was new and worrying. Diagnostic Findings: An MRI without contrast of the sinuses showed the tissue mass had the same color as muscle on certain images. The mass reached forward into the area in front of the upper teeth, suggesting it was growing toward the mouth. Pathology Results: A thin needle biopsy of the mass showed small groups of cells with larger, dark nuclei and slight crowding. The biopsy showed no high-grade signs, indicating the cells were not aggressively abnormal and were likely benign. Special stains were positive for cytokeratin AE1/AE3, p63, and p40, but negative for S100, which helped identify the tumor type. These results led to a diagnosis of ameloblastoma, a rare benign tumor of the sinus. Plan: The surgery removed the side and lowest parts of the mass using a Caldwell-Luc method, achieving almost complete removal. The patient will need regular follow-up visits to check for any return of the growth. Imaging studies will be done periodically as directed by the doctor to ensure the mass does not come back.

Hospital Course:

47-year-old male was admitted following a car accident. The patient presented with forehead abrasion and confusion. A brain CT scan and cervical X-rays showed no hematoma or cerebral edema, but cervical instability at C6-7. The patient was immobilized with a neck collar and closely monitored. Two weeks after admission, the patient complained of severe posterior neck pain (VAS > 9) and bilateral upper extremity numbness. Subsequent surgical stabilization was performed. An anterior cervical plate was positioned, and pilot holes were tapped. The upper left pilot hole was stripped due to repeated drilling, and PMMA augmentation was performed, which resulted in a mass lesion at the spinal canal. C6 corpectomy was promptly performed to remove the mass. Anterior reconstruction with an anterior cervical plate and mesh cage from C5 through C7 was done. Postoperatively, the patient had left side weakness and impairment of the left 4th and 5th digit extension, but he improved without intervention.

Discharge Diagnosis:

Cervical injury with spinal cord compression leading to cervical corpectomy.

Hospital course:

The patient was admitted to the hospital following a car accident. During his hospital stay, he underwent surgical stabilization for cervical instability at C6-7. There were some complications during the procedure, which led to a mass lesion at the spinal canal and cervical corpectomy. The patient had some postoperative weakness and impairment of the left hand digits, but he improved without intervention. The patient was discharged in good condition with a follow-up appointment with a spinal specialist.

A CT scan and neck X-rays showed no blood clot or swelling, but the neck bones were unstable at C6-7.
He wore a neck brace and was watched closely by the medical team during his stay.
Two weeks later, he reported very bad neck pain over nine out of ten and numbness in both arms.
Doctors did surgery to steady his neck by placing a plate in the front and drilling small guide holes.
The left guide hole was damaged from drilling, and bone cement was added, creating a lump in the spinal canal.
Doctors quickly removed the C6 bone to take out the lump and relieve pressure on the spinal cord.
They rebuilt the front of the neck using a plate and a spacer from C5 to C7.
After surgery, he had weakness on his left side and trouble straightening his left ring and little fingers.
But he got better without any extra treatment and his symptoms improved on their own.
Discharge Diagnosis:
He had a neck injury that squeezed his spinal cord, which led to removal of the C6 bone.
Hospital course:
He was admitted to the hospital after a car accident and stayed for treatment and observation.
During his stay, doctors did surgery to steady his neck because the neck bones were unstable at C6-7.
Some problems during the surgery caused a lump in the spinal canal and led to removal of the C6 bone.
After surgery, he had weakness and trouble moving his left hand fingers, but he got better without extra treatment.
He left the hospital feeling well and has a follow-up visit scheduled with a spine specialist.

Hospitalized for: Stenosis of Left Subclavian Artery

Brief Hospital Course: 

The patient, a 4-year-old boy, was admitted with an incidental detection of murmur. Clinical examination revealed low volume radial pulse in the left upper limb and lower BP in the same limb. The right radial pulse was normal. Anthropometrically, his height was 100 cm, and the left upper limb was 10 mm shorter than the right upper limb.  

Echocardiography showed structurally normal heart with RAA and aberrant LSA with flow turbulence. CT angiogram was done, which confirmed the diagnosis. A stenosis of 70-80% just beyond the origin of LSA was detected. The presence of limb length discrepancy justified treatment, and the patient was scheduled for transcatheter placement of stent. 

The procedure was performed successfully, and the patient tolerated it very well. Racer 5 mm × 18 mm stent was positioned across the stenosed segment. Post-procedure angiogram confirmed the stent's correct placement, and good flow was observed in LSA and left axillary artery. The patient was kept on overnight heparin infusion and discharged with oral aspirin.

Follow-up visits on 3 and 6 months showed near-normalization of radial pulse and blood pressure in the left upper limb, and significant improvement of limb length. USG of the left upper limb confirmed a laminar flow pattern in the LSA. The boy has been followed up for the last 4 years, with no remaining limb length discrepancy detected.

Discharge Diagnosis: Stenosis of Left Subclavian Artery.

Discharge Instructions: 

The patient will continue aspirin therapy (as directed by the physician). Follow-up visits should be scheduled as per the physician's instructions. Parents are advised to keep the patient's medical records updated and bring them to each visit.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

Patient Information:
Name: Not provided
Age: 57
Sex: Male

Admission Date: Not provided
Discharge Date: Not provided

Reason for Admission:
Decreased vision in the left eye of 1-month duration

Hospital Course:
The patient was diagnosed with primary intraocular lymphoma (PIOL) based on the results of his diagnostic vitrectomy. As a PCNSL was not detected by magnetic resonance imaging, the patient was treated with weekly intravitreal injections of methotrexate (MTX) for 1 month, followed by monthly maintenance injections for seven more months.

Assessment:
The patient showed significant improvement in his best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA), from 20/25 to 20/16 after 9 months. Fundus examination showed regression of the yellowish lesions in the posterior fundus, changing gradually to atrophy of the RPE. Fundus autofluorescence (FAF) and spectral domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) showed significant improvement in the degree of hyperreflective infiltration in the inner retina, restoration of the RPE and IS/OS junction, and recovery of foveal thickness. Enhanced depth imaging OCT (EDI-OCT) showed a gradual decrease in the subfoveal choroidal thickness during the treatment. The total macular volume reduced significantly after the treatment.

The mean deviation (MD) on standard automated perimetry increased from -13.95 dB before treatment to -7.23 dB after treatment. The mean retinal sensitivity within the central 10° measured with a fundus-related microperimeter increased from 0.3 dB before treatment to 4.1 dB after treatment. Full-field electroretinograms (ERGs) and multifocal ERGs (mfERGs) showed decreased amplitudes.

Final Diagnosis:
Primary intraocular lymphoma (PIOL)

Discharge Instructions:
The patient is advised to follow up with his ophthalmologist regularly for monitoring of his visual acuity and ocular health. Any new or worsening symptoms should be reported to his healthcare provider immediately.
