Admission Diagnosis: Stage I moderately differentiated invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast (ER-/PR+, Her2+), BRCA2 mutation

Hospital Course: 

The patient was diagnosed with stage I moderately differentiated invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast, which was ER-/PR+, Her2+, and also had a BRCA2 mutation. She received neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by a bilateral mastectomy and underwent adjuvant chemotherapy with trastuzumab and pertuzumab. The patient was then started on adjuvant endocrine therapy with toremifene.

Two years after her last treatment, the patient presented with an enlarged left axillary lymph node. Biopsy results showed a recurrence of her breast cancer. Three weeks later, the patient presented to the emergency department with diplopia, weight loss, and frequent urination. Imaging revealed multiple metastases to the brain, liver, and cervical spine.

The patient was started on radiation therapy to the orbits with possible radiation therapy to the pituitary. She was also restarted on trastuzumab and pertuzumab, and began treatment with fulvestrant, goserelin, and zolendronic acid. The patient showed good treatment response with significant improvement in her diplopia.

Discharge Diagnosis: Recurrent metastatic carcinoma of ER/PR-positive breast cancer

Discharge Plan:

The patient remains under close observation and ongoing care for her recurrent metastatic breast cancer. Further diagnostic tests and imaging will be conducted as needed, and additional treatment will be administered as recommended by her oncologist. The patient will be scheduled for regular follow-up appointments to monitor her condition and adjust her treatment plan as necessary.

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 74-year-old
Sex: Female
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Chief complaint:
The patient complained of exacerbation of mild dysphagia and an awareness of a tumor in the left side of her neck.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to our hospital on [REDACTED] with a complaint of mild dysphagia for the past two months, which had recently worsened. Laboratory tests showed normal thyroid function levels. Pharyngoesophagography showed a large diverticulum at the pharyngoesophageal junction. Ultrasonography revealed a hypoechoic lesion present in the posterior bilateral lobe of the thyroid and an isoechoic mass on the left lobe of the thyroid. Cervical CT scan showed a thyroid nodule, bilateral hypopharyngeal diverticula, and an isodensity area with a hyperdensity area, suggesting calcium deposition. A barium swallow pharyngoesophagogram showed a large left-sided diverticulum and a small right-sided diverticulum.

The patient underwent resection of the diverticula and thyroid tumor surgery for improvement of dysphagia. The surgical procedure was approached through a collar incision in the left anterior neck, and the diverticula were visualized under the cricopharyngeus muscle. The left-sided diverticulum was mobilized from the left lobe of the thyroid and the thyroid tumor. The diverticulotomy was performed. The wound was closed in layers with placement of a closed suction drain.

Histopathological examination showed that the diverticula were false diverticula without a muscular layer, and the thyroid tumor was diagnosed as a thyroid adenoma. The patient was started on a clear liquid diet on postoperative day 4. Two years after surgery, the patient remains free of dysphagia.

Diagnosis:
- Mild dysphagia
- Hypopharyngeal diverticula
- Thyroid adenoma

Treatment:
- Surgery for resection of hypopharyngeal diverticula and thyroid tumor

Follow-up:
The patient is advised to continue follow-up care with her primary care physician. No further appointments with our hospital are required.

Patient Name: N/A

Hospital Course:

The patient was referred to our pain clinic due to an 8-day history of postural headache, which occurred following acupuncture treatment to manage chronic lower back pain caused by postlaminectomy syndrome. The patient had undergone L4-5 laminectomy 7 years prior. The physical and neurological examinations were normal. The patient was diagnosed with a postdural puncture headache (PDPH) and was placed on bed rest. An epidural blood patch (EBP) was performed, which failed to relieve the symptoms. A brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was unremarkable, while an MRI myelogram showed an abnormal fluid signal intensity in the left lumbar area, along with the left paraspinal muscle, and soft tissues at the L3-4-5 level, probably due to CSF leakage.

After conservative care, which included bed rest, hydration, and taking acetaminophen, the patient's postural headaches persisted. A repeat fluoroscopically guided interlaminar EBP was performed with minor relief. A transforaminal EBP at the L3-4 and L4-5 levels on the left side was performed. After the transforaminal EBP, the patient's headache and other symptoms subsided without complications.

At the 2-week follow-up, the patient reported being headache-free, and the activities had returned to normal.

Diagnosis:

Postdural puncture headache (PDPH)

Treatment:

Conservative care, including bed rest, hydration, and acetaminophen, was recommended. Epidural blood patches were performed, including an interlaminar approach using autologous blood at the L2-3 level with 15ml, and a repeat of this procedure using the same volume of blood at the L4-5 level. Finally, a transforaminal EBP with 3ml autologous blood was given at each level at L3-4 and L4-5 on the left side.

Follow-up Care:

The patient was discharged after 4 days. At the 2-week follow-up, the patient reported being headache-free, and the activities had returned to normal. The patient was advised to follow-up with their primary care physician if there were any changes in the symptoms.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
- Age: 74
- Gender: Male
- Medical History: Hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, and end-stage renal disease

Hospital Course:
- The patient was transferred to our hospital due to bilateral intermittent claudication that had been ongoing for 6 months before admission.
- The patient had received clopidogrel and cilostazol as medication but refused surgical revascularization.
- Endovascular therapy (EVT) was chosen as the treatment option, and the patient gave written consent.
- EVT was initiated in the right superficial femoral artery chronic total occlusion (SFA-CTO) using the contralateral approach.
- The antegrade approach with the stiff CTO wire resulted in subintimal wiring. Therefore, bidirectional approach with direct distal-SFA puncture was used.
- Retrograde-antegrade rendezvous technique led to wire externalization, but no devices were able to pass the lesion by the antegrade and retrograde approaches.
- Minimal balloon could not pass the lesion, and the needle cracking technique from outside and inside of the vessel could not modify the lesion fully.
- ELA using the Turbo Elite 0.9 mm (Spectranetics, Co., USA) was applied, and it modified the CTO entry-morphology.
- After ELA ablation, the Caravel microcatheter (ASAHI Intecc) finally crossed the lesion using an antegrade approach with the BAlloon Deployment using FORcible Manner (BADFORM) technique, which enabled change of the wire from conventional the 0.014-inch wire to 0.009-inch RotaWire floppy (Boston Scientific) and RotaLink Plus 1.5mm burr ablation.
- Thereafter, we dilated the entire SFA lesion with conventional balloons and simultaneously achieved hemostasis of the distal-SFA puncture point.
- A bare nitinol stent was deployed due to severe dissection of the partial SFA.
- Treating the bilateral iliac arteries with bare nitinol stents followed, resulting in improvement of the right ABI of the patient from being unmeasurable to 0.79, and his intermittent claudication disappeared.
- The ABI and symptoms have remained satisfactory eight months after the current EVT.

Impression and Plan:
- This patient presented with bilateral intermittent claudication that improved after EVT treatment, including ELA and stent deployment.
- The patient's symptoms and ABI remained satisfactory at the eight-month follow-up.

Patient Information: The patient is a 74-year-old man with a history of several chronic conditions.
His medical history includes high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, heart artery disease, and kidney failure requiring dialysis.
Hospital Course: The patient was transferred to our hospital for further evaluation and treatment of his leg condition.
He had leg pain when walking that had been present for six months before admission.
He had been taking clopidogrel and cilostazol but refused surgical revascularization to open the blocked arteries.
He agreed to a minimally invasive procedure called endovascular therapy and gave written consent for his leg condition.
The procedure started in the right thigh artery using a wire from the opposite leg.
The initial attempt with a stiff wire went into the artery wall so we changed our plan.
We then used a two-side approach with a direct puncture lower in the artery to improve access.
We tried to meet the wires from both sides but could not get any device through the blockage.
Even a small balloon and a needle-cracking technique could not open the blockage fully at this stage.
We then used a laser catheter called Turbo Elite to modify the blockage’s entrance to improve flow.
After the laser treatment, a small catheter called Caravel finally crossed the blockage going forward.
This allowed us to switch to a thinner, more flexible wire and a tiny drilling device.
We then opened the whole blocked segment with regular balloons and stopped the bleeding from the puncture site.
A metal stent was placed in the artery because part of it tore to keep the artery open.
We also placed stents in both iliac arteries to improve blood flow to the legs.
After the procedure, the measurement of blood flow in the right leg improved from unable to measure to 0.79.
His leg pain when walking went away and he reported feeling better during daily activities.
Eight months later, the blood flow measurement and symptoms remained good at the follow-up visit.

The procedure included laser treatment and stent placement to keep the arteries open and improve blood flow.
His symptoms and blood flow measurement stayed satisfactory at the eight-month check-up during routine follow-up.

Discharge Summary

Admitted for: Humeral shaft fracture

Hospital course:

The patient was referred to our institution after falling on his right arm resulting in a transverse-oblique humeral shaft fracture. Upon admission, the arm was deformed but there was no neurovascular deficit. Closed reduction was performed and checked by imaging, followed by surgical treatment via anterolateral approach with an antegrade locked IMN using a reamed, unlocked technique. The patient was discharged with a Velpeau bandage after being in beach-chair position on the table.

Rehabilitation and Follow-up:

A rehabilitation program with Want exercises, isometric exercises, and strength training was initiated at 3 weeks after the surgery. The patient reported mild pain at the entry point of the nail during the whole 22-month follow-up period, which remained stable in severity. At the end of the 22 months post-injury, the patient performed daily living activities and demonstrated minimal impairment. The patient was evaluated using the disability of the arm, shoulder, and hand turkey (DASH-T), upper extremity functional index (UEFI), and short-form 36-questionnaire (SF-36) at the 2, 4, 6, 9, 16, and 22 month marks with an overall DASH-T score of 5.83%, UEFI score of 96%, and SF-36 score of 87.7%.

Overall, the patient was discharged with minimal impairment and would benefit from continued rehabilitation.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: ______________

Admission Date: ____________

Discharge Date: ____________

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to our institution with progressive neurological symptoms. He had a history of seropositive Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) that was managed with maintenance methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine and low-dose prednisone. The patient developed fluctuating confusion, word-finding difficulty, right-sided weakness and gait imbalance. An evaluation was done by the neurologist which confirmed the presence of neurological deficits. An MRI scan showed areas of scattered restricted diffusion and enhancement within the cortex and leptomeninges of the left hemisphere near the vertex, suspicious for meningoencephalitis. CSF analysis also demonstrated lymphocytic meningitis with negative, bacterial and fungal cultures. 

The patient was started on antiepileptic medication and a whole-body PET scan was done to rule out underlying malignancy. A bone marrow biopsy was also done to rule out lymphoid neoplasm. An open meningeal biopsy was performed and gross examination revealed thickening and opacification of the meninges. The histopathological findings were consistent with leptomeningeal involvement by nodular rheumatoid meningitis.

Immunosuppressive therapy with monthly cyclophosphamide and high-dose corticosteroids was initiated for 6 months and then the corticosteroids were tapered. The patient's neurological examination improved one month post treatment initiation, although confusion and bilateral postural tremor persisted. Most parkinsonian features also largely resolved following immunosuppressive therapy. 

Repeat MRI 3 months after treatment initiation showed complete resolution of previous findings, and CRP levels also normalized. The patient was eventually transitioned to a long-term care facility due to the persistent behavioral and cognitive deficits with intermittent periods of agitation.

Diagnosis:
Leptomeningeal involvement by nodular rheumatoid meningitis

Course:
The patient was admitted for investigation of progressive neurological symptoms and was treated with immunosuppressive therapy. The patient's neurological examination improved one month post treatment initiation, although confusion and bilateral postural tremor persisted, and most parkinsonian features largely resolved following immunosuppressive therapy. Repeat MRI 3 months after treatment initiation showed complete resolution of previous findings.

Discharge Condition:
The patient has been transitioned to a long-term care facility due to persistent behavioral and cognitive deficits with intermittent periods of agitation.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital for the management of a giant hepatic tumor. She underwent a right hepatectomy during which two well-differentiated hepatocellular carcinomas (HCCs) were removed. The patient recovered well after the surgery and was discharged on postoperative day 17.

Past Medical History:
The patient had no significant past medical history.

Hospital Course:
The patient's hospital course was significant for a sensation of abdominal distension and loss of appetite, at which point she underwent abdominal ultrasonography that discovered a giant hepatic mass in the right lobe. Physical examination was significant for hepatomegaly. Liver function tests showed evidence of nonicteric cholestasis with mild transaminase enzyme level elevation. Screening for viral hepatitis yielded negative results. Levels of the liver-specific tumor marker "protein induced by vitamin K absence-II" were highly elevated. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a giant hypoechoic mass measuring 139 × 120 mm in the right lobe of the liver. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) demonstrated a huge mass that occupied the right lobe of the liver and showed inhomogeneous hyperenhancement in the arterial phase, as well as uniform isoenhancement in the portal venous phase. A low-concentration area indicated the presence of necrosis in the tumor center, and a radiological diagnosis of HCC was therefore posited. The surgical team also discovered a congenital absence of the portal vein that indicated the presence of congenital absence of the portal vein type II. 

Disposition and Follow-up:
The patient was discharged on postoperative day 17 and successfully treated for a small recurrent HCC nodule detected 7 months after the operation with radiofrequency ablation. The patient has been on close follow-up for 6 months without any evidence of further recurrences.

Past Medical History:
The patient had no significant past medical history, meaning she had no serious health issues before this admission.
Hospital Course:
She felt a bloated belly and had no appetite, so doctors did an ultrasound of her abdomen. The ultrasound found a large dark mass in the right part of her liver, measuring about 140 by 120 millimeters. Her physical exam showed that her liver was larger than normal and felt firm upon palpation. Liver tests showed a bile flow problem without yellow skin and a slight rise in liver enzymes. Blood tests for hepatitis A, B, and C viruses came back negative, showing no infection. A liver cancer marker known as PIVKA-II was found to be very high in her blood. The ultrasound measured the mass at about 140 by 120 millimeters in the right liver lobe. A CT scan with contrast showed a huge mass filling the right liver lobe of the liver. The scan showed uneven brightening in the arterial phase and even brightness in the portal venous phase. A dark area in the center of the mass indicated dead tissue, which is called necrosis. Based on these imaging results, doctors believed the mass was liver cancer, also called hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). The surgical team also found that she was born without the main liver vein, known as portal vein type II.
Disposition and Follow-up:
She was discharged from the hospital on day 17 after her surgery for the liver tumor. Seven months later, a small liver cancer nodule was found and treated with radiofrequency ablation. She has had regular follow-up visits for six months with no sign of new cancer returning.

Hospital Course:

The patient was a 43-year-old male with a 17-year history of paraplegia who presented with dark purple discoloration of the left second and third toes. He had been experiencing a cold sensation in both feet for the past year. The patient had a history of hypertension and was taking hydrochlorothiazide-valsartan, kallidinogenase, ranitidine, levosulpiride, phloroglucinol, and loxoprofen. Physical examination showed both feet were cold, although the pulse was palpable on ankles and heels bilaterally. A portable Doppler device showed a decrease in pulse signal intensity on the left side and prolonged capillary refilling time on both toes. Despite a vascular function test showing normal leg circulation levels, the skin over the left toes showed dark discoloration with skin necrosis. The patient's antihypertensive medication was switched to a calcium channel blocker, amlodipine besylate, to address suspicion of Raynaud's phenomenon. Within 3 days, the patient saw a decrease in cold sensation and normalization of capillary refilling time. A medium split-thickness skin graft was performed on the wound, which healed without complications.

Consultations:

A consultation was requested with vascular and plastic surgery, who recommended wound monitoring and a skin graft to address the skin necrosis.

Discharge Condition:

The patient was discharged improved after treatment of his toe discoloration and skin necrosis.

Discharge Medications:

The patient was prescribed amlodipine besylate.

Follow-up:

The patient was advised to follow-up with his primary care physician for further management of his hypertension and any changes to his medication.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Age: 71
Sex: Male
Date of Admission: December 2009
Date of Discharge: March 2012
Reason for Admission: Dyspnea, right-sided chest wall and upper quadrant abdominal pain, pulmonary embolus, multiple coalesced masses in the liver, and AFP significantly elevated.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the Emergency Department in December 2009 with dyspnea, right-sided chest wall, and upper quadrant abdominal pain. He was diagnosed with pulmonary embolus and multiple coalesced masses in the liver with the largest measuring 6 cm x 9 cm x 9 cm in the right lobe of the liver. The pathology from the biopsy was diagnostic of primary HCC, and he was diagnosed with Stage IV T3N0M1 disease. He underwent 70 Gy treatment in 15 fractions to the liver, which was completed in April 2010. Subsequent follow-up imaging showed that the patient's largest liver lesion had decreased in size from over 14 cm to 3 cm, and his pulmonary metastases had completely resolved. From August 2010 till March 2012, the man enjoyed stable disease with normal liver laboratory results and no imaging evidence of disease recurrence. In March of 2012, a small recurrent nodule was found in the right liver, and he underwent hepatic artery embolization with doxorubicin and cisplatin in May of 2012, which resulted in a complete response at that location.

Medical Care:
The patient received radiotherapy alone for the liver lesions, and hepatic artery embolization with doxorubicin and cisplatin for the small recurrent nodule on the right liver.

Diagnostic Evaluation:
The patient underwent diagnostic evaluation in the form of imaging, such as computed tomography and biopsy, which aided in the diagnosis and monitoring of his liver lesions and pulmonary metastases.

Condition on Discharge:
The patient was stable, asymptomatic with a decrease in AFP from 11 460 µg/L to 3.1 µg/L, and no imaging evidence of disease recurrence at the time of his discharge in March 2012.

Follow-Up:
The patient was advised to follow-up with his physician regularly for clinical evaluations and imaging studies for monitoring purposes.

Discharge Medications:
Not applicable.

Disposition:
The patient was discharged with improvement in his condition, normal liver laboratory results, and no imaging evidence of disease recurrence.

Discharge Summary for Patient with Achalasia Cardia

Demographics:
- Patient is a 43-year-old Indian man

Reason for Admission:
- Patient was referred to the gastroenterology department because of dysphagia for both solids and liquids, recurrent vomiting, regurgitating undigested food, and considerable weight loss.

Medical History:
- No significant medical history was reported.

Hospital Course:
- Ultrasound scan of the abdomen showed normal findings.
- Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed a dilated esophageal body and no peristalsis was seen, while the lower esophageal sphincter was tightly closed.
- Retroflexion of the endoscope revealed no mass lesion in the esophagogastric junction or in the cardia.
- Chest X-ray showed an air bubble below the left hemi-diaphragm in the gastric region.
- Barium swallow showed dilated esophagus, "bird beak" appearance of the distal esophagus, and an esophageal air fluid level.
- Diagnosis of primary achalasia cardia was made based on clinical history, examination, upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, and barium swallow X-ray.
- Pneumatic balloon dilatation of the lower esophageal sphincter was performed successfully under sedation with no complications.
- Chest X-ray after the procedure showed two air bubbles under the left hemi-diaphragm in the gastric region, the first of which was confirmed as a colonic air bubble and the second as a gastric air bubble.

Discharge Status:
- Patient was discharged after a successful pneumatic balloon dilatation of the lower esophageal sphincter with no complications.

Instructions:
- Follow up with the primary care physician for further management of achalasia cardia.
- Provide a detailed report of this hospital course to the primary care physician.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 44-year-old Hispanic male who was admitted for the evaluation of bilateral ocular inflammation in the setting of treatment with ipilimumab for metastatic cutaneous melanoma. He had received his third infusion two months prior to presentation, which led to systemic inflammatory side effects from therapy including rash, diarrhea, fever, and persistent rectal abscesses.

Physical Exam:
Upon presentation, the patient had central scotoma in the left eye, and both eyes showed pigment on the endothelium without keratic precipitates. Bilateral optic nerve edema with Paton’s lines and macular edema were noted on fundus examination. Cystic intraretinal and subfoveal fluid was also identified during Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT).

Treatment:
The patient was initially treated with topical therapy with prednisolone acetate and was referred to the uveitis service for further evaluation. Bilateral prednisolone acetate 1% was started four times a day with 0.2% brimonidine tartrate-0.5% timolol maleate ophthalmic solution twice a day and increased to 80 mg of oral prednisone daily. The patient was continually monitored and had his medication doses adjusted to promote healing.

Improvement and Discharge:
Over the course of following three weeks, his vision steadily improved with resolution of the optic nerve and retinal edema and subsequent development of a macular star. At the 2-month follow-up, his vision in both eyes improved to 20/25 and his anterior chamber reaction stabilized at 1+ flare and rare cell while taking prednisolone acetate four times a day. The patient was then lost to follow-up.

Admission Diagnosis: Solitary fibrous tumor of the pleura (SFTP)

Hospital Course: The patient was admitted with biopsy-proven right-sided SFTP and worsening dyspnea on exertion and hypoglycemia. Imaging studies revealed a large heterogeneous mass in the right pleural space, causing collapse of the pulmonary vasculature, cardiac shift and compression of the superior and inferior vena cava. Surgical resection via clamshell sternotomy was planned. A balanced anesthetic was maintained throughout the case and planned exposure of the right femoral artery and vein was performed prior to clamshell incision should cannulation for extracorporeal support be required. Clamshell exposure revealed focal, dense adhesions between the mass and the right upper lobe. Wedge resections of these adhesions resulted in hemorrhage requiring massive transfusion. The following shock states required active management during the case: Obstructive, hypovolemic, and distributive. After control of bleeding and appropriate volume resuscitation, the patient remained hypotensive and required vasoactive infusions. In addition, the patient's intraoperative management was complicated by profound hypoglycemia which required ongoing dextrose therapy until mass resection. The case proceeded with successful surgical resection, and the patient was transported under sedation to the intensive care unit.

Discharge Diagnosis: SFTP

Course in Hospital: The patient's course in the hospital was complicated by massive transfusion requiring management of hypotensive states, distributive shock and hypoglycemia. However, with adequate resuscitation and successful surgical resection, the patient's condition improved. The patient was extubated on day 1 and discharged on day 13 without any complications.

Follow-up: The patient was discharged with follow-up CT imaging scheduled to monitor for residual disease. The patient should also schedule follow-up appointments with her primary care physician and oncologist for further management and surveillance of her condition.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

Patient Information:
Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 67 years
Sex: Female

Chief Complaint:
Moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon. Right hemicolectomy was performed, and the pathology confirmed stage III (pT3N1) adenocarcinoma. Adjuvant chemotherapy was initiated but was discontinued after four of eight cycles due to severe neuropathy. After completion of adjuvant treatment, the patient underwent active surveillance. In November 2012, a recurrence near the right psoas muscle was identified and excised in December. Immunohistochemical workup showed an abnormal mismatch repair profile with loss of MLH1 protein. The patient underwent radiotherapy concurrent with capecitabine, but again, significant neutropenia necessitated a capecitabine dose reduction. In October 2013, the patient relapsed with disease in the L3 spinous process and received 42 Gy of stereotactic radiotherapy in 10 fractions. In June 2014, the tumor recurred at the same site, and the patient underwent palliative resection of the mass.

Enter Personalized OncoGenomics (POG) initiative:
The patient consented to genomic analysis of the tumor resected from the L3 spinous process by the POG initiative at the BC Cancer Agency. The genomic analysis revealed overexpression of FOS and JUN genes that encode the AP-1 transcriptional complex. Immunohistochemical workup confirmed robust expression of c-JUN protein. It was suggested that irbesartan could be a potential option due to the blockade of the renin–angiotensin pathway.

Treatment:
The patient had a pretreatment baseline PET/CT scan and started irbesartan at a dose of 150 mg daily in December 2014. After 5 weeks of therapy, a follow-up PET/CT was performed, and there was virtually a complete functional radiological resolution of her disease. CEA levels decreased from 18 to 3.1.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon.

Discharge Condition:
The patient has been discharged, and her condition is stable. Follow-up visits have been scheduled, and medication and dietary instructions have been provided.

Medications:
Irbesartan 150 mg daily.

Follow-up:
Follow-up appointments have been scheduled. The patient has been advised to adhere to a healthy diet and lifestyle and continue medication as prescribed.

Progressive neuropathy with associated mutation in GSN

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: Confidential
Medical Record Number: Confidential
Date of Admission: Confidential

Hospital Course:
The patient is an 82-year-old female who was admitted to the hospital as an emergency with gross abdominal distension and lower abdominal pain. She had a six-week history of nonspecific malaise, loss of appetite, and dizziness, along with a longstanding history of constipation. Her past medical history included hypertension and impaired glucose tolerance, while her past surgical history included a previous caesarean section.

On examination, the patient had a nontender, grossly distended abdomen with an indentable mass in the lower left quadrant. Blood tests revealed acute renal failure and microcytic anaemia. A CT scan revealed massive dilatation of the sigmoid colon with faecal material within, resulting in bilateral renal tract obstruction. Following a clinical decision, she underwent a laparotomy, during which she was found to have massive colonic dilatation of the sigmoid and descending colon, with dense perirectal fibrosis throughout the length of the rectum. The rectum was resected at the mid rectum, and a Hartman's procedure was performed. Her renal function normalised, and she made an uneventful recovery. 

On histology from the resected specimen, it was observed that the longitudinal muscle layer was degenerate and absent in many areas of the specimen. The myenteric and submucosal plexuses were degenerate where longitudinal muscle was absent, while polyglucosan inclusion bodies were present throughout the longitudinal and circular layers of the muscularis propria, with almost total degeneration of the longitudinal layer, suggesting a myopathic process. The occurrence of longitudinal loss was in areas where the overlying muscle and mucosa were intact indicating that this was likely to be a primary myopathy. There was also a replacement of myocytes in both muscularis layers with elastosis and fibrosis, along with additional areas of elastosis in the submucosa and widespread smooth muscle metaplasia.

Discharge Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with acute renal failure and massive colonic dilatation of the sigmoid and descending colon, with dense perirectal fibrosis throughout the length of the rectum. Histology from the resected specimen revealed a primary myopathy with elastosis and fibrosis.

Follow-Up Care:
The patient is advised to follow a healthy diet and exercise regimen and to attend regular follow-up appointments with the healthcare provider. She is also advised to take appropriate measures to prevent constipation, such as increasing fibre intake and staying hydrated.

Discharge Medications:
None.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient is advised to avoid strenuous physical activity and to take adequate rest for at least two weeks following the surgery. She is also advised to attend regular follow-up appointments with the healthcare provider to monitor her renal and colonic function and to ensure that her postoperative recovery is proceeding smoothly. In case of any unwanted side effects or complications, the patient is advised to immediately contact the healthcare provider.

He is now relatively stable with tracheostomy and GI tube for feeding and restarted very recently treatment with miglustat 200 mg every 8 hours. However, he shows a higher disability score of 21.

The patient's medical condition at the time of discharge was stable.

The patient will be followed up by the neurology department for treatment and management of his condition.

The discharge diagnosis for the patient is a squamous cell carcinoma that invaded the calvarium and surrounding tissues.

The patient’s condition is currently stable and the surgical procedure was successful.

The patient should return to the hospital for follow-up appointments as scheduled by the attending veterinarian. Any changes in appetite, demeanor, or activity level should be reported immediately. A check-up with post-operative imaging should be performed as recommended.

Hospital Course: 
The 64-year-old female patient with a history of Parkinson's disease and anxiety presented with erythema and minimal serous drainage from her left scalp staging incision, three months post bilateral subthalamic nucleus (STN) deep brain stimulation (DBS) surgery. The incision was locally cleansed, and she was prescribed a two-week course of Augmentin. However, a month later, she presented with erythema and a fluctuant mass over the DBS generator in the right subclavicular region. The patient admitted to swimming in a “homemade hot tub” in the woods, which she sterilized using bleach. After the surgical site appearance and interval history were reviewed, the patient was taken to the operating room for explantation. The left connecting lead was severed distal to the connector at the staging incision, and the right subclavicular incision was opened and exposed, resulting in the egress of non-purulent serous fluid. The left lead connector was removed, and the wound site and serous fluid were cultured for aerobic and anaerobic organisms. The wound cultures revealed a light-growth polymicrobial infection, including the species methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA), Enterobacter amnigenus, and Cupriavidus pauculus. The patient was treated with a six-week course of intravenous ceftazidime and discharged. She returned two months later with wound dehiscence and purulence over her right-sided generator. The generator and the connecting lead were explanted. The operative wound cultures remained negative. She was placed empirically on cefepime for two weeks and declined the reconnection of the intracranial leads to a generator.

The patient was admitted to our hospital due to cervical bleeding caused by a giant ulcerous goiter. She had a long-standing history of neglected thyroid carcinoma, which had undergone excisional biopsy 7 years prior, revealing papillary carcinoma (PTC). Despite the diagnosis, the patient refused therapeutic treatment and instead had the growing mass regularly monitored by computed tomography (CT) over the following 7 years.

Physical examination upon admission revealed a cauliflower-like cervical mass with a giant cystic section on the right side, presumably due to the previously diagnosed thyroid carcinoma. Routine laboratory tests, including hematocrit, were within normal limits. The latest CT image showed a large, heterogeneous mass localized to the left thyroid lobe and extended to the anterior neck space, measuring 17 x 12 cm and causing a displacement of the trachea to the right side.

The patient was successfully discharged after managing the surface bleeding with common bedside hemostatic maneuvers and use of local electrocauterization. Despite the success of these treatments, the patient refused any further management, such as surgical debulking and radioiodine therapy.

Follow-up:

The patient is recommended to schedule follow-up appointments with her primary care provider to continue monitoring her condition. If any new developments arise, she is advised to seek medical attention immediately.

The 72-year-old female patient with a long-standing history of neglected thyroid carcinoma was admitted to our hospital with cervical bleeding caused by a giant ulcerous goiter. After managing the surface bleeding, the patient was discharged without further treatment due to her refusal to undergo surgical debulking and radioiodine therapy. She is advised to schedule follow-up appointments with her primary care provider to continue monitoring her condition.

Abdominal CT showed pelvic and peritoneal cavity fluids, occupation of the left lateral lobe of the liver, and an unclear margin of the pancreas. PET-CT suggested swelling of the pancreas and metastases in the liver. The patient received comprehensive internal treatment combined with artificial liver treatment, but his condition deteriorated, and he became unconscious and developed hepatic encephalopathy. He was put on the transplant waiting list and received a liver transplant from a deceased donor on day 4 due to his critical condition. After the transplantation, the patient was sent to the ICU for further treatment.

Postoperative Course:

The patient's condition improved after the transplant, and he was started on immunosuppressive agents. Abdominal CT showed pancreatic swelling with massive exudation and effusion, indicating acute pancreatitis on postoperative day 8. His pathogen culture of various body fluids suggested multiple bacterial infections. An arrow tube was placed around the liver and tail of the pancreas under B-mode ultrasound guidance instead of operative treatment on postoperative day 11, and coffee-like turbid liquids flowed from the arrow tube. 

On postoperative day 20, the patient experienced a sudden increase in heart rate, decrease in blood pressure, increase in blood gas lactate, blurred consciousness, and poor light reflex. He received emergency trachea cannula, continuous renal replacement therapy for anuria, and norepinephrine to maintain blood pressure. On postoperative day 21, he was unconscious and died of septic shock.

CT scan showed fluid in the belly and pelvis, indicating possible infection or inflammation. It also showed a growth in the left part of the liver and an unclear edge of the pancreas. PET scan showed pancreas swelling and cancer spread to the liver, indicating advanced disease. He received medical treatment and artificial liver support, but his condition continued to worsen. He received an emergency breathing tube, kidney dialysis because he was not urinating, and medicine to raise his blood pressure. On day twenty-one, he was unconscious and died from septic shock despite intensive treatment.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: __________     Admission Date: __________     Discharge Date: __________ 

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 34-year-old female at 24 gestational weeks, was admitted to our emergency service with complaints of vomiting, abdominal pain, weakness, and dyspnea. Upon physical examination, the patient showed reduced breath sounds on the left side of the chest and diffuse abdominal tenderness. Laboratory tests revealed several abnormalities including an elevated white cell count, low hemoglobin levels and a low platelet count. A chest X-ray showed free air under the left hemidiaphragm, and a left lateral decubitus abdominal radiograph displayed that the free air moved to the right side. 

During the attempted surgical intervention, an emergency obstetric USG examination was performed which showed the intrauterine fetal demise. The patient was operated on under emergency conditions. A 14 × 8 cm defect was detected in the posterior diaphragm and the spleen was significantly damaged. A large hernia sac was detected in the diaphragmatic cavity. The defect in the posterior diaphragm was closed by primary repair following the insertion of a gastrostomy tube. After the improvement of hemodynamics and oxygen saturation of the patient, a dead fetus was manually delivered via caesarian section and a total gastrectomy followed by Roux-en-Y anastomosis was performed. 

On the 27th day of treatment, the patient died due to brain hypoxia caused by cardiopulmonary arrest. 

Diagnosis: 
The patient's presenting symptoms and pathology were suggestive of an abdominal and cardiothoracic catastrophe, resulting in the intrauterine fetal demise, posterior diaphragm hernia and necrosis of the stomach. 

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient's hospital course was marked by a series of complications from the presenting pathology. Despite surgical intervention the patient developed the intrauterine fetal demise and complications from posterior diaphragm hernia, resulting in the need for a cesarean delivery and complicated surgery to repair multiple organ damage. Ultimately, the patient succumbed to brain hypoxia caused by cardiopulmonary arrest.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 51-year-old female

Admission Date: February 2013

Discharge Date: October 2015

Diagnosis: Recurrent Ameloblastoma

Procedure: Right mandibular resection and reconstruction with nonvascularized free iliac bone followed by dental implant placement and fixed prosthesis

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the department in February 2013 due to discomfort in the mandible. She had been diagnosed with recurrent ameloblastoma and had undergone multiple fenestration procedures in the past. The patient was dissatisfied with the outcomes of previous hospital's treatment policy and came to our department for the complete resection of the tumor. 
After thorough evaluation and diagnosis, we proposed a treatment protocol of radical resection and immediate bony reconstruction using nonvascularized free iliac bone graft. The patient underwent right mandibular resection (teeth 43 to 46; length 35 mm) in March 2013 and was closely monitored for tumor recurrence. 
Follow-up examinations showed no signs of tumor recurrence, but the patient continued to experience right-sided difficulty in mastication. Therefore, a fixed prosthesis was recommended. In November 2014, the mini-plate was removed from the grafted bone, and four dental implants were placed. Subsequently, the patient underwent vestibuloplasty (vestibular extension with periosteal separation procedures) and confirmed osseointegration in all four implants. The final fixed prosthesis was worn by the patient in October 2015. 
The patient's oral hygiene has been regularly managed, and no signs of tumor recurrence or abnormal bone absorption or disintegration of the dental implants have been observed. The patient was discharged in October 2015.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient is advised to continue maintaining good oral hygiene and to follow the regular maintenance therapy schedule. The patient should keep all appointments with the department for proper monitoring of tumor recurrence and dental implant health. If there are any concerns or questions, the patient should contact the department for further consultations.

Hospital Course:
-The patient was admitted to the cardiac catheterization laboratory with sudden onset chest pain associated with anterior ST-segment elevation on the electrocardiogram. The chest pain occurred during a bowel movement and he was found to be in cardiogenic shock upon arrival.
-Emergency diagnostic coronary angiography was performed, revealing severe proximal stenosis in the left anterior descending (LAD) artery. An extravasation of contrast media from the LAD artery into the pericardium was noted, with no flow in the distal LAD artery, resulting in a suspected dehiscence of the left internal mammary artery (LIMA) graft.
-Injection of contrast media discovered that the LIMA graft's flow of contrast only reached the mid-segment and stopped, while the saphenous vein grafts (SVGs) in the right coronary artery (RCA) and circumflex (LCx) artery were patent.
-After diagnostic coronary angiography, the patient experienced pulseless electrical activity cardiac arrest, but spontaneous circulation was achieved with CPR, and an intra-aortic balloon pump was inserted.
-Urgent echocardiography revealed a large global pericardial effusion with right atrial and right ventricular collapse. Emergency pericardiocentesis was performed to aspirate 700 mL of haemorrhagic fluid that contained an organized thrombus.
-Due to on-going haemodynamic compromise and non-availability of cardiac surgery on-site, it was decided to perform percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) to treat the LAD artery stenosis. Following PCI, thrombolysis in myocardial infarction (TIMI) 3 flow was achieved, and no further extravasation was seen at the dehiscence site.
-Assessment of the LIMA graft showed a sluggish flow with extravasation of contrast media into the pericardium, requiring four coils (Tornado Embolisation Microcoils. Cook Medical, Bloomington, IN, USA) for embolization to halt the flow.
-The patient was then transferred to the local cardiac surgery unit and underwent emergency re-sternotomy and evacuation of the blood clots. His haemoglobin level post CABG (4 weeks prior to this admission) was measured at 100 g/L and dropped to 79 g/L following LIMA avulsion. He received 2 units of blood transfusion.
-The echocardiogram post-PCI revealed residual blood clots in the pericardial space that were difficult to extract percutaneously.
-The patient made a full recovery with no neurological sequelae and was discharged after a few days.
-Outpatient review at 3 months confirmed an excellent recovery without report of cardiovascular symptoms. Control coronary angiography was performed at 5 months, and the patient underwent successful PCI to mid and proximal LAD into the left main (LM) artery with LCx ostium optimization.
nemotron_simplification:
Hospital Course:
- The patient went to the heart cath lab with sudden chest pain that showed a front heart attack on ECG.
- The pain started during a bowel movement and he was in shock when he arrived.
- Doctors did an emergency heart artery test and found a tight blockage in the front part of the LAD artery.
- They saw dye leak from the LAD artery into the sac around the heart, with no flow past the blockage.
- This leak indicated a possible tear in the LIMA graft that needed attention to prevent further complications.
- When dye was injected, the LIMA graft only showed flow to its middle part and then stopped.
- The vein grafts in the right and circumflex arteries were open and working, allowing normal blood flow to those areas.
- After the heart artery test, the patient’s heart stopped beating effectively, but CPR restarted circulation.
- Doctors placed an intra-aortic balloon pump to help the heart pump blood more effectively during recovery.
- An urgent ultrasound showed a large fluid buildup around the heart, causing the right chambers to collapse.
- Doctors drained 700 mL of bloody fluid that contained a clot to relieve pressure on the heart.
- Because the patient remained unstable and heart surgery was not available, doctors did a stent procedure to open LAD blockage.
- After the stent, blood flow in the artery was normal (TIMI 3), indicating successful opening.
- No more dye leak was seen at the tear site, showing the leak had stopped.
- The LIMA graft had slow flow and dye leaked into the heart sac; four coils were placed to stop it.
- The patient was moved to the local heart surgery unit for an emergency chest opening to remove blood clots.
- His hemoglobin, which was 100 g/L after his prior bypass surgery, fell to 79 g/L after the LIMA graft tore.
- He received two units of blood to raise his hemoglobin level and improve oxygen delivery.
- The ultrasound after the stent showed leftover blood clots around the heart that were hard to remove with a needle.
- The patient recovered fully with no brain or nerve problems and left the hospital after a few days.
- At three months, an outpatient visit showed an excellent recovery with no reported heart symptoms.
- At five months, a repeat heart artery test was done to check the grafts and plan further treatment.
- A stent was successfully placed in the middle and upper LAD artery to restore blood flow.
- It also reached into the left main artery and improved the circumflex artery opening to enhance blood flow.

Hospital Course:
The 76-year-old male patient presented with visual impairment of his right eye 50 years after receiving penetrating keratoplasty (PKP). This followed an explosion injury that resulted in bilateral corneal opacities before the 1960s trauma. The patient reported seeing his ophthalmologist annually for follow-up examinations for 50 years following his first PKP, and control examinations were conducted in recent years due to primary open angle glaucoma. Cataract surgery was performed externally, 42 years after PKP in the right eye, and six years following surgery, he reported a deterioration of his vision. Follow-up examinations were conducted regularly by his ophthalmologist, with depositing in the periphery of the graft being described 48 years after the first PKP. Upon slit-lamp examination, the graft diameters of the former grafts were 6 mm with a central corneal thickness of 584 µm in the right eye and 544 µm in the left eye. The recipient cornea was cloudy, and gray with an endothelial cell count of 1162 c/mm2 in the right eye and 1320 c/mm2 in the left eye. As a result of progressive visual impairment and discomfort caused by the blurred vision, a repeated PKP was offered on the worse right eye. The patient accepted, and surgery was performed without any complications. The excised primary corneal graft with a rim of the recipient cornea was sent for histopathological analysis.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 96-year-old female with drug-induced agranulocytosis and mild pneumonia

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with severe leucopenia due to drug-induced agranulocytosis, presumably caused by antibiotics. She was also found to have mild pneumonia, which was treated with intravenous meropenem hydrate and oral levofloxacin hydrate for 10 days followed by a short course of sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim for 4 days. She was given subcutaneous injections of filgrastim to treat her neutropenia, which eventually normalized after 6 days and stabilized at around 3000 to 4000/µL after day 13. Her fever receded after day 10, and she was discharged on day 18 without any further complications.

Clinical Findings:
The patient's blood pressure was 136/99 mmHg, pulse rate was 87 beats per minute, and body temperature was 37.4°C during presentation. Her respiratory rate was 20 breaths per minute, and peripheral oxygen saturation was 97%. Chest sounds were normal, and other findings of the physical examination were unremarkable. Full blood count revealed severe leucopenia with a WBC count of 830/µL (neutrophils 7/µL, eosinophils 8/μL, basophils 18/μL, monocytes 378/μL, and lymphocytes 415/μL). A chest radiograph and computed tomography showed mild infiltrative shadow in her left lung.

Medical History:
The patient had a medical history of atrial fibrillation, stroke, hypertension, hypotonic urinary bladder, lower back pain, and gastritis.

Medications:
The patient's daily medications included candesartan, lansoprazole, amlodipine, carbocysteine, zaltoprofen, tranexamic acid, rivaroxaban, bisoprolol, brotizolam, and celecoxib. Candesartan, lansoprazole, amlodipine, and celecoxib were discontinued due to their potential to cause agranulocytosis.

Follow-up:
The patient was discharged from the hospital after the normalization of her neutrophil count and stabilization of her WBC count. She will continue with follow-up appointments with her primary care physician to ensure proper monitoring and further management of her medical conditions.

Hospital Course:

The patient was a 33-year-old female who presented to the hospital with a sudden onset of right-sided weakness. CT scan of the brain showed that the patient had an ischemic stroke which affected the left middle cerebral artery territory. An MRI of the brain revealed altered signal intensity in the left parietal, temporal cortices, and left basal ganglia. The rest of the brain appeared structurally normal, and both cerebellar hemispheres showed no abnormality.

Diagnosis:

The patient was diagnosed with an ischemic stroke in the left middle cerebral artery territory. Additionally, a hypo-dense lesion was found in the medial part of the left basifrontal lobe, in the left Putamen extending superiorly to the left para-ventricular white matter, and around the frontal horn of the left lateral ventricle.

Treatment:

The patient underwent FDG PET/CT as part of routine evaluation before being planned for stem cell transplant for stroke. The PET/CT of the brain revealed reduced FDG uptake in the frontal, parietal, and temporal cortices, and basal ganglia on the left side. Correlative CT revealed a hypo-dense lesion as described above. The patient was treated under the care of the hospital's medical team.

Assessment and Plan:

During the hospital stay, the patient received therapy aimed at preventing further ischemic stroke. The medical team monitored the patient's condition closely and ordered various diagnostic tests, which revealed reduced FDG uptake in the frontal, parietal, and temporal cortices, and basal ganglia on the left side.

Summary:

The patient was admitted to the hospital with an acute onset of right-sided weakness due to an ischemic stroke in the left middle cerebral artery territory. Various diagnostic tests were performed which revealed a hypo-dense lesion in the medial part of the left basifrontal lobe, in the left Putamen extending superiorly to the left para-ventricular white matter, and around the frontal horn of the left lateral ventricle. The patient received treatment for ischemic stroke and was monitored closely by the hospital's medical team.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 40
Gender: Female
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
The patient was referred for an evaluation of right periorbital pain, right eye ptosis, and diplopia that had first appeared 20 days earlier. She had restricted adduction of the right eyeball. Initial MRIs showed enlargement of the right medial rectus muscle with mild contrast enhancement, and additional lesions in the right retrobulbar optic nerve sheath and preseptal area.

MEDICAL MANAGEMENT:
The initial diagnosis was orbital IIP, and the patient was started on 60 mg of prednisone daily for 10 days, which greatly improved her symptoms. The dosage was gradually reduced over the next 8 weeks, but her symptoms relapsed when prednisone was reduced to below 20 mg per day. Azathioprine and mycophenolate mofetil also could not be administered because of potential direct hepatotoxicity. The patient was started on 3 mg of tacrolimus while discontinuing prednisolone over 8 weeks. After 6 months of tacrolimus administration, the right periorbital pain had completely disappeared, and the restriction of right eye abduction had resolved. The second follow-up MRIs were obtained at 16 months after the onset, by which time the lesions had nearly resolved. Tacrolimus was gradually reduced over a period of 7 months before being discontinued, and the patient had no further relapse during the 1-year follow-up.

CLINICAL FINDINGS:
The patient had painful tenderness of the right medial orbital region. Routine serological tests, autoimmune screening tests, and CSF studies all produced normal findings. However, her hepatitis C virus RNA level was 1,724,673 IU/mL in the quantification test, indicating active hepatitis C.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
The patient is advised to follow up with their healthcare provider for further management of hepatitis C. If any orbital IIP concerns arise, they are to contact their healthcare provider immediately.

Hospital Course:

A 42-year-old male with a past medical history of diabetes and hypertension presented to our hospital with recurrent episodes of right limb-shaking, right facial muscles involuntary twitching and slurred speech, which were more prominent with exercise. The patient was initially diagnosed with focal motor seizures but carbamazepine failed to prevent his symptoms. Further investigations including laboratory tests, electrocardiogram, electroencephalography, and imaging studies revealed significant stenosis of the left internal carotid artery (ICA) and scans showed a large heterogeneous plaque at the beginning of the left ICA. The diagnosis of limb-shaking TIA caused by left hemisphere perfusion impairment was considered.

Treatment:

The patient was given fluid replacement therapy, antiplatelet therapy, clopidogrel and aspirin, and statins. ICA angioplasty and stent implantation were performed with excellent restoration flow. No neurological dysfunction was observed post-operation, and the procedure was successful in completely resolving his symptoms. The patient was maintained on antiplatelet therapy and statins after stenting, and no recurrences of his limb-shaking TIA and facial muscles involuntary twitch. 

Clinical courses:

The patient had at least 3 months without any symptoms, and no new TIA. He was discharged to the care of his primary physician with recommendations to continue taking anti-platelets and statins. Follow-up visits were suggested to monitor the progress of the stenosis. The patient follows up with his primary care provider, and no other issues were reported. 

Diagnosis:

Limb-shaking TIA caused by severe left internal carotid artery stenosis. 

Benefit and risk:

The benefit of the ICA angioplasty and stent implantation is that it restored blood flow in the left hemisphere and cleared the symptoms. The patient was maintained on antiplatelet therapy and statins after stenting, and no recurrences of his limb-shaking TIA and facial muscles involuntary twitch. The risks of the procedure may include long-term stent failure, stroke, infection, and bleeding, although no complications were encountered in this case. 

Follow-up:

The patient was advised to follow-up regularly with his primary physician for monitoring and management of his diabetes and hypertension. Further follow-up visits were suggested to monitor the progress of the stenosis, and to adjust the treatment plan if needed. 

Prognosis:

The angioplasty and stenting were successful in resolving the patient's symptoms. The patient had at least 3 months without any symptoms, and no new TIA. The prognosis of this patient depends on his compliance with medical management and follow-up, and his ability to manage his underlying comorbidities, diabetes, and hypertension.

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 42-year-old man with a history of diabetes and high blood pressure.
He had repeated shaking of his right arm and leg, facial twitching, and slurred speech.
These symptoms became worse during physical activity such as walking, exercising, or any effort that increased his heart rate.
Doctors first thought he had seizures that affect movement, but the medicine carbamazepine did not stop the symptoms.
Tests including blood work, heart tracing, brain wave test, and scans showed a major narrowing of the left carotid artery.
The scans also revealed a large, uneven buildup of fatty material at the start of that artery.
Doctors believed the shaking episodes were a mini-stroke caused by reduced blood flow to the left side of the brain.

He received fluids, medicines to prevent blood clots (clopidogrel and aspirin), and a cholesterol-lowering drug (a statin).
Doctors performed a procedure to open and stent the narrowed left carotid artery, which restored blood flow well.
After the procedure, he showed no new nerve problems and his symptoms disappeared completely right away.
He continued taking the clot-preventing medicines and the statin regularly after the stent was placed.
He had no more shaking episodes or facial twitching for several months after the stent procedure.

He went at least three months without any symptoms and had no new mini-stroke reported.
He was discharged to his primary doctor with advice to keep taking the clot-preventing medicines and the statin.
Follow-up visits were advised to check how the narrowing in his artery was changing over time.
He continues to see his primary care provider, and no other problems have been reported.

Opening and stenting the narrowed artery restored blood flow to the left brain and stopped the symptoms.

Hospital Course:

The patient presented to our institution for regular follow-up, 2 years after a right radical nephrectomy for a primary renal cell carcinoma (RCC). The patient was asymptomatic, but an abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan on follow-up revealed a mass in the left adrenal gland. A multidisciplinary team meeting determined that a laparoscopic transperitoneal adrenalectomy was the best course of action.

Procedure:

The patient underwent a laparoscopic transperitoneal adrenalectomy, performed under general anesthesia. The patient was placed in the lateral decubitus position with the left side up. The pneumoperitoneum was established, and a 30° laparoscope and three additional working ports were placed under direct vision. The tumor was exposed and isolated before being excised.

Histological examination:

The histological examination of the specimen demonstrated a metastatic RCC with features similar to the primary renal tumor. All surgical margins were free of tumor.

Outcome:

The postoperative period was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day two. The patient is well and has no recurrence or adrenal insufficiency 18 months post-surgery.

The patient felt fine, but a belly CT scan showed a growth on the left adrenal gland.
A team of doctors decided that keyhole surgery to remove the left adrenal gland was the best choice.
Procedure:
The patient underwent the keyhole surgery while under sleep medicine to keep them comfortable and pain-free.
They lay on the right side and filled the belly with gas to see inside.
Then they placed a small camera and three tools through small cuts to work inside the belly.
They found the growth, carefully separated it from surrounding tissue, and removed it safely and completely.
Histological examination:
Lab tests showed the growth was cancer that had spread from the original kidney tumor.
The edges of the removed tissue were examined and found to be free of any cancer cells.
Outcome:
Recovery was smooth with no complications, and the patient left the hospital after two days.
Eighteen months later, the patient feels fine, with no cancer return or adrenal gland problems.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [Redacted]
Age: 50 years
Sex: Female
Race: South Indian

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to the outpatient department with a productive cough with hemoptysis for the past 2 months. She had a history of pulmonary tuberculosis, which was discontinued within 3 weeks of starting the treatment. She also suffered from diabetes mellitus with peripheral neuropathy for the past 8 years and was taking oral hypoglycemic agents for the same. The patient was diagnosed with an indwelling aspergilloma and was treated with an oral loading dose of Voriconazole followed by an oral maintenance dose. The patient responded well to the treatment, and the hemoptysis resolved after a lobectomy. After 3 weeks, the sputum became negative for acid-fast bacilli. The patient is currently in the 4th month of treatment and is doing well.

Laboratory Results:
Admission baseline investigations showed anemia, and the renal and liver function tests were within normal limits.

Diagnostic Study:
Computed tomogram of the thorax revealed a thick-walled cavity in the right lung upper lobe with an indwelling aspergilloma. 3 sputum samples were tested positive for acid-fast bacilli by Ziehl Neelsen's staining technique. Conventional method of culture on Lowenstein Jensen's medium yielded growth of M. tuberculosis. The anti-tuberculosis drug susceptibility test showed resistance to Isoniazid and Rifampicin but sensitive to Ethambutol, Pyrazinamide, and Streptomycin in their critical concentrations.

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis and an indwelling aspergilloma.

Treatment:
The patient was initially started on a daily dose of Isoniazid, Ethambutol, Pyrazinamide, and Streptomycin. However, after culture demonstrated MDR-TB, Isoniazid was stopped, and oral Levofloxacin and Ethionamide were included in the treatment regimen. Rifampicin was not included due to its interactions with Voriconazole. The patient was given an oral loading dose of Voriconazole 400 mg 12th hourly for 2 doses, which was followed by an oral maintenance dose of 200 mg 12th hourly for 6 weeks.

Follow-up:
After the treatment, the patient was counseled on the importance of adhering to medication and follow-up visits. She was advised to return to the hospital for follow-up visits and monitoring of symptoms.

Summary:
The 50-year-old South Indian woman presented with complaints of productive cough with hemoptysis for the past 2 months. She suffered from diabetes mellitus with peripheral neuropathy and had a history of pulmonary tuberculosis. The patient was diagnosed with an indwelling aspergilloma and treated with an oral loading dose of Voriconazole followed by an oral maintenance dose. Hemoptysis resolved after lobectomy, and the sputum became negative for acid-fast bacilli after 3 weeks. The patient responded well to the treatment and is currently in the 4th month of treatment. The patient was advised to adhere to medication and follow-up visits.

Discharge Summary:

This is a summary of the hospital course of a 62-year-old male with Kearns-Sayre syndrome (KSS) who presented to the emergency department (ED) after two syncopal episodes. He has a past medical history of multi-system involvement including skeletal muscle myopathy, pigmentary retinopathy, heart failure, non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, pulmonary hypertension, chronic heart block, chronic kidney disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and mitral valve prolapse.

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted for syncope secondary to VT, and 150 mg of IV amiodarone bolus was administered. He was started on amiodarone drip at 0.5 mg/min. Follow-up AICD interrogation yielded sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia to the 140s during both syncopal episodes. Chest X-ray revealed right pleural effusion. On day two, the patient was noted to have non-sustained VT with increasing oxygen requirements. A plan was in place to transition the patient from IV to PO amiodarone, but instead, he developed VT storm and was thus continued on amiodarone drip. He was transferred to the critical care unit (CCU) for further monitoring and started on lidocaine drip (1 mg/min) with continued amiodarone and milrinone drips. In the CCU, he continued to have non-sustained VT with symptoms of palpitations despite the AICD reprogramming and medical management. He also continued to have shortness of breath with minimal improvement on bilevel positive airway pressure (BIPAP). Unfortunately, recurrent VT progressed to a VT storm, requiring multiple boluses of IV amiodarone, IV lidocaine, and multiple shocks from his AICD which were futile. The VT storm was refractory to his current medical management. The patient eventually passed away after the withdrawal of care.

Final Diagnosis:

The final diagnosis of the patient was VT storm in the setting of KSS with multi-system involvement including heart failure.

Follow-Up:

The patient was not discharged due to his unfortunate clinical outcome.

The patient was admitted for fainting due to ventricular tachycardia and got 150 mg of IV amiodarone.
He started on an amiodarone drip at 0.5 mg per minute to control his heart rhythm.
Follow-up device check showed sustained fast heart rhythm in the 140s during both fainting spells.
Chest X-ray showed fluid around the right lung, indicating a pleural effusion that needed monitoring.

These treatments did not stop the VT storm and it remained refractory to current therapy.
The patient eventually died after the decision to withdraw life-sustaining care was made due to worsening condition.
Final Diagnosis:
The final diagnosis was VT storm in the setting of Kearns-Sayre syndrome with multi-system involvement including heart failure.
Follow-Up:
The patient was not discharged because he died in the hospital after his condition worsened despite treatment.

The patient, a 36-year-old female, presented to the hospital with a 4-year history of dull pain on the left back and a foreign body on the left side of the spine. She denied hematuria, dysuria, or frequency. The patient was admitted, and a computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed moderate hydronephrosis of the left kidney. A surgical procedure was successfully performed to remove a 3-cm sewing needle that was found around the upper part of the left ureter. A double-J ureteral stent was placed to relieve the obstruction. After 6 months of follow-up, the patient's ureteral obstruction and hydronephrosis were significantly reduced, and the double-J ureteral stent was removed.

Hospital Course Summary:

Patient underwent a right parietal craniotomy for evacuation of a subdural hematoma, with good post-operative progress. The patient was then started on unfractionated heparin infusion, given an intravenous bolus of 5000 U and infusion rate of 1000 U/hr with an aPTT goal of 50 to 70 s for 3 days. Daily echocardiographic evaluation did not reveal any thrombosis in the prosthetic cardiac valves. On the seventh day after surgery, subcutaneous enoxaparin (2 × 0.6 cc) was started, and anti-factor Xa level was monitored until discharge, with a therapeutic range of 0.8 to 1.2 IU/mL. The patient was discharged after her anti-factor Xa level reached 1.1 IU/mL with the recommendation of twice daily 0.6 cc subcutaneous enoxaparin, and the goal INR of 3 to 3.5. Patient delivered a healthy baby via Cesarean delivery under unfractionated heparin treatment, with no complications.

Each day, an ultrasound of the heart showed no clots in the artificial heart valves.
On the seventh day after surgery, the patient began receiving enoxaparin shots under the skin, two doses of 0.6 cc each.
Blood tests for anti-factor Xa were checked until discharge, aiming for a level between 0.8 and 1.2 IU/mL.
The patient was discharged when the anti-factor Xa level reached 1.1 IU/mL, indicating adequate anticoagulation for safety.
The patient should receive 0.6 cc enoxaparin under the skin twice daily and keep the INR between 3 and 3.5.
The patient later gave birth to a healthy baby by cesarean section while receiving heparin, with no problems.

Hospital Course Summary:

This hospital course summary is for a 65-year-old male who was admitted with dyspnea and deteriorating consciousness after ingesting Arvalin(R) that contained ZnP. The patient's history included chronic alcoholism and depression. The patient's laboratory tests indicated low calcium and potassium levels and elevated CRP with low WBC count. After admission, the patient's SpO2 was normalized using a reservoir mask, and he was intubated due to impaired consciousness levels. The patient's lung imaging showed extensive alveolar infiltration, and chest X-rays revealed dull percussion notes and muffled breath sounds. The patient received electrolyte replacement using intravenous crystalloid solutions and polystyrene sulfonate. A central venous catheter was inserted into the right jugular vein, and the patient was sedated with midazolam. The patient was given antibiotics and anti-inflammatory drugs, and his kidney function was monitored. Due to tachycardia and respiratory insufficiency, endotracheal intubation was required again. The patient later underwent tracheostomy. During his psychiatric care, the patient had bronchoscopy, and subacute mucosal inflammation was detected. His tracheostoma was removed after 20 days, and he was discharged after 1 month of psychiatric inpatient care.
nemotron_simplification: Hospital Course Summary: The patient is a 65-year-old man who came with trouble breathing and worsening awareness after swallowing Arvalin containing zinc phosphide. The patient had a history of long-term heavy alcohol use and depression that required care. Blood tests showed low calcium and potassium, high inflammation markers, and a low white blood cell count. The patient’s oxygen level normalized with an oxygen mask, yet he required a breathing tube due to impaired alertness. Lung imaging showed fluid in the air sacs, and chest X-ray indicated signs of fluid in the lungs. The patient received fluids and medicine to correct low calcium and potassium; a catheter was placed in a neck vein. The patient was given midazolam to stay calm, antibiotics for infection, and anti-inflammatory drugs to reduce swelling. Kidney function was checked regularly during the hospital stay to ensure it remained stable and working well. Because of a fast heart rate and trouble breathing, the patient needed another breathing tube. Later, a surgical opening in the neck (tracheostomy) was made to help with breathing and protect the airway. During psychiatric care, a camera look inside the airways showed mild swelling inside the airway lining that needed monitoring. The tracheostomy opening was closed after 20 days, and the patient left the hospital after one month of psychiatric care.

Left chronic subdural hematoma (CSDH)

The patient showed no evidence of neurological deficits after 1-year follow-up, although a CT scan showed that the hematoma remained.

Ongoing monitoring of the patient's condition is recommended to ensure the continued absence of neurological deficits.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to the fast-track ENT clinic with persistent left-sided throat discomfort and pain. The patient reported positive reflux symptoms with heartburn. Medical management was implemented, but it yielded no symptomatic relief. The patient underwent flexible nasendoscopy and a contrast-enhanced MRI scan, which revealed post-cricoid oedema consistent with laryngopharyngeal reflux. As the symptoms continued to persist, a transnasal oesophagoscopy was performed, and a proximal oesophageal lesion was identified. Multiple punch biopsies were taken.

The histological examination of the specimen revealed squamous cell papilloma, which tested positive for human papilloma virus (HPV). Oesophageal manometry and 24-hour oesophageal pH monitoring indicated borderline pathological reflux with some proximal penetration. The patient then underwent complete endoscopic excision of the lesion. Histology confirmed HPV-positive squamous papilloma.

The patient's symptoms resolved after the excision, and the patient received continued anti-reflux treatment, including lifestyle changes. A yearly follow-up confirmed complete remission of symptoms.

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with squamous cell papilloma of the oesophagus, which tested positive for human papilloma virus (HPV).

Procedures:
Transnasal oesophagoscopy was performed, and a proximal oesophageal lesion was identified. Multiple punch biopsies were taken. Complete endoscopic excision of the lesion was performed.

Follow-Up:
A yearly follow-up confirmed complete remission of symptoms. The patient received continued anti-reflux treatment, including lifestyle changes.

Summary:
The patient presented with persistent left-sided throat discomfort with positive reflux symptoms and was diagnosed with squamous cell papilloma of the oesophagus, which was HPV-positive. Anti-reflux treatment was continued with lifestyle changes, leading to complete remission of symptoms. A yearly follow-up confirmed the remission of symptoms.

Discharge Summary: 

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Hospital Course: 

The patient, a 45-year-old male, was admitted to the hospital with symptoms of left flank pain, hypoesthesia, and weakness at both lower extremities. Upon examination, the patient had motor weakness in both lower extremities and elevated deep tendon reflex of the right knee. Diagnostic tests indicated fracture of T8, T9 vertebral body by bone tumor, pathologic fracture of T9 vertebral body by bone tumor, T8–10 myelopathy, and cord compression.

The patient underwent T9 corpectomy and mesh cage insertion with T8–10 posterior screw fixation. Pathological examination confirmed a diagnosis of Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH). The patient underwent radiotherapy at T8–10 spine and showed remarkable improvement in motor weaknesses and hypoesthesia.

The patient has been followed for almost 6 years without any recurrence. Discharge instructions included follow-up care with the primary care physician and regular imaging surveillance to ensure no recurrence of the bone tumor. 

Overall, the patient received excellent medical care from the healthcare team and responded well to treatment.

Hospital Course:
The 27-year-old African-American woman was admitted to the hospital with chest pain, dyspnea on exertion, and a malar rash. Positive tests for anti-nuclear antibodies and anti-double-stranded DNA confirmed SLE-related pericarditis. Transthoracic echocardiography showed severe PH with an estimated RVSP of 92 mmHg and severe right ventricular dysfunction. After initiation of appropriate treatment, the patient showed improvement of muscle weakness and exercise capacity. Repeat transthoracic echocardiography four months later showed a normal right ventricular size and function with an estimated RVSP of 29 mmHg. Repeat right heart catheterization showed a reduction in the mean pulmonary artery pressure, an increase in cardiac output, and a reduction in pulmonary vascular resistance. The patient was started on oral therapy with sildenafil and treprostinil was tapered until discontinuation.

Diagnosis:
SLE-associated PH and polymyositis.

Treatment:
Pulse dose methylprednisolone, intravenous treprostinil, prednisone, and mycophenolate mofetil were prescribed. The patient was discharged on low-dose treprostinil and oral therapy with sildenafil was initiated. Prednisone was tapered over three months.

Follow-up:
The patient showed improvement in her leg weakness and exercise capacity. Repeat transthoracic echocardiography showed a normal right ventricular size and function. Repeat right heart catheterization showed a reduction in the mean pulmonary artery pressure, an increase in cardiac output, and a reduction in pulmonary vascular resistance. The patient continues to be followed up as an outpatient.
