The patient, a 68-year-old male with a history of malignant mesothelioma, was admitted to our department with gradually worsening bilateral low extremity weakness. The patient had previous occupational exposure to asbestos and was diagnosed with asbestosis in 1989. The neurological examination revealed a paraparesis of lower extremities, decreased sensation on the right side below T1, increased reflexes in the lower extremities, and partial Brown–Sèquard syndrome. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the cervical-thoracic spine revealed a hypointense left intramedullary anterolateral lesion at the level of C6–C7, which was strongly enhancing after gadolinium administration.

The patient underwent surgery through median posterior short incision and C6–C7 laminectomy. The intramedullary grayish lesion was completely removed, even though a clear plane was difficult to identify between the tumor and surrounding spinal cord. Pathological examination of the specimen revealed malignant mesothelioma.

The postoperative course was favorable, and the patient's neurological condition improved. Twenty days after surgery, the patient had completely regained normal lower extremity function. However, eight months after surgery, the patient died due to the progression of the thoracic disease.

Overall, the patient’s hospital course was successful and without complications. The patient was discharged in stable condition with appropriate follow-up arranged. The patient's family was informed about the condition and the plan going forward.

Discharge Diagnosis:
- Malignant mesothelioma

Follow-up Recommendations:
- The patient's family should be informed about the condition and the plan going forward.
- Appropriate follow-up should be arranged.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [Name]
Medical Record Number: [Number]

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 38-year-old woman who presented with a six-month history of progressive exertional dyspnea and new onset of syncopal episodes. Auscultation reveals a continuous murmur at the left sternal border. Transthoracic echocardiography reveals an anomalous vascular structure origin from circumflex artery and draining to the main pulmonary artery with significant left to right shunt, mild dilatation of right heart chambers and 60% ejection fraction. Magnetic resonance imaging and coronary angiography confirms the presence of a coronary artery fistula. The pulmonary to systemic flow ratio was calculated as 1.8 to 1. Left anterior mini-thoracotomy was performed, the fistulous tracts were identified, and the fistula on the pulmonary artery side was obliterated with multiple pledgeted 5-0 polypropylene sutures. Transesophageal echocardiography confirmed a successful closure of the fistula, lack of residual shunt and lack of wall motion abnormalities. Electrocardiogram did not show any signs of ischemia. The patient was extubated one hour after completion of the procedure and discharged on the second postoperative day. At 6 and 12 months follow-up, the patient remained free of any cardiovascular symptoms, while echocardiography showed no residual flow. An excellent cosmetic result was achieved.

Hospital Course Summary:
A 38-year-old female presented with dyspnea and syncopal episodes, and murmur on auscultation. The patient's medical examination revealed coronary artery fistula with significant left to right shunt and mild dilatation of the right heart chambers. The patient underwent surgical correction by left anterior mini-thoracotomy, and successful obliteration of the fistulous tracts was noted under transesophageal echocardiography with no residual shunt or wall motion abnormalities seen. The patient remained symptom-free at the six and twelve months follow-up visits, with no residual flow detected on echocardiography.@endsection

The patient, a 61-year-old woman presented to the department with vague neck pain, rachialgia, and left forearm numbness. She was started on corticosteroids and anti-inflammatory medications while waiting for radiological diagnosis. The cervical MRI revealed a left cervical plexus neurinoma, but as the patient's symptoms worsened, an urgent CT scan with 3D reconstruction was performed and the possibility of a vascular lesion was raised. A contrast-enhanced MRI/MRA scan of the cervical region and brain confirmed the presence of a vertebral artery pseudoaneurysm, with a double lumen right above the lesion that was attributed to a vertebral artery dissection. The patient received warfarin and endovascular proximal occlusion of the left vertebral artery to treat this condition. Her thorough history revealed no history of trauma, but the patient had received chiropractic treatment for a sore neck two weeks prior to the onset of symptoms. The MRA verified the absence of an intracranial aneurysm and confirmed the presence of adequate collateral blood supply by the contralateral vertebral artery in the face of a possible vertebral artery occlusion.

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient was admitted for evaluation of an ulcerative lesion on the left side of the lower lip. Biopsies confirmed the diagnosis of well-differentiated infiltrating squamous cell carcinoma, which was staged at T2N0M0 according to TNM guidelines. The patient opted for HDRIB treatment and received five equidistant metallic needles to insert plastic catheters through the tissue. CT image was taken to plan HDRIB treatment. The patient received one fraction of 5.00 Gy on the first day of treatment and two daily fractions of 5.00 Gy for the next 4 days. 

One month post-treatment, the patient had localised acute radiation toxicity with bleeding ulcerative mucositis at the treatment site. The patient was given analgesics, anti-inflammatory drugs, and a mouthwash to treat his symptoms. At the second follow-up, a month later, the ulcer measured 1.5 × 1.5 cm with an indurated area. The LL was epithelialised and tumour-free at his third follow-up, a month later. Finally, a two-year-long evaluation was conducted, which revealed that the patient was asymptomatic and disease-free, albeit mild atrophy and skin hypopigmentation were observed as long-term side effects of the treatment. 

The patient stated that he was pleased with the results and aesthetic outcome of his procedure.

Discharge Summary:

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 60-year-old, morbidly obese male with a medical history of uncontrolled hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus with microvascular complications, stroke without residual weakness, and obstructive sleep apnea who was admitted to the hospital with a three-day history of severe headache. An initial CT scan of the brain showed no evidence of subarachnoid hemorrhage. However, an MRI scan of the brain revealed generalized volume loss.

Physical Examination:
On physical examination, the patient had mild bilateral pedal edema, and we were unable to evaluate jugular venous pulsations due to a thick short neck. Neurological examination was unremarkable, and fundoscopic examination did not reveal any papilledema. Electrocardiogram showed low voltage sinus rhythm. Chest x-ray showed mild left pleural effusion and cardiomegaly. An echocardiogram revealed a large pericardial effusion with features of tamponade.

Diagnostic Studies:
The patient underwent emergent pericardial drainage, and the fluid analysis revealed it as a hemorrhagic pericardial effusion. The septic screen was negative, and vasculitis screening with ANA and ANCA was also negative. A PET CT scan did not detect any malignant focus. An MRI scan of the heart showed basal septal mid-wall myocardial enhancement of non-ischemic pattern, likely due to myocarditis or cardiomyopathy.

Diagnosis:
After ruling out secondary causes of hemorrhagic pericardial effusion, such as malignancy, autoimmune diseases, and TB, our patient was labeled as idiopathic myocarditis leading to chronic pericardial effusion based on MRI scan of the heart.

Management:
The patient's headache was relieved after pericardiocentesis, and his blood pressure stabilized after resuming his home antihypertensive medications. The patient was observed in the hospital for ten days with regular echocardiogram studies. He was asymptomatic and discharged with regular follow-up in the cardiology clinic. The cardiologist outpatient follow-ups with repeated echocardiogram studies for a further five months did not show any fluid reaccumulation. The patient was followed for one year after discharge where he remained clinically stable.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Idiopathic myocarditis leading to chronic pericardial effusion.

Follow-up:
The patient will have regular follow-up in the cardiology clinic to monitor the progress of the patient's condition.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

Admission Date: [Date]
Discharge Date: [Date]
Patient Name: [Name]
Age: 46
Sex: Female
Diagnosis: Schwannoma, Cognard IIa+b Dural Arteriovenous Fistula

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with symptoms of right ear congestion, pulsatile tinnitus, and mild hearing loss. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a lobulated mass at the cerebellopontine angle. An Octreoscan was performed, which showed intense tracer uptake in the mass, thereby supporting the diagnosis of paraganglioma. Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) was conducted, which demonstrated a lack of vascularity associated with the tumor. However, it revealed an incidental discovery of a Cognard IIa+b dural arteriovenous fistula in the right posterior fossa. Due to the extensive volume of the tumor, the patient underwent a staged surgical resection.
The first surgery included a modified radical right neck dissection, right superficial parotidectomy with facial nerve dissection, as well as the initial approach to the tumor and partial extradural resection. One week later, the patient underwent the second stage surgery where the tumor was radically resected using a right transcochlear approach. The right sigmoid sinus was ligated. The facial nerve was mobilized and transposed. Postoperative MRI confirmed complete resection of the tumor. Histological analysis of samples from both surgeries confirmed the tumor not to be a paraganglioma, but instead a schwannoma.
The patient had a long recovery from the surgery due to the lower cranial nerve palsies but has shown gradual improvement. Her latest follow-up MRI showed no evidence of recurrent tumor. DSA revealed large feeders from the right middle meningeal artery (MMA) and occipital arteries into the residual dural arteriovenous fistula. The fistula was embolized utilizing Onyx in the right MMA. Final right common carotid artery (CCA) angiogram demonstrated resolution in arteriovenous shunting. Vertebral artery injection after embolization demonstrated minimal residual shunting via the right anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA). Further intervention was declined by the patient, and angiographic follow-up in one year has been scheduled.

Discharge Medications:
[Not applicable]

Discharge Instructions:
The patient should follow up with their primary care physician as well as their neurologist. It is essential to report any new or recurrent symptoms immediately. The patient should take good care of their health by maintaining a balanced diet and regular exercise routine.

Hospital Course:
The patient, an 8-year-old female child, was admitted to our department due to diminution of vision in the right eye since 5 years, with headache and vomiting since 6 months. On examination, no perception of light was observed in the right eye with normal vision in the left eye. An MRI revealed a cystic lesion at the right temporo-frontal-parietal region measuring 8 × 9 × 6.5 cm. A small rounded nodule was seen on the medial aspect of the cystic lesion at the paraventricular location. The lesion was reported as a cystic astrocytoma/ganglioglioma. Endocrine workup subsequently revealed secondary hypothyroidism.  

Treatment:
The patient underwent right fronto-temporo-parietal craniotomy for drainage and marsupialisation of the cystic lesion. The cystic fluid was yellowish and machine oil-like, containing cholesterol crystals and flecks mostly over the medial side. Histological examination revealed inflamed Rathke's cleft cyst with a cystic wall lined by a flattened to pseudostratified squamous epithelium with congested blood vessels, chronic inflammatory infiltrate in the form of lymphocyte, plasma cells, and lymphoid aggregates.

Outcomes:
Postoperatively, the patient's recovery was uneventful, and the headache and vomiting subsided completely. The patient is in regular follow-up with postoperative MRI at 6 months without any recurrence.

Discharge Diagnosis: Membranous nephropathy

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient, a 60-year-old male, was admitted to our hospital with a two-month history of fatigue and trace lower extremity edema. The patient was also suffering from arthralgias of both knees and hands. Upon examination, it was found that the patient had been diagnosed with newly proteinuria. The patient's nocturia also stood out, alongside an increased urinary frequency.

Physical examination revealed trace lower extremity edema, however, there were no other abnormalities in cardiac, pulmonary, or abdominal exam. The patient had undergone routine cholecystectomy four months prior to admission. Laboratory examination showed a mild elevation in erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Urinalysis revealed 3+ protein but no nitrites or glucose. Renal function was normal. Urine protein was quantified as 10.68 gr/24h.

Further investigation was carried out to determine the cause of membranous glomerulonephritis. The patient was tested for secondary causes which included anti-double stranded deoxyribonucleic acid (anti-dsDNA) antibodies, antinuclear antibodies (ANA), titers for antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA), complement levels, and tests for cryoglobulins and rheumatoid factor. The patient's results were negative or within normal ranges. Serologies for hepatitis A, B, C, and HIV were also non-reactive.

A thoracoabdominal tomography was performed on the patient, which was normal. The renal biopsy showed that the membranous nephropathy was the cause of nephrotic syndrome. IgG deposition was seen along the capillary wall.

Upon review, there was no evidence of acute or chronic infections, nor any other features of related medical issues. The patient was diagnosed with membranous nephropathy.

The patient was discharged in good condition with a diagnosis of membranous nephropathy. The patient received no medications during the hospitalization of his condition.

Follow-Up Instructions:

The patient should seek medical advice from his physician if trace lower extremity edema or any other symptoms recur.

An 8-year-old boy with no significant medical history was admitted to our urgent ophthalmology clinic with a pencil injury to his left eye. 3. Patients should avoid penetrating injuries to the eye.
4. Patients and caregivers should provide immediate medical attention in the event of an eye injury.

The patient is advised to follow up with a pediatric ophthalmologist for regular vision screenings and eye exams. Any changes in vision, pain, or swelling should be reported immediately to their primary care physician.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission Date: [Date of admission]
Discharge Date: [Date of discharge]

Chief Complaint: Fracture of jaw and missing central incisors

History of Present Illness: A 12-year-old female with a history of road side accident was brought to the Department of Oral Surgery with the chief complaint of fracture of lower jaw in parasymphysis region and missing both central incisors. She had no history of orthodontic treatment. On examination, the patient was found to have impacted both lower canine and crowding in both jaws.

Hospital Course: Nonextraction treatment was planned, and the treatment objective was to repair the jaw fracture, regain space for prosthetic replacement of central incisors, relieve crowding, and maintain the existing class I molar relationship. After wiring of the arch to hold the fracture segment on the same day, bone plating was done when the patient was fit for surgery. Once the fracture segment was healed, fixed mechanotherapy was started with Roth, 0.022'' appliances in both maxillary and mandibular arches to align, level and create space for the central incisors. The mandibular canines were kept in place as they were close to the screw and disimpaction was challenging due to their location on the fracture line. Riding pontics were prepared, assessed, and adjusted to the rectangular archwire by stainless steel ligature. The esthetic and smile of the patient was improved after ligating riding pontics.

Summary: The 12-year-old female patient with a history of fracture of lower jaw in parasymphysis region and missing both central incisors due to a road side accident successfully underwent the nonextraction treatment plan. After fixing the fracture segment, the patient's malocclusion was treated with fixed mechanotherapy which aligned and leveled both maxillary and mandibular arches and created space for the central incisors, while keeping the mandibular canines in place due to their location on the fracture line. The final step of the treatment was the preparation and ligating of riding pontics that significantly improved the patient's esthetic and smile.

Albendazole

Involvement of the facial musculature manifesting as a cystic swelling in the bucco-masseteric region consistent with cysticercosis.

The patient should follow up with his primary healthcare provider for continued monitoring.

The patient's condition has improved since admission. He is stable and ready for discharge.

The patient is advised to continue taking his albendazole medication as prescribed. He should avoid tobacco use as it has been associated with cysticercosis. He is encouraged to follow up with his primary healthcare provider for continued monitoring and to report any new or concerning symptoms.

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 37-year-old male with a history of anxiety and migraines who presented to the ED reporting a constant, sharp pain on the right side of his head that had persisted for 12 hours. The patient reported that the pain was typical for his migraine but had not responded to his usual home abortive medication, ibuprofen, or hydrocodone/acetaminophen. 

Physical examination revealed right occipital tenderness upon palpation, but no midline spinal tenderness or cranial nerve deficits. Metoclopramide, normal saline, and diphenhydramine were administered initially, after which the patient reported improvement from a 10/10 to an 8/10 in pain. Subsequently, the patient received an occipital nerve block with 1% lidocaine, and three minutes later, the patient reported further improvement to 2/10 in pain.

Follow-up phone call interview at day 8 revealed complete resolution of the patient's migraine symptoms, and the patient expressed preference for seeking out an occipital nerve block if a migraine were to recur.

Summary:

A 37-year-old male presented with a 12-hour history of severe right-sided head pain consistent with his migraines but unresponsive to his usual home abortive medication. Initial treatment with metoclopramide, normal saline, and diphenhydramine failed to provide adequate relief, but a subsequent occipital nerve block with 1% lidocaine resulted in resolution of the patient's symptoms. Follow-up phone call interview at day 8 revealed continued symptom resolution and expressed patient preference for future use of occipital nerve block.

Medical History:
The patient had multiple rib fractures with right-sided hemothorax following a road traffic accident and underwent thoracostomy tube insertion at the primary treating hospital. She was referred to our tertiary care center after 1½ months from the antecedent injury and was diagnosed with necrotic sloughed-out the right dome of the diaphragm with collapsed right lung.

Hospital Course:
The patient was intubated and shifted to ICU for ventilatory support. A repeat Chest X-Ray and CECT thorax showed bilateral multiple rib fractures, right-sided hemothorax with air foci in the collection, and an indistinct outline of the diaphragm. In view of a possible diaphragmatic injury, the patient underwent right posterolateral thoracotomy. Intraoperatively, necrotic tissues and organized hematomas were removed, and an intercostal tube was placed between the liver and the collapsed lung. No repair of diaphragm could be done. The patient was stable postoperatively but could not be weaned off mechanical ventilation. A tracheostomy was done in view of long-term intubation. Enteral feeds were started through nasogastric tube. After 3 weeks, the patient was transferred to the cardiothoracic surgery unit for further management but could not undergo any surgical procedures and died after 1 month due to her poor general condition.

Condition at Discharge:
The patient had an unfortunate outcome and could not be discharged.

No further plan needed.

None needed.

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 74-year-old
Sex: Female
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Chief complaint:
The patient complained of exacerbation of mild dysphagia and an awareness of a tumor in the left side of her neck.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to our hospital on [REDACTED] with a complaint of mild dysphagia for the past two months, which had recently worsened. Laboratory tests showed normal thyroid function levels. Pharyngoesophagography showed a large diverticulum at the pharyngoesophageal junction. Ultrasonography revealed a hypoechoic lesion present in the posterior bilateral lobe of the thyroid and an isoechoic mass on the left lobe of the thyroid. Cervical CT scan showed a thyroid nodule, bilateral hypopharyngeal diverticula, and an isodensity area with a hyperdensity area, suggesting calcium deposition. A barium swallow pharyngoesophagogram showed a large left-sided diverticulum and a small right-sided diverticulum.

The patient underwent resection of the diverticula and thyroid tumor surgery for improvement of dysphagia. The surgical procedure was approached through a collar incision in the left anterior neck, and the diverticula were visualized under the cricopharyngeus muscle. The left-sided diverticulum was mobilized from the left lobe of the thyroid and the thyroid tumor. The diverticulotomy was performed. The wound was closed in layers with placement of a closed suction drain.

Histopathological examination showed that the diverticula were false diverticula without a muscular layer, and the thyroid tumor was diagnosed as a thyroid adenoma. The patient was started on a clear liquid diet on postoperative day 4. Two years after surgery, the patient remains free of dysphagia.

Diagnosis:
- Mild dysphagia
- Hypopharyngeal diverticula
- Thyroid adenoma

Treatment:
- Surgery for resection of hypopharyngeal diverticula and thyroid tumor

Follow-up:
The patient is advised to continue follow-up care with her primary care physician. No further appointments with our hospital are required.

Patient Name: [Name]
Medical Record Number: [Number]

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 38-year-old woman who presented with a six-month history of progressive exertional dyspnea and new onset of syncopal episodes. Auscultation reveals a continuous murmur at the left sternal border. Transthoracic echocardiography reveals an anomalous vascular structure origin from circumflex artery and draining to the main pulmonary artery with significant left to right shunt, mild dilatation of right heart chambers and 60% ejection fraction. Magnetic resonance imaging and coronary angiography confirms the presence of a coronary artery fistula. The pulmonary to systemic flow ratio was calculated as 1.8 to 1. Left anterior mini-thoracotomy was performed, the fistulous tracts were identified, and the fistula on the pulmonary artery side was obliterated with multiple pledgeted 5-0 polypropylene sutures. Transesophageal echocardiography confirmed a successful closure of the fistula, lack of residual shunt and lack of wall motion abnormalities. Electrocardiogram did not show any signs of ischemia. The patient was extubated one hour after completion of the procedure and discharged on the second postoperative day. At 6 and 12 months follow-up, the patient remained free of any cardiovascular symptoms, while echocardiography showed no residual flow. An excellent cosmetic result was achieved.

Hospital Course Summary:
A 38-year-old female presented with dyspnea and syncopal episodes, and murmur on auscultation. The patient's medical examination revealed coronary artery fistula with significant left to right shunt and mild dilatation of the right heart chambers. The patient underwent surgical correction by left anterior mini-thoracotomy, and successful obliteration of the fistulous tracts was noted under transesophageal echocardiography with no residual shunt or wall motion abnormalities seen. The patient remained symptom-free at the six and twelve months follow-up visits, with no residual flow detected on echocardiography.@endsection

Hospital Course Summary:

Patient was a 71-year-old female who presented to our clinic with an abnormal ECG finding during a scheduled appointment. She had a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, essential hypertension, and dyslipidemia. During the consultation, the ECG reading showed premature ventricular contraction at a 1:1 ratio (ventricular bigeminy) with a heart rate of 46/min. Therefore, various blood investigations were ordered to rule out secondary causes that could have led to the changes in the ECG. An urgent appointment was scheduled a week later to review these results. The patient was also advised to seek urgent medical attention if she felt palpitations or giddiness.

During the second consultation, a week later, the repeat ECG showed atrial flutter with a 3:1 atrioventricular block. All the results of the blood investigations were normal, except for an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) levels. Urgent transthoracic echocardiography revealed a dilated left atrium and ventricle without any myocardial hypokinetic changes. A large echogenic mass measuring 3.1×4.1 cm was identified at the left atrium. The mass was solid and appeared pedunculated, arising from a stalk at the endocardium. The patient had a left ventricular ejection fraction of 54%.

The patient was immediately referred to a tertiary care cardiology clinic where a second transthoracic echocardiography was performed. An imaging diagnosis of left atrial myxoma was confirmed. The tumor measured approximately 2.9×3.1 cm. A paroxysmal atrial fibrillation pattern was observed on the ECG. Warfarin treatment was initiated while aiming for a target international normalized ratio between 2 and 3. Currently, the patient is jointly cared for by the primary care physician and a multidisciplinary team that is helping to manage the anticoagulation therapy. The patient is unwilling to undergo surgery to remove the tumor.

The patient has been advised to continue with the recommended medical management and to seek medical attention immediately in case of any symptoms suggestive of cardiac compromise. The patient has been provided with educational resources to manage their condition and follow up with the healthcare team.

Because of this, doctors ordered blood tests to look for other causes of the heart tracing change.

Hospital Course: 

A 30-year-old male presented with fever and was transferred from a local hospital in Yunnan Province. He was diagnosed with acute purulent appendicitis and underwent an appendectomy seven days prior to admission. On admission, he had a temperature of 39.5°C and a blood pressure of 108/78 mmHg. The rest of his physical examination was normal. The laboratory investigations revealed an elevated white blood cell count and an elevated procalcitonin level. The contrast-enhanced computerized tomography (CT) scan of his abdomen showed an ileocecal abscess with a size of 2.3 cm x 2.9 cm. He was treated empirically with intravenous moxifloxacin before the results of blood culture became available.

Management and Treatment:

On Day 3, gram-positive bacilli were identified in two sets of anaerobic blood cultures. The isolate was identified as E. Lenta using MALDI-TOF MS. The appropriate antibiotics were started, and intravenous meropenem was administered at a dose of 1g every 8 hours. The patient responded promptly to meropenem therapy, and percutaneous or surgical drainage of the abscess was not performed. His fever, elevated procalcitonin level, and leukocytosis resolved without surgical intervention.

Discharge Plan:

No microorganisms were identified in the follow-up blood cultures from Day 5. On Day 10, abdominal color Doppler ultrasonography was normal. After a further 6-day course of intravenous meropenem, the patient recovered and was discharged from the hospital. Follow-up appointments were scheduled to monitor his progress and ensure complete recovery.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with a 2-year history of progressive left greater than the right-hand weakness/myelopathy. On physical examination, left greater than the right-sided atrophy of the thenar/hypothenar eminences, and interosseous muscles were observed. Motor nerve conduction/electromyographic studies showed left greater than the right-sided C7-T1 denervation, while sensory conduction studies were normal.

The patient underwent both neutral and flexion MRI scans, revealing diffuse lower cervical spinal cord swelling most severely at C5-C6. A cervical laminectomy with durotomy was performed to obtain an intramedullary cord biopsy to exclude an intrinsic cord tumor. The biopsy showed focal cord ischemia consistent with intrinsic HD.

A C5-C6 ACDF was performed for anterior decompression. Postoperative cervical MRI showed a reduction of the ischemic C5-C6 cord focus, and the patient exhibited no clinical changes. Follow-up MRI scans over the next two years showed a mild progressive focal atrophy of the cord at the C5-C6 level with selective involvement of the anterior horns.

Discharge Diagnosis:
1. Intrinsic HD with cord ischemia.

Discharge Medications:
N/A

Follow-up:
The patient is advised to follow up with the treating neurologist for regular check-ups and further management of his medical condition. Further scans assessing the disease progression may also be ordered. 

Discharge Condition:
The patient's condition has not improved, but the hospitalization resulted in the successful exclusion of an intrinsic cord tumor and confirmation of the diagnosis of Intrinsic HD. The patient is now able to continue his treatment under the guidance of his neurologist as an outpatient.

Hospital Course:

The patient presented with a nodule at the lower abdominal caesarean section scar, which appeared four years after surgery and gradually increased in size. The mass was clinically diagnosed as a tumor on the abdominal wall and was found to have a black appearance. A fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) was performed and the aspirate was collected on glass slides and was wet fixed and then stained by the Papanicolaou method. The diagnosis given on FNAC was suggestive of scar endometriosis. The cell block findings were confirmatory of endometriosis as they revealed endometrial lining columnar epithelium with subepithelial dense and compact endometrial stroma along with extensive areas of hemorrhage. 

Histopathological findings after complete excision of the nodule also confirmed endometriosis. The patient was found physically fit otherwise and was discharged from the hospital in stable condition.

The patient should follow up with her primary care provider for further evaluation and management of her scar endometriosis. She may need to undergo further imaging and testing to monitor the condition and to determine the most appropriate treatment option. The patient should also be advised to seek medical attention if she experiences any new symptoms or changes in her condition.

On the excisional biopsy, the patient was diagnosed with angiosarcoma with microscopic involvement of the margins.

Hospital Course:

The patient underwent MRI, which showed that the tumor invaded subcutaneous fat with reticular patterns and spread galea aponeurotica and epicranial muscles. PET-CT showed diffuse uptake in the scalp and faint uptake in both level VA lymph nodes. He performed wide excision and treated with free latissimus dorsi flap and split-thickness skin graft. After wide resection and reconstruction surgery, multiple lymph node metastases were detected on PET-CT. After radiotherapy and adjuvant chemotherapy, increased uptake lesions were disappeared.

Summary:

In summary, the patient presented to the hospital with angiosarcoma with microscopic involvement of the margins. The treatment plan included wide excision and reconstruction surgery, followed by radiotherapy and adjuvant chemotherapy, which led to the disappearance of the increased uptake lesions. The patient was discharged in stable condition and instructed to follow up with his primary care physician and oncologist for further evaluation and management.

Discharge Summary:

This is a discharge summary for a 74-year-old woman with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma. The patient was admitted to the hospital due to pain in the right lower chest wall, which was found to be caused by cancer that had spread to multiple areas of the body, including the right lung, mediastinal lymph nodes, liver, and pleural nodules.

The patient was prescribed various medications to manage her cancer, including gefitinib and osimertinib, but after several months of treatment, disease progression was observed.

In September 2017, the patient began receiving a combination of low-dose decitabine and camrelizumab, which resulted in significant improvement in the patient's mediastinal lymph nodes, liver, and pleural nodule metastases. However, after 7 cycles of treatment, the patient's disease progressed again, and she stopped receiving this treatment altogether. 

Throughout the patient's treatment, various markers were measured and showed fluctuations, including an increase in TMB and a decrease in TNB during combined therapy; however, the MSI status and HLA LOH events remained unchanged. 

In May 2019, the patient ultimately passed away from multiple organ failure.

The patient was admitted with fever, myalgia, vomiting, nausea, headache, and abdominal pain. Physical examination revealed hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, rash, and conjunctival injection. Laboratory tests showed acute renal failure, albuminuria, hematuria, and thrombocytopenia. The patient had a history of cutting trees in the forest eight days prior but had not traveled to any other HFRS endemic area.

The patient developed seizures on the third day of hospitalization and was transferred to the Intensive Care Unit. CT and MRI scans showed bilateral hypodensities and hyperintensities in frontal, parietal, and occipital regions. No microhemorrhages were observed. The electroencephalogram showed slow wave activity on the left temporal and frontal lobe.

Blood tests revealed hantavirus IgM and IgG antibodies, indicating HFRS. Other serological tests for Leptospira, HBV, and HCV were negative. The patient refused to have a lumbar puncture.

Treatment included supportive therapy with ceftriaxone, corticosteroids, antiepileptics, saline infusions, electrolytes, antipyretics, and oxygen therapy. The patient was discharged after 16 days and underwent another head MRI after 2 months, which resulted normal.

HOSPITAL COURSE

This patient was admitted to our facility for an intense pruritus on her right arm, which had been ongoing for six months. She also complained of right brachial paresis.

COMORBIDITIES

The patient has a known history of multiple myeloma.

DIAGNOSTIC TESTS AND PROCEDURES

Computed tomography of the cervical spine, magnetic resonance imaging, and electromyography of the brachial plexus were performed, which showed right cervical disc herniation with nerve root compression of C6-C7 and right brachial plexus inflammation (Parsonage-Turner syndrome).

DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS

The patient was treated with methylprednisolone aceponate cream 0.1% and oral hydroxyzine 25mg every 8 hours, which resulted in little improvement of the pruritus. Gabapentin was introduced at 900mg/day, which achieved optimal control after three months of follow-up.

FOLLOW-UP INSTRUCTIONS

The patient was referred to neurosurgery and oncology consultation for additional therapeutic orientation.

SUMMARY

The patient presented with brachial plexopathy, which is attributed to neoplastic infiltration of multiple myeloma. The treatment plan included the application of methylprednisolone aceponate cream 0.1% and oral hydroxyzine 25mg every 8 hours, along with the introduction of gabapentin at 900mg/day. The patient was referred to neurosurgery and oncology for further management.

Reason for Admission: Electrical injury 

Hospital Course: The patient, a 49-year-old male electrician, was brought to the emergency department after an electrical injury from contact with a bare cable while working on a rainy day. He lost consciousness but regained it after hitting his back on a cabinet. On examination, a first-degree burn of about 1 cm diameter was observed on his left hand, which correlated with the injury. Laboratory test results were generally normal except for slightly elevated myoglobin levels. Imaging studies showed no abnormalities. He was discharged on the same day after being diagnosed with an electrical injury.

Reason for Hospital Stay: Mild rhabdomyolysis 

During a subsequent follow-up, the patient developed bilateral lower leg soreness and pain, and mild rhabdomyolysis was suspected due to elevated myoglobin levels. He was advised to rest for 2 months, after which he returned to work. However, during this time, he developed numbness in both hands that gradually worsened, causing him discomfort. 

Diagnosis: Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) and bilateral cubital tunnel syndrome 

The patient presented with numbness in both hands, and physical examination demonstrated the presence of a positive Phalen's test but not Tinel's sign. A nerve conduction velocity (NCV) test revealed bilateral CTS and bilateral cubital tunnel syndrome, and the results were near the lower normal limit.

Treatment: Physical therapy and occupational therapy 

The patient was treated with physical therapy and occupational therapy for about half a year. After a significant improvement in the CTS symptoms, he was able to return to work.

Follow-up: Continued observation 

The patient will continue to be followed up to monitor his progress. No other issues were identified during his hospital stay, and he was discharged with no complications. 

Discharge Medications: None 

Discharge Instructions: The patient was advised to continue to monitor his symptoms and return to the hospital if his condition worsens.

Patient Name: Case 2
Date of Service: [DATE]

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 71-year-old man with metastatic EGFR-mutated adenocarcinoma of the lung. He received first-line afatinib and palliative radiotherapy for a metastatic lesion at T8 of the spine. The primary tumor in his left upper lung initially regressed, but demonstrated apparent enlargement 7 months later. Salvage treatment was given using pemetrexed/cisplatin, and the tumor showed partial regression. The patient underwent maintenance pemetrexed for two years with no major side effects. Chest CT revealed enlargement of the primary tumor, with no evidence of extra-thoracic progression. Exertional dyspnea and chest pain also developed. SABR targeted the tumor in his left upper lung with good results and has been unchanged with postradiation fibrotic changes. Currently, the patient has remained on maintenance pemetrexed for more than 48 months with no evidence of disease recurrence.

Discharge Diagnosis:

Metastatic EGFR-mutated adenocarcinoma of the lung with primary tumor enlargement.

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient with metastatic EGFR-mutated adenocarcinoma of the lung received multiple lines of therapy, including afatinib, palliative radiotherapy, pemetrexed/cisplatin, and maintenance pemetrexed. He also underwent SABR for a targeted tumor in his left upper lung. Despite experiencing slight side effects from chemotherapy, the patient tolerated treatment well and continues to be on maintenance pemetrexed with a favorable response.

The patient, a 65-year-old man with no medical history, was admitted to the hospital after presenting with sudden severe right flank pain and haemodynamic instability. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a right large subcapsular, perirenal, and retroperitoneal haematoma compressing and exerting a mass effect on the kidney.

TREATMENT:
The patient was resuscitated and underwent embolisation to control the bleeding. MRI of the abdomen showed a soft tissue mass confined to the perinephric space. A right open radical nephrectomy was performed, and the nephrectomy specimen revealed an infiltrative spindle cell tumour consistent with synovial sarcoma, monophasic type. Hospital Course:

The patient presented to our institution for regular follow-up, 2 years after a right radical nephrectomy for a primary renal cell carcinoma (RCC). The patient was asymptomatic, but an abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan on follow-up revealed a mass in the left adrenal gland. A multidisciplinary team meeting determined that a laparoscopic transperitoneal adrenalectomy was the best course of action.

Procedure:

The patient underwent a laparoscopic transperitoneal adrenalectomy, performed under general anesthesia. The patient was placed in the lateral decubitus position with the left side up. The pneumoperitoneum was established, and a 30° laparoscope and three additional working ports were placed under direct vision. The tumor was exposed and isolated before being excised.

Histological examination:

The histological examination of the specimen demonstrated a metastatic RCC with features similar to the primary renal tumor. All surgical margins were free of tumor.

Outcome:

The postoperative period was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day two. The patient is well and has no recurrence or adrenal insufficiency 18 months post-surgery.

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to our hospital with symptoms of left upper arm weakness and paresthesia. Physical examination revealed left hemiparesis, with diminished left upper and lower strength, and extensor plantar response on the left side. Cranial multimodal computed tomography (CT) imaging showed hypodensity on cortical and subcortical frontoparietal regions, compatible with ischemic stroke, and cranial Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) revealed occlusion of the M2 segment of the middle cerebral artery.

Clinical Findings:

The patient reported a history of substance abuse, with habitual consumption of heroin, methadone, cocaine, and alcohol, as well as smoking crack cocaine the night before the episode. A toxicological screen yielded positive results for cocaine and opioids, and a carotid ultrasound (CU) showed a large soft plaque with an irregular surface and circumferential blood flow at the distal end, inside the internal carotid artery.

Treatment and Management:

The patient was treated with enoxaparin and warfarin therapy, which resulted in gradual dissolution of the thrombus. The patient's symptoms gradually improved during the next few weeks, and she was discharged from the hospital in good general condition.

Follow-Up:

Despite being discharged in good general condition, the patient continued to abuse drugs and experienced another cerebral stroke a year later.

Conclusion:

The patient presented with left hemiparesis, indicating ischemic stroke, and revealed a history of substance abuse. Treatment with enoxaparin and warfarin therapy resulted in the gradual dissolution of the thrombus, and the patient's symptoms improved over time. However, the patient continued to abuse drugs and was readmitted to the hospital a year later after a second cerebral stroke.

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted with a four-month history of a progressively relapsing painless mass in the neck, despite conservative treatments with antimicrobials and anti-inflammatory medications. A clinical examination showed a firm, oval-shaped mass of approximately 7 cm in the long axis at level IV of the left neck. Imaging studies revealed a left lower neck mass with a heterogeneous short T1 signal and heterogeneous post-contrast enhancement at the lateral aspect of the lesion, consistent with a complex tumor with internal hemorrhage or a pseudoaneurysm.

Diagnosis:

The patient's laboratory survey showed a large elevation in the α-fetoprotein level and the β-human chorionic gonadotropin level. Surgical extirpation revealed a large tumor at the left lower neck measuring approximately 10 cm in length. Pathological examination confirmed the diagnosis of a left testicular immature teratoma of high grade with positive left inguinal lymph node metastases.

Treatment:

The patient received left radical inguinal orchiectomy and left inguinal lymph node dissection. Adjuvant chemotherapy with a bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin regimen was administered soon after completion of surgical interventions. Persistent elevated β-human chorionic gonadotropin levels were observed after a full course of four cycles of monthly chemotherapy with an episode of flare-up, which suggested relapse. Salvage second-line chemotherapy was initiated with a paclitaxel, ifosfamide, and cisplatin regimen thereafter.

Follow-up:

The patient tolerated the treatments well without complications and was discharged from the hospital in stable condition. The patient was advised to follow up regularly with his healthcare team for continued monitoring and management of his condition.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted for a growing, painless neck lump that did not improve with antibiotics and anti-inflammatory drugs.
Exam found a firm, oval lump about 7 cm long in the left lower neck, described as solid and non-tender.
Scans showed the lump had uneven signal and uneven enhancement after contrast, especially on its lateral side.
This pattern suggests a complex tumor that may contain internal bleeding or a blood vessel abnormality.
Diagnosis:
Blood tests showed high levels of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (beta-hCG), indicating possible germ cell tumor.
Surgical exploration revealed a tumor approximately 10 centimeters long in the left lower neck area.
Pathology confirmed the tumor was a high-grade immature teratoma that originated in the left testicle.
Further examination showed the cancer had spread to lymph nodes located in the left groin region.
Treatment:
The patient had surgery to remove the left testicle and the lymph nodes in the left groin.
After surgery, they received adjuvant chemotherapy consisting of bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin, commonly known as BEP.
They completed four monthly cycles of this BEP chemotherapy regimen as planned, with each cycle given every three weeks.
After those cycles, beta-hCG levels stayed high and there was a flare-up, suggesting the cancer had returned.
Because of this, a second chemotherapy regimen with paclitaxel, ifosfamide, and cisplatin (TIP) was started.
Follow-up:
The patient tolerated the treatment well, had no complications, and left the hospital in stable condition.
They were advised to see their healthcare team regularly for ongoing monitoring, follow-up tests, and continued care.

Admission Diagnosis:
Atrial septal defect (ASD), Total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVR), congenital second-degree heart block, 2:1 conduction, mild cyanosis, and pulmonary congestion.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital due to the above-listed conditions. The initial physical examination revealed moderate cyanosis with mildly decreased oxygen saturation values of 85%-94%. A postnatal echocardiogram confirmed the presence of TAPVR and bilateral superior vena cava without bridging vein, interrupted inferior vena cava, and a secundum type ASD. The patient underwent a successful cardiac surgery and permanent pacemaker placement at 9 days of age.

Diagnostic Assessments:
CGH array analysis of a peripheral blood sample revealed an 818 kb duplication of the long arm of chromosome 1, and single-nucleotide polymorphism oligonucleotide microarray analysis indicated a gain of chromosome 1. The duplicated region contained 11 genes, seven of which are OMIM annotated, and four have known disease associations.

Condition on Discharge:
The patient was discharged at 3 weeks of age and was doing well. A 2-month follow-up revealed no complications.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient and her family were educated on the importance of close follow-up with a pediatric cardiologist. They were instructed to monitor the infant's health at home, including daily oxygen saturation levels and feeding patterns. The family was also advised to continue the infant's pacemaker monitoring and receive regular immunizations as recommended by her pediatrician.

Follow-up:
The patient is scheduled for regular follow-up appointments with the pediatric cardiologist and primary care physician to monitor the cardiovascular condition, growth, and development. A clinical genetics evaluation will be recommended to assess the chromosomal abnormality's impact on the patient's long-term health. 

Disposition:
The patient was discharged in stable condition, improved cardiovascular symptoms, and with a positive outlook for long-term outcomes.

Hospital Course

This 51-year-old male weighing 131 kg presented to the ED with altered mental status and slurred speech after undergoing cervical epidural injection. He became unresponsive during the injection with subsequent brief convulsive activity. Emergency medical services was called and found him obtunded with shallow breathing and low oxygen saturations requiring ventilation assistance. On arrival to the ED his breathing was erratic with low oxygen saturations. He remained somnolent with slurred speech, unable to answer questions appropriately or follow commands. On cardiopulmonary monitor, he was noted to have an irregularly irregular heart rhythm. Electrocardiogram showed atrial fibrillation with a rate of 82 beats per minute. Hemodynamically he was stable. Within 60 minutes of ED arrival, the patient’s mental status was back to baseline without recollection of the events that had occurred after the start of the procedure. Imaging studies obtained were all negative. 

Hospital Course: Diagnosis and Treatment

The patient was observed overnight in the hospital and remained asymptomatic and without any further dysrhythmia. He only had chest wall pain, possibly from sternal rub or from any bystander chest compressions that may have been performed when he became unresponsive. Serum/plasma levels of lidocaine and its primary active metabolite, monoethylglycinexylidide (MEGX), were obtained and returned undetectable. Aspirin 325 mg daily was prescribed and a referral to outpatient cardiology was made. 

Condition at Discharge

The patient was discharged with no symptoms and normal mental status.

A 51-year-old man weighing 289 pounds came to the emergency department confused and with trouble speaking after a neck injection.
He became unresponsive during the injection and had a brief seizure, then stopped responding for a short time.
An ambulance was called and found him very drowsy with short breaths and low oxygen levels, needing help to breathe.
When he arrived at the emergency department, his breathing was uneven and his oxygen levels remained low.
He stayed sleepy, spoke unclearly, and could not answer questions or follow directions during his stay.

The patient remains free from recurrence nine months after the second operation.

Patient Name: Confidential

Gender: Male

Discharge Date: [Date]

Admitting Diagnosis: Nasal deformity

Hospital Course:

The patient presented to the otolaryngology clinic with a nasal deformity that had been present for several years, but the patient claimed growth of the mass over the previous year. The patient had no history of alcoholism or dermatological disease. On physical examination, there was a large, pedunculated, swollen, irregular mass measuring 9 cm × 8 cm, occupying the area at the tip and the dorsum of the nose. The remaining head and neck examination was normal.

The lesion was excised completely with sharp scalpel incision and coblation-assisted dissection under general anesthesia. The Artrocare probe of coblation device designed for turbinate surgery was used. Reconstruction of the defect was performed with a full-thickness skin graft obtained from the upper arm. No recurrence was seen during the 1-year follow-up period.

Pathology:

Histopathological examination of the biopsy specimens showed hyperkeratosis of the epidermis, increased sebaceous glands, and cystic expansion of ducts in the dermis. Duct lumen was dilated and filled with keratin plugs. Fibrosis and chronic lymphoplasmocytic cell infiltration were observed around the ducts. Neoplastic cells were not seen.

Summary:

The patient was admitted to the otolaryngology clinic with nasal deformity. The lesion was excised completely with sharp scalpel incision and coblation-assisted dissection under general anesthesia. Reconstruction of the defect was performed with a full-thickness skin graft obtained from the upper arm. The pathology report showed no evidence of neoplastic cells. The patient remained free from recurrence during the 1-year follow-up period.

This is a discharge summary for [Redacted], a 57-year-old female with a history of recurrent breast cancer who was admitted to our facility with bilateral thigh pain and weakness. In the fourth and final phase, she underwent dynamic gait activities including turning her head or body, speed variation, and ambulation over or around obstacles. She was discharged home 29 days after her initial presentation to the hospital, with a marked improvement in functional status as well as subjective reports in confidence and pain.

Upon discharge, the patient demonstrated improvement with pain at 0/10. Her quadriceps and hip strength improved bilaterally. Her TUG test improved to 10 seconds and she was able to ambulate community distances with a walker at discharge. Her Berg Balance Scale results improved to indicate a low fall risk at 55/56. Follow-up appointments were scheduled to monitor her progress.

Admission Diagnosis: Poor oral intake, pneumonia, and hypokalemia
Discharge Diagnosis: Hypokalemia and possible medication-induced hypokalemia

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital for investigation of poor oral intake, hypokalemia, and pneumonia. The patient had discontinued medication for benign prostatic hyperplasia. The patient had been recently diagnosed with cognitive dysfunction and was started on choline alfoscerate and donepezil. Investigations showed hypokalemia and the presence of subtle pneumonia. Further investigations were done to determine the cause of hypokalemia which revealed signs of renal potassium wasting. CT scan showed no abnormalities. A thorough review of the therapeutic agents prescribed for cognitive dysfunction was conducted, which identified donepezil as a possible cause of hypokalemia. Donepezil was immediately discontinued. Potassium supplementation using intravenous and oral formulations was initiated. The patient showed a gradual increase in serum potassium level and on the third day following donepezil cessation, the patient's serum potassium level was 3.5 mmol/L. During this time, proper management of pneumonia was also done. BP was noted to be high for 24 hours after hospitalization and amlodipine and olmesartan were initiated.

Discharge Medications:
Amlodipine and olmesartan were prescribed for BP management.

Follow-up:
The patient was discharged on the ninth day of hospitalization. The patient was advised to continue potassium supplementation for a total of 3 weeks. Olmesartan and amlodipine were prescribed to be continued. The patient was advised to have regular BP monitoring and to follow-up with a primary care doctor.

Instructions to Patient:
The patient was advised to follow a low sodium and low fat diet as well as avoid food high in potassium. The patient was advised to adhere to prescribed medications and avoid over-the-counter medications without consulting a physician. The patient was advised to return to the hospital if any concerning symptoms are noted.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [INSERT NAME]
Sex: Female
Age: 65 years
Medical record number: [INSERT NUMBER]
Discharge Date: [INSERT DATE]

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with complaints of pain and swelling of the left hand along the thenar eminence and the proximal aspect of the thumb. She also had cervical lymphadenopathy. A plain radiograph showed pathological fracture of the base of 1st metacarpal along with lytic lesion at the base of the 1st metacarpal with haziness of the surrounding soft tissue. An ultrasound revealed presence of an abscess. The MRI scan suggested an abscess like picture most likely due to infective etiology and less likely to be neoplastic lesion. 

The patient underwent drainage of abscess and debridement with stabilization of the fracture fragment. Intra-operatively we found thick caseous material within the soft tissue and the fragment at base of the 1st metacarpal was freely mobile similar to a loose body. The fragment was removed and sent for biopsy and culture sensitivity along with the surrounding soft-tissue. A kirschner wire was passed through the 1st carpo-metacarpal joint to stabilize it. 

The biopsy report came back positive for tuberculous osteomyelitis which suggested fibro-collagenous tissue and few bony fragments showing large caseous necrosis with few epitheloidid cell granuloma. The patient was then started on anti-tuberculous treatment emprerically while awaiting the culture report. A Combination of Isoniazid, Rifampicin, Pyrazinamide and ethambutol was started. 

At the end of 5 weeks the kirschner wire backed out partially which was then removed and range of movement exercises were started. The cervical lymphadenopathy regressed by the end of 3 months. The patient had 1 episode of recurrence of cervical lymphandenopathy at the end of 7 months of treatment which eventually regressed on the continuous phase of AKT. 

At the end of one year, the patient had almost complete range of movement with no sequel due to tuberculosis as compared to the opposite hand. Plain radiographs showed some degree of joint remodelling at one year. 

Discharge Medications:
The patient is dispensed her usual home medications.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient is advised to follow up with the orthopedic surgeon regularly and continue taking the prescribed medication. The patient is counselled to adopt a healthy lifestyle and a balanced diet. Any symptoms of recurrence or deterioration should be reported to the physician immediately. Additionally, the patient is advised regarding the importance and significance of regular follow-up, which is critical to the management of her condition.

Follow-up:
The patient is referred to the orthopedic surgeon for follow-up to assess progress and discuss the patient's ongoing management.

Patient Name: [Redacted]

Sex: Male

Date of Admission: [Redacted]
Date of Discharge: N/A

Hospital Course:

The patient presented to the emergency room with massive upper gastrointestinal bleeding and was admitted to the Habib Thameur Hospital. Physical examination revealed diffuse mucocutaneous pallor and a Glasgow Coma Score of 15/15. The patient had tachycardia, hypotension, and enlarged spleen without hepatomegaly. The rectal digital examination was positive for melena. Laboratory investigations showed decreased white blood cell count, thrombocytopenia, and normochromic normocytic anemia. Minor signs of hepatocellular insufficiency were displayed but albuminemia was normal. An acute kidney failure was also noted. The results of the patient’s tests indicated no signs of hepatitis C, hepatitis B surface antigen, and hepatitis B core antibody. 

The patient was stabilized following fluid resuscitation and blood transfusion of two red blood cell concentrates. The patient was treated with a proton-pump inhibitor (omeprazole) and octreotide. An upper gastroduodenoscopy showed the presence of oesophageal varices with massive active bleeding, moderate hypertensive gastropathy, and gastric varicose veins. Several elastics with a first and second kit of ligature were put in place to control the bleeding. An abdominal ultrasound showed the presence of multiple multiloculated cystic formations suggesting multiple liver hydatidosis.

The patient suffered from a cataclysmic re-bleeding causing refractory hemorrhagic shock and disseminated intravenous coagulation leading to death after a week.

Impression:

The patient's clinical history, physical examination, and laboratory investigations suggest multiple liver hydatidosis and acute kidney failure. The patient was treated with a proton-pump inhibitor (omeprazole) and octreotide with the aim of controlling the bleeding. However, the patient suffered from a cataclysmic re-bleeding causing refractory hemorrhagic shock, disseminated intravenous coagulation, and death.

Exam showed very pale skin and mouth tissues and the patient was fully awake and alert.
The patient had a fast heart rate, low blood pressure, an enlarged spleen but normal liver size.
A rectal exam found dark, tarry stool, which is a sign of bleeding in the digestive tract.
Blood tests showed low white blood cells, low platelets, and anemia with normal cell size and color.
There were slight signs of liver trouble, but the albumin level in the blood was normal.
In addition, the patient experienced sudden kidney failure, which means the kidneys stopped working quickly.
Laboratory tests showed no hepatitis B or C infection, which helped rule out viral liver disease.
After receiving fluids and two units of blood transfusion, the patient’s condition stabilized and vital signs improved.
The patient received omeprazole and octreotide to actually try to stop the upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
An endoscopy revealed large bleeding veins in the esophagus, some stomach lining changes, and swollen stomach veins.
Doctors placed several elastic bands around the bleeding veins to stop the blood flow effectively.
Ultrasound showed many cyst-like spots in the liver, suggesting the presence of hydatid disease, a parasitic infection.
Later, the patient bled heavily again, leading to shock that did not respond to treatment.
This caused widespread clotting throughout the blood vessels and led to death after about a week.
Impression:
The patient’s history, exam, and tests point to liver hydatid disease and sudden kidney failure.
Treatment with omeprazole and octreotide was given to try to stop the upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
Despite this treatment, the patient experienced massive re-bleeding, irreversible shock, widespread clotting, and ultimately died.

Hospital Course:
A 24-year-old male was admitted to the emergency department due to multiple gunshot wounds. Physical examination showed that the patient was hemodynamically stable, and no additional findings were noted. 
Further workup including CT scans led to the discovery of a bullet in the right ventricle. Cardiothoracic surgery and cardiology were consulted, and an attempt at endovascular retrieval was made. However, due to the bullet being embedded in the right ventricular trabeculations, a median sternotomy was performed with cardiopulmonary bypass and cardioplegic arrest to successfully remove the bullet. The patient was subsequently transferred to the ICU for further observation. 
On the sixth postoperative day, the patient developed a fever, and further imaging revealed a large pericardial effusion and moderate right pleural effusion with right lower lobe collapse. Pericardiocentesis was performed, and a drain was left in place to evacuate the effusion. The patient's condition continued to improve, and he was stable for transfer to a comprehensive rehabilitation center on the fifteenth postoperative day.

A 24-year-old man came to the emergency room with several gunshot wounds and needed immediate care.
The exam showed the patient's blood pressure and heart were stable, and no other problems were found.
Additional tests, including CT scans, found a bullet inside the right ventricle of the heart.
Heart surgeons and heart doctors were asked to help, and they tried to remove the bullet through a blood vessel.
Because the bullet was stuck in the heart muscle, doctors opened the chest, used a heart-lung machine, and removed it.
After the surgery, the patient was moved to the intensive care unit for close watching.
On the sixth day after surgery, the patient got a fever and needed more tests.
Scans showed a large fluid buildup around the heart, called a pericardial effusion.
They also showed a moderate fluid buildup in the right lung with part of the lung collapsed.
Doctors performed a procedure to remove the fluid around the heart and left a drain to keep draining it.
The patient kept getting better and was well enough to go to a rehab center on day fifteen after surgery.

This is a 48-year-old female patient, who was admitted to our hospital for surgical treatment of a recurrence of squamous cell carcinoma on the left mandible body. She underwent a wide excision and left mandibulectomy followed by a mandible, mouth floor, and tongue reconstruction with a titanium implant and an anterolateral thigh (ALT) free flap. The patient received adjuvant radiation and chemotherapy due to the recurrence of the disease after previous surgery. The patient did not have any suspicious tumor recurrence on the follow-up CT.

The designed implant was manufactured using an A1 metal 3D printer with a biocompatibility material that was composed of titanium, aluminum, and vanadium. The prosthesis appeared well positioned on the radiograph taken after surgery.

The patient was discharged from the hospital and advised to continue follow-up care with the multidisciplinary team. Further information and recommendations for follow-up care were discussed with the patient and their family.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: Not Disclosed
Gender: Female
Age: 80

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with a history of a slow-growing, painless cyst in the right lateral orbital region, which was evaluated through mechanical ptosis, proptosis, and slight hypotropia. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a round mass with no enhancement by gadolinium, and computed tomography (CT) presented with deformation of the right orbit with bone erosion centering on the frontosphenoidal suture and confirmed the diagnosis of a dermoid cyst. The patient declined surgical removal with boney reconstruction and continued with periodic aspiration. Sclerotherapy was performed after obtaining informed consent and aspirating the fluid multiple times. The first sclerotherapy was performed with 10 mL of 1% lidocaine containing 1:100,000 epinephrine and 10 mL of absolute ethanol was instilled, and the cavity was washed again with 10 mL of saline. Second and third sclerotherapies were performed at intervals of 3 months. After the final sclerotherapy, the cyst had shrunk in size, and no re-expansion was seen during a 1-year follow-up after the last sclerotherapy. The patient complained of visual field disturbance due to redundant skin, and a blepharoplasty was performed concomitant with incisional biopsy of the cyst. Histopathological examination showed that the specimen comprised dermis with well-developed sweat and sebaceous glands, compatible with a dermoid cyst.

Condition at Discharge:
The patient's dermoid cyst was treated successfully with sclerotherapy and incisional biopsy. At the time of discharge, the patient demonstrated no evidence of a recurring cyst.

Follow-Up Plan:
The patient will continue follow-up care with her primary care physician near her home residence and is advised to inquire if any new symptoms arise.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 56-year-old male electrician, was admitted to the hospital with chest pain that had lasted for about an hour. The patient had a history of treated hypertension, occasional atypical chest pain, and negative ischaemia induced by stress through exercise stress testing conducted two years ago. On admission, the patient had tachypnoea at rest, and his oxygen saturation was 93%. The ECG showed atrial fibrillation with a heart rate of 90 beats/min, and blood pressure was 175/95 mm Hg.

A cardioversion with DC shock (3 J/Kg body weight) was performed, considering the slightly elevated cardiac enzymes of troponin T and creatine kinase and to exclude coronary disease. Subsequently, a coronary angiography (CAG) was performed, and a suspect of single coronary vessel originating from the right sinus of Valsalva was revealed. The right coronary artery (RCA) showed normal course, no stenoses were present, and no atherosclerotic plaque was found on the MSCT scan.

The patient's left ventricular wall motion and ejection fraction were normal (ejection fraction EF 60%). The patient was discharged with only antihypertensive drug therapy. At the 2-month follow-up, he reported no angina and no exertion dyspnea, and his left ventricular ejection fraction was still normal. The patient was advised to avoid strenuous work (under 6 METs) and work on overhead lines too.

Hospital Course Summary:
The 56-year-old male electrician was admitted to the hospital with chest pain for about an hour. After performing cardioversion and CAG, a multi-slices computed tomography (MSCT) revealed a suspect of single coronary vessel originating from the right sinus of Valsalva, with no stenoses or atherosclerotic plaque and with normal left ventricular wall motion and ejection fraction. The patient was discharged with only antihypertensive drug therapy in stable condition. At the 2-month follow-up, his left ventricular ejection fraction remained normal, and he reported no chest pain or exertion dyspnea. The patient was advised to avoid strenuous work (under 6 METs) and work on overhead lines too.

Hospital Course:

Patient is a 29-year-old female who was admitted at 21 weeks postpartum due to symptoms of diarrhea mixed with blood and abdominal pain. Colonoscopy revealed diffuse inflammation from the rectum to the proximal descending colon with multiple yellow-white color spots consistent with findings of UC. Sulfasalazine was prescribed and the patient's symptoms improved, leading to her discharge after 2 weeks hospitalization. Soon after discharge, sulfasalazine was replaced by mesalazine and the patient resumed breastfeeding.

At 27 weeks postpartum, the patient was admitted for 12 days of educational hospitalization for UC. During this time, a lacto-ovo-semi-vegetarian diet was provided and the patient received guidance on a plant-based diet. Colonoscopy at the end of the hospitalization revealed endoscopic remission of UC. The patient's mesalazine dose was gradually decreased to 0.4 g/day on discharge.

During an interview and questionnaire on lifestyle and dietary habits, the patient reported a dietary change during the postpartum period. The patient stayed at her parent's home for about 3 months after delivery, during which her mother prepared traditional Japanese Washoku meals recommended by the midwife. After returning home, the patient reported a decline in dietary quality and a tendency towards constipation and epigastric distress. This dietary change was assessed by plant-based diet score (PBDS).

Outcome:

The patient was discharged in stable condition and advised to continue a plant-based diet. The patient stopped taking her medication 3 weeks after discharge and remained in remission without medication to the present.

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Date of Admission: [Redacted]
Date of Discharge: [Redacted]

Medical History:
The patient was a 26-year-old female who had been diagnosed with colon cancer six years prior. The patient presented to the hospital for routine control.

Hospital Course:
Upon examination, the patient had no clinical complaints and no apparent physical findings. Further diagnostic evaluation included a contrast-enhanced CCT scan, which identified a perihilar mass with a smooth contour and homogeneous internal structure. Multiple mediastinal lymph nodes were also identified. The patient underwent a positron emission tomography with 2-deoxy-2-[fluorine-18] fluoro- D-glucose integrated with computed tomography (18F-FDG PET/CT), which showed slightly increased 18F-FDG uptake in the identified mass. In addition, the patient underwent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the thorax, which showed a lesion that was isointense with muscle in T1-weighted images, hyperintense in T2-weighted images, and enhanced homogeneously in post-contrast series. Based on the imaging findings and patient history, the following differential diagnoses were considered: metastasis, primary lung cancer, lymphoma, and sarcoidosis.

Results:
In laboratory tests, it was found that the patient's IgG4 value was elevated to 723 mg/dL (135mg/dL).

Diagnosis:
A surgical lung biopsy was performed, and the diagnosis was reported as IgG4-related respiratory disease (IgG4-RRD).

Condition at Discharge:
At the time of discharge, the patient's condition was stable. The patient was provided with information regarding the diagnosis and advised to follow up with their primary care physician for continued management and care.

Follow-Up Care:
Follow-up care was recommended with the primary care physician for continued monitoring and management of the patient's condition.

Summary:
The patient, a 26-year-old female with a history of colon cancer, presented to the hospital for routine control. Diagnostic evaluation identified a perihilar mass with multiple mediastinal lymph nodes, and further testing revealed an elevated IgG4 value. A surgical lung biopsy was performed, and the diagnosis was reported as IgG4-RRD. The patient was advised to follow up with their primary care physician for continued management and care.

The patient was discharged in stable condition with recommendations for follow-up visits as prescribed by the surgical team.

Patient Information:
- Patient: 15-year-old girl
- Diagnosis: Congenital Hyperinsulinism (CHI)
- Treatment: Diazoxide, Octreotide, Lanreotide

Hospital Course Summary:
- Patient with CHI was admitted electively to our pediatric inpatient unit to decide on an alternative medical treatment due to the troublesome hypertrichosis caused by diazoxide.
- Trial off diazoxide was performed whereby, diazoxide was gradually weaned and stopped for 72 hours. However, this led to subsequent development of recurrent symptomatic hypoglycaemia.
- Octreotide (a somatostatin analogue) was then commenced as four times daily subcutaneous injection.
- A good glycemic response was noted at this dose and she was able to tolerate a fast for a period of 24 hours with no evidence of hypoglycaemia.
- Lanreotide (long-acting somatostatin analogue) was commenced as a subcutaneous injection 30 mg once monthly and octreotide was gradually weaned and stopped.
- Continuous blood glucose monitoring system following the administration of lanreotide revealed good glycemic control with no episodes of hypoglycemia.
- Patient developed recurrent symptomatic hypoglycemic episodes after starting fluoxetine. Fluoxetine was discontinued and hypoglycemic episodes resolved within a week.
- Two weeks after the discontinuation of fluoxetine, the patient's depressive symptoms slowly improved over time with the help of counselling.

Final Diagnosis:
- Congenital Hyperinsulinism (CHI)

Follow-up Plan:
- No further specific follow-up needed at this time.

Hospital Course:

A 44-year-old Caucasian male was admitted to the emergency department after being trapped under the transmission system of a vehicle for an unknown amount of time, causing trauma to his chest and lungs. On admission, the patient had gasping breath, palpable regular pulses, and low blood pressure. He was urgently intubated and put on controlled mechanical ventilation due to his altered consciousness and respiratory distress. Upon examination, the patient's chest and upper body were congested, edematous, and covered with petechiae. Bilateral pneumothorax was detected, and bloody fluid was drained from his lungs through the endotracheal tube. The patient's condition improved after bilateral thoracostomies were inserted, draining air and blood. Arterial blood gases showed a pH of 7.246 and high levels of enzymes associated with muscle breakdown. A CT scan revealed mild brain edema and bilateral hemopneumothorax with lung contusions.

The patient was transferred to the ICU, where he was ventilated with volume-control mode, with a gas mixture that was quickly tapered to a fraction of inspired oxygen of 40%. Care was taken to prevent renal complications from potential traumatic rhabdomyolysis, and special attention was given to the brain edema with mannitol administration and frequent neurologic assessments. The patient improved quickly and was extubated on the second day of hospitalization, but remained disoriented and agitated until the fourth day. His facial and thoracic petechiae gradually faded within the next three days. The patient's enzymes returned to normal levels on the seventh day, and he was transferred to the thoracic surgical ward.

Recommendations:

The patient is advised to continue with follow-up appointments with his healthcare provider to monitor his progress. He should avoid activities that may place excessive stress on his chest and lungs, and he should report any changes in his symptoms to his healthcare provider immediately. The patient should also continue to take any medications as prescribed and follow a healthy lifestyle to aid in his recovery. 

For further medical attention, the patient is advised to contact the healthcare provider immediately should he experience any of the following symptoms: chest pain, shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, fever, or cough with abnormal sputum production.
