Hospital Course:

The 8-year-old female patient presented for evaluation of a slowly growing, plaque-like skin lesion on her left chest wall. The lesion was approximately 0.5 cm in maximum diameter in size and was too small and with a light violet color. Ultrasound examination revealed an ovoid, well-demarcated lesion in the subcutaneous region with dermal involvement and without clear separation from the underlying muscle. The patient underwent surgical excision and biopsy, and the pathology report described the specimen as having a white-gray nodular lesion with spindle cells developed in a storiform to whorled pattern. The differential diagnosis included DFSP and Dermatofibroma. A confident diagnosis of DFSP was made based on immunohistochemical expression of CD34 and negative FXIIIA and S100. 

After the diagnosis, the patient underwent extensive imaging and hematological testing which were without pathological findings. Although the margins of the removed mass were healthy, we decided to perform extended surgical excision to decrease the possibility of recurrence. The child's postoperative course was uneventful, and she will be examined every 6 months for the next 3 years for palpation of her scar tissue and examination of her regional lymph nodes to exclude recurrence or the possibility of metastases.

Impression & Plan:

The patient was diagnosed with DFSP based on biopsy. Extended surgical excision was performed, and the patient will undergo regular follow-up appointments. Further treatment is not required at this time.

Patient Name: [Name]

HOSPITAL COURSE:

The patient, a 70-year-old male with rheumatoid arthritis, was admitted with complaints of shortness of breath and productive cough. His RA had been controlled well without any symptoms such as arthritis before the presentation, indicating a low activity of the disease. A blood test showed elevated C-reactive protein, Lactate Dehydrogenase, and soluble interleukin-2 receptor levels. EBV antibody tests confirmed prior infection.

Chest computed tomography revealed interstitial pneumonia affecting the bilateral lower lung fields with multiple nodular shadows. Sputum cytology performed showed atypical lymphoid cells with low cell connectivity, a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, foamy cytoplasm, coarsely granular chromatin and distinct nucleoli. Lung biopsy demonstrated atypical mid- to large-sized lymphoid cells with a high N/C ratio, cleaved nuclei and distinct nucleoli. The patient was diagnosed with MTX-LPD (non-germinal center B-cell-like DLBCL histological type).

Bronchoscopy showed protuberating mucosa with vascular proliferation and bleeding tendency. The patient was treated by withdrawing MTX. Most of the nodules disappeared spontaneously about 3 weeks after MTX withdrawal; thereafter, only tacrolimus was used. The patient was observed for a period of 15 months after MTX withdrawal, and there was no progression of the disease.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSES:

1. MTX-LPD (non-germinal center B-cell-like DLBCL histological type)

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:

1. Continue to take prescribed medications as directed by the primary care physician.
2. Avoid exposure to airborne irritants to prevent respiratory infections.
3. Follow up with regular doctor appointments to monitor health status and medication response.

FOLLOW-UP CARE:

The patient has been referred to a hematologist for ongoing management of lymphoproliferative disorder after MTX withdrawal.

The patient is a 28-year-old male who was treated for PEComa in 2006 and 2014. He underwent a lower anterior resection followed by segmental hepatectomy. The patient is currently undergoing regular surveillance with no recurrence of PEComa identified since the primary surgery in 2006.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to the hospital in November 2006 with symptoms of cramping, abdominal pain, and intermittent melena. Physical examination revealed generalized weakness, dizziness, and massive bloody stool passage. Laboratory tests showed an elevated white blood cell count, low hemoglobin and hematocrit levels, and a normal serum carcinoembryonic antigen level. Diagnostic imaging and biopsy identified a transmural tumor in the rectum, which was later diagnosed as metastatic PEComa.

The patient underwent lower anterior resection in 2006, followed by regular surveillance. The distant liver metastasis progressed slowly over the years, which prompted the patient to undergo segmental hepatectomy in 2014. The pathology report confirmed the presence of metastatic PEComa.

Upon the postoperative analysis, the patient remained free of disease even after 28 months of follow-up.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Metastatic PEComa of rectum and liver

Follow-Up:
The patient is currently undergoing regular surveillance without any reported symptoms or signs of PEComa recurrence. The general clinical examination, subsequent colonoscopies, and abdominal CT scans are performed once every 3 months.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 51-year-old female

Admission Date: February 2013

Discharge Date: October 2015

Diagnosis: Recurrent Ameloblastoma

Procedure: Right mandibular resection and reconstruction with nonvascularized free iliac bone followed by dental implant placement and fixed prosthesis

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the department in February 2013 due to discomfort in the mandible. She had been diagnosed with recurrent ameloblastoma and had undergone multiple fenestration procedures in the past. The patient was dissatisfied with the outcomes of previous hospital's treatment policy and came to our department for the complete resection of the tumor. 
After thorough evaluation and diagnosis, we proposed a treatment protocol of radical resection and immediate bony reconstruction using nonvascularized free iliac bone graft. The patient underwent right mandibular resection (teeth 43 to 46; length 35 mm) in March 2013 and was closely monitored for tumor recurrence. 
Follow-up examinations showed no signs of tumor recurrence, but the patient continued to experience right-sided difficulty in mastication. Therefore, a fixed prosthesis was recommended. In November 2014, the mini-plate was removed from the grafted bone, and four dental implants were placed. Subsequently, the patient underwent vestibuloplasty (vestibular extension with periosteal separation procedures) and confirmed osseointegration in all four implants. The final fixed prosthesis was worn by the patient in October 2015. 
The patient's oral hygiene has been regularly managed, and no signs of tumor recurrence or abnormal bone absorption or disintegration of the dental implants have been observed. The patient was discharged in October 2015.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient is advised to continue maintaining good oral hygiene and to follow the regular maintenance therapy schedule. The patient should keep all appointments with the department for proper monitoring of tumor recurrence and dental implant health. If there are any concerns or questions, the patient should contact the department for further consultations.

The patient, a 29-year-old Caucasian male, was admitted to the hospital due to dyspnea, fatigue, edema of the legs, and abdominal pain. The physical examination revealed LV enlargement with congestive hepatomegaly, symmetrical edema of both lower extremities, and orthopnea. The patient also had a grade III/VI systolic murmur at the upper left sternal border, increased jugular venous pressure, and normal heart sounds. The patient's medical imaging revealed cardiomegaly, a dilated and remodeled, spherical LV, with morphological changes, and multiple mobile thrombi located between apical trabeculations. The patient exhibited ventricular tachycardia episodes, with RBBB morphology, frequent PVC, functional mitral regurgitation due to LV remodeling, decreased LV systolic function, and restrictive LV filling pattern. Additional findings included LV diastolic dysfunction, hepatic and renal infarctions, high levels of NT-pBNP, and moderate tricuspid regurgitation. Genetic tests for Fabry disease, as well as for Gaucher and Niemann–Peck diseases, were negative.

During the patient's hospital course, he was treated with anticoagulants, antiarrhythmics, diuretics, beta-blockers, and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors. After 2 months of anticoagulation and treatment of heart failure, follow-up echocardiographic evaluation detected no thrombi in the apex of the LV between trabeculations, and the patient had no signs of heart failure. A cardioverter defibrillator was implanted for the prevention of sudden cardiac death, and the patient was proposed for cardiac transplantation.

In conclusion, a 29-year-old Caucasian male was admitted to the hospital due to symptoms of LV enlargement with congestive hepatomegaly, symmetrical edema of both lower extremities, and orthopnea. The patient exhibited a restrictive LV filling pattern, hepatic and renal infarctions, and moderate tricuspid regurgitation. Medical management with anticoagulants, antiarrhythmics, diuretics, beta-blockers, and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors was initiated, and the patient was proposed for cardiac transplantation.

Discharge Summary:
Patient: 39-year-old female

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with complaints of foreign-body sensation and epiphora in her left eye. A slit-lamp examination revealed multiple milky-white soft masses on the corneal surface of her left eye. A slight opacity was suspected in the anterior stroma under the slit-lamp examination. Upon investigation, these masses were classified as having a gelatinous dystrophy-like appearance and were located at the cilia-attached region. An OCT scan revealed a large mass under the thinned epithelial layer with no destruction on Bowman’s layer throughout the region. The fellow cornea exhibited a linear subepithelial opacity that was not stained by fluorescein under a slit-lamp examination, and an OCT scan revealed a high-density spot in Bowman’s layer, which was coincident with the cilia-attached region and linear line observed under slit-lamp examination.

Treatment:
To treat the foreign-body sensation, the patient underwent lamellar keratoplasty. The corneal tissues were excised, and the excised specimens were frozen and cut into sections. These sections were incubated with antilactoferrin antibody and fixed with Congo red. Histological analysis revealed that the eosinophilic material was positively stained with Congo red showing apple-green birefringence under polarized light. The material was also positive when using the antilactoferrin antibody, with this area matching the Congo red-positive region.

Outcome:
Postoperative recovery was smooth, and there was no recurrence of amyloid deposition. Ten months after the operation, the corrected visual acuity of the patient’s left eye was 20/20. Epilation of the cilia is performed regularly.

Small bowel obstruction in the midabdomen encased by a thickened peritoneum due to peritoneal fibrosis.

The patient will be monitored for signs of recurrence, but as of the most recent follow-up 28 months after surgery, the patient has shown no signs of recurrence.

The patient presented with a rare case of small bowel obstruction due to peritoneal fibrosis which required surgical intervention. The surgery was successful, and the patient had an uneventful postoperative course with no signs of recurrence at the most recent follow-up.

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient came in because of facial twitching and weakness, loose skin, and a deep groove in the tongue that had gotten worse over four years.
These symptoms caused numbness in the right hand, occasional cramps in the right calf, and less sweating on both hands.
The exam showed slight weakness in the muscles around the eyes and mouth, but no weakness or feeling changes in the arms or legs.
His mother, maternal uncle, and two sisters had similar symptoms, but no relatives outside the Korean family did.
Tests of nerve and muscle function showed problems with both facial nerves, long-term nerve loss in the neck and lower back areas, and reduced sweat gland activity.
To find the cause of the unexplained nerve problem, a whole-exome gene test was done after consent and it found a specific change (p.D214Y) in the GSN gene.
DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS:
Progressive nerve damage linked to a change in the GSN gene.
DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS:
No medication information was given.
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS:
The patient should see their primary care doctor for follow-up.

Discharge Summary:
Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 70-year-old male with a history of chronic myeloid leukemia, peripheral arterial disease, hypothyroidism, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, high cholesterol, and gout, presented with complaints of altered mental status and abdominal pain. On examination, the patient was found to be hypotensive and tachycardic, and a blocked chronic Foley catheter was noted with purulent drainage. The patient was diagnosed with acute kidney injury, leukocytosis, and lactic acidosis upon initial laboratory testing. CT abdomen pelvis without contrast showed gastric pneumatosis with adjacent left upper quadrant portal venous gas along with branching portal venous gas throughout the liver.

Treatment and Management:
The patient was started on a broad-spectrum antibiotic regimen that included cefepime, vancomycin and meropenem. Blood and urine cultures were sent for analysis. The patient was also administered fluid resuscitation, and vasopressor infusion was initiated when blood pressure didn't improve. The general surgery and gastroenterology teams were consulted; esophagogastroduodenoscopy were performed, which revealed proximal stomach ischemia with some necrosis. Biopsies revealed acute hemorrhagic gastritis secondary to ischemia with a recommendation of surgical resection. Surgical resection was deemed inappropriate as the patient was not an eligible candidate due to multiple comorbidities and was managed conservatively.

Follow Up:
The patient's acute renal failure resolved days later, and repeat CT angiography revealed no apparent issues of concern. Thereafter the patient slowly exhibited clinical improvement and repeat EGD revealed gastritis in the proximal stomach with healthy pink mucosa and no signs of ischemia or necrosis. The patient was gradually resumed on an oral diet and was later transferred to the medical floor upon completion of antibiotic therapy. The patient was then discharged to a long-term acute care facility.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission Date: [date]
Discharge Date: [date]

Patient Name: [name]
Age: 68 years
Sex: Male

Medical History:
- Prostate cancer treated with radiation therapy, 3 years ago
- Endoscopic polypectomy for colonic polyps, 1 year ago
- Chronic constipation

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with sudden-onset upper abdominal pain and was found to have a fist-sized mass lesion located between the stomach and pancreas on computed tomography (CT) without contrast. He was initially diagnosed with a malignant tumor with peritonitis carcinomatosa and hospitalized for further examinations and observation. However, the next day, he was found to have intra-abdominal hemorrhage and was transferred to our hospital, a tertiary emergency center, for further diagnosis and treatments.

On arrival at our hospital, the patient was alert and well oriented. A physical examination revealed moderate tenderness in his left upper abdomen with a peritoneal sign. His laboratory data showed mild leukocytosis, moderate anemia, elevated urea nitrogen level, and high serum amylase. The results of a CT with contrast demonstrated an unenhanced, high-density, homogeneous, mass-like lesion located to the ventral side of the pancreatic tail, and a large amount of ascites, which suggested a hematoma and massive intraabdominal hemorrhage. 

An emergency exploratory laparotomy was performed and a 5 cm laceration was found in the mesentery of transverse colon, which arose from the left margin of Treitz's ligament extending in the left direction. Hemostasis was achieved by suture ligations and absorbable hemostat materials were applied on the oozing points. Intraoperative blood transfusion was performed, and the operation was uncomplicated except for temporary paralytic ileus. The patient was discharged in a good postoperative condition on the postoperative day 20.

During the patient's hospital stay, we discovered that he had a history of intractable constipation and had a habit of massaging his abdomen to facilitate defecation, which likely caused the laceration. We advised the patient to avoid massaging his abdomen in the future and to seek medical attention if he experiences any abdominal symptoms.

In summary, the patient with a medical history of prostate cancer, endoscopic polypectomy, and chronic constipation presented with sudden-onset upper abdominal pain and was found to have intra-abdominal hemorrhage due to a mesenteric laceration caused by self-massage for defecation. An emergency exploratory laparotomy was performed to achieve hemostasis, and the operation was uncomplicated except for temporary paralytic ileus. The patient was discharged on the postoperative day 20 with instructions to avoid abdominal self-massage and seek medical attention for abdominal symptoms in the future.

Medical History:
The patient is a 24-year-old male with severe Hemophilia A. He has been receiving Factor VIII replacement therapy three times a week but reported missing the last three doses.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with left medial elbow pain and swelling, along with pain and paresthesias in the ring and small fingers. On examination, there was moderate swelling and tenderness to palpation over the medial epicondyle. Sensation was decreased over the small and ring fingers in the ulnar nerve distribution with intrinsic strength decreased to 4/5 on the MRC grading scale. There was a positive Tinel’s sign at the elbow. The patient was administered Factor VIII and admitted for observation. Following day, the symptoms worsened, and he was taken to the operating room for surgical decompression. The procedure involved decompression of the ulnar nerve at several sites around the elbow. There were no neuroma noted or obvious constriction deformity as seen with chronic compression. 

Discharge Condition: 
The patient was discharged from the hospital and followed up by hematology for maintenance of his Factor VIII levels.

Follow-up Plan: 
At the 6-week follow-up, the patient subjectively reported doing well without activity restrictions, with his paresthesias having completely resolved, and grip strength returned to full 5/5. 

Additional Information:
Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for which identifying information is included in this article.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [redacted]
DOB: [redacted]
Admission Date: [redacted]
Discharge Date: [redacted]
Attending Physician: [redacted]

Admission Diagnosis: West syndrome

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 2-month-old male who previously underwent surgical correction for intraventricular defect, was admitted to the hospital after presenting frequent episodes of inconsolable crying, associated with neck extension, stiffening of the arms and trunk, sometimes followed by swallowing and vomiting. Symptoms were attributed to GERD, and therapy with PPI started, however, no improvement was noticed.

In the following weeks, episodes became even more frequents with exacerbation of symptoms. His mother video-recorded an attack, which showed the presence of flexion spasms. The child eventually underwent fundoplication, but no improvement was noticed. Persistence of symptoms and occurrence of spasms of the arms during acute episodes finally suggested the diagnosis of West syndrome.

IS was then confirmed by EEG while MRI was negative. Despite starting appropriate therapy at 8 months of age, clinical signs of mental retardation were present. Although IS is a rare disorder, diagnosis was suspected based on age and patient history with a complete neurological evaluation.

To our knowledge, this is the first report of IS misdiagnosed as GERD. The attention towards GERD in children may reduce attention towards other peculiar clinical conditions, like in cases we presented. We would suggest considering GERD only in those patients with high risk rate for developing GERD like children with cerebral palsy, in those with surgery complications after oesophageal atresia and/or in any child with very evocative GERD symptoms, such as hematemesis and or chronic vomiting with growth failure.

Discharge Diagnosis: West syndrome

Final Condition at Discharge:
At the time of discharge, the patient continued to experience symptoms of West syndrome, but appropriate therapy was initiated. The patient's family was instructed to follow up with the pediatricians for medication management and further evaluations.

Discharge Medications:
Not Applicable

Follow-Up:
The parents were advised to follow up with a pediatrician for routine well-child visits and to monitor the patient's condition closely. Additional appointments were scheduled with a neurologist for further evaluation and management.

Infantile spasms are rare, but doctors guessed the diagnosis from his age, history, and a full nerve exam.
To our knowledge, this is the first case where infantile spasms were mistaken for reflux disease.
Focusing too much on reflux in babies might make doctors miss other uncommon conditions like this one.
We advise checking reflux only in high-risk babies, like those with cerebral palsy or past esophageal surgery.
Also consider reflux if the baby has signs such as blood in vomit or ongoing vomiting with poor weight gain.

At discharge, the baby still had West syndrome symptoms, but doctors had started the proper treatment.

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted after being diagnosed with cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy (CADASIL). The patient presented with a history of vertigo, migraine headaches, numbness and tingling in her hands and feet, memory loss, fatigue, hypersomnolence, anxiety, and depression. Upon admission, a brain MRI was performed which showed worsening of the white matter hyperintensity with the involvement of bilateral temporal and external capsules.

Treatment:

The patient was not started on any treatment during her initial presentation and her symptoms resolved after a few months. The patient later developed migraine headaches refractory to typical migraine medications, but no treatment was given at that time. The patient was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis by a general neurologist and was referred to an MS clinic where a repeated MRI showed the involvement of bilateral temporal and external capsules leading to a diagnosis of CADASIL. 

Consultations:

The patient received a consultation with a neuroimmunologist, and eventually, the diagnosis was changed based on the new MRI findings and a positive NOTCH3 genetic test.

Follow Up:

The patient was advised to follow up with a neurologist for further management of their CADASIL. 

Discharge:

The patient was discharged from the hospital with a diagnosis of CADASIL and instructions to follow up with a neurologist. There were no complications during their hospital stay.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 52-year-old multiparous African American woman

Diagnosis: Urethral diverticulum

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted after presenting with syncope following a 2-day history of heavy vaginal bleeding, passing large clots, and suprapubic pain. Pelvic examination revealed blood clots in the vagina along with a friable, fibrous ulcerated lesion on the anterior suburethral vagina. A computed tomography scan revealed a soft tissue mass within the lumen of the vagina and an enlarged lymph node in the right ovarian chain. On hospital day 2, the patient underwent an examination under anesthesia with repeat biopsies, which revealed non-diagnostic pathology.

During HDs 3 through 5, the patient’s bleeding decreased significantly, and on HD 6, a second examination under anesthesia revealed biopsies negative for malignancy. A Tonsil clamp was placed into the urethra, and the urology service was intraoperatively consulted, confirming the diagnosis of urethral diverticulum. The diverticulum was excised, and a multilayered repair over the Foley catheter was performed.

On postoperative day 9, the patient re-presented with bleeding, and several rejected sutures in the necrotic tissue were removed. Interrupted mattress sutures were placed to reapproximate the tissue. Final pathology revealed benign squamous mucosa.

Treatment:

Excision of urethral diverticulum and multilayered repair over the Foley catheter.

Follow-up:

In the urology clinic 2 weeks later, a voiding cystourethrogram was performed, revealing no extravasation from the urethra or bladder. A physical examination revealed proper vaginal healing and no defects.

Disposition:

Discharged in stable condition.

Hospital Course:
A 66-year-old female patient was admitted to the Department of Periodontics, M. S. Ramaiah Dental College and Hospital, Bangalore, with the complaint of burning sensation in the gums and bleeding gums for the past one month.

Medical History:
The patient had no relevant drug history or significant medical history. She had not received any dental treatment before.

Examination Findings:
On extra oral examination, the patient had some obvious skin lesions on the scalp and a hyperkeratotic plaque behind her left ear. Intra oral examination of gingiva revealed reddish marginal, attached gingiva and interdental papilla in both maxillary and mandibular anterior region with desquamation of epithelium present in certain regions.

Diagnosis:
Based on the clinical and histopathologic features, the lesion was suggestive of discoid lupus erythematosus.

Treatment:
Hand scaling was performed as gently as possible in order to minimize tissue disruption. Soft tooth brush and mouth rise (chlorhexidine 0.12%) was recommended. Triamcinolone acteonide oral paste was advised to apply two to three times per day.

Follow-up:
The patient was recalled for follow-up and maintenance.

Outside the mouth, she had visible skin spots on her scalp and a rough patch behind her left ear.
Inside the mouth, her gums were red and swollen, with some peeling in certain areas.
Diagnosis:
Based on the exam and tissue test, the signs pointed to discoid lupus erythematosus, a skin condition.
Treatment:
The dentist cleaned her teeth gently to avoid hurting the gums and causing bleeding during the procedure.
She was told to use a soft toothbrush and rinse with chlorhexidine mouthwash twice daily.
She should apply triamcinolone oral paste two to three times each day as directed for relief.
Follow-up:
The patient was asked to return for regular check-ups and care to monitor her condition.

Discharge Summary:

This is a discharge summary for a 50-year-old female patient who presented to our department with an intraoral swelling at the left mandible for six months. The patient underwent surgical excision and reconstruction using a submental island flap, under general anesthesia.

History of Present Illness: The patient reported to our department with swelling and pain in the left mandible region for six months, which grew rapidly after the extraction of lower left back teeth. The patient had no history of fever or difficulty swallowing.

Physical Examination: On extraoral examination, facial asymmetry was noted in the lower left facial region, but there was no evidence of any regional lymphadenopathy. Intraoral clinical evaluation revealed the presence of an expansile mass with anteroposterior as well as buccolingual expansion, extending from the region of the first premolar up to retromolar area, measuring approximately 6x4 cm. The overlying mucosal colour and texture appeared normal.

Diagnostic Tests: A radiographic orthopantomogram revealed a well-defined radiolucent lesion extending from the lower left first premolar to retromolar area. Computed tomography (CT) scans confirmed the presence of aggressive bony resorption of the lower left jaw starting from the premolar region and extending well into the mandibular ramus. Histopathological analysis of a biopsy specimen confirmed an aggressive CGCG.

Hospital Course: The patient underwent surgical excision and reconstruction using a submental island flap, under general anesthesia. The surgical procedure involved extraoral and intraoral approach to excise the lesion completely and a submental island flap for reconstruction. The patient was discharged without any complications.

Follow-up: In subsequent follow-ups, until one year, no evidence of recurrence was observed clinically as well as radiographically. The donor site healed uneventfully with minimal scars, which was present away from aesthetically visible regions of the face.

Summary: A 50-year-old female patient presented with an intraoral swelling at the left mandible for six months and was diagnosed with an aggressive CGCG. The patient underwent surgical excision and reconstruction using a submental island flap, under general anesthesia. The patient was discharged without any complications, and subsequent follow-ups showed no evidence of recurrence.

Discharge Summary: This is a discharge summary for a 50-year-old female patient seen in our clinic today. She came to our department with a swelling inside the mouth on the left lower jaw that lasted six months. The patient had surgery to remove the swelling and rebuild the area with a chin tissue flap. The surgery was performed while the patient was asleep under general anesthesia in the operating room.
History of Present Illness: The patient reported swelling and pain in the left lower jaw for six months, which grew quickly after tooth extraction. The patient reported no fever, no trouble swallowing, and no other systemic symptoms during this period.
Physical Examination: On external exam, the face looked uneven on the left lower side, but no swollen lymph nodes were seen. Inside the mouth, a growing lump was found from the first premolar tooth area to the back of the mouth. The lump measured about 6 by 4 centimeters, and the overlying tissue looked normal in color and texture.
Diagnostic Tests: A panoramic X-ray showed a dark spot in the bone from the first premolar to the back of the mouth. A CT scan confirmed aggressive bone destruction in the left lower jaw, starting at the premolar. The destruction extended into the ramus of the jaw, as clearly seen on the scan. A biopsy examined under the microscope showed an aggressive central giant cell granuloma, confirming the diagnosis.
Hospital Course: The patient underwent surgery to remove the lump and rebuild the area with a chin tissue flap. The surgery was performed while the patient was asleep under general anesthesia in the operating room. The surgeons used both an outside and an inside approach to take out the lump completely. They used the chin tissue flap to repair the surgical site, and the wound healed well. The patient left the hospital with no complications and was discharged home to continue recovery.
Follow-up: At follow-up visits over the next year, no sign of the lump returning was seen by exam or X-ray. The donor site healed well with only a small scar that is not in a visible part of the face.
Summary: A 50-year-old female patient had a six-month swelling inside the left lower jaw that prompted medical evaluation. The swelling was diagnosed as an aggressive central giant cell granuloma after biopsy and imaging. She had surgery to remove it and rebuild the area with a chin tissue flap while asleep under general anesthesia. She left the hospital without problems and follow-up visits showed no return of the lump.

Hospital Course:
The patient was a 33-year-old female who presented with abdominal pain, diarrhea, and fever. She was admitted and subsequently discharged after 2 days of oral ciprofloxacin treatment. However, she was readmitted two days after discharge due to worsening abdominal pain and other symptoms.

Diagnostic Studies:
The patient had a CT scan which revealed a left partially rim enhancing structure 2x2cm, suggestive of a ruptured corpus luteal cyst. There was minimal free fluid in the pelvis and no evidence of other intra-abdominal pathology.

Treatment:
The patient was treated with IV antibiotics and underwent a diagnostic laparoscopy. Generalized profuse seropurulent fluid was taken out, and a normal appendix was identified. The patient was continued on antibiotics and treated for primary streptococcal peritonitis. Her condition improved with conservative symptomatic management, and she was discharged after 10 days of treatment in the hospital. 

Follow-Up:
The patient showed improvement to repeat blood tests which showed the total whites and CRP had normalized. She reported minor lower abdominal pain which resolved spontaneously after conservative symptomatic management. Follow-up was established with the infectious disease team in clinic.  

Plan:
Continued outpatient oral antibiotics with clindamycin per culture sensitivities. Follow-up with the infectious disease team to monitor improvement and continued outpatient care.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 23-year-old male with chronic HCV, presented to our care for combination therapy based on the National Committee for Control and Prevention of viral Hepatitis "C" guidelines in Egypt. The therapy regimen included pegylated interferon α 2a 180 ug/week and ribavirin 1000 mg/day. However, at week 12 of therapy, the patient was discontinued due to a lack of early virologic response.

Discharge Summary:
The patient was diagnosed with HCV in a pre-employment checkup 2 years ago. The patient's BMI was 27.5 and had a liver biopsy score of A2 F2 without steatosis. During therapy, the patient's laboratory parameters recorded OBI with HBV DNA values greater than 2000 IU. To treat this activation, lamivudine was administered and continued for 6 months. During this time, the patient continued to be exposed to both HBV and HCV viral load assessment and HBV was undetected, and the HCV RNA level decreased. The patient discontinued lamivudine due to financial constraints and was exposed to HBV and HCV viral load determination 6 months later, where HBV was undetected, and HCV RNA level decreased to 7062 IU/ml.

Overall, the patient's medical history, including HCV and the occurrence of OBI with HBV DNA values over 2000 IU during therapy, was managed effectively with the use of lamivudine. The patient discontinued lamivudine due to financial constraints and was not followed up for HCV RNA levels. No further course of action was taken at the time of the patient's discharge.

No further steps were taken when the patient left the hospital, and no additional treatment was prescribed.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Name]
Medical Record Number: [MRN]

Admission Date: [Admission Date]
Discharge Date: [Discharge Date]

Diagnosis: Follicular Lymphoma

Hospital Course:

A 72-year-old man presented with an asymptomatic nontender abdominal mass and was found to have a bulky mesenteric mass with a maximum standardized uptake value on PET/CT. Excisional biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of Follicular Lymphoma, which was treated with bendamustine plus rituximab. The patient was followed up on an outpatient basis and has had no recurrent disease to date.

Medical History:

The patient did not have any significant past medical history.

Discussion:

Primary mesenteric tumors are rare, and Follicular Lymphoma is the most common type. The imaging patterns of mesenteric lymphoma at CT can vary, and while the sandwich sign may suggest malignant tumors, its diagnostic performance is unknown. Although the disease may be indolent, vigilance is necessary to ensure early diagnosis. In case of a solid mesenteric tumor, malignant lymphoma should be considered as a priority.

Recommendations:

The patient is advised to continue follow-up with the oncologist and promptly report any symptoms or complications.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 47-year-old edentulous female with maxillary complete denture

Chief Complaint: Dysfunctional maxillary complete denture

History of Present Illness: The patient presented with an unuseful maxillary complete denture, resulting from cervical radiotherapy. She had a limited oral opening and insufficient saliva quantity and flowability.

Hospital Course: The patient's treatment plan consisted of fabricating complete dentures with proper extension of the flanges. Flexible impression trays were used to obtain preliminary impressions for both arches. Custom trays for the final impressions were fabricated with autopolimerized acrylic resin. Final maxillary impressions were made by using polysulfide material alternately for the first and second halves of the sectional trays. Record bases were fabricated and occlusion rims were prepared. A centric relation record was made, and the record was transferred from the patient to a semiadjustable articulator. The try-in was evaluated to verify jaw relations and teeth arrangement. After patient acceptance, final festooning and flasking of the dentures were completed. The final dentures were manufactured using similar designs to that of the record bases. The prostheses were deflasked, finished, and polished. The patient was provided with instructions for cleaning, inserting, and removing the prostheses. She was recalled for follow-up visits to check for the maintenance and her adaptability with the new dentures.

Outcome: The patient reported difficulty in the insertion and removal of denture initially, but progressively, she became used to it.

Follow-up: The patient will continue to be monitored during follow-up visits to check the maintenance and adaptability of her new dentures.

Discharge Summary:
Patient: 47-year-old woman with no teeth who wears an upper denture.
Chief Complaint: The upper denture does not work well.
History of Present Illness: The patient came in because her upper denture was not usable after neck radiation treatment. She could not open her mouth wide and had very little saliva.
Hospital Course: The plan was to make new upper and lower dentures that fit well. Flexible trays were used to take first impressions of both jaws. Custom trays were made from hard acrylic for the final impressions. For the upper jaw, impressions were taken in two parts using a rubber-like material. Record bases and bite rims were prepared from those impressions. A bite registration was made and moved to a special jaw simulator. The denture try-in was checked to make sure the jaw position and tooth placement were correct. After the patient approved the try-in, the dentures were shaped and packed for processing. The final dentures were made using the same design as the record bases. The dentures were removed from the mold, trimmed, smoothed, and polished. The patient received instructions on how to clean, put in, and take out the dentures. She was asked to return for check-up visits to see how the dentures are holding up. These visits also check how well she is getting used to the new dentures.
Outcome: Initially she struggled to insert and remove the denture, but she gradually became comfortable with it.
Follow-up: The patient will keep having follow-up visits to monitor the dentures’ fit and her ability to use them.

Discharge Summary:

Admission Date: [Date]
Discharge Date: [Date]

Patient:
The patient is a 61-year-old Japanese man who was admitted with coxalgia.

Presenting Issues:
The patient presented with coxalgia, a condition that causes pain in the hip joint. Radiography revealed osseous projections at the knee and shoulder joints. The patient had also developed coxarthrosis and severe pain of the right hip joint. The range of motion of the right hip joint was limited in flexion and abduction.

Treatment:
The patient underwent right total hip arthroplasty using the direct lateral approach. A gigantic femoral head and large diameter of the femoral neck were noted. The soft tissue appeared normal, and an incision was made in the articular capsule. Hip dislocation was difficult because of the gigantic femoral head and caused a trochanteric fracture. The bone substance of the greater trochanter, femoral neck, and femoral trochanter was poor and showed bone fragility. An acetabular cup was implanted by press fit without screws at the site of the original acetabulum. An osteotomy was performed in a more distal than usual part of the femoral neck, and a femoral polished tapered stem was implanted using bone cement. The fractured greater trochanter was fixed with tension band wiring using Kirschner wire and nylon tape. The articular capsule, gluteus minimus muscle, gluteus medius muscle, and tensor fasciae latae muscle were repaired.

Outcomes:
Postoperatively, the implant setting was unproblematic, and the exostosis at the femoral neck had been removed. Walking with full weight-bearing was permitted, and there were no complications such as dislocation or infection. Thirteen months postoperatively, the patient had no coxalgia, but the range of motion of the right hip joint was still limited in flexion and abduction. The patient had no limp and no interference with his activities of daily living. There was an ectopic ossification seen radiographically. The patient had returned to his previous work and had no difficulties with everyday activities.

Follow-Up Care:
The patient was discharged from the hospital with a crutch.

Discharge Summary:
Admission Date: [Date]
Discharge Date: [Date]
Patient:
The patient is a 61-year-old Japanese man who was admitted with hip pain during hospital stay.
Presenting Issues:
The patient came in with hip pain, and X-rays showed bony growths at the knee and shoulder joints.
He also had hip arthritis and severe pain in the right hip that limited movement.
He could not move his right hip well when bending the leg or moving it out to the side.
Treatment:
The patient had a hip replacement surgery done from the side of the body to replace the joint.
During surgery, doctors noted a large thigh bone head and a wide thigh bone neck.
The soft tissues looked normal, and a cut was made in the hip joint lining.
Moving the hip out of place was difficult during surgery because of the big bone head.
This difficulty led to a break of the bony bump on the thigh called the greater trochanter.
The bone in the greater trochanter, thigh bone neck, and that bony bump was weak and brittle.
The socket part was placed without screws by pressing it into the original socket spot.
A cut was made lower than usual on the thigh bone neck of the femur.
A polished tapered stem was fixed in place using bone cement to secure the implant.
The broken bony bump, called the greater trochanter, was repaired with wire and tape.
The joint lining and hip muscles (gluteus minimus, gluteus medius, and tensor fasciae latae) were stitched back together.
Outcomes:
After surgery, the implant was set correctly and the extra bone growth on the thigh bone neck was removed.
He was allowed to walk putting full weight on the leg, and there were no problems like dislocation or infection.
Thirteen months after the surgery, he reported no hip pain and felt comfortable during follow-up visits.
He still could not bend his right hip well or move it out to the side.
He walked without a limp and was able to perform his daily activities without any trouble.
Follow-up X-rays showed extra bone forming in an abnormal location around the hip, which is called ectopic ossification.
He returned to his previous job and experienced no difficulty with everyday tasks or work duties.
Follow-Up Care:
The patient was discharged from the hospital and advised to use a crutch for walking support.

Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Diagnosis: 
- Aphakic bullous keratopathy 
- Corneal scarring

Hospital Course: 
The patient underwent penetrating keratoplasty for aphakic bullous keratopathy and corneal scarring. The donor cornea was replaced due to a large dendritic-geographic epithelial ulcer noted immediately after placement. Perioperative administration of intravenous aciclovir was given. Postoperatively, the patient was started on systemic and local antiviral therapy, and local antibiotic treatment. The graft was clear and re-epithelialized at 1 week. Long term prophylactic acyclovir 400 mg was started. However, six months later the patient developed a geographic corneal ulcer involving the graft-host interface with keratic precipitates and corneal edema. The patient was treated with acyclovir 400 mg and topical aciclovir both five times a day for 2 weeks with resolution of the ulcer and residual scarring.

Summary: 
The patient who had aphakic bullous keratopathy and corneal scarring underwent a successful penetrating keratoplasty with the use of a donor corneoscleral disc. The initial donor corneoscleral disc was removed and replaced with a second donor corneoscleral disc which was available. The patient was treated with antiviral and antibiotic medications following the surgery. The patient developed a geographic corneal ulcer, which was treated successfully with antiviral medications. The patient was discharged with instructions for a follow-up within a week.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

Medical History: A 12-year-old female patient was admitted with a history of polyuria, polydipsia, and secondary amenorrhea.
Clinical Findings: A complete preoperative endocrinological assessment revealed mild prolactin hormone elevation, hypothyroidism, and hypocortisolism. Neuroradiological investigation showed a large mass in the sella with compression of the optic chiasm and extending into the third ventricle.
Diagnosis: A craniopharyngioma or a GCT were the suspected diagnoses. However, the symptoms presented by the patient suggested a germinoma.
Procedure: The patient underwent an extended endoscopic endonasal transtuberculum/transplanum approach for tumor removal.
Postoperative Course: The patient demonstrated a significant improvement in her condition with light perception reported in the left eye and improvement in right eye temporal hemianopsia. There were no postoperative complications.
Postoperative Follow-up: Serum levels of AFP, and beta-HCG were checked, suggesting confirmation of germinoma malignancy. The patient was referred to a pediatric oncologist for further treatment, which includes adjunctive chemotherapy and radiation therapy.
Condition at Discharge: The patient was discharged in a normal condition but still receiving desmopressin acetate for diabetes insipidus treatment.
Prognosis: The patient's condition remains optimistic, and a follow-up appointment is necessary.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 71-year-old female, was admitted to our hospital due to anorexia, left inguinal lymph node swelling, low platelet count, and elevated liver enzymes following a tick bite while harvesting. The patient was suspected to have a severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS), and diagnostic tests confirmed SFTS infection based on ELISA and RT-PCR results. 

Clinical Findings:
On admission, the patient presented with mild headache and left inguinal lymph node swelling, with no erythema, rash, or wheal. Laboratory tests revealed low platelet and white blood cell counts, atypical lymphocytes, and elevated liver enzymes.

Treatment:
The patient was treated with adequate fluid replacement therapy due to mild hypovolemia upon admission. Minocycline was administered intravenously, as Rickettsia tsutsugamushi was considered a differential diagnosis. However, treatment with minocycline was discontinued after the definitive diagnosis of SFTS infection.

Outcome:
The platelet count became markedly elevated during hospitalization, and serum transaminases returned to almost normal levels. The patient's anorexia improved, and she was discharged after 13 days without experiencing any fever during her hospitalization. 

Follow-up Plan:
No specific follow-up plan was mentioned in the case report.

She also had low platelets and high liver enzymes after a tick bite while working outdoors.
Doctors thought she might have a serious infection called SFTS, and tests confirmed she had SFTS.
Clinical Findings:
When she arrived, she had headache and swollen lymph node in her left groin, with no redness or rash.
Blood tests showed low platelets, low white blood cells, some unusual lymphocytes, and high liver enzymes.
Treatment:
She received fluids to treat mild low blood volume when she arrived at the hospital.
Doctors gave her the antibiotic minocycline through a vein because they thought she might have another tick-borne illness.
They stopped the minocycline after tests confirmed she had SFTS and no longer needed that antibiotic.

During her stay, her platelet count rose to high levels and her liver enzymes almost returned to normal.
Her loss of appetite got better, and she left the hospital after 13 days with no fever.

The report did not list any specific follow-up appointments, tests, or instructions for her care after discharge.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]
Length of Stay: [REDACTED]

Medical History:
No relevant medical history was reported.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to the emergency clinic with a sudden decrease in vision following a blunt trauma to the right eye with a tennis ball. On presentation, his best corrected visual acuity was hand movement with perception of rays in all quadrants. The patient was managed conservatively with topical steroid eye drops, cycloplegics, and anti-glaucoma medications. The hyphema and vitreous hemorrhage settled down in three weeks, and the patient's visual acuity increased to 20/60. However, the IOP remained high, and prostaglandin analogue bimatoprost 0.01% was added. As the IOP did not show substantial improvement in the following weeks, the patient was advised for filtering surgery under guarded visual prognosis. 
Intraoperatively, there was a vitreous prolapse during deep block excision, which was managed with anterior vitrectomy. On postoperative day one, the visual acuity was 20/125, and the IOP was non-recordable. The patient was treated with topical and oral prednisolone for serous choroidal detachment, and the effusion settled in two weeks. Gradually, the patient's vision and IOP improved, and at the last follow-up visit after three months, the best corrected visual acuity and IOP were 20/25 and 12 mm Hg off any medication, respectively.

Summary:
An 18-year-old male presented with a blunt trauma to the right eye resulting in a decrease in visual acuity and high IOP. The patient was conservatively managed with topical steroid eye drops, cycloplegics, and anti-glaucoma medications, followed by filtering surgery. The intraoperative management included anterior vitrectomy for vitreous prolapse. The patient developed serous choroidal detachment, which resolved with prednisolone treatment. The patient was gradually tapered off prednisolone and showed improvement in visual acuity and IOP at the last follow-up visit after three months.

The patient came to the emergency clinic after a tennis ball hit the right eye and caused sudden vision loss.

The patient was treated with steroid eye drops, eye drops to relax the eye, and medicine to lower eye pressure.

Eye pressure stayed high, so the eye drop bimatoprost was added to lower pressure as needed.

The leaked gel was managed by removing gel from the front part of the eye.
On the first day after surgery, vision was 20/125 and eye pressure could not be measured.
The patient received steroid eye drops and pills for fluid buildup under the eye layer.
The fluid went away in two weeks, and the patient’s eye condition began to stabilize.
Over time, vision and eye pressure got better, showing steady improvement.
At the last check-up three months later, vision with glasses was 20/25.
Eye pressure was 12 mm Hg and no medication was needed.
Summary:
An 18-year-old male was hit in the right eye by a tennis ball, causing sudden vision loss and high eye pressure.
The patient was first treated with steroid eye drops, eye drops to relax the eye, and medicine to lower eye pressure.
Then the patient had surgery to create a new drainage channel for eye fluid.
During surgery, gel leaked from the back of the eye and was removed from the front part of the eye.
The patient developed fluid buildup under the eye layer, which healed with steroid eye drops and pills.
After slowly stopping the steroids, vision and eye pressure improved.
At the three-month follow-up, vision was 20/25 and eye pressure was 12 mm Hg without medicine.

Hospital Course:
The 54-year-old male patient, with a history of smoking and multiple gallstones, underwent intraoperative ERCP followed by LC. A successful endoscopic sphincterotomy was performed to access the gallbladder. The patient had high liver function tests, hyperbilirubinemia, and jaundice, but anesthesia and surgical plans were the same as another patient. The surgical and anesthesia times were 92 and 108 minutes, respectively. After the surgery, the patient didn't require any analgesic medication for the first 12 hours, and their NRS rating was <3/10. However, during the 13th hour, the NRS rating went up to 5/10 on coughing and 3/10 at rest, requiring rescue analgesic. The patient was discharged with a prescription for pain medication after 24 hours.

The patient's condition was monitored postoperatively with adequate treatment. Postoperatively, the patient continued anticoagulation for 8 weeks. To date, the patient remains asymptomatic at rest and exercise.

Hospital Course:

The patient, an 81-year-old female with a significant history of prediabetes and end stage renal disease on hemodialysis, underwent coronary artery bypass graft surgery and replacement of mitral valve with postoperative complications. The patient presented with a dehiscence of the sternal wound, which required wound vacuum assisted closure, as well as a sacral decubitus ulcer, and multiple episodes of sepsis and respiratory failure.

Assessment and Plan:

During the first 45 days of admission, the patient's blood glucose was well-controlled with only 2 units total of sliding scale insulin required. However, soon after the start of intravenous ascorbic acid to aid in sternal wound healing, the patient experienced multiple high FSBG levels over 200 mg/dL, resulting in a total of 9 units of insulin treatment in 24 hours and subsequent FSBG levels remaining high over the next few days. Further investigation revealed a marked discrepancy of greater than 100 mg/dL between simultaneous FSBG and BGMP readings, with BGMP readings ranging from 72 to 146 mg/dL. Given the suspicion for falsely high FSBG readings caused by intravenous ascorbic acid, it was discontinued and FSBG values returned to normal. The patient did not experience hypoglycemia while receiving unnecessary insulin treatment.

Summary:

This discharge summary documents the hospital course of an elderly female with a history of renal disease and prediabetes who underwent coronary artery bypass graft surgery and replacement of mitral valve, complicated by postoperative complications. The patient had high FSBG levels after starting intravenous ascorbic acid, which were believed to be falsely elevated, resulting in unnecessary insulin treatment. The FSBG values returned to normal after discontinuation of intravenous ascorbic acid.

Discharge Summary:
Admission Date: [DATE]
Discharge Date: [DATE]
Patient Name: [NAME]
DOB: [DOB]
Gender: Male

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with complaints of progressive facial asymmetry, difficulty in speech and mastication secondary to restricted movement of the mandible, and intermittent pain in the right TMJ region. The patient reported progressive reduction in the vertical opening and increasing asymmetry of the face with no history of trauma. Clinical examination revealed marked facial asymmetry, and radiographic imaging showed a large radiopaque lesion of the right mandibular condyle. CT scan confirmed a tumor of the right condyle head, and surgical removal of the enlarged condyle via preauricular approach was planned.

A preauricular incision was carried out, and the lesion including the condyle was removed successfully using a surgical bur. The entire specimen was decalcified in 10% formic acid and processed for histopathological examination. Histopathology showed chondrocytes of the cartilaginous cap arranged in clusters in parallel, oblong lacunar spaces, similar to that of the normal epiphyseal cartilage along with regular bony trabeculae. There was no evidence of cartilage islands in underlying bony trabeculae. These features were suggestive of osteochondroma, and the diagnosis of giant osteochondroma was made.
 
Postoperative recovery was uneventful, and periodic follow-up appointments were scheduled. During the latest visit of the patient, it was observed that his facial appearance and mouth opening had returned back to normal, and he had been symptom-free.

Discharge Condition:
The patient has successfully undergone surgical intervention for giant osteochondroma, and he has been discharged from the hospital with good postoperative recovery. The patient has been advised to continue follow-up appointments as scheduled.

Recommendations:
1. The patient is advised to follow up with his physician for periodic check-ups to monitor the condition and ensure a healthy recovery.
2. If any further complications or symptoms develop, the patient should seek medical attention immediately.
3. The patient is advised to continue maintaining healthy dietary habits and exercise regularly.
4. Surgery is not always the first treatment option, and any other treatment options should be discussed in detail with the patient and his caregiver.
5. Patients should be thoroughly educated on their diagnosis and the possible treatment options available to them.

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to our hospital with a diagnosis of chronic rhinosinusitis. He had a history of multiple anaphylactic reactions during surgical procedures and eye examinations performed under general anesthesia at various hospitals, since he was 11 years old. The patient and his relatives had been reluctant to come to the hospital due to extreme fear and discouragement for 10 years after his last episode of anaphylaxis during eye enucleation at the age of 29.

Following his evaluation by the allergist, skin testing was performed for morphine and ketamine, using standard concentrations according to the EAACI recommendation. The first test results were negative but due to his history of severe reactions, further testing was recommended 6 weeks later. The second round of skin tests was positive for ketamine and morphine. Hence, we provided a recommendation for the patient to avoid ketamine and morphine for future anesthetic procedures. The ADR card was updated accordingly, and alternative drugs were suggested, tested negative and were used for the patient's sinus surgery, which was performed without any adverse reactions.

The patient was advised to maintain close observation for allergic symptoms in the case of future anesthetic procedures with alternative drugs. The patient expressed full understanding of the recommendations and was discharged home in good condition. A comprehensive discharge report was provided to the patient and his carers.

Discharge Medications:

None recommended.

Follow-up:

The patient is advised to follow-up with the allergist as needed.

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 16-year-old boy who was admitted to the hospital due to fractures of the left tibia and the right forearm. The tibia fracture was managed with a circular frame, while the forearm fracture was fixed with intramedullary titanium elastic nails. The patient underwent surgery due to metalwork migration, during which the excess material was trimmed and impacted back into the bone. The nail exit holes had a cap of bone substitute applied.
 
Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with periprosthetic fracture of the right forearm and fracture of the left tibia.

Procedure:
The patient underwent corrective osteotomy, creation of an intramedullary canal using the combination drilling technique and insertion of titanium elastic nails. The half-pins were easily removed as they had not bonded to the bone. The wires proved to be more difficult to extract but were ultimately removed. 

Treatment:
The patient received treatment in the form of circular frame and intramedullary titanium elastic nails for fracture management. Surgical intervention was performed due to metalwork migration. 

Follow-up:
Over the course of 18 months, the titanium elastic nails began to migrate and cause some soft tissue irritation. The patient achieved full union and his function returned to his pre-injury state at 1-year follow-up. His range of motion was observed, with a maximum pronation of 25° and supination of 60°. According to the patient, this matched his pre-injury range of motion and he was satisfied with the overall outcome. No further follow-up was necessary.

Date of Discharge: [REDACTED] 

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 78-year-old male, was admitted to the emergency room with complaints of dry cough, fever and malaise persisting for 1 month. He was previously treated with amoxicillin with no improvement. His medical history included diabetes and arterial blood hypertension, for which he was on metformin and amlodipine for 7 years. The patient presented with mildly lethargic orientation, febrile with mild tachycardia, hypoxemia, and crackles in the mid- and lower-lung fields on physical examination. Laboratory tests revealed elevated WBC counts, NLR, ESR, and CRP. The chest radiograph showed diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates. The HRCT showed diffuse interstitial lung involvement with a ground glass pattern. Blood and sputum cultures were negative for bacteria, urine antigen tests for Legionella pneumonia and Streptococcus pneumoniae were negative. Serum immunology tests for autoimmune diseases such as antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies were all negative. A bronchoscopy was then performed, BAL and TBLB were negative for malignancy, bacteria, nocardia, fungi, and mycobacteria. BAL increased cellularity and had a mixed cellularity pattern. In view of the above findings, a diagnosis of Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia (COP) was considered. Treatment with antibiotics was ceased, and the patient was started on prednisone 20mg daily. The patient showed immediate improvement, blood inflammatory markers decreased, and he was discharged after 5 days on prednisone. He was advised to taper off corticosteroids for a total duration of treatment of 6-12 months.

Medical Condition:
Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia (COP)

Treatment:
Prednisone 20mg daily

Follow-up:
The patient has had no recurrence of symptoms at follow-up visits after complete clinical and radiological resolution of his condition.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with high-grade intermittent fever for three days with spontaneous gum bleeding and mild headache. He subsequently developed gradually worsening drowsiness, and was found to have thrombocytopenia with microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA). A diagnosis of thrombotic thrombocytopenia purpura (TTP) was made. He was promptly commenced on therapeutic plasma exchange and 1 mg/kg of oral prednisolone. 

On the fifth day of illness, the patient developed two episodes of generalized tonic-clonic convulsions which progressed into a non-convulsive status epilepticus, requiring elective ventilation in the intensive care unit. On day 18, he developed flaccid paraparesis with sphincter dysfunction. Magnetic resonance imaging showed haemorrhage at multiple spinal levels.

Despite 16 plasma exchanges and high dose steroids, his platelet count remained persistently low, and he was investigated for alternative etiologies. Polymerase chain reaction of serum revealed clinically significant levels of cytomegalovirus (CMV). He was commenced on oral valganciclovir 450 mg/daily for 21 days. After about 6 days of valganciclovir treatment, his platelet count increased, and the MAHA resolved. 

The patient subsequently had regained normal haematological and biochemical parameters with a negative PCR quantification of CMV. He had regained ambulatory status with support and had normal sphincter function. The patient was transferred to a rehabilitation facility for further care.

On the fifth day, he had two seizures with whole-body shaking. These seizures turned into ongoing brain seizure activity without shaking, and he needed a breathing machine in the ICU. On day 18, he developed weakness in both legs and lost bladder/bowel control. An MRI showed bleeding in several spots of his spine. Despite 16 plasma exchanges and high-dose steroids, his platelet count stayed low, so doctors looked for other causes. A blood test found a high level of CMV virus. He started taking valganciclovir 450 mg each day for 21 days. After about six days of valganciclovir, his platelet count rose and the red blood cell breakdown stopped. He then returned to normal blood and chemical levels, and a CMV test came back negative. He was able to walk with help and regained normal bladder/bowel control. The patient was transferred to a rehabilitation facility for further care.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
- Name: [Name Redacted]
- Age: 65-year-old
- Gender: Female
- Diagnosis: Malignant melanoma of the urethra with positive surgical margins

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to our hospital with a 6-month history of difficulty in voiding associated with a small mass at the urethral meatus. Physical examination revealed a small tan-colored polypoid growth protruding from the external urethral meatus, mimicking a urethral caruncle, without any evidence of inguinal lymphadenopathy. Urethral carunclectomy was performed with uneventful postoperative recovery. The pathological examination of the specimen demonstrated malignant melanoma of the urethra with positive surgical margins. Further investigations revealed the presence of residual tumor in the last 0.5 cm of the urethra with no abnormal findings in either the proximal urethra or the urinary bladder. Thus, a radical urethrectomy with bladder preservation and a continent catheterizable stoma (Yang-Monti technique) was performed to achieve 2.5 cm margins. The patient tolerated the procedure well, and there were no complications postoperatively.

Outcome:
The final pathology report revealed a small focus (3mm) of a residual malignant melanoma with negative surgical margins. Currently, one year after the surgery, the patient is in complete clinical remission with no evidence of disease.

Follow-up Recommendations:
The patient will require long-term follow-up with regular monitoring and imaging tests to detect any signs of disease recurrence. The patient is instructed to perform self-intermittent catheterization and remain continent. Follow-up consultations with an oncologist and urologist are advised to monitor the patient's condition and ensure optimal management.

Admission Diagnosis:
Left renal calculus

Chief Complaint:
Poor effort tolerance

History of Presenting Illness:
A 60-year-old woman was admitted with a history of poor effort tolerance. On further evaluation, the patient was diagnosed with left renal calculus and scheduled for left percutaneous nephrolithotomy. During preanesthetic evaluation, the patient's irregularly irregular pulse and abnormal ECG raised concern for an asymptomatic sinus node dysfunction.

Past Medical History:
The patient reported a past medical history of ischemic heart disease with hypertension since 6 months and was on regular treatment. There was also evidence of an asymptomatic sinus node dysfunction, which was resistant to atropine.

Hospital Course:
The patient was given balanced general anesthesia with endotracheal intubation, induced with propofol and vecuronium, and secured under direct laryngoscopy with size 7.0 endotracheal tube. During the surgery, there were repeated episodes of continuous pacing by the temporary pacemaker, followed by a resumption of normal sinus rhythm. Other vital parameters were stable in the intraoperative period. Neuromuscular blockade was reversed with neostigmine and glycopyrrolate. The patient was shifted to the post anesthesia care unit with stable vitals.

Discharge Condition:
The patient was discharged in stable condition on the 5th postoperative day.

Follow-up Care:
The patient was advised to follow-up with their cardiologist for further evaluation and management of their asymptomatic sinus node dysfunction.

Medications on Discharge:
None

Instructions to Patient:
The patient was advised to rest and follow-up with their cardiologist for further evaluation and management of their asymptomatic sinus node dysfunction.

Patient: 45-year-old female
Diagnosis: Multiple myeloma

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with multiple purpuric, ecchymotic lesions over periorbital area, cheeks, front and back of the neck with relative sparing of covered parts for the last 2 years, with a history of minor trauma precipitating these lesions. Skin was easily fragile in most areas. There was a history of multiple episodes of diarrhea and fever in the past 6 months. General examination showed mild pallor and bilateral pedal edema. Skin biopsy finding was suggestive of a bullous lesion with amorphous eosinophilic amyloid deposits. Serum protein electrophoresis and bone marrow aspiration confirmed it to be a case of multiple myeloma. However, radiological evaluations of skeleton were normal. 

Treatment:
The patient was referred to the department of clinical hematology where chemotherapy was started.

Prognosis:
The patient's prognosis will depend on the response to treatment and the stage of multiple myeloma. Close follow-up with clinical hematology is recommended. 

Follow-up:
It is recommended that the patient follow-up with clinical hematology regularly as well as adhere to any prescribed medication regimen.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Date of Admission: [Redacted]
Date of Discharge: [Redacted]

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 68-year-old Japanese man, underwent resection surgery for a leiomyosarcoma at the mediastinum. Due to dissemination in the pleura, the patient received radiation therapy and a second operation. Ten months post-surgery, the patient developed pain and numbness in the left upper limb, and an enhanced solid lesion and a non-enhanced cystic lesion were observed in the apex of the left lung using contrast enhanced CT scan. Ablation using radiofrequency ablation (RFA) was performed after radiation and chemotherapy were deemed ineffective, and surgery was thought to carry a high risk of bleeding. The patient underwent RFA with a LeVeen electrode, with retractable hooks opened for ablation. A total of three ablations were performed, with the output started at 20 W and increased by 10 W every 2 minutes in each session. The procedure was performed under local anesthesia to monitor the appearance of sharp pain of the left upper limb. A maximum output of 80 W and total ablation time of 57 minutes and 14 seconds were achieved. Contrast enhanced CT performed two days after RFA showed that the enhanced solid lesion in the tumor was smaller in size compared to pre-RFA CT. The patient's pain disappeared for approximately 3 months, accompanied by an improvement in motor function disorder. However, the pain of the left upper limb reappeared due to growth of the tumor, three months after RFA.

Condition at Discharge:

The patient's pain had reappeared, and thus, he was discharged from the hospital with instructions to follow up with his healthcare provider.

Instructions:

The patient is advised to follow up with his healthcare provider regarding his condition.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 45 years
Sex: Female
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]
Length of Stay: 7 days

Admitting Diagnosis:
Undifferentiated Spindle Cell Sarcoma Involving the Pancreas

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital urgently due to the acute onset of severe abdominal pain and collapse. Upon examination, she was found to be in class III haemorrhagic shock with distended and diffusely tender abdomen. She was immediately resuscitated with blood transfusions and intravenous crystalloid boluses. Hematological and basic investigations revealed haemoglobin level of 5g/dl and moderate amount of free fluid with mass around the proximal part of the pancreas, respectively. Following which, an emergency exploratory laparotomy was performed, and the source of bleeding was identified as the nidus, which was situated posterior to the body of the pancreas and had ruptured through the inferior border of the pancreas. The histopathological analysis of the biopsy revealed an infiltrating tumour composed of fascicles of spindle cells with oval, vesicular nuclei with scanty eosinophilic cytoplasm that was diagnosed as undifferentiated spindle cell sarcoma, and the tumour was surgically excised.

Treatment:
The patient was managed in the intensive care unit for 4 days and received a course of Ifosfamide and Doxorubicin for 6 months as adjuvant chemotherapy. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography was performed before the commencement of chemotherapy, which showed a 7 × 4.8 × 4.9 cm mass lesion with a thin wall containing hypodense material, attached to the inferior border of the pancreas. There were no other metastatic lesions identified.

Outcome:
The patient recovered following surgery and was discharged 7 days after admission. She was referred to the oncologist and offered a pancreatectomy with excision of the tumour, which was refused. The patient received six months of chemotherapy and finally succumbed to the disease 18 months after the presentation.

Summary:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with undifferentiated spindle cell sarcoma involving the pancreas that was treated with surgery and adjuvant chemotherapy. The patient was discharged following a 7-day hospitalization but eventually succumbed to the disease after 18 months.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [Name]

Date of Admission: [Date of Admission]

Date of Discharge: [Date of Discharge]

Hospitalized for: Stenosis of Left Subclavian Artery

Brief Hospital Course: 

The patient, a 4-year-old boy, was admitted with an incidental detection of murmur. Clinical examination revealed low volume radial pulse in the left upper limb and lower BP in the same limb. The right radial pulse was normal. Anthropometrically, his height was 100 cm, and the left upper limb was 10 mm shorter than the right upper limb.  

Echocardiography showed structurally normal heart with RAA and aberrant LSA with flow turbulence. CT angiogram was done, which confirmed the diagnosis. A stenosis of 70-80% just beyond the origin of LSA was detected. The presence of limb length discrepancy justified treatment, and the patient was scheduled for transcatheter placement of stent. 

The procedure was performed successfully, and the patient tolerated it very well. Racer 5 mm × 18 mm stent was positioned across the stenosed segment. Post-procedure angiogram confirmed the stent's correct placement, and good flow was observed in LSA and left axillary artery. The patient was kept on overnight heparin infusion and discharged with oral aspirin.

Follow-up visits on 3 and 6 months showed near-normalization of radial pulse and blood pressure in the left upper limb, and significant improvement of limb length. USG of the left upper limb confirmed a laminar flow pattern in the LSA. The boy has been followed up for the last 4 years, with no remaining limb length discrepancy detected.

Discharge Diagnosis: Stenosis of Left Subclavian Artery.

Discharge Instructions: 

The patient will continue aspirin therapy (as directed by the physician). Follow-up visits should be scheduled as per the physician's instructions. Parents are advised to keep the patient's medical records updated and bring them to each visit. 

Signed,

The patient was admitted for acute limb ischemia and septic shock secondary to Streptococcus dysgalactiae bacteremia. A workup for infectious endocarditis was initiated and confirmed by transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiogram demonstrating aortic valve vegetations and severe aortic regurgitation.

Hospital Course:
The patient underwent emergent revascularization with left iliac thrombectomy and intravenous antibiotics with gentamicin for 10 days and ceftriaxone for six weeks. Cardiothoracic surgery was consulted, and the patient underwent aortic valve replacement surgery. Upon hemodynamic stabilization, he was discharged to the rehabilitation center one month after the initial hospitalization.

A 56-year-old gentleman with a past medical history of untreated hepatitis C infection, osteomyelitis with right fourth toe amputation, and alcohol abuse presented with paresthesias and a pulseless left leg. Lab work demonstrated normocytic anemia, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and creatinine elevation. Blood cultures were positive for Streptococcus dysgalactiae, and CT angiogram of the left leg demonstrated significant occlusions. The patient was treated for acute limb ischemia and septic shock and underwent an IE workup, which confirmed aortic valve vegetations.

Discharge Medications:
The patient's discharge medications were prescribed by the attending physician and are available in the patient's outpatient medical record.

Follow-up care:
The patient was advised to continue regular follow-up with his primary care physician and cardiothoracic surgeon. Further cardiac rehabilitation is recommended in coordination with the patient's medical team.

The patient was discharged with stable vital signs and improved clinical condition. The patient and family were advised to return to the hospital if any new or worsening symptoms persist.
