Hospital Course Summary:

Admission: 
A 65-year-old female with a history of Hashimoto's disease was admitted to the hospital for malaise and nausea of one-week duration without preceding infection. She had no psychiatric history. She presented with low serum levels of sodium on laboratory findings and inverted T waves on electrocardiogram (ECG).
 
Course: 
After admission, the patient's consciousness levels improved until she presented with paranoia and visual hallucinations four days later. She was delirious and was consulted by psychiatrists, who prescribed quetiapine for her delirium. Furthermore, on the same day, she complained of nausea and was pale and sweating. She was thought to be in a state of acute circulatory failure, and urgent coronary catherization was performed for possible percutaneous intervention. She was diagnosed with Takotsubo cardiomyopathy. Administration of hydrocortisone was initiated, and the hyponatremia and delirium improved dramatically in 3 days. An echocardiogram showed the left ventricular wall motion abnormalities including apical segment to be also markedly improved by 10 days after steroid administration.

Diagnosis: 
Endocrine studies showed decreases in serum cortisol and ACTH and reduced urinary secretion of free cortisol. It was found that the patient was suffering from isolated ACTH deficiency. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed no pituitary lesions or adjacent lesions.

Discharge: 
The patient was discharged in stable condition and instructed to continue taking oral hydrocortisone. She was advised to follow up with her primary care physician and endocrinologist to manage her isolated ACTH deficiency.

She was advised to see her primary care doctor and endocrinologist to manage her isolated ACTH deficiency.

Hospital Course:

47-year-old male was admitted following a car accident. The patient presented with forehead abrasion and confusion. A brain CT scan and cervical X-rays showed no hematoma or cerebral edema, but cervical instability at C6-7. The patient was immobilized with a neck collar and closely monitored. Two weeks after admission, the patient complained of severe posterior neck pain (VAS > 9) and bilateral upper extremity numbness. Subsequent surgical stabilization was performed. An anterior cervical plate was positioned, and pilot holes were tapped. The upper left pilot hole was stripped due to repeated drilling, and PMMA augmentation was performed, which resulted in a mass lesion at the spinal canal. C6 corpectomy was promptly performed to remove the mass. Anterior reconstruction with an anterior cervical plate and mesh cage from C5 through C7 was done. Postoperatively, the patient had left side weakness and impairment of the left 4th and 5th digit extension, but he improved without intervention.

Discharge Diagnosis:

Cervical injury with spinal cord compression leading to cervical corpectomy.

Hospital course:

The patient was admitted to the hospital following a car accident. During his hospital stay, he underwent surgical stabilization for cervical instability at C6-7. There were some complications during the procedure, which led to a mass lesion at the spinal canal and cervical corpectomy. The patient had some postoperative weakness and impairment of the left hand digits, but he improved without intervention. The patient was discharged in good condition with a follow-up appointment with a spinal specialist.
nemotron_simplification:
Hospital Course:
A 47-year-old man came to the hospital after a car crash and had a scrape on his forehead with confusion.
A CT scan and neck X-rays showed no blood clot or swelling, but the neck bones were unstable at C6-7.
He wore a neck brace and was watched closely by the medical team during his stay.
Two weeks later, he reported very bad neck pain over nine out of ten and numbness in both arms.
Doctors did surgery to steady his neck by placing a plate in the front and drilling small guide holes.
The left guide hole was damaged from drilling, and bone cement was added, creating a lump in the spinal canal.
Doctors quickly removed the C6 bone to take out the lump and relieve pressure on the spinal cord.
They rebuilt the front of the neck using a plate and a spacer from C5 to C7.
After surgery, he had weakness on his left side and trouble straightening his left ring and little fingers.
But he got better without any extra treatment and his symptoms improved on their own.
Discharge Diagnosis:
He had a neck injury that squeezed his spinal cord, which led to removal of the C6 bone.

Hospital Course:

This 60-year-old male patient presented to our outpatient clinic with a 1-year history of generalized yellowish ovoid skin-colored papular eruption located on the trunk, groin, and extremities. The patient reported that he first noticed pruritic papules, and 2–3 months later many yellow and ovoid pruritic papules emerged. On skin physical examination, firm, well-defined ovoid skin-colored to yellow papules were seen on the distal and proximal of upper and lower extremities, trunk, groins, and abdomen.

Diagnostic laboratory tests such as full blood cell count with differential, peripheral blood smear, renal, and liver function tests all were normal. Histopathological examination of the skin biopsy from one of the lesion on the trunk revealed proliferation of mast cells with ovoid and spindle nuclei with distinct cytoplasm borders around capillaries, which was compatible with mastocytosis. Based on concurrent clinical and pathological features, we diagnosed our case as xanthelasmoid mastocytosis.

Treatment with H1 antihistamine, cetirizine 10 mg orally nightly and fexofenadine 120 mg for every morning was prescribed for pruritus control which was successful, but eruptions were persistent without any changes. Treatment with phototherapy also recommended to the patient, but despite a 1-year course, no significant improvement was seen in the lesions.

The patient refused further investigations such as bone marrow biopsy or alternative treatments and decided to end the hospital course. The patient was advised to monitor the lesions and seek medical attention if he noticed any changes or deterioration. The patient was discharged with no complications.

Discharge Summary

Patient: 4-month-old male intact Labrador

Hospital Course:

The patient presented with several small skin lacerations of the distal limbs, hock, and tail base. On physical examination, the dog was found to be clinically healthy with normal skeletal development. Several seroma-like swellings were noted in the regions of skin trauma (hocks, tail base). Aspirates taken from these swellings revealed moderate numbers of erythrocytes with fewer neutrophils and macrophages with proteinaceous debris. These findings were consistent with a seroma or hematoma formation, and the dog was treated with amoxycillin/clavulanic acid and firocoxib.

Two months after initial presentation, the patient was examined for ongoing seroma formation and joint abnormalities. Evidence of generalized joint hyperextensibility with a range of motion greater than 180° and skin hyperextensibility and fragility was noted. The dog had a skin extensibility test of 23.5% (normal < 14.5%). A complete blood count revealed mild anemia and serum biochemistry showed a mild hypoalbuminemia and hypoproteinemia. Other serum abnormalities included a moderate hyperphosphatemia, mild elevation in ALP, and decrease in creatinine that were all considered within normal limits for a young dog.

Discharge Diagnosis:

The patient was suspected to have a genetic collagen disease.

Treatment:

The patient was treated with amoxycillin/clavulanic acid and firocoxib. The owners elected to humanely euthanize the patient due to the ongoing joint hypermobility and skin lacerations.

Follow-up Plan:

None.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to the tertiary endometriosis centre with complaints of deep dyspareunia and abdominal pain. Physical examination, vaginal ultrasound, and MRI results indicated the presence of a deep endometriotic lesion at the top of the vagina. The patient underwent laparoscopic resection of the lesion using Sonicision. Post-procedure, the patient presented to the emergency department with vaginal pain and a bloody vaginal discharge after sexual intercourse. Examination revealed a vaginal cuff dehiscence, and a small loop of small intestine was visible in the upper vagina. The peritoneum was closed and the small bowel was repositioned. The patient returned for postoperative check-up and presented with a vaginal cuff dehiscence, which was found to be partly open, and the peritoneum was visible. A different technique was employed for a second repair, namely, to refresh the vaginal edges and perform a two-layer closure of the vagina with the subsequent employment of an omental flap. The omental flap was placed in the pelvis and was attached tension-free to the vaginal cuff closure by interrupted sutures.

Diagnosis:
- Deep endometriotic lesion at the top of the vagina with vaginal cuff dehiscence.

Treatment:
- Laparoscopic resection of the endometriotic lesion using Sonicision.
- Repositioning of the small bowel.
- Refreshment of the vaginal edges and two-layer closure of the vagina with the subsequent employment of an omental flap.

Condition at Discharge:
- Stable.

Follow-Up Care:
The patient was advised to attend follow-up care appointments, undergo regular check-ups, and adhere to the prescribed treatment plan.

None prescribed.

The patient was advised to avoid sexual intercourse for six weeks following the second repair. Additionally, the patient was urged to monitor for any signs of recurrent vaginal cuff dehiscence. Discharge Summary:

This is a discharge summary for a 50-year-old male with a history of diabetes, hypertension and end-stage renal disease. He was admitted to the hospital in December 2020 with fever, decreased urine output, and right sub-costal pain. Initial investigations revealed a significant increase in white blood cell count and C-reactive protein levels. 

A CT scan of the abdomen showed multiple enlarged necrotic lymph nodes in the peripancreatic and portocaval areas with an increase in size compared to a previous scan in March 2020. The patient was referred for an EUS-guided biopsy of the peripancreatic lymph node mass. Histopathology revealed the presence of TB with multiple granulomas composed of epithelioid histiocytes and giant cells. MTB-PCR confirmed the diagnosis of TB. 

The patient was commenced on anti-tuberculosis treatment which significantly improved his condition. Repeat CT scans suggest interval reduction in the sizes of the centrally necrotic lymph nodes in peripancreatic and portocaval locations. Clinically, the patient had improved significantly with no further episodes of pyrexia or abdominal pain. Renal transplantation is planned for the patient once he completes treatment for TB. 

Overall, the patient was discharged with an improved condition and treated for TB. Further follow up is necessary to ensure full recovery.

Discharge Summary: Patient 2

Patient 2, a 45-year-old female, was admitted to hospital due to headache and vomiting in February 2016. Imaging examinations showed an intracranial mass, and the patient received neurosurgical resection of the space-occupying. Postoperative pathological examination indicated non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL). In March 2016, she received whole brain radiotherapy. Cranial MRI after radiotherapy revealed a decrease in the left parietal lobe, basal ganglia, and corpus callosum lesions. In May 2016, the patient underwent chemotherapy for 2 cycles. Two weeks after treatment, she experienced right weakness that gradually progressed to right hemiplegia with muscle strength at 0 level. Due to little symptomatic improvement from conventional therapy of mannitol and dexamethasone for dehydration, cranial MRI was performed, which indicated an increase in left parietal lobe edema.

In July 2016, the patient was started on oral apatinib, which showed remarkable improvement in right hemiplegia symptoms, and her muscle strength was restored to normal. Headache, nausea, and vomiting disappeared. Further details regarding the patient's medical history, clinical course, laboratory test results, medications, and imaging studies can be found in the patient's medical record.

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient was a 50-year-old Chinese male who presented with cough and expectoration of black phlegm for about 2 weeks, sometimes accompanied by bloody sputum and breathlessness. A computed tomography (CT) scan of his chest revealed a rough-edged shadow measuring nearly 32×22×10 mm in the right upper lobe of his lung. The patient was diagnosed with a giant cell carcinoma-like tumor (GCCL) of the lung after undergoing a right-sided upper lobectomy and systematic mediastinal lymphadenectomy. Histopathologic examination of the tumor cells revealed a positive reaction for cytokeratin (CK) and vimentin, while immunostaining for chromogranin A (CgA) and synaptophysin (Syn) was negative.

The patient had several chronic disorders, including a 10-year history of bronchitis and emphysema, and was a smoker with a 30-pack-year history, but had no family history of lung cancer. He underwent combined chemotherapy using gemcitabine and cisplatin for four cycles and was followed up with whole-body radiography examinations every year in a local hospital. As of 7 years after surgery, he remained alive and free from disease progression.

The patient's hospital course was notable for his successful treatment of GCCL, good response to treatment, and his long-term follow-up. The patient was able to communicate clearly and effectively with the healthcare team during his stay. He was compliant with his treatment regimen and was actively involved in discharge planning. The healthcare team discussed the importance of smoking cessation and provided resources for smoking cessation for the patient.

Diagnoses:

1. Giant cell carcinoma-like tumor (GCCL) of the lung.

Discharge Medications:

None.

Follow-Up Care:

The patient is advised to continue yearly follow-up visits with a local hospital to monitor his condition. He is also encouraged to continue smoking cessation efforts.

Admitting Diagnosis: Confusion

Hospital Course:

A 62-year-old African-American male with past medical history of schizophrenia and confusion was admitted to the emergency department. On physical examination, he was lethargic, hypotensive, hypoglycemic, and tachycardic. Initial laboratory studies revealed severe anemia, cytopenia, high serum ferritin level, and elevated soluble CD25. A bone marrow biopsy demonstrated hypercellular bone marrow with erythroid hyperplasia and rare hemophagocytic cells, raising the concern for HLH. A transthoracic echocardiogram was negative for vegetations and infectious workup was negative for viral respiratory PCR, HIV serology, acute infectious hepatitis, cytomegalovirus PCR, and herpes simplex virus (HSV).

The patient was treated with dexamethasone due to underlying severe liver dysfunction, leading to significant clinical improvement. The patient was extubated and steroids were gradually tapered per protocol. His liver enzymes, coagulation studies, platelet count, and ferritin level improved gradually. After 31 days of hospitalization, the patient was discharged home.

Follow-Up Plan:

The patient was advised to follow up with his primary care physician for further management and was provided with a list of his current medications. The patient was informed to schedule a follow-up visit with his primary care physician for a re-evaluation of his medical status, including the need for renal replacement therapy.

Instructions to the Patient:

The patient was advised to continue taking his medications as directed and to follow up with his primary care physician for regular check-ups. The patient was advised to adopt a healthy lifestyle and to maintain regular physical exercise to better manage his condition and prevent further complications.

Summary:

The patient was diagnosed with HLH and was treated with dexamethasone. After a 31-day hospitalization, the patient was discharged home with follow-up instructions for with his primary care physician. The patient was advised to continue his medications and to maintain a healthy lifestyle to manage his condition and prevent further complications.

Hospital Course:

The ten-year-old female patient was admitted with complaints of difficulty in walking and stiffness of both lower limbs, for the past six months. On examination, she had cog-wheel rigidity, increased tone in all the four limbs, power weakness of 4/5 in the lower limbs, and postural tremor and dystonia. Her deep tendon reflexes were exaggerated, while the sensory system, cranial nerve examination, and cerebellar signs were normal. She was diagnosed with dopa-responsive dystonia (DRD) due to the typical diurnal variation of dystonia, and a therapeutic challenge with levodopa/carbidopa was tried, which resulted in a significant decrease in dystonia within two days. Hence, she was treated using a combination of Levodopa, Carbidopa, and Trihexyphenidyl.

Discharge Summary:

Ten-year-old female patient was admitted with complaints of difficulty walking and stiffness in both lower limbs that led to frequent falls. She had cog-wheel rigidity, increased tone, power weakness, postural tremor, and dystonia in all four limbs, with exaggerated deep tendon reflexes. Her sensory system, cranial nerve examination, and cerebellar examination were normal. The patient was diagnosed with DRD as she showed diurnal variation of dystonia and improved significantly after Levodopa/carbidopa therapy. The medication was continued, and the patient showed persistent improvement. The genetic study was planned but could not be conducted due to resource constraints. The patient was discharged in good condition with a plan for follow-up.

The patient, an 86-year-old male, was admitted to our pain-clinic for chronic low back pain and left lower extremity pain for 2 years. The patient reported inadequate pain relief (<50%) and unwarranted side effects with oral analgesics. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the lumbar spine had revealed spinal stenosis, facet degenerative changes, and spondylosis. Per neurosurgery consult, no further surgery was indicated. 

Assessment and Plan:
Upon evaluation, patient was determined to have failed back surgery syndrome with left sacroiliac joint tenderness. Long-term pain relief was defined as pain relief >50% for at least 2 weeks post-injection, and at least 3 months post- Radiofrequency ablation (RFA). However, patient reported absence of any such pain relief. 

Disposition:
The patient was discharged with no further interventions or invasive procedures recommended. The patient was instructed to follow-up with his primary care physician for management of his chronic pain.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 5-year-old Chinese woman, presented to the emergency department with complaints of cough, fever, headache, vomiting, and altered interactions with her parents. She was admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit and diagnosed with sepsis and pneumonia. Empiric antibiotic therapy, immunoglobulin supply, and restricted fluid administration were given. The patient's condition deteriorated, and she became comatose, hypotensive, and suffered from arrhythmia and hypoxia. Electrocardiogram confirmed prolonged Q–T interval while the thyroid test results were received, indicating untreated hypothyroidism secondary to autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto's thyroiditis). Hormone replacement was immediately started, and the patient was administered levothyroxine via nasogastric tube. She also received vasopressor, mechanical ventilation, and continuous renal replacement treatment. Two days after starting levothyroxine, her consciousness was restored, and temperature returned to normal. She was extubated on the fifth day after the initial hormone administration. The dosage of oral levothyroxine was reduced, and she was discharged on a regimen of 3 μg/kg/d once daily.

The patient received levothyroxine, vasopressor, mechanical ventilation, and continuous renal replacement treatment. After two days of hormone therapy, her consciousness was restored, and temperature returned to normal. Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: Undisclosed

Date of Admission: Undisclosed

Date of Discharge: Undisclosed

Admission Diagnosis: Discharging sinuses over the lower anterior abdominal wall

Discharge Diagnosis: Dual infection caused by Mycobacterium szulgai and M. intermedium

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 46-year-old female with a history of laparoscopic appendectomy in 1998, presented with discharging sinuses over the lower anterior abdominal wall for the past two years. The initial incision wound did not heal properly and was later reopened after one month. Despite receiving treatment off and on with multiple injectable and oral antibiotics, there was no definitive microbiological diagnosis prior to admission. The patient did not have any history of local trauma/injury, immunosuppressive drugs/corticosteroids, or tuberculosis.

On admission, a previous surgical scar was noticed on the lower anterior abdominal wall in the midline with a large keloid formed over it. Six sinus openings were noted over the lower anterior abdominal wall with a single sinus discharging pus at the time of presentation. Tenderness was noted over and around the sinuses. Gram variable bacilli and numerous acid-fast bacilli were observed in the discharge. Following culture and antibiotic susceptibility testing, the patient was started on a combination of rifampicin, ethambutol, and clarithromycin.

After one month of therapy, there was no pus discharge from the sinus. The patient was advised to continue the therapy and report back to the hospital after another month. After two months of therapy, the patient was found to be completely all right with no such discharge.

Discharge Medications:

The patient was advised to continue taking rifampicin 600 mg once daily, ethambutol 600 mg once daily, and clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily.

Follow-Up:

The patient was advised to continue with periodic follow-up based upon clinical response and microbiological response.

The patient, a 49-year-old female, was diagnosed with PTC in September 2009. She underwent four neck operations and received two sessions of RAI till May 2015. The patient was diagnosed with RAIR-DTC in August 2014, seven months before her last surgery. In February 2017, she was readmitted to the hospital for the surgical treatment of recurrent tumor in the neck. An enhanced CT scan revealed multiple recurrent lesions in the neck, extensive pulmonary metastases, and metastases behind the left scapula.

Hospital Course:
The patient participated in a phase II, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter clinical trial of anlotinib in RAIR-DTC (registration number: NCT02586337) from March to August 2017. The patient took placebo during the initial treatment period, which resulted in progression.

The patient subsequently underwent open label therapy with anlotinib in September 2017. Imaging evaluations were conducted in every two cycles for the first 12 cycles, and then every four cycles. The target tumors under the right anterior sternocleidomastoid muscle, under the right subclavian, and behind the left posterior scapula were treated, and other recurrent tumors in the neck and extensive lung metastases were not treated.

The patient received a total of 52 cycles of anlotinib. The target lesions were reduced by 93.79%, and no new lesions emerged. The patient experienced adverse events such as hypertension, tachycardia, twitching of the hand and foot, diarrhea, hand-foot syndrome, and headache during the clinical trial. Most were grade 1 or 2, and most were controlled by medication.

Recurrent thyroid cancer with pulmonary and scapular metastases

The patient underwent multiple neck operations and received two sessions of RAI before participating in a clinical trial of anlotinib.

The patient, a five-year-old female, presented with a swelling in the left lumbar region. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a multinodular plexiform tumor within the subcutaneous planes of the lumbosacral region, extending from L1 to S1 vertebral levels. The final pathologic diagnosis was plexiform schwannoma. The patient was asymptomatic and showed no sign of recurrence on one year clinical follow-up.

Further follow-up is recommended as per standard guidelines. Family and patient education regarding necessary follow-up guidelines and potential adverse events has been provided. The patient was discharged in stable condition.

The patient is a 6-year-old female with mosaic Turner syndrome who was referred for cardiac evaluation secondary to her genetic condition. Physical exam revealed short stature, nevi on skin, and a broad-based gait. An echocardiogram was remarkable for severe apical and posterior wall left ventricular hypertrophy with a spongy appearance. The patient is being managed conservatively since she is clinically asymptomatic. Her follow-up visits with cardiology show preserved cardiac function (ejection fraction of 54% on the right side and 53% on the left side). She is receiving multidisciplinary care as an outpatient.

The patient is recommended to receive continuous follow-up visits with cardiology to monitor her cardiac function. She is advised to continue with multidisciplinary care as an outpatient.

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 70-year-old female with congestive heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and end-stage renal disease, was admitted to the general surgery clinic with a radiographic finding of a CCF. During workup for upper gastrointestinal bleeding, a CT enterography incidentally revealed a fistulous connection between her gallbladder and the proximal transverse colon. She reported right upper back pain that was unrelated to meals in the clinic. She had no abdominal tenderness and her liver function tests were within normal limits.

Medical Management:

The patient was hospitalized for surgical repair of the CCF with cholecystectomy, using the da Vinci Xi robotic system. The evaluation revealed an inflammatory connection between the gallbladder fundus and the proximal transverse colon, which was successfully separated. The gallbladder was dissected in a top-down fashion and a critical view of safety was obtained. Locking robotic clips were applied to the cystic duct and cystic artery, and the structures were transected. The colotomy was closed in a two-layer running fashion.

Outcome:

The patient recovered uneventfully and was discharged on the second postoperative day. Histopathological examination of the specimen revealed no evidence of malignancy, and the patient was seen in the clinic without postoperative complaints.

Her belly was not tender, and her liver tests were normal.
Medical Management:
She was hospitalized for surgery to fix the gallbladder-colon link and remove her gallbladder using a robot. The evaluation showed an inflamed connection between the gallbladder and colon, which was successfully separated. The gallbladder was removed from top to bottom, and a safe view was obtained. The patient's medical history was unremarkable except for a diagnosis of RCC.

Discharge instructions were given to the patient, and he was advised to follow up with his urologist regularly. The patient is doing well without any evidence of disease. No further therapy is planned at this time.

The patient was admitted for the treatment of RCC with synchronous liver metastases. The patient was treated with a combination of ipilimumab and nivolumab, with SBRT to the primary tumor. The patient developed a kidney dysfunction, which was managed with prednisone and mycophenolate. Imaging showed a remarkable response, and the patient underwent consolidative nephrectomy. The patient is doing well without any evidence of disease, and no further therapy is planned at this time.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with back pain and claudication pain in both lower limbs. After evaluation, she was found to have degenerative scoliosis with malalignment of global sagittal and coronal balance with lumbar canal stenosis. Surgical intervention was warranted after the failure of an appropriate conservative trial. She underwent instrumentation from T10 to pelvis and interbody fusion was done at multiple levels using the standard posterior approach. Post-operatively, the patient was doing fine and was kept on regular follow-up.

During the six-year follow-up period, the patient presented with generalized back pain. Evaluation revealed breakage of both rods at the dorso-lumbar junction and breakage of the left side rod between the S1 screw and the S2-iliac screw. "Vacuum phenomenon" can be seen in the disc space corresponding with the site of breakage of the rod on CT scan. The solid bony union is appreciated in the rest of the construct. Conservative management was chosen, involving trigger point injections, analgesics, and physiotherapy. 

Outcome:
After five years of conservative management, the patient was completely asymptomatic. No further treatment was necessary, and the patient was discharged on [redacted] after a [redacted] day hospital stay with recommendations for regular follow-up care.

Tests showed a wear-and-tear spine curve, poor front-back and side alignment, and narrowing of the lower spinal canal.
Because non-surgical treatment such as physical therapy and medicines did not relieve symptoms, surgery was needed.
Surgeons placed metal rods and screws from the upper back to the pelvis and fused spine bones at several levels.
After surgery, the patient felt well, had no complications, and attended regular follow-up visits for monitoring.
During a six-year follow-up period, the patient experienced widespread back pain that prompted further evaluation.
Tests showed both metal rods broke at the upper-lower back joint, and the left rod broke near the pelvis screws.
A CT scan showed a gas collection in the disc where the rod broke, called a vacuum phenomenon.
The remaining parts of the spinal fusion showed solid bone healing with no gaps on imaging.
Doctors chose non-surgical care, including trigger point injections for muscle knots, pain medicines, and regular physical therapy.
Outcome:
After five years of non-surgical treatment, the patient had no symptoms and felt completely well.
No additional treatment was required, and the patient did not need further surgery or medicines.
The patient was discharged on [redacted] after a [redacted]-day hospital stay and advised to continue regular follow-up care.

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the emergency department with complaints of general weakness and poor oral intake. Her medical history includes diabetes, hypertension, severe osteoarthritis, and a recent episode of urinary tract infection treated with antibiotics.

Physical examination showed dehydration and hypotension. Laboratory results revealed elevated serum calcium levels, elevated creatinine levels, and decreased serum magnesium levels. The patient was diagnosed with UTI sepsis and admitted to the intensive care unit. Antibiotics and massive hydration were administered, leading to stabilization of her vital signs.

On the third hospital day, the patient’s serum calcium level decreased following the administration of saline and calcitonin. However, the level began to increase again from the third day of calcitonin administration. Further diagnostic workup, including contrast-enhanced computed tomography of chest and abdomen and whole body bone scintigraphy, ruled out malignancy.

Laboratory results revealed a suppressed PTH–vitamin D axis and secondary adrenal insufficiency may have contributed to her hypercalcemia.

Treatment with hydrocortisone (1.5 mg/kg) was initiated from the tenth hospital day and led to the normalization of serum calcium levels. Her general weakness and anorexia improved subsequently. The patient was lost for follow-up, and adequate monitoring for bone mineral density was recommended.

She was moved to the intensive care unit. She got antibiotics and lots of fluids, which helped her vital signs become stable. On the third day in the hospital, giving saline and calcitonin lowered her calcium level. But the calcium level started to rise again after the third day of calcitonin. More tests, including a CT scan of the chest and belly and a bone scan, did not find cancer. Lab results showed low PTH and vitamin D activity. A weak adrenal gland may have contributed to the high calcium. Starting on the tenth day, she received hydrocortisone (1.5 mg per kg) and her calcium returned to normal. Her weakness and poor appetite got better afterward. The patient was lost to follow-up, and checking her bone density was recommended.

Hospital Course:
The patient, an 89-year-old male, was admitted with complaints of cough and haemoptysis. The patient had a history of bronchiectasis in the right middle lobe bronchus for 30 years. One month before admission, the patient suffered a massive haemoptysis, which was controlled through bronchial artery embolization. However, haemoptysis recurred, and the patient was admitted to our hospital. Bronchoscopy performed on the patient showed active bleeding from the right middle lobe bronchus, which was temporarily controlled through haemostatic medications and cryotherapy.

Management:
On the next day, an 8 mm x 3 cm silicon stent was deployed using biopsy forceps after multiple attempts. Another customized stent with a diameter of about 6 mm was placed from the right intermediate bronchus to the right lower lobe bronchus, to avoid stent migration. Bleeding stopped promptly after the placement of stents. The patient received successive antibiotic therapy, and no obvious complication of obstructive pneumonia developed.

Outcome:
One month after the operation of stents implantation, the patient experienced complete atelectasis of the right middle and lower lobe with the complication of right pleural effusion. The patient received further surgery to remove the silicon stent inside the right intermediate bronchus. Thoracic puncture and drainage were done after stent extraction for relieving pleural effusion. Post-operation CT scan reviewed the patient's chest and revealed the right lower lobe recruitment. The patient did not experience any more haemoptysis during the three-month follow-up time and left the hospital ten days after stent extraction.

The bleeding returned, leading to his admission to the hospital for further care.
A lung exam with a scope showed active bleeding from the right middle lobe, briefly stopped with medicines and freezing.
Management:
The next day, doctors placed an 8 mm by 3 cm silicone tube in the airway using a special tool after several tries.
They also put a custom-made 6 mm tube from the middle airway to the lower lung airway to keep it from moving.
Bleeding stopped quickly after the tubes were placed, and the patient’s condition stabilized.
He received antibiotics over several days, and no lung infection from blockage developed.
Outcome:
One month after the tube placement, the right middle and lower lung parts collapsed and fluid built up around the lung.
He had surgery to remove the silicone tube from the middle airway, and the procedure was successful.
After the tube was taken out, a needle was used to drain the fluid around the lung.
A chest scan after the procedure showed the lower lung had reopened and was working better.
He did not cough up blood again during the three-month check-up and left the hospital ten days after the tube removal.

The patient presented with binocular vertical diplopia after an assault. Physical examination revealed restricted right ocular motion in temporal downward gaze with no scleral injection, bony step-off, enophthalmos, or proptosis. Head and orbital CT were negative for injury while the CT scan incidentally revealed a maxillary mucosal retention cyst. Ophthalmology was consulted and forced duction testing was performed, confirming gaze restriction. The patient was taken to the operating room where a trapdoor fracture with entrapment of the inferior rectus muscle was diagnosed and repaired. Retrospective review of the CT revealed soft tissue density with radiodensity characteristics consistent with herniation of orbital fat and entrapped muscle fibers.

Hospital Discharge Summary:

This 26-year-old male presented with binocular vertical diplopia following an assault. Upon physical examination, restricted right ocular motion was noted with no signs of injury. A maxillary mucosal retention cyst was incidentally detected on CT. Ophthalmology was consulted and confirmed the gaze restriction through forced duction testing. A trapdoor fracture with entrapped inferior rectus muscle fibers was diagnosed and repaired in the operating room. Retrospective CT evaluation led to the detection of herniation of orbital fat and entrapped muscle fibers. The patient was discharged without any further complications and with appropriate follow-up arranged.

Hospital Course: The patient, a 50-year-old male, presented at Dankook University Dental Hospital with complaints of pain and swelling at his left TMJ and numerous radiopaque masses around the joint on panoramic radiography. The patient showed spontaneous and opening pain and swelling at the left TMJ, but showed no tenderness or limitation of mouth opening. Through imaging tests, including panoramic imaging, CBCT, and MR imaging, numerous radiopaque loose bodies of various shapes and sizes surrounding the left condyle, and hypertrophy with sclerotic changes on the anterior and lateral sides of the temporal bone, the articular eminence, and the articular fossa were observed. A surgical excision under general anesthesia was performed to remove approximately 120 pieces of the loose bodies. Histopathologic examination confirmed the diagnosis of synovial chondromatosis. On a postoperative panoramic image, remaining flat hypertrophy of the articular eminence was observed, without any loose bodies. The patient's symptoms were relieved, and no signs of recurrence were observed at 1-month and 3-month follow-up visits.

The patient, a 68-year-old female, was admitted to the Department of General and Vascular Surgery and Angiology with chronic epigastric pain. An abdominal ultrasound revealed a fluid-filled tumor situated between the common iliac arteries. Further imaging studies were conducted, including a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis, which revealed a neoplasm in the presacral space. An arterial and venous Doppler ultrasound was performed, followed by a direct phlebography, revealing a large venous aneurysm of the right common iliac vein with an adhering thrombus and large collateral circulation. Anticoagulant treatment with rivaroxaban was administered, and the patient received this treatment for two years without any complications or aneurysm growth.

Discharge Summary

Patient: 22-year-old male

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with bilateral muscular atrophy and tremor of the distal upper extremities with insidious onset 5 years ago. Cold exposure worsened the symptomatology. Clinical examination revealed symmetrical muscular atrophy of the hands and forearms and reduced muscular strength during flexion, extension, and abduction of the fingers and flexion, extension of the wrist, as well as reduced tendon reflexes from the affected neurotomes. Electroneurophysiology and electromyography showed signs of chronic motor neuron lesion, bilaterally. Magnetic resonance images (MRI) acquired in neutral position showed loss of cervical lordosis and focal cord atrophy at C5-C6 level. MRI acquired in flexion revealed widening of the posterior epidural space. Postcontrast images showed uniform enhancement of the epidural space. The enhancement was reduced in the neutral position. After considering all the findings, the diagnosis of HD was made, and the patient was treated conservatively.

Diagnosis:
Hirayama Disease (HD)

Summary:
The patient's symptoms were consistent with HD, and was diagnosed based on the MRI findings in neck flexion. The patient was treated conservatively and is being discharged at this time. Further monitoring and follow-up are recommended.

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient presented with painful, red raised lesions on the right forearm with fever, which gradually coalesced to form larger lesions. The patient had a prior history of upper respiratory tract infection and similar episodes three years back. On examination, a large erythematous plaque was present on the right upper extremity along with small erythematous plaques on both upper limbs, right side of the neck, and chest. Few lesions showed typical “relief of mountain range appearance”. Local temperature was raised in all the lesions. Superficial nerves were not thickened and sensations on the plaques were normal. Histopathology showed a diffuse infiltrate consisting predominantly of mature neutrophils located in the upper dermis without evidence of primary leukocytoclastic vasculitis.

Treatment:
The patient was initially treated with tablet dapsone 100 mg HS with dramatic early improvement, and relapse on discontinuation. The second episode was treated with a combination of dapsone and oral prednisolone started at 30 mg/day and gradually tapered over 4 weeks. The patient is now in remission and discharged. 

Follow-Up Instructions:
The patient is advised to follow-up with their primary care provider for further evaluation and management.

The patient came in with painful red bumps and a fever, and had a recent cold or throat infection before.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital for the management of a giant hepatic tumor. She underwent a right hepatectomy during which two well-differentiated hepatocellular carcinomas (HCCs) were removed. The patient recovered well after the surgery and was discharged on postoperative day 17.

Past Medical History:
The patient had no significant past medical history.

Hospital Course:
The patient's hospital course was significant for a sensation of abdominal distension and loss of appetite, at which point she underwent abdominal ultrasonography that discovered a giant hepatic mass in the right lobe. Physical examination was significant for hepatomegaly. Liver function tests showed evidence of nonicteric cholestasis with mild transaminase enzyme level elevation. Screening for viral hepatitis yielded negative results. Levels of the liver-specific tumor marker "protein induced by vitamin K absence-II" were highly elevated. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a giant hypoechoic mass measuring 139 × 120 mm in the right lobe of the liver. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) demonstrated a huge mass that occupied the right lobe of the liver and showed inhomogeneous hyperenhancement in the arterial phase, as well as uniform isoenhancement in the portal venous phase. A low-concentration area indicated the presence of necrosis in the tumor center, and a radiological diagnosis of HCC was therefore posited. The surgical team also discovered a congenital absence of the portal vein that indicated the presence of congenital absence of the portal vein type II. 

Disposition and Follow-up:
The patient was discharged on postoperative day 17 and successfully treated for a small recurrent HCC nodule detected 7 months after the operation with radiofrequency ablation. The patient has been on close follow-up for 6 months without any evidence of further recurrences.

The patient presented with tenderness on the dorsoradial aspect of the scaphoid of the left wrist due to an unhealed proximal pole fracture and a broken headless screw. Physical examination showed an active range of motion from 30o extension to 40o flexion, 20o radial deviation, and 30o ulnar deviation. Plain X-ray and computed tomography confirmed the fracture and the broken screw. Surgery was performed by two certified orthopedic hand surgeons to remove the implant and replace it with a more antegrade central fixation carried out using a 2.8-mm headless screw. A pure cancellous autograft bone was harvested from the distal radius through a dorsal window just proximal to Lister’s tubercle, which was compressed in a syringe and packed into the cavity within the bone with a small impactor.

The patient was discharged after being placed in a removable long opponens splint for two weeks. The Colles cast was applied postoperatively. The tenderness of the wrist that originated from the non-healed scaphoid bone disappeared after three months, and wrist extension was reported as 60° and flexion as 40°. Radiographic signs of healing in the nonunion area without bone resorption were observed after three months. The patient returned to work five months after the last surgery with a good functional condition. The bridging trabecula was found on CT scans in two planes at nine months.

Unhealed proximal pole fracture and broken headless screw.

Surgery was performed by two certified orthopedic hand surgeons to remove the implant and replace it with a more antegrade central fixation carried out using a 2.8-mm headless screw. Discharge Summary:

Patient: 53-year-old male nurse diagnosed with HCV infection 

Hospital Course:
In January 2011, the patient was evaluated at the Outpatient Infectious Diseases clinic for abnormal liver function tests. His HCV RNA was 660,000 IU/mL, genotype 3a. A liver biopsy showed chronic active hepatitis with Metavir A2 necroinflammatory grading and F2 fibrosis. The patient was considered eligible for antiviral treatment and started therapy with PEG-IFN-α-2a and ribavirin in March 2011. Treatment was well tolerated, and HCV RNA became negative by the fourth week and remained undetectable during the entire 24-week treatment regimen. ALT normalized within the first 3 weeks of treatment. The patient underwent post-treatment follow-up until September 2012, and a new biopsy revealed a mild reduction in Metavir grading and staging (A1 and F1, respectively).

Hospitalization:
Nine weeks after finishing the antiviral therapy, the patient developed symmetrical polyarthritis with joint pain and edema in the wrists, knees, shoulders, and metacarpophalangeal joints, associated with prolonged morning stiffness. MRI detected bone erosions with juxta-articular osteopenia in the wrist, knee, and hand joints, revealing a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Rheumatoid factor and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody testing were positive. 

Treatment:
The patient was treated with prednisone and NSAIDs for two months, followed by methotrexate and sulfasalazine with a quick and favorable response to treatment. 

Discharge:
The patient was discharged home in satisfactory condition with a prescription for methotrexate and sulfasalazine. Follow-up with Rheumatologist and Gastroenterologist was advised.

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 79-year-old male with advanced prostate cancer who presented with a mass on the tip of his urethral meatus. Biopsy confirmed squamous cell carcinoma, and the patient underwent partial penectomy and lymph node dissection which revealed positive right inguinal lymph nodes (three out of seven) with pathologic T2N2M0 disease. Adjuvant chemotherapy was administered with low dose carboplatin and paclitaxel, and radiation was delivered to the right inguinal region.

The patient developed disease recurrence with nodal involvement nine months later and was treated with additional chemoradiation with curative intent, including another round of low dose carboplatin and paclitaxel, and radiation to the left pelvic region. He responded well, but eventually developed disease progression and was considered for second-line therapy with the PD-L1 inhibitor atezolizumab.

After approximately two years of treatment with atezolizumab, the patient developed bullous pemphigoid, an immune-mediated toxicity of the skin commonly associated with those agents. Prednisone was administered and the patient had quick resolution of his blistering symptoms.

At the time of this report, the patient has shown near complete response and has been placed on treatment holiday. Follow-up appointments have been scheduled to monitor progress.
nemotron_simplification: Hospital Course: The patient is a 79-year-old man with prostate cancer that has spread to other parts over time. He first noticed a growth on the opening of his urethra, called the meatus of the penis. A biopsy showed the growth was a type of skin cancer called squamous cell carcinoma. He had surgery to remove part of his penis and to take out lymph nodes in his right groin. Three of the seven lymph nodes removed had cancer, and the cancer stage was T2N2M0. After surgery, he received low-dose chemotherapy with carboplatin and paclitaxel and radiation to his right groin. Nine months later the cancer returned in lymph nodes, so he got more chemo and radiation aiming to cure it. This treatment included another round of low-dose carboplatin and paclitaxel and radiation to his left pelvis. He improved at first, but later the cancer grew again and doctors considered using the drug atezolizumab. After about two years on atezolizumab, he got bullous pemphigoid, an immune-related skin side effect of the drug. He was given prednisone and his blistering symptoms cleared up quickly, and he felt better. Now his cancer is almost gone and he is taking a break from treatment to recover. Follow-up visits are scheduled to check his progress and make sure the cancer does not come back.

Admitting Diagnosis: Achalasia

Hospital Course:

The patient was a 29-year-old female with a history of mild progressive dysphagia who presented with severe dysphagia. The patient had been diagnosed with achalasia three years ago but refused any treatment options. She was given ferrous sulfate capsules for iron therapy by her general practitioner about a month earlier, which led to the development of severe dysphagia after three weeks. She was referred to a gastroenterologist for further evaluation.

On admission, the patient had no odynophagia, nausea, or vomiting. Physical examination was unremarkable.

A barium swallow esophagography showed a dilated esophagus with a bird's beak appearance of the lower esophageal sphincter and a filling defect in the distal part of the esophagus. An EGD revealed a dilated esophagus and an elliptical-shaped, black-colored bezoar in the distal part of the esophagus. There were no ulcers or erosions in the esophagus. The lower esophageal sphincter was severely spastic.

Attempts were made to fragment and push the bezoar into the stomach, but it was discontinued due to high LES pressure and resistance and the risk of aspiration. Finally, the bezoar was retrieved with a basket.

An esophageal manometer was carried out and the results were compatible with the diagnosis of achalasia. In the next endoscopic session, achalasia balloon dilation (size 30 mm) was successfully applied.

The patient was asymptomatic during the 3-year follow-up.

Discharge Condition:

The patient's condition improved after treatment with achalasia balloon dilation. The patient was discharged in good condition and was advised to follow up with her gastroenterologist as scheduled.

Discharge Medications:

N/A

Follow-up:

The patient was advised to follow up with her gastroenterologist as scheduled.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 79-year-old male

Reason for Admission: Progressive dysphagia and weight loss

Medical History: None provided

Hospital Course:

Upon admission, the patient presented with symptoms including hematemesis, melena, fever, cough, and yellow sputum. Blood analysis revealed severe anemia, high leukocyte and neutrophil levels, and a low albumin level. A sputum smear indicated the presence of gram-positive cocci.

An endoscopy identified an elongated lump on 1 side of the vertical axis of the esophagus. The mass extended progressively for 15 cm along the esophageal longitudinal axis and invaded half of the esophageal circumference. Biopsy revealed the tumor to be a malignant melanoma, positive for S-100 and HMB-45, and negative for cytokeratin and carcinoembryonic antigen markers.

Computed tomography showed inflammation of the lungs and no evidence of distant metastasis. Additionally, a physical examination revealed no pigmented lesions at the skin, eyes, rectum, or other locations.

Due to the advanced age of the patient and comorbidities including hypoproteinemia, infection, and severe anemia, surgery, chemotherapy, or radiotherapy were not performed. The patient was discharged without receiving treatment.

Follow-up:

Approximately 1 month after discharge, the medical team was informed of the patient's death.

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 50-year-old male with a history of a pruritic plaque on his left hand, was admitted to the dermatology department for assessment. The plaque started as a small, erythematous papule that gradually increased in size over several months and became a larger, scaly plaque. The patient also experienced pruritus and a tingling sensation. Topical steroid treatment provided temporary relief; however, the plaque did not resolve. A biopsy was performed due to the unusual morphology of the plaque, revealing spongiotic dermatitis compatible with nummular dermatitis. Further treatment with potent topical steroids provided only temporary flattening of the plaque.

Several months later, the patient returned with ulceration of the center of the plaque and subcutaneous nodules in a sporotrichoid pattern extending from his left fifth digit superiorly to his elbow. Culturing a biopsy confirmed fish-tank granuloma, caused by M. marinum. The patient reported a history of having a salt-water fish tank and had lost several fish weeks after the onset of symptoms, although there was no necropsy.

Antimicrobial susceptibility testing showed sensitivity to amikacin, clarithromycin, doxycycline, ethambutol, moxifloxacin, rifabutin and rifampin, and resistance to ciprofloxacin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Treatment with doxycycline and azithromycin provided no clinical improvement after 3 months of continuous therapy. Treatment was switched to moxifloxacin and clarithromycin, and the patient applied local heat to the affected skin for several hours per day using a reusable heat pack. The patient was referred to a plastic surgeon for excision of the subcutaneous nodules on his left hand, wrist, and arm. After 3 months of the new antibiotic regime and excision of the nodules, the patient's ulcerated plaque healed, and the excised subcutaneous nodules did not recur. 

The patient remained in hospital for 17 months before clinical resolution of the disease was confirmed. The patient was discharged following confirmation of resolution of the disease with no further medical follow-up required.

He was discharged with no further follow-up needed.

Reason for Admission: Shortness of breath

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the emergency department with shortness of breath and increasing dyspnea. She was found to have a large goiter that was compressing the trachea and causing respiratory distress. The patient was quickly transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU) where she was intubated using rapid sequence induction to relieve respiratory distress. Subsequent cerebral and thoracic computed tomography (CT) scans revealed a large goiter plunging into the upper mediastinal orifice, which was removed successfully by thyroidectomy 48 hours after admission. Prior to reversal of the neuromuscular blockage, the tube balloon was deflated, and the diagnosis of tracheomalacia was almost confirmed. The endotracheal tube was left in place for 24 hours, and then removed the next day without incident.

Course of Treatment:
The patient received corticotherapy (dexamethasone at 12 mg per day for two days) prior to thyroidectomy to accelerate fetal lung maturation. Surgery was completed without incident, as no intraoperative tracheostomy was necessary. Patient was treated with levothyroxin sodium tablets 75mcg/day post-surgery.

Follow-Up Plan:
Patient was discharged from the hospital on the 5th postoperative day without any complications. Pathology showed multinodular goiter with areas of atypical hyperplasia, but no sign of malignancy. Patient gave birth to a healthy newborn four weeks later.

Recommendations:
Patient should continue taking levothyroxin sodium tablets 75mcg/day as prescribed. She should follow up with her primary care physician for monitoring of her thyroid function and any potential complications related to the goiter removal.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Name]
Medical Record Number: [Number]

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 29-year-old male of Syrian origin, was admitted for evaluation of a painless right-sided testicular swelling that had been present for 12 months. Upon clinical examination, he had a nontender enlarged right testis. Further evaluation with alpha-fetoprotein (α-FP) and beta human chorionic gonadotropin (β-HCG) tumor markers revealed negative results. An ultrasound scan of the scrotum showed a 7-cm hypoechoic, hypervascular, and cystic mass replacing the right testis. A right radical inguinal orchidectomy was performed, and a staging computed tomography scan was negative for lymphatic or metastatic disease.

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient was diagnosed with Sertoli cell sarcoma (SCS) with undifferentiated sarcoma confined to the testis. The tumor was composed of small, intermediate, and large epithelioid cells arranged in sheets with broad areas of necrosis. Microscopic features of these cells were consistent with SCS. Additionally, there were ill-defined areas of undifferentiated sarcoma composed of highly pleomorphic, epithelioid, and spindle-shaped cells with high mitotic activity invested in fibrous and fibromyxoid stroma. The tumor did not extend beyond the tunica albuginea. The spermatic cord and epididymis were uninvolved, and no lymphovascular invasion was identified.

Treatment:
The histological diagnosis was SCS with undifferentiated sarcoma confined to the testis. Further oncological treatment with adjuvant chemotherapy was strongly advised, but the patient declined and moved to a different locality.

Follow-up:
The patient should be advised to receive regular follow-up consultations for potential recurrence of the tumor, and to notify his healthcare provider if he develops any symptoms concerning for the same.

Clinical Course:
The 9-year-old male patient presented at the clinic with multiple papular lesions on his left cheek. The patient had a history of cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL) located in his nose two years ago that was successfully treated with intralesional meglumine antimonate injection. Dermatological examination on admission revealed multiple, coalescing, rough, slightly elevated, yellowish-brown papular lesions measuring 3-6 mm in diameter on the left cheek. Giemsa staining of the skin biopsy showed numerous leishmania parasites in their amastigote form. The patient was diagnosed with lupoid CL based on his medical history, clinical, and microscopy findings. The patient was started on weekly intralesional meglumine antimonate injection for four weeks, and significant improvement was observed in the patient's lesions.

Hospital Course:
The patient's hospital course was uneventful. The patient did not encounter any complications or adverse drug reactions during his hospital stay. The patient tolerated the treatment well and had no complaints of pain or discomfort.

Condition on Discharge:
On discharge, the patient's condition had improved significantly with no visible papular skin lesions on the left cheek.

Follow-Up Plan:
The patient was advised to maintain good hygiene practices and avoid exposure to sandflies. The patient was scheduled for a follow-up visit with the dermatology clinic in two months to monitor for recurrence of skin lesions or signs of CL.

N/A

- Monitoring for potential recurrence of lupoid cutaneous leishmaniasis or any other skin lesions on the left cheek
- Review of the patient's clinical response to four weekly intralesional meglumine antimonate injection therapy.

Clinical Course:
The patient is a 9-year-old boy who came to the clinic with several small bumps on his left cheek.
He had an infection called leishmaniasis in his nose years ago that was cured with medicine injected into the sores.
On exam, the bumps were rough, slightly raised, yellowish-brown and measured 3 to 6 millimeters across.
A lab test of a skin sample showed many leishmania parasites in their tissue form.
Based on his past infection, the exam and the test, the doctor diagnosed him with lupoid cutaneous leishmaniasis.
This type is a form of skin leishmaniasis that looks like lupus and is named for its appearance.
He started receiving weekly injections of medicine directly into the bumps for four weeks and his lesions got much better.
Hospital Course:
The patient's stay in the hospital was smooth with no problems or bad reactions to the medicine.
He tolerated the treatment well and reported no pain or discomfort during his time there.
Condition on Discharge:
At discharge, the patient's skin on the left cheek showed no visible bumps and his condition had improved a lot.
Follow-Up Plan:
The patient was told to keep good hygiene and stay away from sandflies to prevent new infection.
He is scheduled for a dermatology check-up in two months to watch for return of skin lesions or leishmaniasis signs.

N/A

The patient will be watched for possible return of lupoid cutaneous leishmaniasis or other skin lesions on the left cheek.

The patient underwent regular outpatient department follow-ups for 18 months, and no lesions were found postoperatively.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Patient Name: [REDACTED] 
Age: 84 years 
Sex: Male 
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]
 
HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient presented to the otolaryngology clinic with a scalp lesion with a progressive enlargement over 2 months following the MMS surgery. The biopsy confirmed the presence of invasive squamous cell carcinoma in the setting of severe solar elastosis. A surgical extirpation was performed, creating a 5 × 7 cm defect (35 cm2) that extended down to the level of the galea. Reconstructive options were discussed, and the physician elected to use vCPM. vCPM was placed on the wound in direct contact with the galea, followed by Adaptic® dressing. The patient returned to the clinic on day 7 after the first vCPM application, and a second 5 × 5 cm vCPM graft was placed on the fully granulated wound. The patient returned on day 14, at which time the defect had reduced to approximately 3 × 5 cm (15 cm2) and substantial re-epithelialization was noted. Based on the appearance of the wound, a third application was not deemed necessary. At the day 21 follow-up, the patient's wound had completely closed with minimal scarring. Six months following treatment, the wound remained closed with continued improvement in the hyperemia. The patient experienced no complications and was very pleased with the outcome.
 
DIAGNOSIS:
Invasive squamous cell carcinoma in the setting of severe solar elastosis
 
DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
The patient is advised to follow up with the physician for regular monitoring of the wound healing progress. Any signs of infection or delayed wound healing should be immediately reported to the physician.
 
FOLLOW-UP:
Follow-up appointments are scheduled with the physician for regular monitoring of the wound healing progress.

Hospital Course:

This 58-year-old female presented with sudden painless decreased vision in the left eye (LE) for 1 month. She had no history of any Valsalva maneuver or trauma. BCVA in the RE was 20/20 and LE was 20/200.

Assessment and Findings:

Fundus examination as well as OCT LE showed hemorrhagic PED at the fovea and sub-ILM hemorrhage at inferonasal macula. LE EDI-OCT confirmed the presence of pachychoroid in the BE. ICG did not reveal any hyperfluorescence in the LE due to masking by the hemorrhagic PED.

Treatment and Outcome:

With a provisional diagnosis of PCV, she was treated with LE IVB injection. At 1-month follow-up, her LE vision improved to 20/125. Fundus examination revealed the disappearance of sub-ILM hemorrhage with a reduction in the size of hemorrhagic PED which were confirmed on OCT. 

Conclusion:

The patient was discharged with improved vision after receiving LE IVB injection therapy. Follow-up visits and monitoring may be necessary to ensure that the patient’s condition is properly managed going forward.

Her right eye vision was normal (20/20) and her left eye vision was poor (20/200).
Assessment and Findings:
Eye exam and scans showed a bleeding spot under the retina at the center of vision.
They also showed a small bleed beneath the inner retinal layer near the nose side of the macula.
Further scans confirmed thickened choroid in both eyes, a sign of the pachychoroid condition seen in the patient.
The dye test did not show any abnormal fluorescence because the bleed blocked the view.
Treatment and Outcome:
Based on a tentative diagnosis of polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy, she received an injection of medication into her left eye.
One month later, her left eye vision improved from 20/200 to 20/125 after the injection.
Exam showed the inner bleed disappeared and the bleeding spot got smaller, confirmed by scans.
Conclusion:
The patient was discharged with better vision after the left eye injection and advised to continue monitoring.
She will need regular follow-up visits and monitoring to keep her condition under ongoing control.

The patient presented with abnormal uterine bleeding requiring transfusion. A large, firm, 6 cm mass in the cervix was found on examination, and a biopsy confirmed high-grade invasive cervical adenocarcinoma, which was an unusual variant of cervical mucinous adenocarcinoma. The patient underwent concurrent chemoradiation with weekly cisplatin followed by a brachytherapy boost. Significant tumor shrinkage was observed during brachytherapy. However, at a one-month follow-up, a 1.5 cm, firm, nodular mass within the cervical canal was found, confirmed by PET/CT, which was consistent with residual tumor. The patient underwent adjuvant hysterectomy in the form of an exploratory laparotomy, total abdominal hysterectomy, and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, which revealed residual cervical tumor measuring up to 1.6 cm in greatest dimension.

CONDITION AT DISCHARGE:
The patient is without complaints and has maintained normal bowel and bladder function. At a 12-month follow-up, she continues to show no evidence of disease, and the patient feels well with no complaints.

Follow-up appointments have been scheduled in accordance with the treating physician's recommendation.

Patient: 58-year-old man
Reason for Admission: Weight loss, jaundice, and abdominal pain
Diagnosis: Obstructive jaundice due to a well-differentiated pancreatic adenocarcinoma
Treatment: Three cycles of chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and infusional 5-fluorouracil.
Outcome: Significant reduction in local disease, leading to a curative Whipple procedure
Post-operative Status: Surgical margins free of disease

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with weight loss, jaundice, and abdominal pain that were consistent with obstructive jaundice. Laboratory findings were indicative of pancreatic adenocarcinoma. The patient underwent an endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration biopsy, which confirmed the diagnosis of a well-differentiated pancreatic adenocarcinoma. At the same time, a biliary stent was placed. 
The patient received three cycles of chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and infusional 5-fluorouracil, resulting in a significant reduction in local disease. Based on his favorable response, the patient underwent a Whipple procedure with curative intent, and histopathological analysis of the specimen demonstrated free surgical margins from disease. 

The patient made an uneventful recovery and was discharged from the hospital with a recommendation for a follow-up visit in the near future. The patient was advised to continue regular follow-up with his healthcare provider for further evaluation and management of his condition.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admitted for failure to thrive and extreme weight loss, a 56-year-old male presented with a history of refractory, sero-negative migratory arthritis and occasional episodes of abdominal pain and diarrhea. During initial testing, the patient exhibited neutrophilia, increased ESR, CRP levels, and abnormal WBC counts.

Over the course of several admissions, the patient's clinical condition continued to deteriorate, with thrombocytopenia and macrocytic anemia being added to his list of symptoms. Additionally, it was noted that he suffered from bilateral stenosis and total occlusion of the left internal carotid artery at the origin, among other issues.

Despite extensive testing and repeated hospital stays, the patient's condition remained mysterious, and no diagnosis was reached. However, he did test positive for Tropheryma whipplei PCR in the blood, which suggested the presence of Whipple's disease. Confirmation via small bowel biopsy was obtained, and the patient started a course of antibiotics for the disease.

As the patient's condition continued to decline, he was placed into hospice care, where he eventually passed away.

Overall, the patient's complex medical history and illness resisted easy diagnosis and treatment, despite a thorough course of testing and interventions.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information: Mrs. X, 96-year-old female.

Chief Complaint: Dementia, physical restraints, and nasogastric tube.

Hospital Course:

Mrs. X was admitted to the hospital with a history of dementia, physical restraints and having nutrition via the nasogastric tube for the past three years. She was restrained with mittens as she attempted to remove the nasogastric tube. Her risk of aspiration pneumonia was high with a swallowing reflex time of 9.5 seconds. Repetitive saliva swallowing test also revealed the risk of aspiration.

Treatment and Intervention:

The patient received the extracts of traditional Chinese medicine Banxia Houpu Tang (BHT) through NGT for four weeks. This resulted in significant improvement in her swallowing reflex time which reduced to 3.5 seconds. The results of the repetitive saliva swallowing test also showed improvement. Oral feeding was subsequently initiated, starting from gelatinous foods to mixed ground foods of approximately 800 kcal. The nasogastric tube and physical restraints were later removed.

Outcome:

Mrs. X's oral intake improved significantly after receiving BHT extracts, and this facilitated the removal of her nasogastric tube and physical restraints. She was discharged in a stable condition, with instructions to continue her medication and follow-up with her primary care physician.

Follow-up:

Mrs. X was advised to continue her medication, eat a nourishing and balanced diet, follow-up with her primary care physician, and attend regular monitoring appointments for her swallowing reflex time.

She received nutrition through a nose-to-stomach tube and wore mittens to stop her from pulling it out.
Her risk of lung infection from food or liquid entering the lungs was high because swallowing took 9.5 seconds.
A test that counts saliva swallows also showed a high risk of lung infection from food or liquid entering lungs.
Treatment and Intervention:
The patient received herbal medicine called Banxia Houpu Tang through the nose-to-stomach tube for four weeks.
This improved her swallowing time from 9.5 seconds to 3.5 seconds, showing better muscle function.
The saliva swallow test improved, indicating less risk of lung infection from food or liquid entering lungs and better safety.
She then began eating soft, jelly-like foods and later soft, mashed foods that gave about 800 calories each day.
The nose-to-stomach tube and the devices that limit movement were removed after her swallowing improved.
Outcome:
The patient's oral intake improved a lot after the herbal medicine, allowing removal of the tube and the movement-limiting devices.
She was discharged in stable condition, with instructions to keep taking her medicine and see her primary care doctor.
Follow-up:
The patient was told to continue her medicine, eat a healthy balanced diet, and see her primary care doctor.
She was also advised to have regular check-ups to measure her swallowing time and ensure safety.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 33-year-old, Malaysian male, presented to the hospital following a nocturnal seizure. Prior to admission, the patient had flu-like symptoms, loss of appetite, and general myalgia. On admission, he was disoriented but had no lateralizing symptoms or signs. The patient experienced post-ictal periods of approximately 30 minutes and had a 21-second asystole during the third seizure. A permanent pacemaker was placed to address this complication.

The patient's neurological exam was unremarkable except for gaze-evoked nystagmus, thought to be a side effect of the administered phenytoin. Despite administration of anticonvulsant medication and subsequent optimization of phenytoin, the patient continued to have recurrent seizures. He developed additional symptoms such as right-sided headache, right ear pain, tenderness, and an unusual sound in the right ear which evolved into a hallucination of music. The patient also developed complex partial seizures, indicating the possibility of HSV encephalitis.

Investigations:
LPs performed on two separate occasions showed no abnormality other than a slightly elevated protein level. CT scans of the head with contrast were normal, and a SPECT scan showed a slight decrease in perfusion of the left side compared to the right. A repeat EEG showed nonspecific abnormality of the right temporal lobe.

Treatment:
The patient was started on a course of acyclovir, and over the first week of therapy, there was significant improvement. Seizures and headaches resolved, but the hallucination of music persisted for several days. The patient was discharged to complete a three-week course of acyclovir. While tapering the anticonvulsants, there were breakthrough seizures, so the patient remains on levetriacetam and phenytoin.

Summary:
The patient was diagnosed with possible HSV encephalitis, which was successfully managed with acyclovir therapy. The patient was discharged with instructions to continue the full course of medication and remain on anticonvulsants.

The patient, a 4-month-old female, was admitted to the hospital due to poor eye contact. She was delivered at 35 weeks of gestation and had an unremarkable family history. The patient was diagnosed with Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA) due to the presence of esotropia and nystagmus, and the extinguished electroretinogram (ERG) in both eyes. Cycloplegic refractive errors were also noted, which were subsequently addressed. A slit lamp examination, fundus examination, and systemic evaluation for any metabolic and organ abnormalities were conducted, but no significant findings were observed except for the aforementioned ocular symptoms.

Diagnostic evaluations were performed, which included genetic testing for CRX, CRB1, GUCY2D, AIPL1, RDH12, RPE65, LRAT, RPGRIP1, and TULP1. However, the results were unremarkable. A brain MRI revealed the presence of a prominent enlargement in the subarachnoid space of both frontal convexities, and absence of the septum pellucidum. However, no focal lesions were found, and the size of the corpus callosum and white matter myelination were normal. Follow-up MRI scans showed the absence of the septum pellucidum, but with stable external hydrocephalus. A diagnosis of septo-optic dysplasia was considered, however, the normal appearance of the optic nerve and normal pituitary function left the diagnosis doubtful.

Medical History:
The patient did not have any notable medical history aside from the ocular and neuroimaging findings with LCA and the subarachnoid space abnormalities observed in the brain MRI scans.

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient, a 4-month-old female, was admitted to the hospital for poor eye contact. She was diagnosed with LCA, and further diagnostic evaluations including genetic testing and a brain MRI were conducted. Follow-up MRI scans showed the absence of the septum pellucidum, but with stable external hydrocephalus. At the age of 3 years, the patient showed moderate developmental delay. No noteworthy medical history was obtained during her hospital course.

The patient, a 36-year-old female, presented to the hospital with a 4-year history of dull pain on the left back and a foreign body on the left side of the spine. She denied hematuria, dysuria, or frequency. The patient was admitted, and a computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed moderate hydronephrosis of the left kidney. Hospital Course: A 73-year-old male patient presented with severe postoperative hypertension following coronary artery bypass grafting. The patient had a medical history of type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, coronary heart disease, prostate cancer, and long-standing hypertension that had become harder to control during the past 2 years. The patient's family history was unremarkable, except for cases of sudden death among maternal relatives. A CT scan showed a small right adrenal mass, and biochemical testing revealed high levels of normetanephrines with no signs of familial syndromes. A meta-iodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) scan showed intense and moderate uptake of a 2 × 2 × 3 cm mass of the right adrenal gland with no distant metastases detected. The patient underwent adrenalectomy and was diagnosed with pheochromocytoma, confirmed by histology post-operatively. The patient has been discharged and will now continue with outpatient follow-up.

Summary of Hospital Stay: The patient was admitted due to severe postoperative hypertension that was difficult to manage despite medication. After further investigation, the diagnosis of Pheochromocytoma was confirmed by histology post-operative. The patient underwent adrenalectomy, and no complications were encountered during the procedure. The patient has been discharged and will be followed up in the outpatient clinic.

Diagnosis: Pheochromocytoma is a chromaffin cell tumor of the adrenal gland. It causes the excess production of catecholamines, including epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine, resulting in variable symptoms of hypertension, palpitation, headache, sweating, and blurred vision.

Treatment: The patient underwent adrenalectomy to remove the tumor, after which there were no complications. The patient will continue to monitor and manage chronic conditions, including diabetes, dyslipidemia, and hypertension, with appropriate medication and lifestyle changes.

Prognosis: The prognosis is dependent on the size of the tumor, degree of malignancy, and any additional risk factors or comorbidities that the patient may have. In this case, the adrenal mass was small, and the Ki-67 proliferation index was less than one percent. Therefore, the patient's prognosis is positive.

Follow-up: The patient has been discharged and will return to the outpatient clinic for regular follow-up care to manage chronic conditions and monitor for recurrence or metastasis. Appropriate testing, including urine and plasma metanephrine levels, will be done to evaluate the patient's recovery.
